name: KIT
gene_function: KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally involved in regulated activation of RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR and STAT3 signaling in the presence of stem cell factor (SCF).

variants.variant_description: KIT W557_K558delinsE affects the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the KIT protein. KIT exon 11 deletions have been shown to result in constitutive phosphorylation of KIT and increased MAPK and AKT activation [PMID: 17699867, 14645423, 25239608].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating KIT mutations (particularly exon 11 deletions) are present in most gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [PMID: 9438854, 15930355, 28481359]. Compared with GISTs harboring KIT exon 9 mutations or wild-type KIT, GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations have a worse recurrence-free survival and overall survival [PMID: 16135486].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved adjuvant therapy for the treatment of patients with KIT-positive unresectable and/or metastatic GIST [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2026]. Clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 11 mutations, in general, are associated with sensitivity to imatinib [PMID: 14645423, 18955451, 24638003]. Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines. Sunitinib (category 1) is recommended as a preferred second-line option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST previously treated with imatinib [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2026]. Of note, no alterations associated with resistance were detected in this specimen.

variants.variant_description:
Mutations in KIT exon 11 encoding the juxtamembrane domain are recurrently identified in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [PMID: 9438854, 15930355, 28481359]. The specific mutation found in this tumor has been shown to be a gain-of-function mutation with transforming properties [PMID: 14645423, 15790786,16397263,16434489].

KIT exon 11 mutations - including V560G - are well-described and occur most frequently in those arising from mucosal membranes and acral skin and less commonly from conjunctival and cutaneous sites [1,2]. Like other exon 11 mutation, KIT V560G has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signalling [3,4].

Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations (including exon 11 deletions) including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, etc. While imatinib has not been FDA-approved for the treatment of melanoma, several studies have shown that patients with melanoma harboring KIT exon 11 mutations respond to imatinib [5-7] and possibly other tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib and nilotinib [8-10]. While KIT V560G is uncommon, limited studies have suggested that mutations affecting this codon confers sensitivity to these agents [8,9]. In addition, other mutations within exon 11 which have similar functional affects are associated with TKI sensitivity. The current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma with imatinib [11].

variants.variant_description: While deletions and substitutions are more common in KIT exon 11 [PMID: 9438854], duplication mutations have been described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST), in particular involving the 3' end of exon 11 [PMID: 14681327]. While the effect of this specific variant on protein function is not well characterized, the recurrent nature of this variant suggests that is pathogenic, likely resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signaling.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activated KIT mutations (particularly exon 11 deletions) are present in most gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [PMID: 9438854, 15930355]. GIST with exon 11 duplications occur predominantly in the stomach and have a favorable clinical course [PMID: 14681327, 33673554] (in contrast to exon 11 deletions which have an inferior prognosis [PMID: 16135486]).
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved adjuvant therapy for KIT (CD117)-positive GIST. Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2026]. While clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 11 deletions are associated with sensitivity to imatinib [PMID: 24638003, 18955451, 14645423] and GIST with exon 11 insertions have a superior prognosis [PMID: 14681327, 16135486], one study found no clinical benefit was observed among patients with KIT exon 11 insertions compared to KIT wild-type GIST [PMID: 24638003], though this may reflect a small sample size.  
 
Sunitinib is FDA-approved for GIST after disease progression or intolerance to imatinib [PMID: 19737946]. No secondary mutations known to be associated with acquired TKI-resistance [PMID: 15930355, 17875769, 16954519] were detected.

variants.variant_description: Two KIT mutations were identified affecting exons 11 and 17. The KIT W557R mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the KIT protein. Pathogenic KIT exon 11 mutations, such as W557R, result in consitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signaling as well as oncogenic transformation [PMID: 9438854]. The second KIT mutation affects exon 17 and results in an amino acid subsitution.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: KIT exon 11 mutations  are well-described in approximately 80% of patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [PMID: 9438854, 15930355, 1464543]. KIT exon 17 mutations, including N822K, frequently arise as secondary resistance mutations in patients receiving treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors [PMID: 19737946, 15930355, 16954519, 17875769, 22614970].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved adjuvant therapy for KIT (CD117)-positive GIST. Clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 11 mutations, in general, are associated with sensitivity to imatinib [PMID: 14645423, 18955451, 24638003]. Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations is a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. However, preclinical and clinical studies found that KIT exon 17 mutations have been identified as secondary mutations associated with imatinib-resistance in GIST [PMID: 18623623, 18488160, 25239608]. The most recent NCCN guidelines recommend sunitinib as a preferred second-line option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST previously treated with imatinib; however, sunitinib has been shown to have minimal activity against tumors with KIT exon 17 mutations [PMID: 19164557, 19861442, 19390946]. Regorafenib is a preferred third-line option following imatinib and sunitinib, and ripretinib is a preferred fourth-line option after treatment with imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025].

Compared with GISTs having KIT exon 9 mutations or wild-type KIT, GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations have a worse recurrence-free survival and overall survival [PMID: 16135486].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved adjuvant therapy for the treatment of patients with KIT-positive unresectable and/or metastatic malignant GIST [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. Clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 11 mutations, in general, are associated with sensitivity to imatinib [PMID: 14645423, 18955451, 24638003]. Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines. Sunitinib (category 1) is recommended as a preferred second-line option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST previously treated with imatinib [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. Of note, no alterations associated with resistance were detected in this specimen.

variants.variant_description: The D572G mutation detected in this specimen is characterized as a likely oncogenic exon 11 mutation, is infrequently reported in patients with melanoma, and results in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signalling  [1-3,6-7]. KIT mutations are present in 10%–15% of melanomas of mucosal (most frequently vulvovaginal primaries, but also anorectal and sinonasal) and acral (ie, non–hair-bearing surfaces of palms and soles, nailbeds) origin. They are also present on 2%–3% of chronically sun-exposed skin, but extremely rarely on skin with intermittent sun exposure. Thus, clinical features can guide the decision whether to perform KIT mutation testing and possibly other tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib and nilotinib [4,5,17].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The multikinase inhibitor imatinib is NCCN-compendium listed for the treatment of patients with metastatic or unresectable melanoma with activating KIT exon 11 and 13 alterations [9-13,17]. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines KIT mutations may occur in multiple “hotspots” across the gene and differ in their sensitivity to KIT inhibitor therapy (eg, imatinib, sunitinib, nilotinib). KIT exon 11 and exon 13 mutations (eg, W557R, V559D, L576P, K642E) appear to have a high level of sensitivity to KIT inhibition.  KIT exon 17 mutations (eg, D816H) appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors. KIT amplifications appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors [17-19]. This specimen harbors both KIT D572G mutation as well as low level amplification of KIT.

variants.variant_description:
KIT exon 11 deletion and KIT exon 17 single nucleotide substitution
V569_L576del(;)Y823D
 
Two pathogenic KIT mutations are identified in this specimen. KIT exon 11 mutations, such as KIT V569_L576del, are well-described in patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [1]. Approximately 80% of patients with GIST have a mutation in the gene encoding the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase; another 5%–10% of GIST have a mutation in the gene encoding the related PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinase. Specific mutations in KIT or PDGFRA show some correlation with tumor phenotype, but mutations are not strongly correlated with the biologic potential of individual tumors. The accumulated data show that KIT mutations are not preferentially present in high-grade tumors, and can also be found in small incidental tumors as well as tumors that have an indolent course [2-6]. The second KIT mutation identified, Y823D, is located within exon 17 and resides within the activation loop domain. Y823D is classified as likely oncogenic and pathogenic [7,8]. KIT mutations identified in the tyrosine kinase domain (exon 13 and exon 17), as is V654A, often arise as secondary resistance mutations in patients treated with imatanib [6,9-12].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: GIST have different response rates to imatinib based upon the tumor mutation status: KIT exon 9 mutations have a lower response rate and progression-free survival (PFS) than exon 11 tumors at 400 mg, but dosing at 400 mg BID has been associated with better PFS. In patients with KIT exon 11 mutations, median PFS and OS were longer for those with secondary exon 13 or 14 mutations compared to those with exon 17 or 18 mutations. According to the most recent NCCN guideliens sunitinib appears to have activity against tumors with KIT adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding pocket mutations (exons 13 and 14) that confer resistance to imatinib, but has little activity against tumors with imatinib-resistant mutations in the KIT activation loop (exons 17 and 18), as in this specimen [6,9-12]. Another TKI that can be considered is nilotinib where clinical benefit may be specific to patients with secondary KIT exon 17 mutations [6].

variants.variant_description: Two KIT mutation were detected in this specimen: V560D and N822K (in a subclonal population). KIT exon 11 mutations - including V560D - are well-described and occur most frequently in those arising from mucosal membranes and acral skin and less commonly from conjunctival and cutaneous sites [1,2]. Like other exon 11 mutation, KIT V560G has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signalling [3,4].The KIT N822K, exon 17, mutation identified in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain and is characterized as oncogenic [1,3-4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis. KIT mutations may occur in multiple “hotspots” across the gene and differ in their sensitivity to KIT inhibitor therapy (eg, imatinib, sunitinib, nilotinib). KIT exon 11 and exon 13 mutations appear to have a high level of sensitivity to KIT inhibition. Whereas, KIT exon 17 mutations  appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors. KIT amplifications appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors [15]. The KIT exon 17 N822K mutation has been identified in disease progression gastrointestinal tumors (GISTs) collected from patients treated with either imatinib or sunitinib. While the multikinase inhibitors imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib and ripretinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with KIT-mutant GIST, their clinical utility in patients with KIT N822K mutant melanoma is unknown [5-14].
 
N822K is well-described in patients with progressive disease during treatment with imatinib or sunitinib [PMID: 18623623, 18488160, 26316776]. This mutation has also been functionally shown to confer resistance to imatinib [PMID: 18488160, 24205792, 31085175]. In preclinical studies, cells with the N822K mutation have demonstrated sensitivity to ponatinib [PMID: 21482694], sunitinib [PMID: 31217744, 31085175], avapritinib [PMID: 29093181], regorafenib [PMID: 31085175], desatinib [PMID: 23149070], midostaurin [PMID: 31085175], crenolanib [PMID: 31182436], flumatinib [PMID: 24205792], ripretinib [PMID: 31085175], BPR1J373 [PMID: 27512117], RMC-4550 [PMID: 37992684].

KIT exon 11 deletion mutations, as detected in this specimen, are well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumor [1].

KIT exon 11 mutations - including V560D - are well-described and occur most frequently in those arising from mucosal membranes and acral skin and less commonly from conjunctival and cutaneous sites [1,2]. Like other exon 11 mutation, KIT V560D has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signalling [3]. Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations (including exon 11 deletions) including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, etc. While imatinib has not been FDA-approved for the treatment of melanoma, several studies have shown that patients with melanoma harboring KIT exon 11 mutations respond to imatinib [4-6] and possibly other tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib and nilotinib [7-9]. While KIT V560D is uncommon, limited studies have suggested that this mutation also confers sensitivity to these agents [1,7]. The current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma with imatinib [10]. Clinical trials are underway investigating the clinical utility of imatinib and other agents for KIT-mutated melanoma.

One study found that second-line sunitinib induced higher clinical benefit (PR or stable disease for ≥6 months) in patients with imatinib resistant/intolerant GISTs with primary KIT exon 9 mutations than those with KIT exon 11 mutations. Median PFS and OS were significantly longer for patients with KIT exon 9 mutations or non-mutated KIT than those with KIT exon 11 mutations. In patients with KIT exon 11 mutations, median PFS and OS were longer for those with secondary exon 13 or 14 mutations compared to those with exon 17 or 18 mutations. Although sunitinib appears to have activity against tumors with KIT adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding pocket mutations (exons 13 and 14) that confer resistance to imatinib, it has little activity against tumors with imatinib-resistant mutations in the KIT activation loop (exons 17 and 18)[6,9-12].

variants.variant_description:
The W557R mutation detected in this specimen is well-described in melanoma [1-7]. This mutation and other KIT exon 11 mutations occur most frequently in melanomas arising from mucosal membranes and acral skin and less commonly from conjunctival and cutaneous sites [8]. KIT W557R has also been described as a germline variant associated with familial gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [9,10]. This test cannot distinguish between germline and somatic variants; therefore, genetic counseling and possible germline testing may be indicated.

KIT W557R mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the KIT protein. Pathogenic KIT exon 11 mutations, such as W557R, result in consitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signaling as well as oncogenic transformation [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma with imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib or riperetinib [17]. Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations (including exon 11 deletions) including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, etc. While imatinib has not been FDA-approved for the treatment of melanoma, several studies have shown that patients with melanoma harboring KIT exon 11 mutations respond to imatinib [11-13] and possibly other tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib and nilotinib [14-16]. While there is limited clinical data concerning KIT W557R due to the low incidence of this mutation, available studies have suggested that this mutation also confers sensitivity to these agents [6,7]. Clinical trials are underway investigating the clinical utility of imatinib and other agents for KIT-mutated melanoma.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: According to the most recent NCCN guidelines, approximately 80% of GIST have a mutation in the gene encoding the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase; another 5%–10% of GIST have a mutation in the gene encoding the related PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinase. The presence and type of KIT and PDGFRA mutations are not strongly correlated with prognosis. Specific mutations in KIT or PDGFRA show some correlation with tumor phenotype, but mutations are not strongly correlated with the biologic potential of individual tumors. The accumulated data show that KIT mutations are not preferentially present in high-grade tumors, and can also be found in small incidental tumors as well as tumors that have an indolent course [8].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: GIST have different response rates to imatinib based upon the tumor mutation status: KIT exon 9 mutations have a lower response rate and progression-free survival (PFS) than exon 11 tumors at 400 mg, but dosing at 400 mg BID has been associated with better PFS. In randomized trials evaluating imatinib in the advanced disease setting, the presence of a KIT exon 11 mutation was associated with better response rates, median progression-free survival (PFS), and median overall survival (OS) than KIT exon 9 mutations or non-mutated KIT or PDGFRA [8,2-10].

Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [13-16]. No secondary mutations known to be associated with acquired TKI-resistance [15-16] were detected in this specimen. GISTs have different response rates to imatinib based upon the tumor mutation status: KIT exon 9 mutations have a lower response rate and progression-free survival (PFS) than exon 11 tumors at 400 mg, but dosing at 400 mg BID has been associated with better PFS. Most PDGFRA mutations are associated with a response to imatinib, with the exception of D842V, which is unlikely to respond to imatinib and most other approved TKIs for GIST except for avapritinib [13].

KIT V559A affects the juxtamembrane domain (exon 11) of the KIT protein [PMID: 15837988]. V559A results in constitutive phosphorylation of KIT and increased MAPK and AKT activation in patient samples and cultured cells [PMID: 15837988, 19047099]. KIT exon 11 mutations are most common in GISTs of all sites, whereas KIT exon 9 mutations are specific for intestinal GISTs and PDGFRA exon 18 mutations are common in gastric GISTs [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025].

The V559A mutation detected in this specimen has been described in melanoma, particularly acral or mucosal melanoma [1-6,8]. This mutation has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signalling [7-8].

Sunitinib (category 1) is recommended as a preferred second-line option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST previously treated with imatinib [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 11 mutations, in general, tend to be associated with sensitivity to imatinib [5-7], an FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) for KIT-positive GIST. TKIs sunitinib, regorafenib, ripretinib are common FDA-approved options if resistance is found, whereas nilotinib, sorafenib, and pazopanib are among potential alternatives. 
 
The exon 11 mutation W557G lies within the juxtamembrane domain and results in constitutive phosphorylation in cell culture [8] and is predicted to lead to Kit gain of function and is predicted to be sensitive to imatinib [9].
 
However, the exon 13 mutation V654A lies within the protein kinase domain and is commonly associated with imatinib resistance as well as resistance to other TKIs [10-11].
 
N822K is well-described in patients with progressive disease during treatment with imatinib or sunitinib [PMID: 18623623, 18488160, 26316776]. This mutation has also been functionally shown to confer resistance to imatinib [PMID: 18488160, 24205792, 31085175]. In preclinical studies, cells with the N822K mutation have demonstrated sensitivity to ponatinib [PMID: 21482694], sunitinib [PMID: 31217744, 31085175], avapritinib [PMID: 29093181], regorafenib [PMID: 31085175], desatinib [PMID: 23149070], midostaurin [PMID: 31085175], crenolanib [PMID: 31182436], flumatinib [PMID: 24205792], ripretinib [PMID: 31085175], BPR1J373 [PMID: 27512117], RMC-4550 [PMID: 37992684].
 
In addition, the exon 17 N822K lies within the activation loop in the protein kinase domain of Kit and results in activation and signaling [12-13] and has also been identified as a secondary mutation associated with TKI resistance [14].

The KIT K558N variant detected in this specimen is rare, but has been described in gastrointestinal stromal tumor [1-3]. However, this variant has also been described as a germline polymorphism (rs200375589). The functional effect of this variant (if any) or the KIT protein has not been evaluated.

Low-level MYC copy number gain (equivocal for amplification): 
A low-level copy number gain of the MYC gene was detected (approximately 4-6 copies; considered equivocal for amplification). MYC (c-MYC) is a transcription factor involved in growth signaling, and amplification of MYC has been reported in a wide variety of solid tumors [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified solid tumors; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [2-4].

variants.variant_description: The W557R mutation detected in this specimen is well-described in melanoma [1-7]. This mutation and other KIT exon 11 mutations occur most frequently in melanomas arising from mucosal membranes and acral skin and less commonly from conjunctival and cutaneous sites [8]. KIT W557R has also been described as a germline variant associated with familial gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [9,10]. This test cannot distinguish between germline and somatic variants; therefore, genetic counseling and possible germline testing may be indicated. A W557_K558delinsRR mutation (also designated W557_K558>RR) was also identified in this specimen. This mutation results for a second base substitution (c.1673A>G) in addition to the c.1669T>C substitution resulting in the W557R mutation described above. This second mutation is present at a lower variant allele frequency. Because there is a low-level copy number gain of the KIT gene, the lower allele frequency could result from one of several copies of KIT acquiring this mutation or from tumor heterogeneity. While there are no known reports of this specific mutation, complex deletion, insertion and substition mutations affecting codons W557 and K558 are well-described in various neoplasms, particularly GIST [11]. Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations (including exon 11 deletions) including GIST, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, etc. While imatinib has not been FDA-approved for the treatment of melanoma, several studies have shown that patients with melanoma harboring KIT exon 11 mutations respond to imatinib [12-14] and possibly other tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib and nilotinib [15-17]. While there is limited clinical data concerning KIT W557R (and no clinical data for W557_K558delinsRR) due to the low incidence of this mutation, available studies have suggested that this mutation also confers sensitivity to TKI therapy [6,7]. The current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma with imatinib [18]. Clinical trials are underway investigating the clinical utility of imatinib and other agents for KIT-mutated melanoma.

Like other exon 11 mutation, KIT V560D has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signalling [3]. While KIT V560D is uncommon, limited studies have suggested that this mutation also confers sensitivity to these agents [1,7]. The current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma with imatinib [10]. Two KIT mutations were identified affecting exons 9 and 17. KIT A502_Y503dup is located within the extracellular domain of exon 9 and is characterized as pathogenic and oncogenic. Although the majority of KIT mutations are located in exon 11, 13% have been reported in exon 9. Approximately 80% of patients with GIST's have a mutation in the gene encoding the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase; another 5%–10% of GIST have a mutation in the gene encoding the related PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinase [NCCN - GIST, Version 1.2026]. The second KIT mutation affects exon 17 and results in an amino acid subsitution.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: KIT exon 9 mutations  are well-described in approximately 13% of patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [PMID: 9438854, 15930355, 1464543]. KIT exon 17 mutations frequently arise as secondary resistance mutations in patients receiving treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors [PMID: 19737946, 15930355, 16954519, 17875769].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved adjuvant therapy for KIT (CD117)-positive GIST. Patients with GIST's have different response rates to imatinib based upon the tumor mutation status: KIT exon 9 mutations have a lower response rate and progression-free survival (PFS) than exon 11 tumors at 400 mg, but dosing at 400 mg BID has been associated with better PFS [NCCN - GIST, Version 2.2024][PMID: 14645423, 18955451, 24638003]. Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 9 mutations is a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [NCCN - GIST, Version 1.2025]. However, preclinical and clinical studies found that KIT exon 17 mutations have been identified as secondary mutations associated with imatinib-resistance in GIST [PMID: 18623623, 18488160, 25239608].

variants.variant_description: Two KIT mutations were detected in this specimen: K642E and N822K. The K642E mutation detected in this specimen is a known oncogenic exon 13 mutation in melanoma [PMID: 25148578, 28481359, 21325067, 15990278, 19802003] that affects the tyrosine kinase domain, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signaling [PMID: 15990278, 19802003] as well as transformation in culture [PMID 11073817]. The KIT N822K mutation identified in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain and is characterized as oncogenic [PMID: 24205792, 18623623, 26956871, 20633291].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, and systemic mastocytosis. KIT mutations may occur in multiple “hotspots” across the gene and differ in their sensitivity to KIT inhibitor therapy (eg, imatinib, sunitinib, nilotinib). KIT exon 11 and exon 13 mutations appear to have a high level of sensitivity to KIT inhibition, whereas KIT exon 17 mutations  appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors. The KIT N822K mutation is well-described in patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors with progressive disease during treatment with imatinib or sunitinib [PMID: 18623623, 18488160, 26316776] and has been functionally shown to confer resistance to imatinib [PMID: 18488160, 24205792, 31085175].  According to the most recent NCCN Guidelines, while imatinib is not a preferred agent for patients with KIT-mutated melanoma, it may be useful for those who are ineligible for or unresponsive to more effective therapies [NCCN Guidelines Melanoma: Cutaneous, Version 2.2026].

However, KIT S628N has been associated with sensitivity (in vitro) to TKI therapies including imatinib and desatinib [PMID: 25317746, 25317746].

variants.variant_description:
KIT K642E is a rare mutation located in exon 13 with a frequency of approximately 1-2% although the majority of KIT exon 13 mutations in GISTs are reported to be K642E [PMID:18246046]. K642E results in an amino acid substitution affecting the ATP binding pocket within the kinase domain of the KIT protein. This mutation has been shown to be activating [PMID: 10702394] and described in both sporadic GIST and patients with familial GIST. K642E is most often identified as a secondary mutation associated acquired resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in gastrointestinal stromal tumors [PMID:17193822].

The K642E mutation detected in this specimen is a known oncogenic exon 13 mutation in melanoma [PMID: 25148578, 28481359, 21325067, 15990278, 19802003] that affects the tyrosine kinase domain, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signaling [PMID: 15990278, 19802003] as well as transformation in culture [PMID 11073817].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Sunitinib appears to have activity against tumors with KIT (ATP)-binding pocket mutations (exons 13 and 14) that confer resistance to imatinib. As such current NCCN guidelines recommended sunitinib (category 1) as a preferred second-line option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST previously treated with imatinib [NCCN GIST v1.2025]. Given the rarity of primary exon 13 KIT mutations initial response to imatinib is less clear. One report of a patient with GIST harboring the V654A variant showed imatinib resistance and rapid progression [PMID:16954519]. However, a case report of a patient with this same mutation, K642E, had a robust and prolonged response to imatinib [PMID: 19383335].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: KIT mutations are present in 10%–15% of melanomas of mucosal (most frequently vulvovaginal primaries, but also anorectal and sinonasal) and acral (ie, non–hair-bearing surfaces of palms and soles, nailbeds) origin [PMID: 28467829, 28720667, 35706047].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Treatment with KIT inhibitor therapy (e.g., imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, ripretinib) is considered useful in certain circumstances for KIT mutated melanoma [NCCN Guidelines Melanoma: Cutaneous, Version 2.2025]. The multikinase inhibitor imatinib has demonstrated clinical efficacy in patients with metastatic or unresectable melanoma with activating KIT exon 11 and 13 alterations [PMID: 21642685, 23775962, 18510589, 20545949, 22261812]. Clinical efficacy of nilotinib has also been reported in these patients [PMID: 28327988].
For the specific mutation detected in this specimen - K642E - responses to imatinib have been reported in melanoma patients [PMID: 20372153, 21642685, 23775962] and preclinical data has also supported potential efficacy of other inhibitors including sunitinib [PMID: 31205508, regorafenib [PMID: 21170960], ponatinib [PMID: 25239608], axitinib [PMID: 31205508], ninteanib [PMID: 35194937], and IDRX-12 [PMID: 37223931, 40018846].

variants.variant_description: The K642T mutation detected in this specimen is less common than K642E mutation which is a well-described oncogenic exon 13 mutation in melanoma, resulting in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signalling [1-5].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: KIT mutations are present in 10%–15% of melanomas of mucosal (most frequently vulvovaginal primaries, but also anorectal and sinonasal) and acral (ie, non–hair-bearing surfaces of palms and soles, nailbeds) origin. They are also present on 2%–3% of chronically sun-exposed skin, but extremely rarely on skin with intermittent sun exposure. The more common K642E is a well-described somatic mutation in melanoma. K642T has been described as a germline mutation associated with hereditary predisposition to gastrointestinal stromal tumors [6-7]. Sequencing of non-neoplastic tissue demonstrated that the mutation is somatic (not present in non-neoplastic tissue).
diseases.therapeutic_implications: The multikinase inhibitor imatinib is NCCN-compendium listed for the treatment of patients with metastatic or unresectable melanoma with activating KIT exon 11 and 13 alterations [8-13]. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines KIT mutations may occur in multiple “hotspots” across the gene and differ in their sensitivity to KIT inhibitor therapy (eg, imatinib, sunitinib, nilotinib). KIT exon 11 and exon 13 mutations (eg, W557R, V559D, L576P, K642E) appear to have a high level of sensitivity to KIT inhibition.  KIT exon 17 mutations (eg, D816H) appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors. KIT amplifications appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors [8,14-15]. One case report also demonstrated evidence of imatinib sensitivity for the K642T mutation.

variants.variant_description:
The KIT D816V mutation identified in this specimen affects the protein kinase domain (exon 17) of the KIT protein. This mutation results in constitutive activation of KIT and drives the differentiation, proliferation, and survival of mast cells [PMID: 19787646, 30007460, 23593539].

The KIT D816V mutations identified in this specimen affects the protein kinase domain (exon 17) of the Kit protein [1]. This mutation confers a gain of function on Kit, as indicated by constitutive phosphorylation of Kit in cultured cells [PMID: 25148578].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating mutations in the tyrosine kinase 2 domain (exon 17) of the KIT gene, especially KIT D816V, are the molecular hallmark of systemic mastocytosis and are identified in approximately 90% of cases, depending on subtype [WHO Haematolymphoid Tumors (5th ed)].

Preclinical data and clinical data in other neoplasms suggest that this mutation may be senstive to inhibitors such as midostaurin [11], repretinib [11], avapritinib [12] or ponatinib [13].

KIT Y823H mutation has rarely been reported in melanoma [2] and has been documented in several other tumor types including gastronintestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [3] and seminomas [4] and confers a gain of function on Kit, as indicated by constitutive phosphorylation of Kit in cultured cells [4-5].

However, several clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 17 mutations (including Y823H) has been identified as secondary mutations associated with imatinib-resistance in GIST [1,14-15].

variants.variant_description: KIT mutations have been identified in a variety of neoplasms, including more commonly gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST), leukemias, and systemic mastocytosis, but has also been identified in a subset of thymic carcinomas (including those with KIT D820 alterations) [1]. The D820Y mutation seen in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain (exon 17) of the Kit protein and results in constitutive phosphorylation and transformation [2, 3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis. In general, thymic carcinomas with KIT mutations have shown response to imatinib and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors; however, preclinical and clinical studies found that KIT exon 17 mutations (including D820Y) have been identified as secondary mutations associated with imatinib-resistance in GIST [4-6] indicating caution when choosing specific therapies. 
 
Preclinical studies have also suggested tumors harboring KIT D820 mutations may have resistance to sunitinib and regorafenib but may be sensitive to ponatinib, cabozantinib, and avapritinib [6-8]. In addition, a case report of thymic carcinoma with a KIT D820E mutation was treated with soratetinib and demonstrated a partial response [9].

variants.variant_description: The KIT N822K, exon 17, mutation identified in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain and is characterized as oncogenic [1,3-4]. KIT mutations are present in 10%–15% of melanomas of mucosal (most frequently vulvovaginal primaries, but also anorectal and sinonasal) and acral (ie, non–hair-bearing surfaces of palms and soles, nailbeds) origin. They are also present on 2%–3% of chronically sun-exposed skin, but extremely rarely on skin with intermittent sun exposure. Thus, clinical features can guide the decision whether to perform KIT mutation testing [15].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis. KIT mutations may occur in multiple “hotspots” across the gene and differ in their sensitivity to KIT inhibitor therapy (eg, imatinib, sunitinib, nilotinib). KIT exon 11 and exon 13 mutations appear to have a high level of sensitivity to KIT inhibition. Whereas, KIT exon 17 mutations  appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors. KIT amplifications appear to have minimal or no sensitivity to KIT inhibitors [15]. The KIT exon 17 N822K mutation has been identified in disease progression gastrointestinal tumors (GISTs) collected from patients treated with either imatinib or sunitinib. While the multikinase inhibitors imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib and ripretinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with KIT-mutant GIST, their clinical utility in patients with KIT N822K mutant melanoma is unknown [5-14].
 
N822K is well-described in patients with progressive disease during treatment with imatinib or sunitinib [PMID: 18623623, 18488160, 26316776]. This mutation has also been functionally shown to confer resistance to imatinib [PMID: 18488160, 24205792, 31085175]. In preclinical studies, cells with the N822K mutation have demonstrated sensitivity to ponatinib [PMID: 21482694], sunitinib [PMID: 31217744, 31085175], avapritinib [PMID: 29093181], regorafenib [PMID: 31085175], desatinib [PMID: 23149070], midostaurin [PMID: 31085175], crenolanib [PMID: 31182436], flumatinib [PMID: 24205792], ripretinib [PMID: 31085175], BPR1J373 [PMID: 27512117], RMC-4550 [PMID: 37992684].

variants.variant_description: KIT is altered in a variety of tumor types, but mutations are rare in non-small cell lung carcinoma [1]. The KIT D820G mutation identified in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain (exon 17) of the Kit protein [2]. While KIT D820G has not been previously reported in lung carcinoma, it has been documented in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) following therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors and hematopoietic neoplasms (acute myeloid leukemia and mast cell neoplasms) [3-5]. However, this mutation has not been fully biochemically characterized.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, etc, although the affect in lung carcinoma harboring KIT mutations is unknown. Preclinical and clinical studies found that KIT exon 17 mutations (including D820G) have been identified as secondary mutations associated with imatinib-resistance in GIST [5-7]. Preclinical studies have also suggested tumors harboring KIT D820G mutations may have resistance to sunitinib and regorafenib but may be sensitive to ponatinib, cabozantinib, and avapritinib [7-9]. Additional clinical studies are warranted to better understand this therapeutic significance of this mutation.

KIT Y823D mutation identified in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain (exon 17) of the Kit protein [1]. While KIT Y823D mutation has not been previously reported in melanomas, it has been documented rarely in several tumor types including gastronintestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [2] and seminomas [3] and confers a gain of function on Kit, as indicated by constitutive phosphorylation of Kit in cultured cells [3-4].

While the KIT Y823D mutation identified in this specimen  has not been reported in melanomas, it has been idenitifed in several cancers including gastrointestinal stromal tumors [1] and seminomas [2] amd confers a gain of function on Kit, as indicated by constitutive phosphorylation of Kit in cultured cells [2-3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of several neoplasms with TKI-sensitive KIT mutations including gastrointestinal stromal tumor, chronic myeloid leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, etc. While imatinib has not been FDA-approved for the treatment of melanoma, several studies have shown that patients with KIT-mutated melanoma (particulary exon 11 mutations) respond to imatinib [5-9] and possibly other tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib and nilotinib [10-12].  However, several clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 17 mutations (including Y823D)  has been identified as secondary mutations associated with imatinib-resistance in GIST [1,13-14].

variants.variant_description: Mutations in KIT exon 11 encoding the juxtamembrane domain are recurrently identified in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [PMID: 9438854, 15930355, 28481359]. While this specific variant has not been described, KIT exon 11 deletion mutations in general result in constitutive activation of KIT and downstream growth signaling as well as oncogenic transformation [PMID: 9438854]. Compared with GISTs having exon 9 mutations or wild-type KIT, GISTs with exon 11 mutations have a worse recurrence-free survival and overall survival [PMID: 16135486].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved adjuvant therapy for KIT (CD117)-positive GIST. Clinical data on the sensitivity of this specific mutation is not available due to the rarity of this mutation, however, clinical studies have shown that KIT exon 11 mutations, in general, are associated with sensitivity to imatinib [PMIDs: 14645423, 18955451, 24638003]. Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 11 mutations is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, v1.2025]. Sunitinib is FDA-approved for GIST after disease progression or intolerance to imatinib [PMID: 19737946]. No secondary mutations known to be associated with acquired TKI-resistance [PMIDs: 15930355, 16954519, 17875769] were detected.

variants.variant_description: KIT A502_Y503dup is located within the extracellular domain of exon 9 and is characterized as pathogenic and oncogenic. Although the majority of KIT mutations are located in exon 11, 13% have been reported in exon 9. Approximately 80% of patients with GISTs have a mutation in the gene encoding the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase; another 5%–10% of GISTs have a mutation in the gene encoding the related PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinase [NCCN - GIST, Version 1.2026].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved as an adjuvant therapy for KIT (CD117)-positive GIST. Patients with GISTs have different response rates to imatinib based upon the tumor mutation status: KIT exon 9 mutations have a lower response rate and progression-free survival (PFS) than exon 11 tumors at 400 mg, but dosing at 400 mg BID has been associated with better PFS [NCCN - GIST, Version 2.2024][PMID: 14645423, 18955451, 24638003]. Treatment of GIST with KIT exon 9 mutations is a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [NCCN - GIST, Version 1.2026]. Of note, no alterations associated with resistance were detected in this specimen.

variants.variant_description: Two KIT mutations were detected. One mutation (A502_Y503dup) is a duplication involving exon 9 which encodes the extracellular domain for the KIT protein. This mutation is the most common affecting exon 9 and exon 9 mutations, in general, are most common within intestinal GISTs [PMID: 9438854, 15930355, 28481359, 24061512]. The second KIT mutation (V654A) affects exon 13 and results in an amino acid subsitution affecting the ATP binding pocket of the KIT protein. This mutation has been shown to be activating [PMID: 17363509, 33024275] and has been described as a secondary mutation associated acquired resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (see below) [PMID: 35035701, 15685537, 18623623, 37105265].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved adjuvant therapy for KIT (CD117)-positive GIST. GISTs have different response rates to imatinib based upon the tumor mutation status: KIT exon 9 mutations have a lower response rate and progression free survival (PFS) than exon 11 tumors at 400 mg, but dosing at 400 mg BID has been associated with better PFS [PMID: 24638003]. Dose escalation is currently recommended for GIST with exon 9 mutations that progress [NCCN GIST v2.2024].
 
However, KIT V654A is assoicated with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [PMID: 35035701, 15685537, 18623623, 37105265]. KIT V654A has been associated acquired resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) imatinib [PMID: 35035701, 15685537, 18623623] and avapritinib [PMID: 37105265]. This mutation also appears to confer resistance to ponatinib based on preclinical studies [PMID: 25239608]. Other TKIs such as axitinib [PMID: 31205508], motesanib [PMID: 20633291] and CHMFL-KIT-031 [PMID: 29340041] have been shown to overcome resistance in preclinical studies.

variants.variant_description:
Evidence of an ALK gene fusion was detected by initial screening for 5' to 3' imbalance and confirmed by ALK break-apart FISH. ALK gene fusions involving a variety of fusion partners are well-described and result in constitutive activation of ALK kinase domain and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 10216106, 17625570, 8122112].

Two KIT variants were detected. KIT V654A affects the ATP binding pocket. This mutation has been shown to be activating [1-2] and has been described as a secondary mutation associated aquired resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (see below) [3-6]. KIT K509I has been described as both a somatic mutation (in mastocytosis) [7-8] and a germline variant associated with a predisposition to mastocytosis [9-11]. It is uncertain if these variants affect the same allele (in cis) or oppositive alleles (in trans).

diseases.diagnostic_implications:
ALK gene fusions have been described at a low incidence (<1%) in melanoma [PMID: 35871080, 24445538, 25602801, 27776007, 24698967, 29920315]. Gene fusions including ALK are more common in Spitz neoplasms, including benign Spitz tumors and spitzoid melanomas [PMID: 24445538, 25602801, 27776007, 24698967, 29920315].

KIT mutations are well-described in melanoma, particularly acral or mucosal melanoma [12].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Several studies have shown a clinical response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) among patients with NSCLC [PMID: 23724913, 28475456, 25470694, 26598747, 26708155, 28586279, 28126333, 26973324, 24670165]. The efficacy of crizotinib in other cancers with ALK fusions is referred to in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines, but no specific treatment recommendation is given [National Comprehensive Cancer Network Guidelines - Melanoma: Cutaneous. Version 2.2025].

While several studies have shown that patients with melanoma harboring KIT exon 11 mutations respond to imatinib [13-15], the mutations in this specimen do not involve exon 11. KIT V654A has been associated acquired resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) imatinib [3-5] and avapritinib [6]. This mutation also appears to confer resistance to ponatinib based on preclinical studies [16]. Other TKIs such as axitinib [17], motesanib [18] and CHMFL-KIT-031 [19] have been shown to overcome resistance in preclinical studies. KIT K509I is associated with sensitivity to TKI including imatinib, dasatinib and midostaurin [7-10].

KIT D496N 
This variant has been reported as a germline variant in population databases (rs143179681) with the hightest gnomAD frequency among African/African Americans (0.03%). There are no known reports in which this variant was shown to be somatic; however, evaluation of non-neoplastic tissue would be required to definitively exclude a somatic mutation.
ClinVar entries for this variant include both VUS (3) and likely benign (1). In silico analysis of this variant suggests that it does not alter protein function. 
This variant is most likely a benign, germline polymorphism, but is being reported due to the conflicting ClinVar interpretations.

While KIT D817V mutation has rarley reported in melanomas [1], it has been documented rarely in several tumor types including gastronintestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [2] and seminomas [3] and confers a gain of function on Kit, as indicated by constitutive phosphorylation of Kit in cultured cells [3-4]. KIT R804G has not been reported in melanomas before and has not been biochemically characterized.

variants.variant_description:
KIT amplification (approximately 11 copies)
 
Copy number gains (amplification) of KIT:
A copy number gain (amplification) was detected in KIT. It is understood from the provided pathology report that this patient has a poorly differentiated carcinoma from an unknown primary location. KIT gene amplifications occur in a subset of melanomas, gliomas and small cell lung carcinomas, among other tumors (OncoKb Aug 2023). KIT gene amplifications are reportedly not correlated with KIT protein overexpression in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and medulloblastomas [1,2]. However, KIT amplifications have been correlated with protein overexpression in both ovarian dysgeminomas [3] and recurrent gliomas [4]. KIT amplification has been associated with tumor progression in seminomas [5]. In a study of 11 patients with melanoma harboring amplified, wildtype KIT, the response rate with imatinib treatment was 0% [6].

KIT amplification is well described in melanoma, occurring in approximately 3% of cutaneous melanomas [1] and possibly higher in mucosal melanomas [2].

PDGFRA R841K:
PDGFRA (platelet derived growth factor receptor alpha) is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. R841K is a rare PDGFRA mutation which has been identified in at least one melanoma [1] and one gastrointestinal stromal tumor [2]. It has been shown in preclinical studies to be activating/oncogenic and responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) imatinib and crenolanib [1]. KIT amplification is well described in melanoma, occurring in about 10-15% of cases and having no clear association with location or etiology [3]. While tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) such as imatinib are recommended in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines for the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma [4], several studies have shown that melanomas with KIT amplification are not as responsive to imatinib [5-7] or nilotinib [8-10] treatment. In a phase 2 study of metastatic melanoma patients, 1 out 3 patients with KIT amplification achieved a partial response [5]. In other studies, none of eleven and four patients with KIT amplification alone responded to imatinib [6,7]. For nilotinib, 1 out 15 patients with KIT amplification achieved a partial response to nilotinib in one study [8] while none of two and six patients with KIT amplification responded in other studies [9,10].

PDGFRA R841K:
PDGFRA (platelet derived growth factor receptor alpha) is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. R841K is a rare PDGFRA mutation which has been identified in at least one melanoma [1] and one gastrointestinal stromal tumor [2]. It has been shown in preclinical studies to be activating/oncogenic and responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) imatinib and crenolanib [1]. KIT amplification is well described in melanoma, occurring in about 10-15% of cases and having no clear association with location or etiology; it is about equally common in lesions arising on acral, mucosal and chronically sun-damaged skin [3]. While TKIs such as imatinib are recommended in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines for the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma [4], their role in KIT-amplified cases is less clear. In a small phase II clinical trial, 5 of 26 patients with melanoma harboring KIT mutations responded to nilotinib, however none of the 8 patients with KIT-amplified melanoma responded [5]. Similarly, a phase II trial of imatinib in 25 patients with melanoma harboring KIT mutations or amplification found that disease control rates were correlated positively with KIT mutations but not KIT amplification [6]. Clinical trials are underway investigating the clinical utility of TKIs and other agents for KIT-amplified and PDGFRA-mutant melanoma. The close homology between KIT and PDGFRA leads to similar sensitivity to TKIs, which in turn results in overlapping clinical trial enrollment criteria and the possibility of a dual mechanism of response to therapy in this case. Michigan Medicine is currently participating in a phase 2 cliinical trial (NCT02272998; UMCC 2015.088) evaluating the efficacy of the TKI ponatinib and a phase 1 clinical trial (NCT02219711; UMCC 2015.040) evaluating the efficacy of the TKI MGCD516. Trials outside of Michigan include a phase I/II trial of pembrolizumab and imatinib at Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center and other locations (NCT02812693), and a Phase I trial of DCC-2618 (NCT02571036, multiple locations in USA).

KIT copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain (approximately 13 copies) involving the KIT gene was detected, consistent with gene amplification. Amplification of KIT is well-described in NSCLC [1,2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified NSCLC; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [5-7].

name: BRAF
gene_function: BRAF is a serine-threonine kinase involved in growth signaling, downstream of EGFR within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.

variants.variant_description:
Studies investigating the functional effect of several G469 mutations have demonstrated intermediate constitutive kinase activation of BRAF as well as downstream MAPK signaling [PMID: 15035987, 26343582, 28783719]. In contrast with BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations which result in constitutively active monomers, G469Y and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner [PMID: 26343582, 28783719]. Class II BRAF mutations are identified in a variety of CNS tumors [PMID: 3480497].

The BRAF G469V mutation detected in this specimen has been described in biliary cancer [1] as well as other cancers including lung cancer NSCLC [PMID: 28481359,24297085], colorectal cancer [PMID: 15729718] and melanoma [PMID: 15948115]. Studies investigating the functional effect of several G469 mutations have demonstrated intermediate constitutive kinase activation of BRAF as well as downstream MAPK signaling [PMID: 15035987, 26343582, 28783719]. In contrast with BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations which result in constitutively active monomers, G469V and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner [PMID: 26343582, 28783719].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: BRAF class II mutations including BRAF G469V are insensitive to the RAF-targeted inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib [PMID: 26466569].

Based on preclinical studies, "class 2" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [6,7]. However, newer compounds such as BGB659 and PLX8394 have proven effective against these "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [6,8,9]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have been shown to be effective against "class 2" BRAF mutations in preclinical studies [6,7].

BRAF class II mutations including BRAF G469V are insensitive to the RAF-targeted inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib [6] . Laboratory data suggest that cancer cells with oncogenic, non-V600 BRAF mutations may be sensitive to novel BRAF inhibitors such as plixorafenib [De La Fuente, M, et al. JCO. 2023 ASCO annual meeting vol 41, number 16 supplement].

There is no FDA-approved therapy or specific therapy recommended for NSCLC with non-V600 BRAF mutation by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines. 
 
While the combination of dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with a BRAF V600E mutation, these drugs are not approved for non-V600 BRAF mutations like G469V. Based on preclinical studies, "class 2" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [PMID: 26343582, 28783719]. However, newer compounds such as BDTX-4933, BGB659, PLX8394 and AZ628 have proven effective against these "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [PMID: 26343582, 27834212, 29662630]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have been shown to be effective against "class 2" BRAF mutations in preclinical studies [PMID: 26343582, 28783719, 29662630]. In a phase 1 trial, clinical responses to the ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523) have been reported in NSCLC with non-V600 BRAF [PMID: 29247021].

variants.variant_description:

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Vemurafenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with ECD harboring a BRAF V600 mutation. According to the most recent NCCN Guidelines, vemurafenib is a preferred regimen for BRAF V600E-mutant ECD in the first-line or subsequent-line. However, the FDA-approved dose is associated with significant toxicity that often results in discontinuation, dose interruption, or dose modification. Dabrafenib is another recommended regimen [NCCN Guidelines Histiocytic Neoplasms, Version 1.2026].
 
BRAF V600E mutations are associated with sensitivity to BRAF inhibitor therapies such as vemurafenib [PMID: 21483012, 21639808]. The VE-BASKET study and others have found that vemurafenib monotherapy shows efficacy in patients with BRAF V600-mutant Erdheim-Chester disease specifically, although dermatologic adverse events were frequent complications [PMID: 29188284, 25422482].  As of a result, Vemurafenib was approved by the FDA for treatment of Erdheim-Chester disease in patients harboring a V600 mutation [PMID: 30120160].  However, in other tumor types such as melanoma, monotherapy typically results in resistance to BRAF inhibitors within a year, and thus, the combination of BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy results in improved survival and/or more prolonged response as well as reduced cutaneous adverse events (e.g. squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma and photosensitivity) [PMID: 25399551, 23020132, 26037941, 25287827, 25265494, 25037139, 31732523, 29573941, 25440439]. Several BRAF + MEK inhibitor combinations are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600-mutated metastatic melanoma and have been shown to be clinically efficacious including dabrafenib + trametinib [PMID: 25399551, 23020132, 26037941, 25287827], vemurafenib + cobimetinib [PMID: 25265494, 25037139, 31732523], and ecorafenib + binimetinib [PMID: 29573941]. In Erdheim-Chester disease patients, there is also evidence to suggest combination BRAF and MEK inhibition in the setting of progressive disease or treatment-related toxicities of BRAF monotherapy [PMID: 32642685].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Dabrafenib & Trametinib (FDA-approved):
   The combination of the BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib and the MEK inhibitor trametinib are FDA-approved for advanced solid tumors with BRAF V600E mutations.  In several case reports and cohort studies, patients with BRAF V600E-mutated papillary craniopharyngioma have demonstrated tumor reduction after being treated with the BRAF inhibitor debrafenib and the MEK inhibitor trametinib [PMID: 26498373, 28918496, 28425764, 31675726, 33285519, 35023192, 35155453, 37683921, 39158090] or to the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib [PMID: 26115708]. 
 
   Other BRAF inhibitors including vemurafenib, dabrafenib, encorafenib as well as MEK inhibitors such as trametinib, selumetinib (AZD6244) and binimetinib (MEK162) are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma, non small cell lung cancer and/or anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with BRAF V600E mutations.

The RAF inhibitor dabrafenib in combination with the MEK1/2 inhibitor trametinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with BRAF V600E-mutant solid tumors. In a phase 2 trial of vemurafenib in metastatic or unresectable BRAF-mutant PTC, 10 of 12 (83.3%) of patients demonstrated a partial response [6]. In a phase 1 trial of dabrafenib in metastatic BRAF-mutant differentiated thyroid cancer, a response rate of 64% (9/14) was reported [7].  NCCN guidelines recommends dabrafenib/trametinib for patients with papillary carcinoma harboring BRAF V600E mutations that have progressed following prior treatment with no satisfactory alternative treatment options [8].

BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib and dabrafenib as well as MEK inhibitors such as trametinib, selumetinib (AZD6244) and binimetinib (MEK162) are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E mutations. The combination of dabrafenib and trametinib is FDA-approved for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with BRAF V600E. In a phase 2 trial of vemurafenib in metastatic or unresectable BRAF-mutant PTC, 10 of 12 (83.3%) of patients demonstrated a partial response [8]. In a phase 1 trial of dabrafenib in metastatic BRAF-mutant differentiated thyroid cancer, a response rate of 64% (9/14) was reported [9]. In melanoma patients, the combination of a BRAF inhibitor with a MEK inhibitor is more efficacious than either therapy alone and reduces the risk of RAS-driver secondary neoplasms such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma [10]. Increased efficacy associated with combined BRAF and MEK inhibition has also been reported in preclinical studies of thyroid carcinoma cells [11]. Consideration of treatment of advanced PTC not amenable to RAI therapy with vemurafenib or dabrafenib is currently a category 2A recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [12].
diseases.prognostic_implications:
BRAF V600E is associated with an inferior prognosis in patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma, particularly when this mutation co-occurs with TERT mutations (not assessed by this panel) [3-5,8].

This mutation is associated with an inferior prognosis and a higher incidence of lymph node metastases [3-5], particularly when this mutation co-occurs with TERT mutations (not assessed by this panel) [6]. In one study, the recurrence rate among patients with both BRAF and TERT mutations was 68.6% compares to 8.7% among patients with neither mutation [6]. TERT status may be assessed by separate single-gene testing. This information may be used for risk stratification based on guidelines from the American Thyroid Association [7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) NSCLC Panel has preference stratified the first-line therapy options for patients with BRAF p.V600E mutation–positive metastatic NSCLC. Dabrafenib plus trametinib is a preferred treatment option. If combination therapy with dabrafenib plus trametinib is not tolerated, single-agent therapy with dabrafenib or vemurafenib are treatment options; therefore, these agents are categorized as “useful in certain circumstances" [PMID: 27283860, 28919011; NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026].
 
The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) NSCLC Panel recommends dabrafenib/trametinib or binimetinib/encorafenib as preferred first-line therapy options for patients with BRAF V600E mutation-positive advanced or metastatic NSCLC. The Panel also recommends dabrafenib/trametinib or binimetinib/encorafenib as subsequent therapy options if the patient with a BRAF V600E mutation did not previously receive a BRAF inhibitor [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026].

The detection of BRAF V600E (or other MAPK pathway alteration) fulfills a diagnostic criterion for ganglioglioma according the the 5th edition WHO. The frequency of BRAF V600E in gangliogliomas ranges from 10%-60%, depending on the site, with highes frequencies in cortical tumors and lowest in spinal cord tumors [PMID: 20156809, 21274720, 23435618, 23442159, 23583981, 23609006, 23633565, 24238153, 24529209, 26810070, 26826417, 27984673, 28986151, 29058119, 29880043, 32289278]. BRAF V600E is also well-described in other types of glioma, including pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, extra-cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, and epithelioid glioblastoma [PMID: 21274720, 25346165, 23552385].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
On March 16, 2023, the FDA approved the combination of dabrafenib (BRAF inhibitor) with trametinib (MEK inhibitor) for pediatric patients 1 year or older with low-grade glioma with BRAF V600E who require systemic therapy. This combination is also approved for unresectable and metastatic tumors with BRAF V600E.

While there are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for BRAF-mutated gliomas, BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib and debrafenib as well as MEK inhibitors such as trametinib, selumetinib (AZD6244) and binimetinib (MEK162) are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E mutations. Several small clinical studies have suggested that BRAF and/or MEK inhibitors may also be effective in the treatment of  low-grade gliomas with BRAF V600E mutations, including ganglioglioma [5-8], pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma [9-12], pilocytic astrocyoma [13,14], and desmoplastic infantile astrocytoma [15]. There are also case reports of high-grade gliomas with BRAF V600E responding to these therapies [16,17]. Preclinical data from gliomas in mice [18] as well as clinical data in melanoma patients [19] suggest that the combination of a BRAF inhibitor with a MEK inhibitor is more efficacious than either therapy alone and reduces the risk of RAS-driver secondary neoplasms such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

Dabrafenib+Trametinib
According to most recent NCCN guidelines, adjuvant dabrafenib/trametinib combination therapy is a recommended option for patients with resected stage III or recurrent disease and who harbor a BRAF V600-activating mutation. Dabrafenib/trametinib is not the preferred first-line regimen for most patients with stage IV disease [NCCN Guidelines Melanoma: Cutaneous Version 2.2026].

variants.variant_description:
RAF is a serine/threonine kinase that plays a key role in the regulation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade [1], which under physiologic conditions regulates the expression of genes involved in cellular functions, including proliferation [4]. Genetic alterations in BRAF are found in a large percentage of melanomas, thyroid cancers and histiocytic neoplasms as well as a small fraction of lung and colorectal cancers. The most common BRAF point mutation is V600E, which deregulates the protein's kinase activity leading to constitutive BRAF activation, as BRAF V600E can signal as a monomer independently of RAS or upstream activation [5]. BRAF mutations are most commonly found in the 600th codon (V600), most frequently V600E (80%) but also including V600K (15%) and V600R/M/D/G (5%) [3].  BRAF V600D is a known oncogenic and likely pathogenic mutation [2]. The product of these alterations is a BRAF kinase that can activate MAPK signaling in an unregulated manner and, in some instances, is directly responsible for cancer growth [1].

RAF is a serine/threonine kinase that plays a key role in the regulation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade (PMID: 15520807), which under physiologic conditions regulates the expression of genes involved in cellular functions, including proliferation (PMID: 24202393). Genetic alterations in BRAF are found in a large percentage of melanomas, thyroid cancers and histiocytic neoplasms as well as a small fraction of lung and colorectal cancers. The most common BRAF point mutation is V600E, which deregulates the protein's kinase activity leading to constitutive BRAF activation, as BRAF V600E can signal as a monomer independently of RAS or upstream activation (PMID: 20179705). Other BRAF mutations have been found that affect the protein's propensity to dimerize (PMID: 12068308). BRAF V600D is a known oncogenic and likely pathogenic mutation [2]. The product of these alterations is a BRAF kinase that can activate MAPK signaling in an unregulated manner and, in some instances, is directly responsible for cancer growth (PMID: 15520807).

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Extensive clinical trial data have shown that compared with BRAF V600E, patients with BRAF V600K-mutated metastatic melanoma may have slightly lower response/benefit when treated with BRAF ± MEK inhibitors. Less frequent mutations affecting codon 600 (including V600R/M/D/G) also may benefit from these therapies [3]. Randomized clinical trials are ongoing to compare front-line systemic targeted therapy (BRAF/MEK) to immune therapy with checkpoint inhibitors. Results will help define the best approach for initial therapy [3]. BRAF inhibitors have been shown to have clinical activity in unresectable metastatic melanomas with BRAF V600 mutations. Co-administration of inhibitors of MEK, a signaling molecule downstream of BRAF, potentiates these effects. Efficacy and safety data from large randomized trials testing BRAF and MEK inhibitors have significantly impacted the recommended treatment options for patients with BRAFmutation positive unresectable advanced melanoma [3]. Based on the results from the COMBI-AD trial, adjuvant dabrafenib/trametinib combination therapy is a recommended option for patients with resected stage III or recurrent disease and who harbor a BRAF V600-activating mutation. The RAF-targeted inhibitors encorafenib, dabrafenib and vemurafenib, alone or in combination with the MEK1/2-targeted inhibitors binimetinib, trametinib and cobimetinib respectively, are FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with BRAF V600E/K mutant melanoma.

The RAF-targeted inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib are NCCN-listed as monotherapy for the treatment of BRAF V600E-mutant Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis and vemurafenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600-mutant Erdheim Chester Disease.

KRAS Q61H:
KRAS is a membrane-bound GTPase normally involved in signal transduction upon activation by a growth factor receptor (e.g. EGFR). The Q61H mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of KRAS as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. Somatic RAS mutations are generally mutually exclusive with other prominent driver mutations (e.g., BRAF V600E as seen in this sample). However, they have been rarely described in association with a concurrent BRAF V600 mutation; more importantly, RAS mutations have infrequently been identified as an acquired resistance mechanism to BRAF inhibitor or other therapies in a variety of tumors.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
KRAS mutations are associated with primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies such as cetuximab and panitumumab [2-4]. Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in KRAS-mutated neoplasms [5]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have been disappointing [6-8]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [9], CDK4/6 [10-12], ERBB3 [13], histone deacetylase [14], STAT3 [15] and PI3K inhibitors [16,17]. However, as noted above, acquired KRAS mutations have been identified as a potential mechanism of resistance to BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy [18-22].
Relevant Clinical Trials: 
No clear eligibility for clinical trials with concomitant BRAF and KRAS mutations.

V600_K601delinsEI are very rare although has been reported in cutaneous melanoma, and there are rare reports of other complex BRAF alterations involving codons V600 and K601 in cutaneous melanomas [2-4]. The BRAF V600E mutation identified in this specimen results in constitutive activation of BRAF and downstream growth signaling [1]. This mutation is well-described in several types of glioma, particularly ganglioglioma, pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, extra-cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, and epithelioid glioblastoma [2-4]. In addition, a dinucleotide deletion/insertion within codon 601 is also present on the same allele (in cis) as the BRAF V600E. This specific mutation is very rare and has not been reported in low-grade gliomas, although occasional other BRAF class 2 mutations have been documented. The effect of this specific mutation on BRAF structure and kinase activity is uncertain. There are, however, a few case reports of this very rare complex BRAF alteration involving codons V600 and K601 in cutaneous melanomas [5,6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
BRAF V600E mutations are associated with sensitivity to BRAF inhibitor therapies such as vemurafenib [5-6]. While melanoma patients invariably develop resistance to BRAF inhibitors - typically within a year - the combination of BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy results in improved survival and/or more prolonged response [7-14] as well as reduced cutaneous adverse events (e.g. squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma and photosensitivity) [7,15]. More recently, the FDA approved atezolizumab in combination with cobimetinib and vemurafenib for patients with BRAF V600 mutation-positive unresectable or metastatic melanoma. Median progression-free survival was 15.1 months for those treated with atezolizumab in combination with cobimetinib and vemurafenib versus 10.6 months for those treated with cobimetinib and vemurafenib only [17].

In general, “class 2” BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g.vemurafenib, dabrafenib) when seen in isolation. One of the abovementioned case reports found that the two patients with melanoma and complex V600/K601 mutations did achieve an increased response when BRAF/MEK targeted therapy was initiated [3].
