In one study, the recurrence rate among patients with both BRAF and TERT mutations was 68.6% compares to 8.7% among patients with neither mutation [8]. TERT status may be assessed by separate single-gene testing. This information may be used for risk stratification based on guidelines from the American Thyroid Association [9].

variants.variant_description:
MAP2K1 P124S:
MAP2K1 encodes the protein MEK1 - a dual specificity kinase involved in growth signaling within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, downstream of BRAF and NRAS/KRAS. While MAP2K1 mutations are not well-described in anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, activating MAP2K1 mutations, including P124S, are well-described in other cancers including melanoma [1-4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
As noted above, combination therapy with the BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib and the MEK inhibitor trametinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with no satisfactory locoregional treatment options. While some MAP2K1 mutations can be seen as a mechanism of acquired resistance to BRAF and/or MEK inhibitor therapy [2], the P124S mutation detected in this sample is most often observed as a pre-treatment MAP2K1 mutation [3,4]. This mutation results in activation of MEK1 and MAPK signaling, but at much lower level than the BRAF V600E or MAP2K1 E203K mutation [1,3] and this mutation frequently co-occurs with other mutations activating MAPK signaling [3,4] (as seen in this specimen). Preclinical studies have suggested that this mutation confers intermediate sensitivity to BRAF inhibitors [3,4], and an observational study of 123 melanoma patients with BRAF V600E and MAP2K1 P124 mutations suggested that this mutation is associated with diminished response to BRAF inhibitors [4]. However, this mutation appears to be be highly sensitive to MEK inhibitors (e.g. trametinib) as well as ERK inhibitors (e.g. VX-11e), based on preclinical studies [4].
Clinical Trials Currently Recruiting Patients:
No known active clinical trials specifically recruiting anaplastic thyroid carcinoma patients with MAP2K1 mutations.

BRAF V600K and MAP2K1 P124S:
BRAF is a serine-threonine kinase and MAP2K1 encodes the protein MEK1 - a dual specificity kinase. Both BRAF V600K [1,2] and MAP2K1 P124S [3-6] are well-described in melanoma and are not commonly see in other neoplasms. The presence of these two mutations strongly favors a diagnosis of melnoma. Both mutations result in consitutive activation of MAPK signaling [1,3,5]. MAP2K1 P124S results in weaker activation of MAPK signaling than the BRAF V600 or MAP2K1 E203K mutations [3,5] and frequently co-occurs with other mutations activating MAPK signaling [5,6] (as seen in this specimen). BRAF V600 mutations in melanoma are associated with younger age and are often seen in melanoma arising from sites with only intermediate sun exposure [2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
BRAF V600 mutations are associated with sensitivity to BRAF inhibitor therapies such as vemurafenib [7,8]. While melanoma patients invariably develop resistance to BRAF inhibitors - typically within a year - the combination of BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy may result in a more prolonged response [9]. While MAP2K1 mutations can be seen as a mechanism of acquired resistance to BRAF and/or MEK inhibitor therapy [4], P124S is most often observed as a pre-treatment MAP2K1 mutation [5,6] (as in this specimen). Preclinical studies have suggested that this mutation confers intermediate sensitivity to BRAF inhibitors [5,6], and an observational study of 123 patients with BRAF V600E and MAP2K1 P124 mutations suggested that this mutation is associated with diminished response to BRAF inhibitors [6]. However, this mutation appears to be be highly sensitive to MEK inhibitors (e.g. trametinib) as well as ERK inhibitors (e.g. VX-11e), based on preclinical studies [6]. 
 
Several BRAF and MEK inhibitors are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF-mutated metastatic melanoma. The combination of debrafenib and trametinib, vemurafenib and cobimetinib or encorafenib and binimetinib are currently a category 1 recommendations for metastatic melanoma within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [10].

EGFR E746_A750del:
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a receptor tyrosine kinase. The in-frame exon 19 deletion identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: This mutation is also associated with clinical response to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,2]. The TKI therapies erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and osimertinib are all FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions. While no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified, the BRAF V600E mutation described above is expected to confer resistance to TKI therapy as this mutation is downstream of EGFR within MAPK signaling.

variants.variant_description:
BRAF V600E and N581S:
Two BRAF mutations - V600E and N581S - were detected at roughly equal variant allele frequencies. While both mutations - particularly V600E - have been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1,2], the presence of two BRAF mutations has not been described in the literature. While BRAF V600E results in constitutive activation of BRAF and downstream mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling [1], N581S (like other "class 3" BRAF mutations) results in reduced kinase activity. However, N581S is associated with RAS-dependent augmentation of MAPK signaling [3-5]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers. In epithelial tumors including NSCLC, the requisite RAS activation associated "class 3" BRAF mutations appears to come from activated receptor tyrosine kinases including EGFR.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The combination of dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with a BRAF V600E mutation and this treatment is currently a category 2A recommendation in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [6-8]. However, the BRAF inhibitors vemurafenib and debrafenib are NOT effective in treating "class 3" BRAF mutations like N581S since they preferentially inhibit activated BRAF monomers (class 1 mutations) [5]. Of note, newer RAF inhibitors such as PLX8394, BGB659 and AZ628 have demonstrated an ability to inhibit RAF dimers [4,9,10]. In addition, since the requisite RAS activation associated "class 3" BRAF mutations in NSCLC appears to come from activated receptor tyrosine kinases including EGFR, targeting of these receptors may be efficacious. NSCLC cell lines and patient-derived xenografts harboring "class 3" BRAF mutations were shown to be sensitive to the anti-EGFR antibody cetuximab [5]. In another preclinical study, "class 3" BRAF mutations conferred sensitivity to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor desatinib [11]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of RAS and BRAF) also inhibit the growth of cell lines and patient-derived xenografts with these mutations [5]. Finally, ERK inhibitors also act downstream of BRAF and in a recent phase 1 clinical trial, a subset of NSCLC with class 2 or 3 BRAF mutations responded to the ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523) [12].

variants.variant_description: Both BRAF V600E [1] and MAP2K1 E203K [2-5] are well-described in melanoma. While BRAF V600E is associated with sensitivity to BRAF inhibitor therapies such as vemurafenib [6,7], MAP2K1 E203K is associated with resistance to vemurafenib [4]. MAP2K1 mutations (including E203K) are frequently seen as a mechanism of acquired resistance to BRAF and/or MEK inhibitor therapy [3,4]. Clinical trials investigating the utility of ERK inhibitors in advanced stage cancer patients include NCT03415126 (phase 1 of ERK inhibitor ASN007; multiple centers including Cancer & Hematology Centers of Western Michigan, Grand Rapids, MI), NCT02711345 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LTT462; New York, NY and Houston, TX) and NCT02857270 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LY3214996 alone or in combination with other agents; multiple centers outside the midwest). variants.variant_description: The BRAF D594E mutation detected in this specimen is very rare. However, other mutations affecting codon D594 including D594N, D594A, and D594G are slightly more common, albeit still infrequent, and have been described in various tumors including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-3]. D594E (like other "class 3" BRAF mutations) results in absent kinase activity (kinase-dead), but is associated with RAS-dependent augmentation of MAPK signaling [4-6]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers. Of note, the mutation in this specimen is present at a very low level (3% variant allele frequency) below what would be anticipated based on the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells (30%). This observation may indicate that the mutation is subclonal.

The BRAF G469E mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon, but has been described as a somatic mutation in multiple cancers including melanoma [1], colorectal cancer [1], head and neck squamous cell carcinoma [2], cholangiocarcinoma [3]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers.

The BRAF N581I mutation identified in this specimen is an uncommon mutation within the tyrosine kinase domain of BRAF that has been described in melanoma [1,2]. While this mutation is thought to abrogate BRAF kinase activity, it has been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation in a RAS-dependent manner [3]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to CRAF heterodimers. While BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, debrafenib) are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E mutation, these inhibitors are not FDA-approved for BRAF non-V600 mutations. In addition, because BRAF inhibitors block activated BRAF monomers but do not affect the formation of heterodimers, they are not expected to be effective for "class 3" BRAF mutations as demonstrated in preclinical experiments [3]. While MEK inhibitors (e.g. trametinib, cobimetinib) are also FDA-approved specifically for melanoma with BRAF V600E/K, preclinical experiments have shown that N581I and other "class 3" BRAF mutations are sensitive to MEK inhibition [3]. The NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060) includes a treatment arm (R) for advanced solid tumors with non-V600 mutations (treatment is trametinib). Other clinical trials currently enrolling patients with non-V600 mutated melanoma include NCT02296112 (phase 2 of trametinib, multiple centers outside Michigan).

The BRAF G469L mutation identified in this specimen has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1]. Other mutations involving codon 469 (including G469A, G469R, G469V and G469S) have also been described in NSCLC [2-9]. Studies investigating the functional effect of several G469 mutations have demonstrated constitutive activation of BRAF as well as downstream MAPK signaling [9-11]. In NSCLC, the absence of an EGFR mutation (and the presence of a BRAF mutation) is associated to resistance to EGFR-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors [12,13]. Several BRAF and MEK inhibitors are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF-mutated melanoma. Several case reports and case series have demonstrated a response of BRAF V600E-mutated NSCLC to BRAF inhibitor therapy [14-17]. A recent clinical trial also provides data suggesting that combined BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy may be even more efficacious [17]. Vemurafenib alone is unlikely to be beneficial in NSCLC with BRAF mutations other than V600 including G469L - as demonstrated in one case report [1]. However, preclinical studies have demonstrated in vitro efficacy of dabrafenib and trametinib (alone and more so in combination) in NSCLC with BRAF G469 mutations [9]. In addition, two case reports have demonstrated a clinical response to sorafenib in NSCLC harboring these mutations [5,7].

The impact of this non-V600 BRAF mutation on response to anti-EGFR therapy is uncertain and, according to NCCN guidelines, "patients with BRAF mutations other than V600E may be considered for anti-EGFR therapy" [NCCN - Colon Cancer, v2.2025].
 
BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib (which are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF-mutated melanoma) have not shown a clinical benefit as monotherapy in CRC [PMID: 26460303], possibly due to activation of EGFR signalling [PMID: 22281684]. The BRAF G469R mutation detected in this specimen is a well-described, oncogenic mutation that occurs in melanoma [1-2] and other cancers [1]. In contrast to BRAF V600E, V600K, and other "class 1" BRAF mutations, which result in constitutively active monomers, G469R and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner [3-6].

The BRAF G469R mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon, but has been described in patients with glioma, esophageal and gastric adenocarcinomas, NSCLC, melanoma, and other cancers [PMID: 31466300, 28481359, 24297085, 23833300, 27105513]. D594G (like other "class 3" BRAF mutations) results in absent kinase activity (kinase-dead), but is associated with RAS-dependent augmentation of MAPK signaling [PMID: 15035987, 26343582, 28783719]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers.

BRAF G469 mutations (including G469R) are well described in NSCLC [1-9]. Studies investigating the functional effect of several G469 mutations have demonstrated intermediate constitutive kinase activation of BRAF as well as downstream MAPK signaling [9-13]. In contrast with BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations which result in constitutively active monomers, G469R and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner (in contrast with "class 3" mutations) [12,13]. While the combination of dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with a BRAF V600E mutation, these drugs are not approved for non-V600 BRAF mutations like G469R. Based on preclinical studies, "class 2" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [12]. However, newer compounds such as BGB659 and PLX8394 have proven effective against these "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [12,14]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have also been shown to effective against "class 2" BRAF mutations in preclinical studies [12]. The NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060) includes an open treatment arm (R) for advanced solid tumors with non-V600 mutations (treatment is trametinib); however, this arm is temporarily suspended and a 70 patient expansion is being considered. Another treatment arm for BRAF non-V600 mutations (Z1L; treatment with ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523)) is anticipated to open in the Summer of 2018. Other relevant clincal trials include NCT02974725 (phase 1 of RAF inhibitor LXH254 and ERK inhibitor LTT462; Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA) and NCT02857280 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LY3214996; multiple centers outside Michigan).

MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have been shown to be effective against "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [3-5,7] as well as limited clinical studies in melanoma patients [6-8]. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommends treatment of metastatic or unresectable melanomas harboring BRAF non-V600 mutations with trametinib (category 2A) [9]. There is also some preclinical [10-11] and clinical [10] evidence in melanoma that "class 2" mutations may be sensitive to dual MAPK inhibition (BRAF and MEK).

Newer RAF inhibitors such as PLX8394, BGB659 and AZ628 have demonstrated an ability to inhibit RAF dimers [PMID: 26343582, 27834212, 29662630]. In epithelial tumors, including NSCLC, the requisite RAS activation associated "class 3" BRAF mutations appears to come from activated receptor tyrosine kinases including EGFR. ERK inhibitors act downstream of BRAF, and in a recent phase 1 clinical trial, a subset of NSCLC with class 2 or 3 BRAF mutations responded to the ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523) [PMID: 29247021]; however, there are no known clinical studies in other tumor types.

The BRAF N581S mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon, but has been described as a somatic mutation in multiple cancers including colorectal cancer [1] and melanoma [2,3]. BRAF mutations in hepatocellular carcinoma are relatively uncommon but do occasionally occur. Some studies have shown an association with more aggressive behavior and resistance to TKI therapy [11]. N581 mutations (like other "class 3" BRAF mutations) results in reduced kinase activity, but is associated with RAS-dependent augmentation of MAPK signaling [4-6]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers.

Equivocal for ERBB2 (HER2) amplification:
A low-level copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene (considered equivocal for true ERBB2 amplification) was detected. ERBB2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. ERBB2 amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression and oncogenic growth has been described in NSCLC [1,2]. While anti-ERBB2 antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. afatinib) have been shown to be effective in other ERBB2-amplified neoplasms such as breast cancer [3], results from small clinical trials in NSCLC with ERBB2 amplification have shown only limited efficacy [4,5]. The potential benefit of these therapies is also uncertain due to the BRAF mutation described above as well as the low-level copy number gain in this specimen. Because this sample was found to have an equivocal copy number gain using this assay, evaluation using an alternative method (e.g. FISH) is recommended before any clinical action is taken based on these results.

BRAF mutations in class 2 and 3 are more likely to harbor concurrent KRAS mutations.

variants.variant_description: TAX1BP1-BRAF gene fusions are rare but have been described in melanoma [1], low-grade glioma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, pilocytic astrocytoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma [2]. Other oncogenic BRAF gene fusions leading to constitutive activation of BRAF and downstream signaling have been described in a variety of neoplasms including pilocytic astrocytomas, melanoma and Sptiz tumors, thyroid cancer, lung cancer, colorectal caner, and pancreatic cancer [1,3-7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Preclinical studies have suggested that cancers with TAX1BP1-BRAF fusions [1] and other BRAF fusions [8-9] may be sensitive to MEK inhibitors e.g. trametinib, selumetinib. Clinical trials [10-12] and case reports [1,13-18] have reported clinical responses to MEK inhibitors in neoplasms with BRAF fusions. 
 
Cancers with BRAF fusions are NOT expected to be sensitive to vemurafenib. In fact, in vitro experiments have shown paradoxical activation of BRAF activity and MAPK signaling in cells with BRAF rearrangements that are treated with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib and the multikinase inhibitor sorafenib [19-21]. As a clinical corollary, treatment of pilocytic astrocytoma patients with sorafenib resulted in acceleration of tumor growth [19].

variants.variant_description: FAM131B (exon2)::BRAF(exon9) results in an in-frame fusion of the first two exons of FAM131B and exons 9 and above of BRAF. BRAF rearrangements result in loss of the N-terminal BRAF inhibitory domain, causing RAS-independent dimerization and leading to constitutive activation. The FAM131B gene fusion has been shown to result in constitutive activation of BRAF and downstream MAPK signaling [1].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: BRAF alterations are commonly found in pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, with activating mutations being most frequent. Although uncommon, BRAF rearrangements, including the FAM131B::BRAF rearrangement, have also been reported in association with this tumor [1]. BRAF rearrangements are rare in high-grade gliomas and most commonly associated with low-grade gliomas such as pilocytic astrocytoma [2,3,4,5]. The presence of this rearrangement may provide evidence in support of the diagnosis of pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma in the right clinical context. These rearrangements have also been associated with a superior prognosis in pilocytic astrocytoma [6,7,8].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: The FAM131B::BRAF rearrangement may also have therapeutic applications. BRAF rearrangements result in loss of the N-terminal BRAF inhibitory domain, causing RAS-independent dimerization and leading to constitutive activation. Because of this, BRAF rearrangements are less sensitive to treatment by RAF inhibitors, similar to other class II BRAF alterations [10].  Some in vitro experiments have shown a paradoxical activation of BRAF activity and MAPK signaling in cells with BRAF rearrangements that are treated with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib and the multikinase inhibitor sorafenib [11,12]. As a clinical corollary, treatment of pilocytic astrocytoma patients with sorafenib resulted in acceleration of tumor growth [12]. Preclinical data has suggested that MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib may be more efficacious [12].

Alterations of the MAPK pathway appear to be a universal feature of pilocytic astrocytomas [1,2]. BRAF rearrangement (particularly KIAA1549-BRAF rearrangements) are the most common of these alterations, occurring in approximately two thirds of pilocytic astrocytomas [PMID: 19373855,: 23817572]. These rearrangements have also been associated with a superior prognosis [PMID: 20044755, 21610142] and are rare in other types of low-grade gliomas or high-grade gliomas.

Alterations of the MAPK pathway appear to be a universal feature of pilocytic astrocytomas [PMIDs: 19373855, 23817572]. BRAF rearrangement (particularly KIAA1549-BRAF rearrangements) are the most common of these alterations, occurring in approximately two thirds of pilocytic astrocytomas [PMIDs: 19373855, 23817572]. These rearrangements are rare in high-grade gliomas and are uncommon among other types of low-grade glioma including grade II diffuse gliomas, gangliogliomas and pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma [PMIDs: 19373855, 19543740, 25382612]. Therefore, the presence of this rearrangement may provide evidence in support of the diagnosis of pilocytic astrocytoma in the right clinical context. These rearrangements have also been associated with a superior prognosis [PMIDs: 20044755, 21610142].

Most WHO grade 1 pilocytic astrocytomas in pediatric patients contain BRAF fusions or, less commonly, BRAF V600E mutations, especially those arising in the posterior fossa; such tumors are rarely high grade [NCCN Guidelines Central Nervous System Cancers Version 5.2024]. diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The MEK inhibitor selumetinib is NCCN-compendium listed as a treatment option for patients with BRAF fusion-positive pilocytic astrocytoma [PMIDs: 23533272, 24803676, 28002790, 28339824, 31151904, NCCN Guidelines Central Nervous System Tumors Version 1.2026].

NCCN Guidelines [v. 1.2025] recommend the type II BRAF inhibitor tovorafenib (category 2A) or a MEK inhibitor - selumetinib or trametinib (category 2A) for the treatment of gliomas with BRAF fusions with recurrent or progressive disease. Clinical responses to tovorafenib have by reported in the phase 2 trial "FIREFLY-1" [PMID: 37978284]. Phase 1 [PMID: 28339824] and phase 2 [PMID: 31151904] clinical trials have shown a clinical response to selumetinib in pediatric pilocytic astrocytomas with KIAA1549-BRAF fusions. 
 
In vitro experiments have shown a paradoxical activation of BRAF activity and MAPK signaling in cells with BRAF rearrangements that are treated with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib and the multikinase inhibitor sorafenib [PMID: 23533272, 24803676]. As a clinical corollary, treatment of pilocytic astrocytoma patients with sorafenib resulted in acceleration of tumor growth [PMID: 24803676].
diseases.prognostic_implications: BRAF fusions are associated with better prognosis in pediatric low-grade astrocytoma [PMIDs: 20044755, 21610142, NCCN Guidelines Central Nervous System Cancers Version 1.2026].

variants.variant_description: The TRIM24-BRAF fusion protein results from an inversion of chromosome 7 that contains the BRAF kinase domain [1,4]. TRIM24-BRAF fusions has been found in melanoma and in one paper up to 8% of melanomas without other molecular alterations harbored BRAF fusions [2]. In another large scale study 14 melanomas harbored BRAF fusions, 9 of which featured an epithelioid and spindle cell histology characteristic of  Spitzoid melanoma. Of the total 531 melanomas evaluated, the enrichment of BRAF fusions in Spitzoid melanomas compared to non‐Sptizoid tumors was highly significant (p = 0.0001) [3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There is promising clinical data in patients with BRAF fusion-positive melanoma treated with the FDA-approved MEK1/2-targeted inhibitor trametinib. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines BRAF fusions have shown responses to MEK inhibitors and non-specific RAF inhibitors (eg, sorafenib). Trametinib is recommended as second line or subsequent therapy for patients with melanomas harboring BRAF fusions [5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The BRAF inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib are NOT effective in treating "class 3" BRAF mutations since they preferentially inhibit activated BRAF monomers (class 1 mutations) [6]. Newer RAF inhibitors such as PLX8394, BGB659 and AZ628 have demonstrated an ability to inhibit RAF dimers [5,7,8]. In epithelial tumors including NSCLC, the requisite RAS activation associated "class 3" BRAF mutations appears to come from activated receptor tyrosine kinases including EGFR. NSCLC cell lines and patient derived xenografts harboring "class 3" BRAF mutations were shown to be sensitive to the anti-EGFR antibody cetuximab [6]. In another preclinical study, "class 3" BRAF mutations conferred sensitivity to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib [9]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of RAS and BRAF) also inhibit the growth of cell lines and patient-derived xenografts with these mutations [6]. Finally, ERK inhibitors also act downstream of BRAF and in a recent phase 1 clinical trial, a subset of NSCLC with class 2 or 3 BRAF mutations responded to the ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523) [10].  In addition, it is uncertain how this mutation and the KRAS alteration below may interact and affect therapy; however, targetting downstream effectors like ERK is likely to be most efficacious.

The absence of an activating EGFR mutation and the presence of a KRAS mutation is associated with primary resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) [9-10]. Some studies have demonstrated a modest response of KRAS-mutant NSCLC to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib [11]. In a phase 2 trial, KRAS-mutant NSCLC treated with trametinib (GSK1120212) showed a similar progression free survival and response rate as docetaxel [11]. While some clinical trials have suggested that the combination of a MEK inhibitor and docetaxel may be more efficacious than docetaxel alone [12-13], a large clinical trial failed to show any improvement in progression free survival for the combination of selumetinib (AZD6244) and docetaxel compared to docetaxel alone [14]. In preclinical studies, treatment of lung cancer cells with a MEK inhibitor induces a compensatory response involving FGFR1 leading to adaptive resistance while the combination of MEK and FGFR1 inhibition resulted in greater sensitivity than MEK inhibition alone [15]. The combination of a MEK inhibitor with other agents such as PI3K inhibitors [16], histone deacetylase inhibitors [17], or CDK4/6 inhibitors [18-19] has also demonstrated improved antitumor activity in preclinical studies.  The effects of the above BRAF mutation with this KRAS alteration are uncertain with regards to therapy, although targetting downstream effectors are predicted to be most promising.

BRAF D594A has been described in patients with small bowel adenocarcinoma [1], as well as a number of other cancers including melanoma, lung and colorectal adenocarcinoma [2]. D594A is classified as a class III hypoactivating mutation which lies within the kinase domain of the protein. This missense mutation results in a kinase-dead (or with “lower than wildtype kinase activity”) protein [3, 4]. Biological characterization of the BRAF D594A mutation has demonstrated that it is RAS dependent in its activation of the MAPK pathway, signals as a dimer with CRAF, and typically co-occurs with another driver mechanism that amplifies RAS signaling [6,7]. In patients with melanoma BRAF D594A typically co-occurs with an activating RAS mutation or NF1 inactivation, whereas when observed in non-small cell lung or colorectal cancers, it is associated with receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) hyperactivation at the protein level [4,6]. In this specimen there is a concurrent activating KRAS mutation. Please see separate interpretation.

While the BRAF D594A mutation identified in this specimen has not been described in colorectal cancer (CRC), this mutation has been described in melanoma [PMID: 25537974, 23273605, PMID: 25148578] and other mutations affecting the same codon - particularly D594G - are well described in CRC [PMID: 27404270, 26386083]. While this mutation is thought to abrogate BRAF kinase activity, it has been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation in a RAS-dependent manner [PMID: 20141835]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to CRAF heterodimers. In contrast with BRAF V600E, limited data suggest that BRAF D594G is not associated with microsatellite instability (MSI) or a poor prognosis [PMID: 27404270].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The current National Comprehenisve Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines state that human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) alterations, MSI-H/dMMR, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, and tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H) are enhanced in patients with small bowel adenocarcinoma (SBA) compared to colorectal carcinoma (CRC) and may reveal greater importance of targeted or immunotherapeutic treatments compared to current CRC treatment algorithms [5]. However, specific targeted therapy recommendations are not provided at this time.

The impact of this BRAF mutation on response to anti-EGFR therapy is uncertain; however, in vitro experiments have shown that D594A and other "class 3" BRAF mutations are sensitive to inhibition of receptor tyrosine kinase activity by cetuximab (with or without MEK inhibition) [PMID: 28783719] and dasatinib [PMID: 22649091]. In a multicenter pooled study, 50% of colon cancer patients harboring class 3 BRAF mutations responded to anti-EGFR therapy (n=28) [PMID: 31515458].
 
BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib (which are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF-mutated melanoma) have not shown a clinical benefit as monotherapy in CRC [PMID: 26460303], possibly due to activation of EGFR signalling [PMID: 22281684]. In addition, because BRAF inhibitors block activated BRAF monomers but do not affect the formation of heterodimers, they are not expected to be effective for "class 3" BRAF mutations [PMID: 28783719]. Emerging data suggests that there may be utility when BRAF inhibition is combined with EGFR, MEK and/or PI3K inhibition, though clinical data on kinase-dead mutations like D594A is lacking [PMID: 27729313, 28363909].

BRAF G466E
The class III hypoactivating [4,5] exon 11 BRAF G466E missense mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein and renders BRAF kinase-dead (or with “lower than wildtype kinase activity”) [1,2,3]. This mutation has been reported in melanomas, lung and colorectal cancers, and in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia. Biological characterization of the BRAF G466E mutation has demonstrated that it is RAS dependent in its activation of the MAPK pathway, signals as a dimer with CRAF, and typically co-occurs with another driver mechanism that amplifies RAS signaling. Thus, when BRAF G466E is observed in melanoma, it typically co-occurs with an activating RAS mutation (as in this case) or NF1 inactivation, whereas when observed in non-small cell lung or colorectal cancers, it is associated with receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) hyperactivation at the protein level.

The BRAF G466E mutation detected in this specimen is rare, but has been been described in various tumors including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-3]. G466E (like other "class 3" BRAF mutations) results in absent kinase activity (kinase-dead), but is associated with RAS-dependent augmentation of MAPK signaling [4-6]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While BRAF G466E is sensitive to MEK inhibition by targeted inhibitors such as trametinib, it is insensitive to RAF monomer inhibitors such as vemurafenib. Based on preclinical studies, "class 3" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [4]. Clinical studies have also shown that melanoma patients with nonV600 BRAF mutations do NOT respond to BRAF inhibitor monotherapy [8]. However, newer compounds such as BGB659 and PLX8394 have proven effective against these "class 3" mutations in preclinical studies [4,9]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have also been shown to be effective against "class 3" BRAF mutations in preclinical studies [4]. Limited clinical studies have also shown a modest benefit among melanomas with nonV600 BRAF mutations (including "class 3" mutations) to MEK inhibitor monotherapy (overall response rate 40%; progression-free survival 3.7 months; n=5) and to combined BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy (overall response rate 28%; PFS 3.3 months; n=18; likely due to activity of the MEK inhibitor) [8].

The BRAF inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib are NOT effective in treating "class 3" BRAF mutations since they preferentially inhibit activated BRAF monomers (class 1 mutations) [6]. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines BRAF mutations other than those involving codon 600, are observed in patients with NSCLC. However, the impact of those mutations on therapy selection is not well understood at this time [7].

MAP2K1 D67N:
MAP2K1 encodes the protein MEK1 - a dual specificity kinase involved in growth signaling within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, downstream of EGFR, NRAS/KRAS and BRAF. The D67N mutation detected in this specimen has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-3] and has been shown to be oncogenic resulting in constitutive activation of MEK1 and downstream signaling in cell culture [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
While neither the CAP/AMP/ASCO guidelines nor the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend MAP2K1 mutational status be used as a predictive molecular biomarker for response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy (cetuximab, panitumumab) [4,5], colorectal cancers with activating MAP2K1 mutations are not expected to respond to these therapies since MEK1 is downstream of EGFR within MAPK signaling. Multiple studies have identified MAP2K1 mutations as a potential mechanism of primary resistance to anti-EGFR therapies [6,7]. Some MAP2K1 mutations, such as MAP2K1 F53C/L, can also been seen as a mechanisms of acquired resistance to BRAF inhibitor therapy [8,9], although the significance of MAP2K1 D67N specifically in regards to BRAF inhibitor therapy remains to be fully elucidated.
 
Several MEK inhibitors including trametinib (GSK1120212), selumetinib (AZD6244) and cobimetinib (XL518) are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600 mutated melanoma. This mutation, however, has been shown to be resistant to at least some MEK inhibitors such as selumetinib (AZD6244) [10]. Given the relative rarity of the MAP2K1 D67N mutation, little is known about the potential utility of MEK inhibitors as well as inhibitors acting downstream within the MAPK signaling pathway (e.g. ERK inhibitors).

variants.variant_description: The BRAF V600E mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) and is known to result in constitutive activation of BRAF as well as downstream MAPK signaling [1-3]. This mutation is associated with decreased overall survival in CRC [2-4]. In addition, when present along with microsatellite instability (MSI), as is seen in this patient, BRAF V600E is strongly associated with sporadic MSI i.e. NOT associated with a germline mutation within a mismatch repair gene (Lynch syndrome) [5,6]. The BRAF R603X mutation is present on the opposite allele and causes premature truncation of the protein, presumably leading to loss-of-function. This is a rare variant but has been described in multiple tumor types including endometrium and stomach [7-8].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Anti-EGFR Antibody Therapy: While the current CAP/AMP/ASCO guidelines do not recommend BRAF mutational status be used as a predictive molecular biomarker for this purpose [9], the current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines state that BRAF V600E mutation makes response to panitumumab or cetuximab highly unlikely unless given with a BRAF inhibitor [10]. CAP/AMP/ASCO guidelines do recommend BRAF testing for prognostic stratification (as well as for CRC with MLH1 loss) [9].
 
On April 8, 2020, encorafenib with cetuximab was FDA-approved for metastatic CRC with BRAF V600E with disease progression on one or two prior regimens. Median overall survival was 8.4 months in the encorafenib plus cetuximab arm compared to 5.4 months in the control arm (either irinotecan or FOLFIRI with cetuximab). 
 
Other Therapies: While studies have not shown a clinical benefit of BRAF inhibitors as monotherapy in CRC [9] due to activation of EGFR signaling [12], several studies suggest that there is utility when BRAF inhibition is combined with EGFR, MEK and/or PI3K inhibition [13-17]. The NCCN guidelines recommend encorafenib + (cetuximab or panitumumab) as a non-first line treatment option for CRC with BRAF V600E.

BRAF p.[G466A;V471L]:
Two BRAF single nucleotide substitutions affecting the same allele were detected - G466A and V471L. The BRAF G466A mutation identified in this specimen is an uncommon mutation within the tyrosine kinase domain of BRAF that has been described in melanoma [1,2]. In contrast with BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations which result in constitutively active monomers, G466A and other "class 3" mutations have been shown to abrogate BRAF kinase activity and to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation in a RAS-dependent manner [3-5]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to CRAF heterodimers. There are no known reports of BRAF V471L, and the effect of this variant on protein function and oncogenesis is uncertain.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While both BRAF inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) and MEK inhibitors (e.g. trametinib) are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation, these drugs are not approved for non-V600 BRAF mutations like G466A. Based on preclinical studies, "class 3" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [4]. Clinical studies have also shown that melanoma patients with nonV600 BRAF mutations do NOT respond to BRAF inhibitor monotherapy [7]. However, newer compounds such as BGB659 and PLX8394 have proven effective against these "class 3" mutations in preclinical studies [4,6]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have also been shown to be effective against "class 3" BRAF mutations in preclinical studies [4]. Limited clinical studies have also shown a modest benefit among melanomas with nonV600 BRAF mutations (including "class 3" mutations) to MEK inhibitor monotherapy (overall response rate 40%; progression-free survival 3.7 months; n=5) and to combined BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy (overall response rate 28%; PFS 3.3 months; n=18; likely due to activity of the MEK inhibitor) [7].

variants.variant_description: The BRAF L597S mutation detected in this specimen (as well as other mutations of this codon including L597R and L597Q) are uncommon, but have been described in melanoma [1-4] and other cancers [5-8]. This mutation has been shown to result in constitutive activation of BRAF and downstream MAPK signaling [1] and to induce cell proliferation in in vitro studies [9]. However, in contrast with BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations which result in constitutively active monomers, L597S and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner (in contrast with "class 3" mutations) [10,11].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While several BRAF and MEK inhibitors are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutations, these drugs are not approved for non-V600 BRAF mutations like L597S. Based on preclinical studies, "class 2" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [10,11]. However, newer compounds such as BGB659 and PLX8394 have proven effective against these "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [10,12,13]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have shown efficacy against "class 2" BRAF mutations in preclinical studies [10,11] including cells with BRAF L597R/S/Q mutations [1]. In one case report, a patient with metastatic melanoma harboring a BRAF L597S mutation responded significantly to treatment with the MEK inhibitor TAK-733 [1]. ERK inhibitors which act further downstream within MAPK signaling are also being investigated in clinical trials (see below).

The BRAF G464V mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon, but has been described in NSCLC [PMID: 23833300, 27545006, 12068308, 24297085] and other cancers [PMID: 27545006, 12068308]. Low-level BRAF copy number gain (equivocal for amplification):
A low-level copy number gain of the BRAF gene (approximately 4-6 copies; considered equivocal for amplification) was detected. BRAF copy number gains have been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1], and frequently co-occurs with BRAF mutations (as observed in this specimen). However, in this specimen, the copy number gain appears to affect the wild-type (non-mutated) BRAF allele. It is not known if the low-level copy number gain observed in this specimen is sufficient to significantly affect BRAF expression and signaling. It is also unknown if this copy number gain affects sensitivity to targeted therapies.

variants.variant_description: The BRAF codon D594 mutations identified in this specimen have been described in small bowel adenocarcinoma [1], as well as a number of other cancers (in particular, melanoma) [2]. While codon D594 mutations are thought to abrogate BRAF kinase activity, they have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation in a RAS-dependent manner [3]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to CRAF heterodimers. In contrast to BRAF V600E, limited data suggest that BRAF D594G is not associated with microsatellite instability (MSI) or a poor prognosis in colorectal carcinoma (CRC) [4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The current National Comprehenisve Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines recommend treating small bowel adenocarcinoma with systemic therapy according the NCCN Guidelines for CRC [5]. As such, the impact of this BRAF mutation on response to anti-EGFR therapy is uncertain; however, in vitro experiments have shown that D594A and other "class 3" BRAF mutations are sensitive to inhibition of receptor tyrosine kinase activity by cetuximab (with or without MEK inhibition) [6] and desatinib [7]. BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib (which are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF-mutated melanoma) have not shown a clinical benefit as monotherapy in CRC [8], possibly due to activation of EGFR signaling [9]. In addition, because BRAF inhibitors block activated BRAF monomers but do not affect the formation of heterodimers, they are not expected to be effective for "class 3" BRAF mutations [6]. Emerging data suggests that there may be utility when BRAF inhibition is combined with EGFR, MEK and/or PI3K inhibition, though clinical data on kinase-dead mutations like D594A is lacking [10,11]. Furthermore, the clinical significance of these mutations in the context of a strongly activating KRAS exon 2 mutation, which predicts primary resistance to anti-EGFR therapies, is uncertain (see above for details).

variants.variant_description: The E586K mutation detected in this specimen is very rare but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1]. Similar to V600E (and other "class 1" BRAF mutations), the E586K mutation results in increased BRAF kinase activation and dimerization with correpsonding increased downstream MAPK pathway activity [2, 3]; thus, it is presumed to be an activating oncogenic mutation [4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no studies that have specifically examined the response of the E586K mutation to targeted therapy. Although this mutation is likely functionally similar to V600E (and other "class 1" BRAF mutations), it is unclear whether it would necessarily respond to combination targeted therapy with dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) -- the FDA-approved treatment for patients with metastatic BRAF V600E-positive NSCLC. Furthermore, the variant fraction of the E586K mutation in the current specimen is relatively low (approximately 10%), suggesting that this alteration may be subclonal.

The variant lies within the kinase domain of BRAF and has been shown to result in increased kinase activity and activation of downstream MAPK signaling [1-3]. While this assay cannot reliably distinguish between germline and somatic variants, the allele frequency of this variant in comparison with the estimated tumor percentage is more consistent with a somatic mutation. In preclinical studies, the BRAF S467A was found to be sensitive to MEK inhibitors including CI-1040 and PD0325901. The agents being investigated within the clinical trials described above act downstream of BRAF and therefore may be effective in inhibiting MAPK activation associated with both the KRAS and BRAF mutations.

KRAS L19F: 
KRAS is a membrane-bound GTPase normally involved in signal transduction upon activation by a growth factor receptor (e.g. EGFR). The L19F mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC). This mutation results in more weak activation KRAS and downstream growth signaling than more common KRAS mutation affecting codons 12, 13 and 61 [1,2]. However, the BRAF mutation described below is expected to augment the MAPK activation associated with this mutation (see discussion below). While KRAS codon 12, 13 and 61 mutations are associated with primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies such as cetuximab and penitumumab [3-5], the impact of less common mutations like L19F is not well-established. The utility of other agents for KRAS-mutated CRC, such as MEK inhibitors, is currently under clinical investigation. Clinical trials currently enrolling patients with KRAS-mutated CRC include NCT03415126 (phase 1 trial of ERK1/2 inhibitor ASN007; Cancer and Hematology Centers of Western Michigan, Grand Rapids, MI), NCT02079740 (phase 1/2 trial of the MEK inhibitor trametinib combined with navitoclax; Dana Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA), NCT03101839 (phase 1 trial of KRAS inhibitor AZD4785, multiple centers outside Michigan), NCT02613650 (phase 1 trial of mFOLFIRI with MEK inhibitor MEK162; Huntsman Cancer Institute, Salt Lake City, UT), NCT02703571 (phase 1/2 of ribociclib and trametinib; multiple centers outside Michigan), NCT02906059 (phase 1 of Wee1 inhibitor AZD1775 with ironotecan; Laura and Isaac Perlmutter Cancer Center, New York, NY). The BRAF G466V mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon, but has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [6-8] and other cancers. G466 mutations (like other "class 3" BRAF mutations) result in diminished kinase activity, but are associated with RAS-dependent augmentation of MAPK signaling [9-11]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers. Therefore, this mutation is expected to augment the MAPK activation initiated by the weakly activating KRAS mutation described above. Of note, the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib is NOT effective in treating "class 3" BRAF mutations since it preferentially inhibits activated BRAF monomers (class 1 mutations) [11]. MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of RAS and BRAF) have been shown to inhibit the growth of cell lines and patient-derived xenografts with class 3 BRAF mutations [11]. ERK inhibitors also act downstream of BRAF and in a recent phase 1 clinical trial, a subset of NSCLC with class 2 or 3 BRAF mutations responded to the ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523) [12]. Finally, newer RAF inhibitors such as PLX8394 and BGB659 have demonstrated an ability to inhibit RAF dimers [10,13]. The NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060) includes a treatment arm in development (Z1L) investigating the utility of the ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523) for advanced solid tumors with non-V600 mutations. This arm is anticipated to open late in 2018. Other relevant clincal trials include NCT02428712 (phase 1/2 of RAF inhibitor PLX8394; multiple centers including Karmanos Cancer Institute, Detroit, MI), NCT02974725 (phase 1 of RAF inhibitor LXH254 and ERK inhibitor LTT462; Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA), NCT02857280 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LY3214996; multiple centers outside Michigan), NCT01306045 (phase 2 trial of MEK inhibitor selumetinib (AZD6244); National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD), and NCT03051035 (phase 1 of ERK inhibitor KO-947; Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN and Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia, PA).

While the specific BRAF mutation identified in the specimen has not been described in intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN), other BRAF mutations have been described in IPMN [1-3] and A598_T599insV has been described in melanoma [4] and papillary thyroid carcinoma [5]. No known funtional studies have characterized this mutation. BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib and debrafenib as well as MEK inhibitors such as trametinib are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E mutations. The responsiveness of BRAF A598_T599insV mutations to these agents is unknown. There is a single report of a patient with melanoma harboring a BRAF A598_T599insV mutation that responded to the combination of a BRAF inhibitor (dabrafenib) and a MEK inhibitor (trametinib) [4]. The BRAF A598_T599insV mutation is NOT one of the inclusion variants for either the BRAF V600 arm (ARM-H) or the BRAF non-V600 arm (ARM-R). The TAPUR trial (NCT02693535) includes a treatment arm (group 13; regorafenib) for BRAF-mutated advanced cancer. Other relevant clincal trials include NCT02428712 (phase 1/2 of BRAF inhibitor PLX8394 in advanced unresectable BRAF-mutated tumors; multiple centers including Karmanos Cancer Institute; Detroit, MI), NCT03415126 (phase 1 of ERK-inhibitor ASN007 in advanced solid tumors; Cancer and Hematology Centers of Western Michigan; Grand Rapids, MI), NCT02857270 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LY3214996 in advanced/metastatic cancer; multiple centers outside Michigan) and NCT01531361 (phase 1 of vemurafenib with sorafenib or crizotinib in advanced cancers; MD Anderson Cancer Institute; Houston, TX).

The BRAF G464V mutation detected in this specimen is rare, but has been described in NSCLC [1,2] and other cancers [3]. Other mutations affecting codon G464 including G464E have also been described [3,4]. Studies investigating the functional effect of several G469 mutations have demonstrated intermediate constitutive kinase activation of BRAF as well as downstream MAPK signaling [3,5-5]. In contrast with BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations which result in constitutively active monomers, G464V and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner (in contrast with "class 3" mutations) [12,13]. While the combination of dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with a BRAF V600E mutation, these drugs are not approved for non-V600 BRAF mutations like G464V. Based on preclinical studies, "class 2" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [6,7]. However, newer compounds such as BGB659 and PLX8394 have proven effective against these "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [6,8]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have been shown to be effective against "class 2" BRAF mutations in preclinical studies [6,7]. The impact of the concomitant KRAS mutation described below on response to these therapies is uncertain. The NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060) includes an open treatment arm (R) for advanced solid tumors with non-V600 mutations (treatment is trametinib); however, this arm is temporarily suspended and a 70 patient expansion is being considered. Another treatment arm for BRAF non-V600 mutations (Z1L; treatment with ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523)) is anticipated to open in the Summer of 2018. Other relevant clincal trials include NCT02974725 (phase 1 of RAF inhibitor LXH254 and ERK inhibitor LTT462; Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA) and NCT02857280 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LY3214996; multiple centers outside Michigan).

The BRAF G469L mutation identified in this specimen has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1]. Other mutations involving codon 469 (including G469A, G469R, G469V and G469S) have also been described in NSCLC [2-9]. Studies investigating the functional effect of several G469 mutations have demonstrated constitutive activation of BRAF as well as downstream MAPK signaling [9-11]. In NSCLC, the absence of an EGFR mutation (and the presence of a BRAF mutation) is associated to resistance to EGFR-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors [12,13]. Several BRAF and MEK inhibitors are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF-mutated melanoma. Several case reports and case series have demonstrated a response of BRAF V600E-mutated NSCLC to BRAF inhibitor therapy [14-17]. A recent clinical trial also provides data suggesting that combined BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy may be even more efficacious [17]. Vemurafenib alone is unlikely to be beneficial in NSCLC with BRAF mutations other than V600 including G469L - as demonstrated in one case report [1]. However, preclinical studies have demonstrated in vitro efficacy of dabrafenib and trametinib (alone and more so in combination) in NSCLC with BRAF G469 mutations [9]. In addition, two case reports have demonstrated a clinical response to sorafenib in NSCLC harboring these mutations [5,7].

name: MAP2K2
gene_function: MAP2K2 encodes the protein MEK2 - a dual specificity kinase involved in growth signaling within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, downstream of BRAF and NRAS/KRAS [PMID: 32641410].

variants.variant_description: Although the Q60R has not been functionally characterized, MAP2K2 Q60P is known to be oncogenic, and therefore MAP2K2 Q60R is considered likely oncogenic [PMID:PMID: 32641410]. Activating MAP2K1 mutations are well-described in various neoplasms [PMID: 22197931, 35123694, 22817889, 24982505, 25202140].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved therapies for MAP2K1-mutated solid tumors. Limited clinical data suggest that MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and cobimetinib may be effective against various cancers harboring oncogenic MAP2K1 mutations [PMID: 36455195].

variants.variant_description: MAP2K2 mutations are identified in approximately 5% of patients with melanoma [PMID: 24463458]. MAP2K2 F57CT has been shown to cause activation of MEK2 and downstream signaling [PMID: 16439621].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no FDA-approved or NCCN-compendium listed treatments specifically for patients with MAP2K2 F57C mutant solid tumors. The MEK inhibitors cobimetinib and trametinib are NCCN compendium-listed for the treatment of histiocytic neoplasms with MAPK pathway mutations, including MAP2K2 mutations [NCCN Histiocytic Neoplasms, Version 3.2024].

variants.variant_description: MAP2K2 mutations are identified in approximately 5% of patients with melanoma [2]. MAP2K2 K61T has been shown to cause activation of MEK2 and downstream signaling [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no FDA-approved or NCCN-compendium listed treatments specifically for patients with MAP2K2 K61T mutant melanoma.

variants.variant_description: The F57L mutation detected in this specimen is rare, but has been described in plasma cell myeloma and breast cancer [1-3]. While the MAP2K2 F57L mutation has not been biochemically characterized, mutations affecting the same codon including F57C has been shown to cause activation of MEK2 and downstream signaling [4]. Additionally, mutations affecting this codon, including F57L, have also been described as germline variants associated with cardio-facio-cutaneous (CFC) syndrome [4-6]. Genetic counseling with possible germline testing is recommended if there is any clinical concern for a germline MAP2K2 mutation.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Because MEK2 is downstream of BRAF within the MAPK pathway, this mutation is expected to confer some degree of resistance to BRAF inhibitors. The susceptibility of this specific mutation to MEK inhibitors (e.g trametinib, selumetinib, binimetinib, cobimetinib) is not known.

variants.variant_description:
Two EGFR mutations were detected - G719A and T790M. Because these two mutations affect different exons, it is not known if these two mutations affect the same allele (in cis) or different alleles (in trans). These two mutations are present at similar variant allele frequencies (28% and 27%). EGFR G719 amino acid substitution mutations, including G719A, are well-described mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream MAPK and PIK3CA signalling [PMID: 26206867, 23242437, 28531810, 27785061, 18372921, 18036700, 17285735, 22776705, 16205628, 15118073]. G719X mutations may occur in isolation or with other EGFR mutations [PMID: 26206867, 23242437, 28531810, 27785061, 18372921, 18036700, 17285735]. T790M is most commonly observed as a mechanism of acquired resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) [PMID: 17085664, 15728811, 15737014]. This mutation results in increased EGFR affinity for adenosine triphosphate and reduced binding to EGFR TKI [PMID: 18227510].
 
There is no known history of treatment with TKI therapy. The incidence of EGFR T790M prior to TKI therapy (TKI-naïve) is dependent on the detection methods employed, but when observed, has often been described at low variant allele frequencies [PMID: 33116639, 35884570, 26973206, 30936123, 25882755], unlike this specimen. 
 
Germline EGFR T790M mutations have also been described in association with a germline predisposition to NSCLC [PMID: 16258541, 17510392, 22588155, 24736066, 34869019]. The variant allele frequency of the T790M mutation is similar to that of the G719A mutation and is below 50% (28%); however, this allele frequency may be altered by somatic copy number alterations. Evaluation of non-neoplastic tissue (e.g., peripheral blood) is required to differentiate germline from somatic mutations. NCCN guidelines recommend evaluation for a germline mutation if T790M is identified in absence of prior TKI therapy [v. 5.2025].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While several studies have suggested that G719 mutations are more sensitive to second-generation EGFR inhibitors (e.g. afatinib) than first-generation EGFR inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib) [PMID: 26206867, 22776705, 16205628, 26206867, 27240419, 21531810, 26051236] and afatinib is also the only inhibitor that is FDA-approved for the treatment of lung cancers harboring these mutations, EGFR T790M confers resistance to most EGFR inhibitors and is commonly seen as mechanism of acquired resistance to TKI therapy [PMID: 17085664, 15728811, 15737014, 17020982]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [PMID: 27959700, 24893891] and is currently FDA-approved for this application. Osimertinib has also demonstrated efficacy for G719X mutations [PMID: ] and is (along with afatinib) one of the two preferred therapies for EGFR G719X. With these two mutation, osimertinib would be preferred. No molecular alterations associated with acquired resistance to osimertinib [PMID: 29883838, 29406987] were identified in this specimen.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in gliomas affect the extracellular domain - as seen in this specimen. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [11]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [12-16]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [11-13]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [11].
EGFR T790M confers resistance to most EGFR inhibitors and is commonly seen as mechanism of acquired resistance to TKI therapy. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation and is currently FDA-approved for this application [17].

While the second generation EGFR TKI afatinib is efficacious in NSCLC with G719 mutations [11-13] and is FDA approved in this context, T790M confers resistance to first and second generation EGFR TKI [10]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [14-15] and is currently FDA-approved for this application [16]. Treatment of EGFR T790M+ NSCLC with osimertinib is also a category 1 recommendation in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [17].  No molecular alterations associated with acquired resistance to osimertinib [18-19] were identified in this specimen.

EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations, as identified in this specimen, are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. Exon 20 insertions are the third most common EGFR mutations; they occur in approximately 2% of patients with NSCLC and 4% to 12% of patients with EGFR mutations [17].

EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations, as identified in this specimen, are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. A copy number gain of the EGFR gene was also detected, consistent with EGFR amplification. EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-4]. EGFR amplification that is present prior to TKI therapy more commonly affects the mutant EGFR allele [2-4] as appears to be the case in this sample.

EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations, as identified in this specimen, result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073, 30854234]. Diagnositc:
In-frame insertions within exon 20 have recently been described in a subset of diffuse midline gliomas with H3K27me3 loss [PMID: 32303840, 33130881]. EGFR mutations are a diagnostic criterion for diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered according to the 5th edition WHO.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Recommended treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertions is described in NCCN guidelines [NCCN - Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, version 5.2026]. Carboplatin/pemetrexed + amivantamab-vmjw (Rybrevant) is considered the preferred first-line systemic therapy with amivantamab-vmjw, sunvozertinib and datopotamab deruxtecan-dlnk indicated as potential subsequent therapies following progression. Amivantamab-vmjw in combination with carboplatin and pemetrexed was FDA approved in March of 2024 for locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertions. 
 
Most EGFRex30 alterations are associated with lack of resonce to first, second and thir generation EGFR TKI therapy with select exceptions: A763_Y764inFQEA which is associated with sensitivity to TKI therapy and A763_Y764insLQEA which may be associated with sensitivity to first and third generation TKI therapy  [NCCN - Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, version 5.2026] [PMID: 18676761, 27468240, 29702285, 26354527, 26051236, 26051236, 29740957, 21220471].

EGFR exon 20 insertions (other than A763_Y764insFQEA) are associated with primary RESISTANCE to achievable doses of the first-generation, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies that are currently FDA-approved for some EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [2,3]. Several studies have shown a more robust in vitro response of exon 20 mutated lung cancer to second-generation, irreversible EGFR inhibitors such as afatinib [4-6]; however, the IC50 values observed may fail to correspond with achievable plasma concentrations [7] and a recent clinical trial investigating the utility of afatinib demonstrated disappointing results in NSCLC patients with exon 20 insertions [8]. In cell lines and xenografts with EGFR exon 20 insertions, response to osimertinib was superior to afatinib [9-11]. However, based on several small series and case reports, clinical responses to these agents among patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions have been limited to partial responses in a subset of patients [9,12-17].
A newer EGFR inhibitor - poziotinib, Spectrum Pharmaceuticals - was specifically designed to inhibit EGFR exon 20 insertions. Based on in vitro studies, this inhibitor is able to overcome the steric hindrance that limits efficacy of other inhibitors and can be 40 to 100 times more potent than afatinib or osimertinib in cells with EGFR exon 20 insertions (IC50 0.3 - 1.84nM) [18]. In an ongoing phase 2 trial at MD Anderson (NCT03066206), poziotinib demonstrated an objective response rate of 73% (8 of 11) in NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions [18]. Another EGFR inhibitor designed for exon 20 insertions - TAK-788 (AP32788) - was also shown to potently inhibit EGFR exon 20 mutations in preclinical studies (IC50 21-33 nM) [19]. In early clinical studies, partial responses were observed in 3 of 14 evaluable NSCLC patients with EGFR or ERBB2 exon 20 insertions [20]. Other novel EGFR inhibitors with preclinical evidence of efficacy include TAS6417 [21],"compound 1A" [22] and tarloxotinib [23].

The FDA recently granted accelerated approval for 2 different therapies targeting EGFR exon 20 insertions in NSCLC. Mobocertinib (Exkivity) approval was based on a study with an overall response rate of 28% and median duration of 17.5 months [2]. Amivantamab-vmjw (Rybrevant) is a bispecific antibody whose approval was based on a study with an overall response rate of 40% and median duration of 11.1 months [3]. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) NSCLC Panel recommends testing for EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations in eligible patients with metastatic NSCLC based on data showing the efficacy of amivantamab-vmjw or mobocertinib as subsequent therapy options for patients with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutation-positive metastatic NSCLC and on the FDA approvals [17].
 
EGFR exon 20 insertions, such as EGFR S768_D770dup, (other than A763_Y764insFQEA) are associated with primary resistance to achievable doses of the first-generation, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies that are currently FDA-approved for some EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [4-5]. While second-generation irreversible EGFR inhibitors such as afatinib and third-generation inhibitors such as osimertinib demonstrate superior efficacy in preclinical studies [6-9], these drugs also fail to achieve significant clinical efficacy [10-16].

While there are no FDA-approved therapies or NCCN recommended therapies for gliomas with EGFR mutations, 2 different therapies targeting EGFR exon 20 insertions are FDA-approved for NSCLC with these mutations. Mobocertinib (Exkivity) is an EGFR inhibitor, specifically targeting EGFR with exon 20 mutations, whose approval in NSCLC was based on a study with an overall response rate of 28% and median duration of 17.5 months [PMID: 34647988]. This drug demonstrated limited intracranial activity in brain metastases of NSCLC tumors with EGFR exon 20 insertions. 
 
Amivantamab-vmjw (Rybrevant) is a bispecific antibody whose approval in NSCLC was based on a study with an overall response rate of 40% and median duration of 11.1 months [PMID: 34339292]; however, this drug is not expected to cross the blood brain barrier. EGFR exon 20 insertions are associated with primary resistance to achievable doses of the first-generation, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies that are currently FDA-approved for some EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [PMID: 18676761, 27468240]. While second-generation irreversible EGFR inhibitors such as afatinib and third-generation inhibitors such as osimertinib demonstrate superior efficacy in preclinical studies [PMID: 21764376, 29483211], these drugs also fail to achieve significant clinical efficacy [PMID: 29702285, 26354527, 26051236, 26051236, 29740957, 21220471]. 
 
Preclinical data has demonstrated sensitivity to specific TKIs using primary astrocyte models with exon 20 kinase domain insertions. The same group identified four patients with bithalamic gliomas harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions who were treated with TKIs (afatenib, osimertinib, or trametinib) and results were encouraging, suggesting a survival benefit [PMID: 32303840].

EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations (like the one identified in this specimen) are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. However, this type of mutation most commonly occurs in lung adenocarcinoma and is only exceptionally observed in other tumor types [2]. For example, an EGFR exon 20 insertion has been reported in lung adenosquamous carcinoma [3], and interestingly, EGFR exon 20 indel mutations are well-described in sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma (SNSCC) that are associated with synchronous or metachronous inverted sinonasal papillomas (ISP) [4].

The EGFR-MET bispecific antibody amivantamab, alone and in combination with chemotherapy, is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations such as N771_H773dup and is NCCN recommended as first line therapy option [2]. Additionally, recently the FDA granted accelerated approval to sunvozertinib (Zegfrovy) for adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) exon 20 insertion mutations whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy [5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Amivantamab-vmjw - a bisepecific antibody directed against EGFR and MET is FDA-approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with EGFR exon 20 insertions and has demonstrated preclinical [3] and clinical [4-5] activity in these cancers. Amivantamab with chemotherapy demonstrated improved PFS and intracranial PFS compared to chemotherapy alone in EGFR-mutant NSCLC that has progressed on osimertinib [6].
 
Preclinical data and limited clinical studies have demonstrating evidence supporting the potential utility of EGFR inhibitors (afatinib, osimertinib) in patients with bithalamic gliomas harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions [1].
 
Importantly, EGFR exon 20 insertions are associated with primary resistance to achievable doses of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies; particularly first-generation, reversible EGFR TKI therapies that are currently FDA-approved for EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [7-8]. While a better in vitro response of exon 20 mutated lung cancer cells to second-generation, irreversible EGFR inhibitors such as afatinib was observe [9-11], clinical trials investigating the utility of afatinib demonstrated disappointing results in NSCLC patients with exon 20 insertions [12]. 
 
An EGFR inhibitor designed for exon 20 insertions - Mobocertinib (TAK-788) was shown to potently inhibit EGFR exon 20 mutations in preclinical studies (IC50 21-33 nM) [13]. In early clinical studies, partial responses were observed in a minority of NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions [1,14-15]. 
 
Poziotinib (Spectrum Pharmaceuticals) is another newer EGFR inhibitor designed to inhibit EGFR exon 20 insertions [16]. This medication was associated with clinical response among EGFR exon 20 mutated lung cancers [16-17], but was also associated with significant toxicity [17].

Current FDA-approved EGFR inhibitor therapies have limited efficacy in neoplasms with EGFR exon 20 insertions. Patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions (other than A763_Y764insFQEA) are resistant to these medications [5,6]. However, preclinical studies have shown that SNSCC cells with these mutations are more sensitive to irreversible EGFR inhibitors, including afatinib (FDA-approved in NSCLC), neratinib (FDA-approved for breast cancer) and dacomitinib (PF-00299804) [4]. Similar results were obtained from prelinical studies of other cell types harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions [7-11]. In cell lines and xenografts with EGFR exon 20 insertions, response to osimertinib was superior to afatinib [12-14]. However, based on several small series and case reports, clinical responses to these agents among patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions have been limited to partial responses in a subset of patients [12,15-20]. A newer EGFR inhibitor - poziotinib, Spectrum Pharmaceuticals - was specifically designed to inhibit EGFR exon 20 insertions. Based on in vitro studies, this inhibitor is able to overcome the steric hindrance that limits efficacy of other inhibitors and can be 40 to 100 times more potent than afatinib or osimertinib in cells with EGFR exon 20 insertions [21]. In an ongoing phase 2 trial at MD Anderson (NCT03066206), poziotinib demonstrated an objective response rate of 73% (8 of 11) in NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions. Questions or requests regarding expanded access (compassionate use) for Spectrum Pharmaceuticals can be submitted at EAP@sppirx.com. Clinical trials investigating the utility of poziotinib (NCT03066206, NCT03318939) are currently restricted to NSCLC patients.

EGFR exon 20 insertions are associated with primary resistance to achievable doses of the first-generation, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies that are currently FDA-approved for EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [3,4]. Several studies have shown a more robust in vitro response of exon 20 mutated lung cancer to second-generation, irreversible EGFR inhibitors such as afatinib [5-7]; however, a recent clinical trial investigating the utility of afatinib demonstrated disappointing results in NSCLC patients with exon 20 insertions [8]. 
 
A newer EGFR inhibitor (poziotinib; Spectrum Pharmaceuticals) was specifically designed to inhibit EGFR exon 20 insertions. [9]. In an ongoing phase 2 trial at MD Anderson (NCT03066206), poziotinib demonstrated an objective response rate of 73% (8 of 11) in NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions [9]. Preliminary results from the ZENITH20 study (NCT03318939), however, found a response rate in patients with exon 20 insertion NSCLC of just 14.8% with poziotinib, and significant toxicity requiring dose reduction was identified in 68% of patients [15]. Other novel EGFR inhibitors with preclinical evidence of efficacy include TAS6417 [12],"compound 1A" [13] and tarloxotinib [14]. Preclinical data has demonstrated sensitivity to specific TKIs using primary astrocyte models with exon 20 kinase domain insertions. The same group identified four patients with bithalamic gliomas harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions who were treated with TKIs (afatenib, osimertinib, or trametinib) and results were encouraging, suggesting a survival benefit [1].
