The EGFR exon 20 insertion mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. However, this mutation is associated with primary resistance to achievable doses of first generation, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies currently FDA-approved for some EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [2]. Several studies have shown a more robust in vitro response of exon 20 mutated lung cancer to second generation, irreversible EGFR inhibitors such as afatinib [3-5]; however, the IC50 values observed may fail to correspond with achievable plasma concentrations [6] and a recent clinical trial investigating the utility of afatinib demonstrated disappointing results in NSCLC patients with exon 20 insertions [7]. However, there is emerging evidence that a third-generation TKI (osimertinib) which is currently FDA-approved for NSCLC with EGFR T790M mutation, may be also be effective for exon 20 insertions [8]. Clinical trials are underway investigating the utility of other TKI (e.g. AP32788, EGF816) and other agents such as luminespib (AUY922; an HSP-90 inhibitor) for NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertions.

EGFR exon 20 insertions (other than A763_Y764insFQEA) are associated with primary resistance to achievable doses of the first-generation, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies that are currently FDA-approved for EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [3,4]. A newer EGFR inhibitor (poziotinib; Spectrum Pharmaceuticals) was specifically designed to inhibit EGFR exon 20 insertions. [9]. In an ongoing phase 2 trial at MD Anderson (NCT03066206), poziotinib demonstrated an objective response rate of 73% (8 of 11) in NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions [9]. Preliminary results from the ZENITH20 study (NCT03318939), however, found a response rate in patients with exon 20 insertion NSCLC of just 14.8% with poziotinib, and significant toxicity requiring dose reduction was identified in 68% of patients [15]. Another EGFR inhibitor designed for exon 20 insertions [TAK-788, Mobocertinib] was also shown to potently inhibit EGFR exon 20 mutations in preclinical studies (IC50 21-33 nM) [10]; in early clinical studies, partial responses were observed in 3 of 14 evaluable NSCLC patients with EGFR or ERBB2 exon 20 insertions [11]. Results from the ongoing Phase 1/2 trial (NCT02716116) of mobocertinib in previously treated patients with exon 20 insertion -mutant NSCLC tumors found an overall response rate of 43% [16]. Amivantamab also received FDA breakthrough therapy designation and the ongoing Phase 1 CRYSALIS study (NCT02609776) has shown promising preliminary results. Other novel EGFR inhibitors with preclinical evidence of efficacy include TAS6417 [12],"compound 1A" [13] and tarloxotinib [14]. Preclinical data has demonstrated sensitivity to specific TKIs using primary astrocyte models with exon 20 kinase domain insertions. The same group identified four patients with bithalamic gliomas harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions who were treated with TKIs (afatenib, osimertinib, or trametinib) and results were encouraging, suggesting a survival benefit [1].

variants.variant_description: EGFR mutations are well-described in sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma (SNSCC) which are associated with synchronous or metachronous inverted sinonasal papillomas (ISP) [1]. These mutations were identified in 88% of ISP and 77% of ISP-associated SNSCC but were not found in any SNSCC without an associated with ISP [1]. In another study, EGFR mutations in these tumors were mutually exclusive with HPV infection and either an EGFR mutation or HPV infection was present in all cases, suggesting that these two events represent the essential oncogenic drivers of these tumors [2]. The majority of EGFR mutations in ISP-associated SNSCC are exon 20 insertions - in contrast with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). These mutations were shown to result in constitutive activation of EGFR as well as downstream mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling [1]. Current FDA-approved EGFR inhibitor therapies have limited efficacy in neoplasms with EGFR exon 20 insertions. In preclinical studies, ISP-associated SNSCC cells with an EGFR exon 20 insertion were relatively resistant to reversible EGFR inhibitors including erlotinib and gefitinib - both of which are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with certain EGFR mutations [1]. As a clinical correlary, patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions (other than A763_Y764insFQEA) are resistant to these medications [3,4]. However, preclinical studies have shown that SNSCC cells with these mutations are more sensitive to irreversible EGFR inhibitors including afatinib (FDA-approved in NSCLC), neratinib (FDA-approved for breast cancer) and dacomitinib (PF-00299804) [1]. Similar results were obtained from prelinical studies of other cell types harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions [5-9]. In cell lines and xenografts with EGFR exon 20 insertions, response to osimertinib was superior to afatinib [10-12]. However, based on several small series and case reports, clinical responses to these agents among patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions have been limited to partial responses in a subset of patients [10,13-18]. A newer EGFR inhibitor - poziotinib, Spectrum Pharmaceuticals - was specifically designed to inhibit EGFR exon 20 insertions. Based on in vitro studies, this inhibitor is able to overcome the steric hindrance that limits efficacy of other inhibitors and can be 40 to 100 times more potent than afatinib or osimertinib in cells with EGFR exon 20 insertions [19]. In an ongoing phase 2 trial at MD Anderson (NCT03066206), poziotinib demonstrated an objective response rate of 73% (8 of 11) in NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions. Questions or requests regarding expanded access (compassionate use) for Spectrum Pharmaceuticals can be submitted at EAP@sppirx.com. Clinically trials investigating the utility of poziotinib (NCT03066206, NCT03318939) are restricted to NSCLC patients.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Some observational studies have suggested that MYC amplification may be associated with acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors [5]. There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified NSCLC; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [6-8]. Clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of some of these agents (particularly BET bromodomain inhibitors) are ongoing. Michigan Medicine is currently participating in one such study - a Phase 1/2 study investigating the safety and preliminary efficacy of the BET bromodomain inhibitor INCB057643 in advanced stage malignancies (NCT02711137; UMCC 2016.052). As this sample was equivocal for MYC amplification by this assay, evaluation of MYC status using different method (e.g. FISH) is recommended, if clinically indicated.

Two EGFR mutations affecting adjacent codons (S768I and V769L) are present on the same allele. This combination of mutations (also designated SV768IL) has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-7] as has S768I combined with other mutations [8-9]. S768_V769delinsIL has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activations of EGFR and downstream ERK and AKT signaling [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While afatinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR S768I, studies concerning TKI sensitivity when S768I is combined with V769L have been mixed. In one report, a patient harboring these mutations was resistant to afatinib [2], while, in another, a response was reported [3]. In other reports, the combination of these mutations conferred resistance to gefitinib [4] and osimertinib [1]. Case reports have identified S768_V769delinsIL in association with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [1,5]. Given the inconsistency and relative paucity of data on this mutation, the clinical implications of this finding is uncertain.

EGFR amplification and EGFR A289D:
A copy number gain involving the EGFR gene was detected, consistent with EGFR amplification. EGFR amplification associated with increased EGFR expression is well-described in gliomas [PMID: 2981413; NCCN Guidelines Central Nervous System Tumors, Version 1.2026] and frequently co-occurs with EGFR variant III (vIII) [PMID: 16133418], which was NOT observed in this specimen. The A289D mutation detected in this specimen is well-described in gliomas of varying grade [PMID: 17177598, 28855349, 28481359]. Other mutations affecting this residue, including A289T and A289V, have also been described in glioma [PMID: 17177598, 28855349, 28481359, 17143531]. These mutations lie within the extracellular domain of EGFR [PMID: 17177598] and have been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [PMID: 17177598, 29533785].

The A289D mutation detected in this specimen is well-described in gliomas of varying grade [PMID: 17177598, 28855349, 28481359]. Other mutations affecting this residue, including A289T and A289V, have also been described in glioma [PMID: 17177598, 28855349, 28481359, 17143531]. These mutations lie within the extracellular domain of EGFR [PMID: 17177598] and have been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [PMID: 17177598, 29533785].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: According to WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System, 5th edition, EGFR amplification (or TERT promoter mutation, gain of chromosome 7 and loss of chromosome 10, necrosis or microvascular proliferation) may be important for grading of tumors [WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System, 5th edition]. Several studies have shown that diffusely infiltrative astrocytomas lacking the histologic features of glioblastoma (necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation) but having one of the molecular hallmarks (EGFR amplification; +7/-10 or TERT promoter mutation) have similar clinical outcomes as typical grade 4 glioblastomas, and may be treated as such [PMIDs: 3029105, 28575485, 29016839, 23604523, 26087904, 30187121, 25783747, 29052002].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for gliomas with EGFR amplification or mutations. Multiple therapies such as vaccines, EGFR inhibitors, EGFR antibodies, CAR T-cells, RNA-based therapies, among others, have been evaluated for gliomas with EGFR amplification and/or EGFRvIII and have shown mixed results [PMIDs: 23248284, 23363814, 25586468, 27020557, 24310612, 15035290, 19825799, 25140039, 25939761, 19491283, 20345222, 25696001, 12205508, 12743604, 25895099]. 
 
Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in glioma affect the extracellular domain - as seen in this specimen. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [PMID: 22588883]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [PMID: 24120142, 15035290, 23363814, 26423602, 25140039]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [PMID: 22588883]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [PMID: 22588883].

Although the EGFR R108S mutation has not been specifically characterized, other EGFR R108 mutations affect the extracellular domain and have been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [PMID: 23917401, 29731991]. Similar mutations affecting the extracellular domain are also identified in glioblastomas [PMID: 17177598, 37446288].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The EGFR mutation detected in this specimen affects the extracellular domain instead of the tyrosine kinase domain, as seen with most EGFR mutations observed in gliomas. Studies have shown that these extracellular domain mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in non-small cell lung cancer (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [PMID: 22588883, 37446288]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [PMID: 24120142, 15035290, 23363814, 26423602, 25140039]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [PMID: 22588883, 20459769].

variants.variant_description:
The V774M mutation affects the tyrosine kinase domain of the EGFR protein and has been reported in gliomas [PMID: 28481359] and is well-described in other neoplasms [PMID: 23242437, 31007929, 21531810, 29858019, 16863509].

The EGFR V774M mutation detected in this specimen is uncommen but has been described mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-5]. This mutation frequently co-occurs with other EGFR mutations on the same allele including S768I [2] and H773L [3-5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Osimertinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with certain EGFR exon 20 mutations, and case reports of patients with lung cancer with EGFR V774M reported sensitivity to osimertinib [PMID: 36842378, 39062751]; however, the potential efficacy in gliomas is unknown.

The impact of the EGFR V774M mutation on treatment sensitivity is uncertain. In one case report, a patient with V774M did not respond to erlotinib [1], and, in another report, a patient with H773L and V774M did not respond to afatinib [5].

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations were detected, both affecting the same allele. The EGFR L861Q mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073, 16205628]. The EGFR L833F mutation identified in this specimen is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of EGFR and has not been functionally characterized. These mutations have been previously described in NSCLC [PMID: 40713215].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Recommended treatment for NSCLC with EGFR L861Q mutations is described in NSCL-24 of NCCN guidelines [NCCN - Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, version 1.2026]. Afatinib (Gilotrif) or osimertinib (Tagrisso) are considered the preferred first-line systemic therapies.
 
While several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation, only afatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR L861Q. Both preclinical [PMID: 27240419, 28088511, 29285266] and clinical [PMID: 25589191, 26051236, 28088511, 26051236] studies have demonstrated the sensitivity of this mutation to afatinib while preclinical [PMID: 27240419, 19147750] and clinical [PMID: 24419415, 28645631] studies suggest that erlotinib and gefitinib are less effective for this mutation. However, studies have shown efficacy of osimertinib in NSCLC with L861Q alterations [PMID: 31825714]. 
 
There is limited clinical data on the efficacy of TKI therapy in patients with multiple EGFR mutations affecting the same allele. A case report of a patient with NSCLC with EGFR [L833F; L861Q] reported response to afatinib and a combination of osimertinib and bevacizumab [PMID: 34621884]. A retrospective study of 81 patients with NSCLC with compound EGFR mutations showed response to TKIs in patients with EGFR [L833F; L861Q] and similar mutations [PMID: 40713215].

variants.variant_description: The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073]. The L858R mutation results in activation of the tyrosine kinase domain, and is associated with sensitivity to the small-molecule EGFR TKIs [PMIDs: 15118073, 19483740, NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 3.2026]. The EGFR A859S mutation identified in this specimen is rare but has been described in patients with NSCLC [PMID: 28572459, 33324543, 40989709]. The functional effect of the A859S mutation is not well characterized; however, the EGFR A859T mutation at the same residue has not been shown to cause activation of EGFR [PMID: 17877814].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
NSCLC with EGFR L858R is sensitive to multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies. According to NCCN Guidelines, osimertinib is a preferred first-line EGFR TKI option for NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R (or exon 19 deletion). Other recommended first-line therapies include lazertinib+amivantamab-vmjw (Lazcluze+Rybrevant) or osimertinib with pemetrexed and cisplatin/carboplatin [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 3.2026]. The effect of the EGFR A859S mutation on sensitivity to TKI therapy has not been well characterized.
 
Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified in this specimen.

variants.variant_description: This variant has been described in lung cancer specimens [PMID: 17285735, 21030498, 29489023, 30121391, 33224870, 36188595, 36380563, 40713215]. This mutation lies within exon 20 and affects the kinase domain of the EGFR protein, but has not been functionally assessed in any known study. Therefore, the impact of this variant on protein function (if any) is not known. However, several in silico algorithms predict that this variant alters protein function. This variant has been described concomitantly with other, known pathogenic, EGFR mutations e.g., G719 mutations [PMID: 29228562, 33224870, 36188595, 40713215].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The potential sensitivity of this variant (in isolation) to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy has not been evaluated in any known study.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations are detected, both affecting the extracellular domain of the EGFR protein. A289V [PMID: 29533785]  and G598V [PMID: 17177598] have both been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: EGFR A289V [PMID: 17143531, 28481359, 28201779, 23917401, 17177598] and G598V [PMID: 17177598, 23917401, 24140581, 25471132, 18772396, 28855349, 19284481] have both been recurrently reported in gliomas, as have other EGFR mutations affecting the extracellular domain.
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in gliomas affect the extracellular domain - as seen in this specimen. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [PMID: 22588883]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [PMID: 22588883, 24120142, 15035290, 26423602, 25140039]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [PMID: 22588883, 24120142, 15035290]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [PMID: 22588883].

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations were detected. E746_A750del is a well-described exon 19 deletion in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that affects the kinase domain of the EGFR protein and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073]. A289V affects the extracellular domain and has also been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [PMID: 29533785].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: While EGFR E746_A750del and other exon 19 deletions are common in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), extracellular domain EGFR mutations, such as A289V, are more commonly reported in gliomas [PMID: 17143531, 28481359, 28201779, 23917401, 17177598]. However, extracellular domain mutations have been reported at a low incidence in NSCLC and do NOT appear to be mutually exclusive with other prominent NSCLC drivers alterations. In on ASCO abstract (e20532, 2019) concerning 10,100 NSCLC patients, EGFR extracellualr domain mutations were reported in 0.36% of NSCLC including 0.23% affecting codon A289 (A289V, A289D, A289T, A289Y) [J Clin Oncol. 2019;37(15 suppl):e20532]. 81% of these patients harbored concomitant EGFR kinase domain mutations - most commonly L858R (72%), but also exon 19 deletions (17%) and other kinase domain mutations. In another abstract presented at the 2022 World Conference on Lung Cancer (EP16.03-019), 2,065 NSCLC patients were found to harbor extracellular domain mutations within circulating tumor DNA with 50% harboring other driver mutations including 17% with EGFR kinase domain mutations, 22% with KRAS mutations, 6.5% with ERBB2 mutations, 1.8% with MET exon 14 skipping mutations, 1.4% with BRAF V600E, and 1% with kinase gene fusions [J Thor Oncol. 2022;17(9 suppl):S596].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
EGFR Exon 19 Deletion Mutation
EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutations are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [PMID: 15118073, 24929780, 28841389, 19483740]. Osimertinib is a third-generation oral EGFR TKI FDA approved for the treatment of patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR alterations. Osimertinib monotherapy and osimertinib in combination with platinum and pemetrexed chemotherapy are both indicated for the first-line treatment of adults with metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R mutation [NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology - Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 8.2025]. Single-agent erlotinib, afatinib, gefitinib, or dacomitinib are other recommended first-line treatment options. 
 
EGFR Extracellular Domain Mutation
Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [PMID: 22588883]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [PMID: 22588883, 24120142, 15035290, 26423602, 25140039]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [PMID: 22588883, 24120142, 15035290]. However, in one ASCO abstract (e20532, 2019), 6 NSCLC patients harboring L858R and an EGFR extracellualr domain mutation who were treated with TKI therapy achieved a 2-month disease contraol rate of 83% with 2 patients having 10-month PFS, and 3 patients treated for 2, 5 and 12 months respectively who were still on treatment [J Clin Oncol. 2019;37(15 suppl):e20532]. Therefore, this extracellular domain mutation may not confer resistance to the above therapies shown to be efficacious in NSCLC with exon 19 deletions.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations were detected - E746_A750del and T790M. These two mutations are present at different variant allele frequencies (55% and 12%, respectively). Because these two mutations affect different exons, it is not known if these two mutations affect the same allele (in cis) or different alleles (in trans). The EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073]. T790M is most commonly observed as a mechanism of acquired resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) [PMID: 17085664, 15728811, 15737014]. This mutation results in increased EGFR affinity for adenosine triphosphate and reduced binding to EGFR TKI [PMID: 18227510]. There is no known history of treatment with TKI therapy. The incidence of EGFR T790M prior to TKI therapy (TKI-naïve) is dependent on the detection methods employed, but when observed, has been described at low variant allele frequencies [PMID: 33116639, 35884570, 26973206, 30936123, 25882755]. Germline EGFR T790M mutations have also been described in association with a germline predisposition to NSCLC [PMID: 16258541, 17510392, 22588155, 24736066, 34869019]. The variant allele frequency of the T790M mutation is below 50% (12%); however, this allele freqency may be altered by somatic copy number alterations in this specimen. Evaluation of non-neoplastic tissue is required to differentiate germline from from somatic mutations.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutations are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [PMID: 15118073, 24929780, 28841389, 19483740], EGFR T790M confers resistance to most EGFR inhibitors and is commonly seen as mechanism of acquired resistance to TKI therapy [PMID: 17085664, 15728811, 15737014, 17020982]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [PMID: 27959700, 24893891] and is currently FDA-approved for this application. No molecular alterations associated with acquired resistance to osimertinib [PMID: 29883838, 29406987] were identified in this specimen.

This mutation has been rarely reported in small cell lung cancer [PMIDs: 15741570, 21430269, 16837691, 22941188, 30550363, 24828667].

Because these two mutations affect different exons, it is not known if these two mutations affect the same allele (in cis) or different alleles (in trans). T790M is most commonly observed as a mechanism of acquired resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) [2-5]. This mutation results in increased EGFR affinity for adenosine triphosphate and reduced binding to EGFR TKI [6]. There is no known history of treatment with TKI therapy. The incidence of EGFR T790M prior to TKI therapy (TKI-naïve) is dependent on the detection methods employed, but when observed, has only been described at low variant allele frequencies [7-11], as seen in this specimen.

The EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. An EGFR copy number gain was also detected. EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-4]. EGFR amplification that is present prior to TKI therapy more commonly affects the mutant EGFR allele [2-4], as appears to be the case in this sample.

CDK4 copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain involving the CDK4 gene was detected, consistent with CDK4 amplification. CDK4 encodes a cyclin dependent kinase that normally phosphorylates the retinoblastoma gene product (Rb) during the G1/S transition. Amplification of CDK4 resulting in increased CDK4 expression has been described at a low incidence in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1].

MET amplification:
A copy number gain of the MET gene was detected (approximately __ copies), consistent with MET amplification. Amplification of MET resulting in increased MET expression is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-3]. MET amplification is a well-described mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [4-7]. Of note, this patient has undergone TKI treatment based on the previously identified activating EGFR mutation. The origninal, pre-treatment lung biopsy specimen did NOT demonstrate the MET copy number gain identified in the current specimen. Therefore this acquired copy number alteration may reflect a mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy.

The EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. A low-level EGFR copy number gain (considered equivocal for amplification) was also detected. EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-4].

MET and KRAS amplification:
Copy number gains involving the MET gene (approximately __ copies) and KRAS gene (approximately __ copies) were detected. MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase and KRAS is a membrane-bound GTPase downstream of MET (and EGFR) within MAPK pathway growth signaling. Amplification of MET [1-8] and KRAS [8-10] are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Amplification of each of these genes (particularly MET) has been described as a mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [4-8,11]. Of note, this patient has undergone TKI treatment based on the previously identified activating EGFR mutation. The origninal, pre-treatment lung biopsy specimen did NOT demonstrate the MET or KRAS copy number gains identified in the current specimen. Therefore this acquired copy number alteration may reflect a mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy.

MYC copy number gain (equivocal for amplification): 
A copy number gain (approximately __ copies) of the MYC gene was detected, consistent with MYC amplification. MYC (c-MYC) is a transcription factor involved in growth signaling. Amplification of MYC, as seen in this specimen, is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and may be associated with a poor prognosis, particularly in early stage disease [1-4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutations are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [PMID: 15118073, 24929780, 28841389, 19483740]. Osimertinib is a third-generation oral EGFR TKI FDA approved for the treatment of patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR alterations. Osimertinib monotherapy and osimertinib in combination with platinum and pemetrexed chemotherapy are both indicated for the first-line treatment of adults with metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R mutation [NCCN Guidelines - Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026]. Single-agent erlotinib, afatinib, gefitinib, or dacomitinib are other recommended first-line treatment options. All of these are category 1 recommendations and are appropriate for patients with performance status 0–4. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified. 
 
EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutations are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [PMID: 15118073, 24929780, 28841389, 19483740]. Osimertinib is a third-generation oral EGFR TKI FDA approved for the treatment of patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR alterations. In the first-line setting, the NCCN NSCLC Panel recommends single-agent osimertinib, osimertinib in combination with (carboplatin or cisplatin)/pemetrexed, or lazertinib + amivantamab-vmjw as preferred and category 1 options for patients with advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or L858R mutations. Single-agent afatinib, dacomitinib, erlotinib, gefitinib, or lazertinib are first-line treatment options that may be useful in certain circumstances [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

While EGFR L858R is associated with sensitivity to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib) [1,12], EGFR T790M confers resistance to most EGFR inhibitors and is commonly seen as mechanism of acquired resistance to TKI therapy [2-5]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [13-14] and is currently FDA-approved for this application [15]. No molecular alterations associated with acquired resistance to osimertinib [16-17] were identified in this specimen.

This mutation is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,5] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [6]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [6]. One study has suggested that copy number gains involving the EGFR mutant allele (as seen in this specimen) is associated increased benefit from EGFR TKI therapy [7]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M) were identified.

The impact of this copy number alteration on response to EGFR TKI therapy is uncertain. In one study, concurrent CDK4 amplification was identified in pre-treatment samples from 10% (21/200) of lung cancers with EGFR mutations, and, in this study, CDK4 amplification was NOT associated with resistance to EGFR inhibitors [2].
 
A phase 2 study of the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib (PD-0332991) showed clinical efficacy in well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcoma with CDK4 amplification [3]. In one case report, a NSCLC patient with a sensitive EGFR mutation and CDK4 amplification responded to the combination of an EGFR inhibitor and a CDK4/6/ inhibitor [4].

While EGFR exon 19 deletions are associated with sensitivity to FDA-approved EGFR inhibitors (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and osimertinib), the MET and KRAS copy number alterations also detected in this specimen have been associated with acquired resistance to EGFR inhibitor therapy (see Therapeutic Implications for copy number alterations below).

Both preclinical [12,13] and several clinical reports have shown that patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC with acquired TKI resistance resulting from MET amplification respond to combined EGFR and MET TKI therapy [14-19]. Acquired resistance to combined MET and EGFR TKI therapy in MET-amplified, EGFR-mutant NSCLC (by a variety of mechanisms) has also been described [14,15,20]. KRAS amplification may mitigate response to dual EGFR/MET inhibitor therapy since NRAS activates MAPK signaling downstream of both EGFR and MET. KRAS amplification has been implication as a potential mechanism of acquired resistance of MET exon 14-mutant NSCLC to crizotinib [21].

Some observational studies have suggested that MYC amplification may be associated with acquired or primary (intrinsic) resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors [5]. There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified NSCLC; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [6-8]. Clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of some of these agents (particularly BET bromodomain inhibitors) are ongoing. Michigan Medicine is currently participating in one such study - a Phase 1/2 study investigating the safety and preliminary efficacy of the BET bromodomain inhibitor INCB057643 in advanced stage malignancies (NCT02711137; UMCC 2016.052). As this sample was equivocal for MYC amplification by this assay, evaluation of MYC status using different method (e.g. FISH) is recommended, if clinically indicated.

Some observational studies have suggested that MYC amplification may be associated with acquired or intrinsic resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors [5-6]. There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified NSCLC; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [7-9].

Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a receptor tyrosine kinase. The in-frame exon 19 insertion/deletion mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073].

EGFR L747_A750delinsP and EGFR amplification:
An activating, oncogenic EGFR mutation [1] as well as amplification of the WILD-TYPE allele of EGFR was detected in this specimen. Of note, the EGFR T790M mutation detected in a previous specimen from this patient (SU-16-10339) was NOT detected in this specimen. The absence of EGFR T790M in tumor specimens from patients treated with osimertinib whose tumors were previously found to harbor T790M is well-decribed [5]. However, amplification (approximately __ copies) of the WILD-TYPE allele of EGFR was detected in this specimen.  EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-4]. While EGFR amplification that is present prior to TKI therapy more commonly affects the mutant EGFR allele [2-4], EGFR amplification can also be acquired during TKI therapy [5-9] and frequently involves the wild-type allele [6,7], as appears to be the case in this sample.

CDK4 copy number gain (amplification):
CDK4 encodes a cyclin dependent kinase that normally phosphorylates the retinoblastoma gene product (Rb) during the G1/S transition. Amplification of CDK4 resulting in increased CDK4 expression has been described at a low incidence in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1]. While this copy number alteration was not present with the previously evaluated liver biopsy, there are no known descriptions of CDK4 amplification as a mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy.

MET amplification:
A copy number gain of the MET gene was detected (approximately 7 copies), consistent with MET amplification. Amplification of MET resulting in increased MET expression is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-3]. MET amplification is a well-described mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [4-7]. Of note, this patient has undergone TKI treatment based on the previously identified activating EGFR mutation. While the origninal, pre-treatment specimen  was not evaluated for copy number alterations, the liver biopsy did NOT contain the MET copy number gain identified in the current specimen. Therefore this acquired copy number alteration may reflect a mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy.

CCND1 copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain of the CCND1 gene was detected, consistent with CCND1 amplification. CCND1 encodes cyclin D1, a protein that interacts with cyclin dependent kinases (CDK), regulating Rb activity and cell cycle progression. Putative cyclin D1 amplification has been described in a small subset of lung adenocarcinoma [1]. While this copy number alteration was not present with the previously evaluated liver biopsy, there are no known descriptions of CDK4 amplification as a mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutations are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [PMID: 15118073, 24929780, 28841389, 19483740]. Osimertinib is a third-generation oral EGFR TKI FDA approved for the treatment for patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR alterations. Osimertinib monotherapy and osimertinib in combination with platinum and pemetrexed chemotherapy are both indicated for the first-line treatment of adults with metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R mutation [NCCN Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Version 3.2025]. Single-agent erlotinib, afatinib, gefitinib, or dacomitinib are other recommended first-line treatment options. All of these are category 1 recommendations and are appropriate for patients with performance status 0–4. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

The EGFR exon 19 deletion detected in this specimen is associated with sensitivity to the FDA-approved EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies [1,10] and treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [11]. However, this patient is noted to have had progressive while on erlotinib and later while on osimertinib. Acquired amplification of the wild-type allele of EGFR (as observed in this specimen) has been described in association with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [5-9]. In addition, one study showed that, in cell lines, the introduction of amplification of the wild-type allele (but not the mutant allele) was sufficient to confer resistance to third-generation TKI therapy. This study also showed that cotreatment with a TKI and cetuximab overcame EGFR amplification-mediated resistance. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [6]. One study has suggested that copy number gains involving the EGFR mutant allele (as seen in this specimen) is associated increased benefit from EGFR TKI therapy [7].

This mutation is also associated with clinical response to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,2]. Several of these inhibitors including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and osimertinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions. While no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (e.g. T790M) were identified, the copy number alterations also detected in this specimen may impact response to EGFR TKI therapy and/or other therapies (see Therapeutic Implications for copy number alterations below).

A phase 2 study of the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib (PD0332991) showed clinical efficacy in well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcoma with CDK4 amplification [2]. The impact of the copy number alteration on response to EGFR and/or MET TKI therapy is uncertain.

Both preclinical [8,9] and several clinical reports have shown that patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC with acquired TKI resistance resulting from MET amplification respond to combined EGFR and MET TKI therapy [10-15]. Acquired resistance to combined MET and EGFR TKI therapy in MET-amplified, EGFR-mutant NSCLC by a variety of mechanisms has also been described [10,11,16].

Preclinical studies have shown that cells with CCND1 amplification may be sensitive to CDK4/6 inhibitors e.g. palbociclib (FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer), ribociclib, and abemaciclib [2]. However, within the studies published thusfar, no clear association has been demonstrated between CCND1 amplification status and response to these agents [3,4]. The impact of the copy number alteration on response to EGFR and/or MET TKI therapy is uncertain.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
While EGFR exon 19 deletions (including E746_A570del) are associated with sensitivity to first, second, and third generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, osimertinib) [1][2], EGFR C797S confers resistance to pyrimidine-based EGFR inhibitors such as osimertinib [3-9]. However, in the absence of an EGFR T790M resistance mutation (not detected in this specimen), there is some evidence to suggest that tumor regression can be achieved with erlotinib or gefitinib in EGFR C797S-mutant tumors who have acquired resistance to osimertinib, though the duration of response and benefit may be limited [10].
 
Preclinical studies suggest that the combination of histone deacetylase inhibitor vorinostat and tyrosine kinase inhibitor brigatinib [11] or fluorinated quinazoline EGFR inhibitors [12] may overcome resistance associated with T790M and C797S. A small clinical study suggests low potential efficacy (objective response rate 10%) associated with the combination of cetuximab and brigatinib [13-14]. New EGFR inhibitors such as JND3229 and BBT-176 have also shown preclinical evidence of activity against EGFR exon 19 deletion, T790M and C797S. Recently, a phase I/II clinical trial of BBT-176, a new EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitor cleared by the FDA as an investigational new drug for the treatment of EGFR C797S-mutant non-small cell lung cancer, has been initiated and is currently recruiting NSCLC patients in Korea who have progressed following prior therapy with an EGFR TKI agent (NCT04820023).

PDGFRA and KIT amplification:
Amplification of chromosomal segment 4q12 encompassing both PDGFRA and KIT was detected in this sample. Amplification of PDGFRA and KIT is well-described in NSCLC [1,2]. 
 
It is not known if these amplification events are associated with primary or acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy. There are no know clinical studies reporting KIT and/or PDGFRA amplification in association with resistance to anti-EGFR therapy. However, there is a report of EGFR-mutated xenografts acquiring resistance EGFR inhibitors in the context of KIT overexpression [3]. In clinical studies of ALK-rearranged lung cancers, amplification of KIT [4] and KIT overexpression [5] has been associated with acquired resistance to crizotinib. It is not know if amplification of KIT and PDGFRA was present prior to TKI therapy in this patient (DL-13-01190; CN-13-00373) since only EGFR mutational status was evaluated.
 
In preclinical studies, cells with PDGFRA and KIT amplification were sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies including sunitinib and imatinib [1,6]. However, there is very little clinical data concerning the efficacy of these therapies [2]. Relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02272998 (phase 2 of ponatinib; University of Michigan) and NCT02219711 (phase 1 of TKI MGCD516; University of Michigan).

Median progression-free survival was 19.4 months in the ramucirumab plus erlotinib arm compared with 12.4 months in the placebo plus erlotinib arm.

Two EGFR mutations were detected - E746_A750del and T790M. These two mutations are present at similar variant allele frequencies (38-39%). Because these two mutations affect different exons, it is not known if these two mutations affect the same allele (in cis) or different alleles (in trans). The EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073]. T790M is most commonly observed as a mechanism of acquired resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) [PMID: 17085664, 15728811, 15737014]. This mutation results in increased EGFR affinity for adenosine triphosphate and reduced binding to EGFR TKI [PMID: 18227510]. There is no known history of treatment with TKI therapy. The incidence of EGFR T790M prior to TKI therapy (TKI-naïve) is dependent on the detection methods employed, but when observed, has been described at low variant allele frequencies [PMID: 33116639, 35884570, 26973206, 30936123, 25882755]. Germline EGFR T790M mutations have also been described in association with a germline predisposition to NSCLC [PMID: 16258541, 17510392, 22588155, 24736066, 34869019]. The variant allele frequency of the T790M mutation is similar to that of the L858R mutation and is below 50% (39%); however, this allele freqency may be altered by somatic copy number alterations in this specimen. Evaluation of non-neoplastic tissue is required to differentiate germline from from somatic mutations.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in glioma affect the extracellular domain - e.g. the P596L mutation detected in this specimen. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [PMID: 22588883]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [PMID: 25140039, 26423602, 23363814, 15035290, 24120142]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [PMID: 22588883]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [PMID: 22588883].
 
T790M is the most common mechanism of acquired resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) [PMID: 15728811, 15737014, 17020982]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation and is currently FDA-approved for this application [PMID: 24893891]. However, the potential efficacy in gliomas and in the context of a concomitant extracellular domain mutation is uncertain.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: EGFR amplification, resulting in EGFR overexpresssion, has been described in approximately 10-19% in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma [1-6].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: EGFR gene amplification has been associated with response to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapies such as gefitinib and erlotinib in some studies [10] but not others [11-12]. EGFR was not associated with response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies such as cetuximab [13].
diseases.prognostic_implications: EGFR amplification is associated with an inferior prognosis (shorter progression-free and overall survival) in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma [7-9].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are mixed outcomes with anti-EGFR treatment (e.g., cetuximab, necitumumab) in part depending on the underlying malignancy. With an undetermined primary malignancy, it is difficult to assess the implications for treatment [12-27].

While anti-EGFR trials in unselected patients with GEC have not demonstrated any efficacy [4-6], some studies have suggested that anti-EGFR antibodies (e.g. cetuximab) [7,8] and/or tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. gefitinib) [9] may be efficacious in GEC with EGFR amplification. In addition, several studies have suggested that EGFR amplification is associated with an even greater response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy in KRAS wild-type CRC [10-14].

There are mixed outcomes with anti-EGFR treatment (e.g., cetuximab, necitumumab) in part depending on the underlying malignancy. With an undetermined primary malignancy, it is difficult to assess the implications for treatment. For example, whereas CRC may have augmented response, gliomas have shown mixed results with various targeted therapies, and even for head and neck SCC (where cituximab is FDA approved) the response rates are not high and EGFR amplification may not predict response [12-27].

While there are several studies investigating the combined impact of EGFR activation mutations and EGFR amplification [PMID: 26141217, 28202511], there are no known clinical studies that have reported the response of NSCLC with EGFR amplification in the absence of an EGFR mutation to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

One study has suggested that amplification involving the EGFR mutant allele is associated with increased benefit from EGFR TKI therapy [6], whereas acquired amplification of the wild-type allele of EGFR has been described in association with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [5].

While anti-EGFR trials in unselected patients with GEC have not demonstrated any efficacy [4-6], some studies have suggested that anti-EGFR antibodies (e.g. cetuximab) [7,8] and/or tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. gefitinib) [9] may be efficacious in GEC with EGFR amplification.

There are known studies specifically investigating EGFR targeted therapies in ganglioneuroblastoma. In gliomas, multiple therapies - vaccines, EGFR inhibitors, EGFR antibodies, CAR T-cells, RNA-based therapies, etc. - have been evaluated for gliomas with EGFR amplification and/or EGFR vIII and have shown mixed results [2-16].

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for breast cancer with EGFR amplification. Preclinical studies have suggested that anti-EGFR antibodies (and possibly in combination with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors) may be an efficacious in breast cancer with EGFR amplification [4]. In clinical trials, the addition of the anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies cetuximab and/or panitumumab to cisplatin, carboplatin or anthracycline-based therapies may (modestly) improve response rates in triple-negative breast cancer [5-7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies such as cetuximab are FDA-approved for the treatment of head and neck squamous cell caricinoma and other cancers expressing EGFR. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors are FDA-approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer with specific EGFR mutations. However, clinical studies have shown that EGFR copy number is NOT predictive of response to these agents in either head and neck or lung squamous cell carcinoma [8,9].

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of biliary tract cancers. In other types of cancer, such as esophageal cancer, colorectal cancer, head and neck cancer and glioma, clinical studies have shown mixed results regarding the association between EGFR amplification and response to anti-EGFR antibodies and/or tyrosine kinase inhibitors [5-11]. As this sample was equivocal for EGFR amplification by this assay, evaluation of EGFR status using different method (e.g. EGFR FISH) is recommended, if clinical indicated.

In preclinical studies, EGFR amplification was associated with response to the anti-EGFR antibody cetuximab [9-12]. In clinical studies, anti-EGFR antibodies have not proven effective in gastric carcinoma as a whole (i.e. not selecting for EGFR-amplified cancers) [13-16]. However, several early clinical studies have suggested that EGFR amplification and/or overespression may be associated with response to treatment regimens containing anti-EGFR antibodies including cetuximab with cisplatin and cepecitabine [17], cetuximab with FOLFOX6 [18], cetuximab with oxaliplatin/leucovorin/5-fluoruracil [19] or nimotuzumab with ironotecan [20]. In another phase 2 trial, the EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor erlotinib was active in patients with gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma but not gastric, and no molecular correlate was found to be predictive of response [22]. In a phase 2 study, no clear response to lapatinib was shown in gastric cancers with overexpression [23].

The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073]. In patients with NSCLC, the two most commonly found EGFR gene mutations are deletions in exon 19 (with conserved deletion of the LREA sequence) in 45% of patients with EGFR mutations and a point mutation in exon 21 (L858R in 40%), as in this specimen. Both mutations result in activation of the tyrosine kinase domain, and both are associated with sensitivity to the small-molecule EGFR TKIs [PMIDs: 15118073, 19483740, NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 3.2026].

EGFR L858R with EGFR low-level copy number gain (equivocal for amplification):
EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1].  A low-level EGFR copy number gain was also detected. EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-3]. EGFR amplification that is present prior to TKI therapy more commonly affects the mutant EGFR allele [2-3], as appears to be the case in this sample.

CDK4 copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain involving the CDK4 gene was detected, consistent with CDK4 amplification. CDK4 encodes a cyclin dependent kinase that normally phosphorylates the retinoblastoma gene product (Rb) during the G1/S transition. Amplification of CDK4 resulting in increased CDK4 expression has been described at a low incidence in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1].

MYC copy number gain (amplification): 
A copy number gain of the MYC gene was detected, consistent with MYC amplification. MYC (c-MYC) is a transcription factor involved in growth signaling. Amplification of MYC, as seen in this specimen, is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and may be associated with a poor prognosis, particularly in early stage disease [1-4].

EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1].  A low-level EGFR copy number gain was also detected (approximately 4-6 copies; considered equivocal for amplification). EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-4]. EGFR amplification that is present prior to TKI therapy more commonly affects the mutant EGFR allele [2-4], as appears to be the case in this sample.

MET amplification:
A copy number gain of the MET gene was detected (approximately __ copies), consistent with MET amplification. Amplification of MET resulting in increased MET expression is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-3]. MET amplification is a well-described mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [4-7]. Of note, this patient has undergone TKI treatment based on the previously identified activating EGFR mutation. The origninal, pre-treatment lung biopsy specimen  did NOT demonstrate the MET copy number gain identified in the current specimen. Therefore this acquired copy number alteration may reflect a mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
NSCLC with EGFR L858R is sensitive to multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies. According to NCCN Guidelines, osimertinib (Tagrisso) is a preferred first-line EGFR TKI option for NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R (or exon 19 deletion). Other recommended first-line therapies include lazertinib+amivantamab-vmjw (Lazcluze+Rybrevant) or osimertinib with pemetrexed and cisplatin/carboplatin [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026]. 
 
NSCLC with EGFR L858R is sensitive to multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies. According to NCCN Guidelines, osimertinib (Tagrisso) is a preferred first-line EGFR TKI option for NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R (or exon 19 deletion). Single-agent erlotinib, afatinib, gefitinib, or dacomitinib are other recommended first-line treatment options [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 3.2026]. 
 
Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified in this specimen.

In patients with NSCLC, the two most commonly found EGFR gene mutations are deletions in exon 19 (with conserved deletion of the LREA sequence) in 45% of patients with EGFR mutations and a point mutation in exon 21 (L858R in 40%), as in this specimen. Both mutations result in activation of the tyrosine kinase domain, and both are associated with sensitivity to the small-molecule EGFR TKIs, such as afatinib, dacomitinib, erlotinib, gefitinib, and osimertinib [1,2,3]. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [3]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified in this specimen.

The impact of this copy number alteration on response to EGFR TKI therapy is uncertain. In one study, concurrent CDK4 amplification was identified in pre-treatment samples from 10% (21/200) of lung cancers with EGFR mutations, and, in this study, CDK4 amplification was NOT associated with resistance to EGFR inhibitors [2]. However, in osimertinib acquired resistance, abnormal cell cycle regulation has been reported to be common, including CCND1, CCNE1, CDK4, CDK6 amplification and CDKN2A mutations [3-4].
 
A phase 2 study of the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib (PD-0332991) showed clinical efficacy in well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcoma with CDK4 amplification [5]. In one case report, a NSCLC patient with a sensitive EGFR mutation and CDK4 amplification responded to the combination of an EGFR inhibitor and a CDK4/6/ inhibitor [6].

Some observational studies have suggested that MYC amplification may be associated with acquired or intrinsic resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors [5-6]. There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified NSCLC; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [7-9].

This mutation is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,5] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR L858R including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [6]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [6]. One study has suggested that amplification involving the EGFR mutant allele is associated with increased benefit from EGFR TKI therapy [7]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

Both preclinical [8,9] and several clinical reports have shown that patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC with acquired TKI resistance resulting from MET amplification respond to combined EGFR and MET TKI therapy [10-15]. There are no known descriptions of all three variants affecting the same allele; however, G719S (and other mutations affecting G719) are frequently associated with other concomitant EGFR mutations. G719S is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and is known to result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1-2]. E709 mutations, including E709K, have also been described in a small subset of NSCLC [3-4]. E709 mutations frequently co-occur with other EGFR mutations including G719 mutations (as seem in this specimen) [5]. The K714N mutation is rare, but has also been described in NSCLC [6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While several studies have shown that G719 mutations in NSCLC are also sensitive to these inhibitors [7-14] and afatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR G719 mutations, the efficacy of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors with a single allele affected by all three mutations is unknown as there are no descriptions of specific set of mutations. However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitive EGFR mutation (G719S, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [3-6]. The impact of the K714N mutation on potential sensitivity to these therapies is unknown.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The FDA recently granted accelerated approval for 2 different therapies targeting EGFR exon 20 insertions in NSCLC. Mobocertinib (Exkivity) approval was based on a study with an overall response rate of 28% and median duration of 17.5 months [2]. Amivantamab-vmjw (Rybrevant) is a bispecific antibody whose approval was based on a study with an overall response rate of 40% and median duration of 11.1 months [3]. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines, EGFR exon 20 (EGFRex20) mutations (other than EGFR p.T790M) are a heterogeneous group, some of which are responsive to targeted therapy and that require detailed knowledge of the specific alteration. Most EGFRex20 alterations are generally associated with lack of response to first-, second-, and third-generation EGFR TKI therapy, with select exceptions: p.A763_Y764insFQEA is associated with sensitivity to TKI therapy and p.A763_Y764insLQEA may be associated with sensitivity to first- and third-generation TKI therapy [16]. G719D
Several studies have suggested that G719 mutations are more sensitive to second-generation EGFR inhibitors (e.g. afatinib) than first-generation EGFR inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib) [1-2,13-17]. Afatinib is also the only tyrosine kinase inhibitor that is FDA-approved for the treatment of lung cancers harboring these mutations.

Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in glioma often affect the extracellular domain - as is the case for G598V. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [18-20]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [11-12,18, 21-22]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [11-12,18]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [18].

However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitiviting EGFR mutation (G719X, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [1-4].

However, the EGFR mutation in this specimen affects the extracellular domain. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR kinase inhibitors typically employed in NSCLC [12]; response to these inhibitors among glioblastoma patients in clinical studies has been disappointing [13-15]. A phase 1/2 study of afatinib with or without temozolomide in recurrent glioblastoma patients showed a non-statistically significant correlation between EGFRvIII expression and minimally improved outcome with afatinib therapy [17]. Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, preclinical and clinical studies have shown that extracellular mutations (like P596R) [9-13] and exon 20 (like V774M) [14-16] are poorly inhibited by these EGFR inhibitors.
 
Newer agents targeting EGFR have demonstrated evidence of potential efficacy in lung cancer with EGFR exon 20 mutations; however, these agents do NOT demonstrate good brain penetration. A newer EGFR inhibitor, mobocertinib (EXKIVITY; TAK-788) was recently (9/15/2021) approved by the FDA for the treatment of lung cancer with EGFR exon 20 insertions [17]. However, this drug has demonstrated disappointing CNS penetration. Amivantamab, an EGFR/MET bispecific antibody, received FDA breakthrough therapy designation and the ongoing Phase 1 CRYSALIS study (NCT02609776) has shown promising preliminary results. This medication would also not be active across the blood brain barrier. A newer EGFR inhibitor poziotinib has shown significant potency for EGFR exon 20 mutations [18]. However, in the ZENITH20 trial involving poziotinib in lung cancer patients with EGFR exon 20 mutations, the reported overall response rate was 30% and many patients experienced significant toxicity at the doses evaluated [19].

EGFR E709_T710delinsD
EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase that is activated by EGF family extracellular ligands. Binding of EGFR by its ligands, including EGF ligands and transforming growth factor alpha, activates downstream signaling pathways including the canonical MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascades. EGFR exon 18 deletions (including  E709_T710delinsD) are less common but well-described mutations in non-small cell lung cancer [1-4].  According to NCCN guidelines, many of the less commonly observed alterations in EGFR, which cumulatively account for ~10% of EGFR-mutation positive NSCLC (ie, exon 19 insertions, p.L861Q, p.G719X, p.S768I), are also associated with responsiveness to certain EGFR TKIs, such as osimertinib and afatinib, and should be considered on a mutation-specific basis, when possible [12]. EGFR  E709_T710delinsD lies just outside of the protein kinase domain and is characterized as oncogenic.

Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with acquired TKI resistance (such as T790M) were identified.

EGFR variant III (EGFRvIII):
EGFR variant III (vIII) is a rearrangement that results in the deletion of exons 2 through 7, fusing exon 1 with exon 8 and is known to be oncogenic. This molecular alteration is well-described in patients with glioblastoma [PMID: 2981413, 16133418, 2168866, 2236070, 1584765, 1557402, 8845302, 8700557]. EGFRvIII results in a receptor incapable of binding any ligand but with constitutive, low-level signaling [PMID: 26282175, 9006938], partially due to impaired endocytosis and degradation [PMID: 17372273]. This molecular alteration frequently co-occurs with EGFR amplification which was observed in this case.

EGFR variant III (vIII) is a rearrangement that results in the deletion of exons 2 through 7, fusing exon 1 with exon 8. This molecular alteration is well-described in many different neoplasms, particularly non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-4] as well as glioblastomas [5-8]. Several studies have suggested this mutation occurs exclusively in squamous cell carcinoma - not in adenocarcinoma [1-4]. EGFRvIII effects the extracellular domain of the EGFR protein and has been shown to be oncogenic [9,10] rendering the EGFR receptor incapable of binding any ligand but with consititutive, low-level signaling [11,12], partially due to impaired endocytosis and degradation [13].

The in-frame deletion of exons 2 though 7 within the EGFR gene (also known as EGFRvIII) is well described in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) [1-4]. This deletion has been shown to be oncogenic [5,6] rendering the EGFR receptor incapable of binding any ligand but with consititutive, low-level signaling [7,8], partially due to impaired endocytosis and degradation [9]. This molecular alteration frequently co-occurrs with EGFR amplification which was not observed in this case [10]. The molecular alteration is associated with inferior prognosis [11,12]. There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for gliomas with EGFRvIII. While early studies intimated the therapeutic potential of anti-EGFRvIII vaccines [13,14], results from a recent phase 3 trial have been disappointing [15], possibly due to dynamic regulation of EGFRvIII expression [16]. First generation EGFR inhibitors, which are efficacious in EGFR-mutant lung cencer, have not been effective in GBM with EGFRvIII [17,18]. Studies investigating the utility of second and third generation EGFR inhibitors are underway [19,20]. While anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies (efficacious in RAS-WT colorectal cancer) have proven ineffective in GBM [21], antibody-based therapies directed at EGFRvIII (e.g. mAB806, 125I mAB425, bscEGFRvIIIxCD3) have shown promising preclinical and early clinical results [22-24]. Other immune-based therapies including T cells with chimeric antigen receptor (CART-T cells) have also shown promising preclinical and early clinical results [25]. Finally, RNA-based therapies are currently being evaluated in preclinical studies [26,27]. Relevant clinical trials in the US currently recruiting patients include NCT01454596 (phase 1/2 trial of CAR T cells with chemotherapy, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD), NCT02664363 (phase 1 trial of CAR T cells, Preston Robert Tisch Brain Tumor Center at Duke, Durham, NC) and NCT02343406 (phase 2 of anti-EGFR antibody ABT-414, multiple centers outside Michigan).

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for gliomas with EGFRvIII. Multiple therapies - vaccines, EGFR inhibitors, EGFR antibodies, CAR T-cells, RNA-based therapies, etc. - have been evaluated for gliomas with EGFR amplification and/or EGFRvIII and have shown mixed results [PMID: 23248284, 23363814,25586468, 27020557, 24310612, 15035290, 19825799, 25140039, 25939761, 19491283, 20345222, 25696001, 12205508, 12743604, 25895099, 25696001]. In gliomas with MGMT promoter methylation, EGFRvIII upregulates DNA mismatch repair, resulting in increased temozolomide sensitivity [PMID: 32066879].

Preclinical studies have shown that extracellular mutations like EGFRvIII are poorly inhibited by EGFR inhibitors that bind competitively with ATP in the active "type I" EGFR comfirmation (all EGFR inhibitors FDA-approved for NSCLC; erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, and osimertinib) [1,14] and the response to these inhibitors among gliobastoma patients in clinical studies has been disappointing [15-17]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [1,14]. Neratinib and lapatinib are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of HER2+ breast cancer.

variants.variant_description:
Two EGFR mutations were detected - L858R and T790M. Because these two mutations affect different exons, it is not known if these two mutations affect the same allele (in cis) or different alleles (in trans). These two mutations are present at similar variant allele frequencies (38-39%). The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 15118073]. T790M is most commonly observed as a mechanism of acquired resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) [PMID: 17085664, 15728811, 15737014]. This mutation results in increased EGFR affinity for adenosine triphosphate and reduced binding to EGFR TKI [PMID: 18227510].
 
There is no known history of treatment with TKI therapy. The incidence of EGFR T790M prior to TKI therapy (TKI-naïve) is dependent on the detection methods employed, but when observed, has only been described at low variant allele frequencies [PMID: 33116639, 35884570, 26973206, 30936123, 25882755], unlike this specimen. 
 
Germline EGFR T790M mutations have also been described in association with a germline predisposition to NSCLC [PMID: 16258541, 17510392, 22588155, 24736066, 34869019]. The variant allele frequency of the T790M mutation is similar to that of the L858R mutation and is below 50% (39%); however, this allele freqency may be altered by somatic copy number alterations in this specimen. Evaluation of non-neoplastic tissue is required to differentiate germline from from somatic mutations.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While EGFR L858R is associated with sensitivity to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib) [PMID: 15118073, 19483740], EGFR T790M confers resistance to most EGFR inhibitors and is commonly seen as mechanism of acquired resistance to TKI therapy [PMID: 17085664, 15728811, 15737014, 17020982]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [PMID: 27959700, 24893891] and is currently FDA-approved for this application. No molecular alterations associated with acquired resistance to osimertinib [PMID: 29883838, 29406987] were identified in this specimen.

In one review [2], the response rate among NSCLC harboring exon 19 insertions (n=18) was 56% with median time to progression of 10.4 months. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified in this specimen.
