A copy number gain of the MYC gene was detected, consistent with MYC amplification. MYC (c-MYC) is a transcription factor involved in growth signalling. MYC amplification resulting in MYC overexpression is well-described in cervical squamous cell carcinoma [1-3].

The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. The low- level EGFR V592I is rare and has not been described in NSCLC and has not been functionally or biochemically characterized. EGFR copy number gain was also detected. EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Preclinical studies have demonstrated potential efficacy of BET bromodomain inhibitors in other cancers with MYC amplification [4-7]. Other preclinical studies have suggested that inhibition of CDK7 and CDK12/13 may be efficacious [8].

L858R mutation is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,5] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR L858R including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [6]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [6]. One study has suggested that amplification involving the EGFR mutant allele is associated with increased benefit from EGFR TKI therapy [7].No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E709 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI reponse is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity.  Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations were detected on the same allele (in cis). EGFR A289V [1-5] and G598V [1,6-8] have both been reported in gliomas. These mutation affects the extracellular domain and have been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [9].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in gliomas affect the extracellular domain - as seen in this specimen. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [10]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [10-14]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [10-12]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [10].

variants.variant_description: Two nucleotide substitutions (c.2497T>C, L833V and c.2512C>G, L838V) were detected on the same allele of EGFR. Both L833V and L838V mutations are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and nearly always co-occur with another amino acid subsitution, most commonly on the same allele [1-8], as seen in this specimen. L833V has also been known to co-occur with the H835L [1-8] and L858R mutation [9-11]. L838V has also been described in association with L858R [8].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with specific EGFR mutations (e.g. exon 19 deletions, L858R) including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and osimertinib. These drugs are not approved for the mutation(s) detected in this specimen and little clinical information is available regarding their impact on response to TKI therapy (due to their rarity). In case reports, 2 patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR L833V and H835L compound mutations achieved a near-complete response to gefitinib without progression until 34 weeks following the initiation of TKI therapy [1] or stable disease [7]. Another patient with this mutation (as well as an E709K mutation) achieved a partial response on afatinib [2]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified.

L833V has also been known to co-occur with the L858R mutation [9-11].

Diagnostically significant molecular alteration
EGFR amplification with multiple EGFR mutations:
A copy number gain involving the EGFR gene was detected (approximately 10 copies), consistent with EGFR amplification. EGFR amplification associated with increased EGFR expression is well-described in gliomas [1] and frequently co-occurs with EGFR variant III (vIII) [2], which was NOT observed in this specimen. EGFR mutations have also been reported in gliomas, with A289V (extracellular domain) and V774M (kinase domain) being relatively common.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Absence of IDH mutation and the presence of EGFR amplification in gliomas appearing histologically as WHO grade II or III may follow an aggressive course, and therefore in the right context these may be a grade IV glioblastoma according to the 5th edition WHO classification [3]. This designation is based on the observation that IDH-wildtype gliomas histologically grade II or III with EGFR amplification (or +7/-10 or TERT promoter mutation) have clinical outcomes similar to IDH-wildtype glioblastoma [4-10].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for gliomas with EGFR amplification or mutations. The interactions of the EGFR amplification and multiple mutations on potential response to therapy are uncertain.

variants.variant_description: The P699L mutation detected in this specimen is a rare mutation identified previously in lung neoplasia [1].This variant is within exon 18 and is not a commonly recurrent alteration found in cancer. Its function is therefore still uncertain.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. In the rare reported variant within a lung adenocarcinoma of P699L, this patient did not respond to TKI treatment [1]. EGFR inhitor use in melanomas has shown some promise when combined with other treatments to increase apoptosis and invasiveness, but these studies have not be performed on patients with this specific variant [2,3]. In other tumor types, preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [4].

variants.variant_description: An EGFR exon 19 deletion as well as a single nucleotide substitution were detected affecting the same allele. EGFR exon 19 deletion/insertion mutations are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. A755D has been described in combination with exon 19 deletion/insertion mutations [2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
This mutation is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1-5] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. The FDA has also approved ramucirumab in combination with erlotinib for first line treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 (L858R) mutations. Median progression-free survival was 19.4 months in the ramucirumab plus erlotinib arm compared with 12.4 months in the placebo plus erlotinib arm.
 
For earlier stage disease (stage IB to IIIA), adjuvant osimertinib was shown to result in improved disease-free survival (90% disease-free at 24 months compared to 44% for placebo; ADAURA trial) [6].
 
Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [7]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [7]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations are detected. EGFR A289V has been reported in gliomas [1-4]. This mutation affects the extracellular domain and has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [5]. EGFR V774M has also been reported in gliomas [6] as well as other neoplasms, particularly lung cancer [7-11]. This mutation lies with exon 20, encoding the kinase domain of EGFR.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, preclinical and clinical studies have shown that extracellular mutations (like A289V) [12-16] and exon 20 (like V774M) [17-19] are poorly inhibited by these EGFR inhibitors.
 
Newer agents targeting EGFR have demonstrated evidence of potential efficacy in lung cancer with EGFR exon 20 mutations; however, these agents do NOT demonstrate good brain penetration. A newer EGFR inhibitor, mobocertinib (EXKIVITY; TAK-788) was recently (9/15/2021) approved by the FDA for the treatment of lung cancer with EGFR exon 20 insertions [20]. However, this drug has demonstrated disappointing CNS penetration. Amivantamab, an EGFR/MET bispecific antibody, received FDA breakthrough therapy designation and the ongoing Phase 1 CRYSALIS study (NCT02609776) has shown promising preliminary results. This medication would also not be active across the blood brain barrier. A newer EGFR inhibitor poziotinib has shown significant potency for EGFR exon 20 mutations [21]. However, in the ZENITH20 trial involving poziotinib in lung cancer patients with EGFR exon 20 mutations, the reported overall response rate was 30% and many patients experienced significant toxicity at the doses evaluated [22].

variants.variant_description: Three EGFR exon 18 mutations - G719S, E709K and K714N - were detected. G719S (and other mutations affecting G719) is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and is known to result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1-2]. E709 mutations, including E709K, have also been described in a small subset of NSCLC [3-4]. E709 mutations frequently co-occur with other EGFR mutations including G719 mutations (as seem in this specimen) [5]. The K714N mutation is rare, but have also been described in NSCLC [6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation. Several studies have shown that G719 mutations in NSCLC are also sensitive to these inhibitors [7-14] and afatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR G719 mutations.
 
No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E709 or K714 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI response is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity. However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitive EGFR mutation (G719S, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [3-6].
 
Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

This EGFR R108G mutation affects the extracellular domain and has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [1, 6]. Similar mutations affecting the extracellular domain are also very frequent in glioblastomas [4].

Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in non-small cell lung cancer (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [7]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [8-12]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [7]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [7].

variants.variant_description: EGFR exon 19 deletion mutations including the one seen here are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), resulting in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. A low-level EGFR copy number gain was also detected (approximately 4-6 copies; considered equivocal for amplification). EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [2-4]. EGFR amplification that is present prior to TKI therapy more commonly affects the mutant EGFR allele [2-4], as appears to be the case in this sample.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The EGFR mutation detected in this sample is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1, 5-7] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib osimertinib, and dacomitinib. In May 2020, the FDA also approved ramucirumab in combination with erlotinib for first line treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 (L858R) mutations. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [8]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [8]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified. One study has suggested that amplification involving the EGFR mutant allele is associated with increased benefit from EGFR TKI therapy [9].

variants.variant_description:
Alterations in EGFR have frequently been reported in gliomas [PMID: 23917401, 28201779, 28481359, 17177598, 25079552]. The EGFR R108K mutation affects the extracellular domain and has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [PMID: 23917401, 29731991]. Similar mutations affecting the extracellular domain are also identified in glioblastomas [PMID: 17177598, 37446288].

An EGFR R108K mutation was detected in this specimen - identical to the mutation detected within the left temporal brain mass. This mutation has been shown to be oncogenic, conferring anchorage-independent growth and tumorigenic potential when stably expressed in NIH-3T3 cells [1]. This mutation has NOT been described in a primary lung cancer. However, the mutation has frequently been reported in gliomas [1-4]. Similar mutations affecting the extracellular domain are also very frequent in glioblastomas [4] but are rare in primary lung cancers [5]. There are also individual reports of this mutation ocuring in gastroesophageal cancer [4] and liposarcoma [6]. Therefore, molecular data from this specimen suggests that this tumor is more likely to represent a metastasis rather than a primary lung cancer.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The EGFR mutation detected in this specimen affects the extracellular domain instead of the tyrosine kinase domain, as seen with most EGFR mutations observed in gliomas. Studies have shown that these extracellular domain mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in non-small cell lung cancer (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [PMID: 22588883, 37446288]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [PMID: 24120142, 15035290, 23363814, 26423602, 25140039]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [PMID: 22588883, 20459769].

Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, the EGFR mutation detected in this specimen affects the extracellular domain - not the tyrosine kinase domain. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [7]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among gliobastoma patients has also been disappointing [8-12]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [7]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [7].

variants.variant_description: The EGFR single nucleotide substitution resulting in an EGFR I744V mutations seen in exon 19 of this specimen (present at an allele frequency of 15%, less than expected for the estimated tumor cellularity) has been rarely described as a somatic mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-4]. This specific mutation has not been functionally characterized in any known study.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While multiple tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies are FDA-approved for metastatic NSCLC for certain known sensitizing EGFR mutations (e.g., erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib), none are specifically approved for NSCLC harboring an EGFR I744V mutation.  There have been rare reports of NSCLC patients with this I744V alteration treated with a TKI, with mixed response: one progression (erlotinib) and one partial response (gefitinib) [1, 2]. Given the relative paucity of data on this mutation, the clinical implications of this finding is uncertain.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations - E709V and G719A - were identified within exon 18 on the same allele (in cis). EGFR G719 amino acid substitution mutations, including G719A, are well-described mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream MAPK and PIK3CA signalling [1-10]. E709 mutations, including E709V, have also been described in NSCLC [1-10] but has not been biochemically characterized. While G719X mutations may occur in isolation or with other EGFR mutations, E709 mutations always co-occur with other EGFR mutations including G719X, L861Q and L858R [1-7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation; however, afatinib appears to be the most effective for G719 mutations [1,8,9] and is currently the only FDA-approved treatment of NSCLC with EGFR G719 mutations. No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E709 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI reponse is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity. However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitiviting EGFR mutation (G719X, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [1-4]. Importantly, no mutations associated with TKI resistance were detected.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations - G719A and L707W - were identified within exon 18 on the same allele (in cis). EGFR G719 amino acid substitution mutations, including G719A, are well-described mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream MAPK and PIK3CA signalling [1-10]. L707W, has also been described in NSCLC [11] but has not been biochemically characterized. G719X mutations may occur in isolation or with other EGFR mutations [1-7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation; however, afatinib appears to be the most effective for G719 mutations [1,8,9] and is currently the only FDA-approved treatment of NSCLC with EGFR G719 mutations. No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E707 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI reponse is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity.  Importantly, no mutations associated with TKI resistance were detected.

variants.variant_description:
Two EGFR mutations - L858R and I744M - were identified. Because these mutations affect different exons, it is unknown if they are present on the same allele (in cis) or opposite alleles (in trans). The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. EGFR I744M has been rarely described in lung carcinoma, including one patient who harbored a concomitant EGFR L858R, similar to that seen in this specimen [2-3]. While not extensively studied, there is some in vitro evidence suggesting this mutation harbors oncogenic properties [3].

Low-level MYC copy number gain (equivocal for amplification): 
A low-level copy number gain of the MYC (c-MYC) gene was detected (considered equivocal for amplification). MYC (c-MYC) is a transcription factor involved in growth signaling. Amplification of MYC, as seen in this specimen, is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and may be associated with a poor prognosis, particularly in early stage disease [1-4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The L858R mutation is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,4] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR L858R including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [5]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation. 
 
No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR I744 mutations, and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI response is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity. While one report of a patient harboring a single EGFR I744M mutation showed sensitivity to TKI therapy [3], another report demonstrated lack of response [6]. However, the tumor with compound EGFR L858R and I744M mutations reported previously in the literature did show sensitivity to gefitinib [2]. 
 
Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified NSCLC; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [5-7]. In addition, MYC amplification is associated with DNA damage [8] raising the possible utility of therapies targeting DNA damage repair deficiencies such as PARP inhibitors and ATR kinase inhibitors.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations – V843L and T790M - were detected. Because these mutations affect different exons, it is unknown if they are present on the same allele (in cis) or opposite alleles (in trans). V843L mutation is a rare mutation that has been previously reported in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and is known to result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. T790M, detected at a low level in this specimen, is the most common mechanism of acquired resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) [2-5]. This mutation results in increased EGFR affinity for adenosine triphosphate and reduced binding to EGFR TKI [6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, one study [1] reported that patient with V843L mutations did not respond to first- generation TKIs. T790M confers resistance to first and second generation EGFR TKI [6]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [7-8] and is currently FDA-approved for this application [9]. Treatment of EGFR T790M+ NSCLC with osimertinib is also a category 1 recommendation in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [10].  No molecular alterations associated with acquired resistance to osimertinib [11-12] were identified in this specimen.

variants.variant_description:
Somatic variant of uncertain clinical significance
EGFR S768_V769delinsIL:
Two EGFR mutations affecting adjacent codons (S768I and V769L) are present on the same allele. This combination of mutations (also designated SV768IL) has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-7] as has S768I combined with other mutations [8-9]. S768_V769delinsIL has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activations of EGFR and downstream ERK and AKT signaling [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While afatinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR S768I, studies concerning TKI sensitivity when S768I is combined with V769L have been mixed. In one report, a patient harboring these mutations was resistant to afatinib [2], while, in another, a response was reported [3]. In other reports, the combination of these mutations conferred resistance to gefitinib [4] and osimertinib [1]. Case reports have identified S768_V769delinsIL in association with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [1,5]. Given the inconsistency and relative paucity of data on this mutation, the clinical implications of this finding is uncertain.

variants.variant_description: EGFR V843L and T790M:

EGFR [G719C;S768I]:
Two EGFR mutations are detected - G719C in exon 18 and S768I in exon 20.These mutations affect the same allele of the EGFR gene. Both EGFR G719 mutations (including G719C) and the S768I mutation detected are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream MAPK and PIK3CA signalling [1-14]. Both mutations frequently co-occurs with other EGFR mutations as seen in this specimen [1-7,12-14].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Afatinib (Gilotrif) is FDA-approved for metastatic NSCLC harboring specific EGFR mutations including both S768I and G719 mutations. Several studies have suggested that G719 and S768I mutations are more sensitive to second-generation EGFR inhibitors (e.g. afatinib) than first-generation EGFR inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib) [1,8,9,15-18]. Afatinib is also the only tyrosine kinase inhibitor that is FDA-approved for the treatment of lung cancers harboring these mutations. The treatment of metastic EGFR-mutated NSCLC with an EGFR inhibitor is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [19]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with acquired TKI resistance (such as T790M) were identified.

variants.variant_description:
Low level EGFR copy number gain:
A low copy number gain affecting the EGFR gene, consistent with equivocal for amplification, was detected in this specimen. EGFR copy number gain is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) but more frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [1-3] (seen in this specimen). Studies have suggested that EGFR copy number gain in NSCLC is associated with an inferior prognosis, particularly in squamous cell carcinoma [4,5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While several studies have investigated the combined impact of EGFR activation mutations and EGFR amplification [6,7], there are no known clinical studies investigating the response of NSCLC with EGFR amplification in the absence of an EGFR mutation to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. However, several studies have suggested that anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies (e.g. cetuximab, necitumumab), in combination with chemotherapy, immunotherapy or antiangiogenic therapy are more efficacious in NSCLC with EGFR amplification (particularly squamous cell carcinoma) [8-10].

variants.variant_description: This single nucleotide substitution has been described as a somatic mutation in non-small cell lung cancer [1,2], colorectal cancer [3,4] and endometrial cancer [5]. This mutation has not been functionally characterized in any known study.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: In preclinical studies, EGFR A864V was shown to confer sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) afatinib and sapitinib (AZD8931) [3]. A non-small cell lung cancer patient harboring an EGFR A864V mutation was reported to respond to the combination of EGFR inhibitor gefitinib with fulvestrant [1].

variants.variant_description: The tandem nucleotide substitution resulting in an EGFR L747P mutation in exon 19 detected in this specimen is rare, but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-2]. EGFR L747P is located in the terminal hydrophobic center of the βchain of the N terminal in the kinase domain. Functional studies have found that this mutation changes the structure of the hydrophobic center and causes continuous activation of EGFR kinase [3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While multiple TKI therapies are FDA-approved for metastatic NSCLC for certain known sensitizing EGFR mutations (e.g. erlotinib, gefinitinib, afatinib, osimertinib), none are specifically approved for NSCLC harboring an EGFR L747P mutation. Several case reports have described patients with EGFR L747P-mutant tumors who did not respond to first and third generation EGFR-TKI’s, suggesting that this mutation might confer primary resistance [4-5]. However, there is one case report of a patient with an EGFR L747P mutant lung adenocarcinoma who responded to afatinib therapy [3]. Another study identified 9 patients with EGFR L747P mutations; 2 of the 3 patients treated with afatinib achieved a partial response [1]. A similar small series of patients with uncommon EGFR mutations also suggested response with afatinib [2].

variants.variant_description: The EGFR L861Q mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1,2]. The EGFR G724A mutation also identified in this specimen is much more rare, but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [3]. This mutation has not been functionally or clinically characterized. The impact of this mutation on response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy is uncertain. Of note, the mutations are present on separate amplicons, and thus, it cannot be determined whether they are present on the same or different alleles. An EGFR copy number gain was also detected. EGFR amplification is well-described in NSCLC and, as in this case, frequently co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations [4-6]. EGFR amplification that is present prior to TKI therapy more commonly affects the mutant EGFR allele [4-6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefinitib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation; however, only afatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR L861Q. Both preclinical [7-8] and clinical [8,10] studies have demonstrated the sensitivity of this mutation to afatinib while preclinical [7,12] and clinical [13,14] studies suggest that erlotinib and gefitinib are less effective for this mutation. One study has suggested that amplification involving the EGFR mutant allele is associated with increased benefit from EGFR TKI therapy [15]

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations - L858R and E709V - were identified. Because these mutations affect different exons, it is unknown if they affect the same allele (in cis) or opposite alleles (in trans). The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. E709 mutations, including E709V, have also been described in NSCLC [1-11] but has not been biochemically characterized. E709 mutations virtually always co-occur with other EGFR mutations including G719X, L861Q and L858R [3-9].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The L858R mutation is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,2] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR L858R including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [12]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [3]. 
 
No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E709 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI response is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity. However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitive EGFR mutation (G719X, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [3-6].
 
Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance (such as T790M or C797S) were identified.

variants.variant_description: The tandem nucleotide substitution resulting an EGFR G779F mutation detected in this specimen is rare, but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMID: 29765525, 31715539, 15788655, 28481359, 16467085, 27875527], as have other mutations affecting this codon including G779S [PMID: 18676761, 17626639, 18172267], G779D [PMID: 21057810] and G779C [PMID: 17285735]. The recurrent nature of this mutation in lung cancer suggests that it is likely oncogenic; however, functional studies have not been performed to determine the effect of this mutation on protein function.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are no known clinical studies that have investigated the sensitivity of this particular EGFR mutation to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. 
 
Other EGFR exon 20 mutations, particularly insertion mutations, are more common and (other than A763_Y764insFQEA) are associated with primary resistance to achievable doses of the first-generation, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies that are currently FDA-approved for some EGFR-mutated NSCLC (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [PMID: 18676761, 27468240]. Several studies have shown a more robust in vitro response of exon 20 mutated lung cancer to second-generation, irreversible EGFR inhibitors such as afatinib [PMID: 16818618, 18408761, 18089823]; however, the IC50 values observed may fail to correspond with achievable plasma concentrations and a recent clinical trial investigating the utility of afatinib demonstrated disappointing results in NSCLC patients with exon 20 insertions [PMID: 26051236]. Similarly, osimertinib has demonstrated preclinical activity with on partial response in a subset of patients in clinical studies [PMID: 26051236, 29483211]. 
 
A newer EGFR inhibitor (poziotinib; Spectrum Pharmaceuticals) was specifically designed to inhibit EGFR exon 20 insertions. Based on in vitro studies, this inhibitor is able to overcome the steric hindrance that limits efficacy of other inhibitors and can be 40 to 100 times more potent than afatinib or osimertinib in cells with EGFR exon 20 insertions (IC50 0.3 - 1.84nM) [PMID: 29686424]. In an ongoing phase 2 trial at MD Anderson (NCT03066206), poziotinib demonstrated an objective response rate of 73% (8 of 11) in NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions [PMID: 35820397]. Another EGFR inhibitor designed for exon 20 insertions [TAK-788 (AP32788)] was also shown to potently inhibitor EGFR exon 20 mutations in preclinical studies (IC50 21-33 nM) [PMID: 33632773]; in early clinical studies, partial responses were observed in 3 of 14 evaluable NSCLC patients with EGFR or ERBB2 exon 20 insertions [PMID: 33632773]. Other novel EGFR inhibitors with preclinical evidence of efficacy include TAS6417 [PMID: 29748209],"compound 1A" [PMID: 29978938] and tarloxotinib [PMID: 33710795].

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations - L858R and E709V and G719A - were identified within exon 18 on the same allele (in cis). EGFR G719 amino acid substitution mutations, including G719A, are well-described mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream MAPK and PIK3CA signalling [1-10]. E709 mutations, including E709V, have also been described in NSCLC [1-10] but has not been biochemically characterized. While G719X mutations may occur in isolation or with other EGFR mutations, E709 mutations always co-occur with other EGFR mutations including G719X, L861Q and L858R [1-7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Of the available EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), afatinib appears to be the most effective for G719 mutations [1,8,9] and is currently FDA-approved for metastatic NSCLC with EGFR G719 mutations. No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E709 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI reponse is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity. However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitiviting EGFR mutation (G719X, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [1-4].

variants.variant_description: The V292 detected in this sample is within the extracellular domain of EGFR and has been reported (rarely) as a somatic variant in colorectal cancer [1-2]. However, this variant has also been reported as a germline (inherited) variant (rs150549265). While the variant allele frequency (approximately 27%) is more suggestive of a somatic variant, a germline variant cannot be definitively excluded. There are no known studies to determine the effect of this variant (if any) on protein function. The clinical significance of this variant is uncertain.

Two EGFR mutations - R108K and A289V - were detected. Because these two mutations were detected in separately sequenced regions, it is uncertain if they affect the same allele (in cis) or opposite alleles (in trans). Both mutations have been reported in glioma [1-5]. These mutations affect the extracellular domain and have been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for gliomas with EGFR amplification or mutations. The interactions of the EGFR amplification and multiple mutations on potential response to therapy are uncertain.

variants.variant_description:
EGFR G719A and L707W:
Two EGFR variants - G719A and L707W - affecting the same allele were detected in this specimen. EGFR G719 amino acid substitution mutations including G719A are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream MAPK and PIK3CA signalling [1-5]. The L707W variant also detected is rare, but has been described in NSCLC [6-8][9], often co-occurring with G719A [6-8]. Unlike G719A, L707W has not been biochemically characterized - the affect of this variant (if any) on protein function is unknown.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation; however, only afatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR G719 mutations. Importantly, no mutations known to be associated with TKI resistance were detected.

variants.variant_description: The P596L mutation detected in this specimen has been reported as a somatic mutation in gliomas of varying grade [1-5], as have other substitution mutations affecting the same amino acid including P596R [6]. These mutations lie within the extracellular domain of EGFR. The functional affect of P596L on protein function has not been investigated; however, the recurrent nature of this mutation suggests that it may be a driver mutation.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in glioma affect the extracellular domain - as seen in this specimen. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) which inhibit the active "type I" confirmation [7]. Response to these inhibitors in clinical studies among glioblastoma patients has also been disappointing [8-12]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [7]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib fails to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [7].

variants.variant_description: While the specific EGFR mutation identified in this specimen has not been reported, other exon 19 duplications/insertions in this region have been reported in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and have been shown to result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1-3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Both preclinical [3] and limited clinical studies [2-6] have suggested that EGFR exon 19 duplications/insertions are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy (e.g. erlotinib, afatinib and gefitinib). In one review [3], the response rate among NSCLC harboring exon 19 insertions (n=18) was 56% with median time to progression of 10.4 months. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified in this specimen.

variants.variant_description: The EGFR L858R and C797S mutations identified in this specimen are both well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), resulting in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling [1-9]. Of note, EGFR T790M was NOT detected in this specimen.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While EGFR L858R is associated with sensitivity to first, second and third generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) [1,9,10], EGFR C797S confers resistance to pyrimidine-based EGFR inhibitors such as osimertinib [2-9]. However, both preclinical [3,4] and clinical [5-8] studies indicate that NSCLC harboring EGFR C797S (in the absence of EGFR T790M in cis) retain sensitivity to quinazoline-based inhibitors such as erlotinib, gefitinib and afatinib. Patients treated with first or second generation EGFR inhibitor monotherapy following the acquisition of C797S can subsequently acquire an EGFR T790M mutation; therefore, combination therapy (osimertinib + first or second generation inhibitor) may prevent or delay progression [8], though the acquisition of EGFR T790M and C797S in cis would confer resistance to both therapies [5-8].

variants.variant_description: The EGFR V769L mutation identified in this specimen is rare, but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-6]. The effect of this mutation on EGFR protein function has not been evaluated. While this mutation often co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations including L858R [2-6], no other EGFR mutations were detected in this specimen.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While multiple TKI therapies are FDA-approved for metastatic NSCLC certain known sensitizing EGFR mutations (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib), none are specifically approved for NSCLC harboring an EGFR V769L mutation. Potential sensitivity to EGFR inhibitors to EGFR V769L mutated NSCLC has only been evaluated in the context of a concurrent EGFR S768I mutation. There are conflicting individual patient reports of NSCLC patients with EGFR V769L and S768I with response to afatinib [4] and primary resistance to afatinib [5] and gefitinib [6].

variants.variant_description:
EGFR p.[S768I; V769L] (also designated S768_V769delinsIL):
Two EGFR mutations affecting adjacent codon (S768I and V769L) are present on the same allele. This combination of mutations (often designated S768_V769delins IL) has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-6] as has S768I combined with other mutations [7,8].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While afatinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR S768I, studies concerning TKI sensitivity when S768I is combined with V769L have been mixed. In one report, a patient harboring these mutations was resistant to afatinib [1], while, in another, a response was reported [2]. In another report, [S768I; V769L] was resistant to gefinitib [3]. There is also one report of [S768I; V769L] identified in association with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [4]. Given the inconsistency and relative paucity of data on this mutation, the clinical implications of this finding is uncertain.

variants.variant_description: The EGFR D761Y mutation identified in this specimen is rare, but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-4]. The effect of this mutation on EGFR protein function has not been evaluated. While this mutation often co-occurs with activating EGFR mutations including L858R [1-4], no other EGFR mutations were detected in this specimen. One study [1] posited that D761Y represents an acquired, secondary resistance mutation to tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy; however, this study did not evaluate a pretreatment sample for the presence of this mutation, and other studies [2-4] have reported this mutation prior to any TKI treatment.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While multiple TKI therapies are FDA-approved for metastatic NSCLC certain known sensitizing EGFR mutations (e.g. erlotinib, gefinitinib, afatinib, osimertinib), none are specifically approved for NSCLC harboring an EGFR D761Y mutation. Potential sensitivity to EGFR inhibitors to EGFR D761Y mutated NSCLC has only been evaluated in the context of a concurrent EGFR L858R mutation. Preclinical studies have shown L858R/D761Y mutated cells to have modestly diminished sensitivity to gefinib compared to cells harboring L858R alone [1,2,5]. Individual cases of NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R and D761Y have reported a LACK of response to gefitinib [1-3]. However, prelinical studies have also suggested that irreversible EGFR inhibitors, particularly third-generation inhibitors (e.g. osimertinib, rociletinib), may be capable of overcoming this modest resistance [5].

variants.variant_description: The EGFR R776H mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-9] as have R776C mutations [10,11]. These mutations frequently co-occur with other EGFR mutations [1-7,10,11] including G719A [1-3]. In one report, a germline EGFR R776H variant was present within multiple family members who developed NSCLC including a patient who harbored a somatic G719A mutation on the same allele as the R776H variant [12]. While the allele frequencies of the R776H and G719A variants - both approximately 25% - in comparison with estimated percentage of neoplastic cells (approximately 50%) are suggestive of somatic mutations, this assay cannot definitively distinguish germline from somatic mutations without evaluating non-neoplastic tissue. EGFR R776H/C mutations have been shown to result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream growth signaling [13]. EGFR R776H mutations activate EGFR in a dimerization-dependent manner by preferentially adopting the acceptor position in the asymmetric dimer as well as increasing phosphorylation of monomeric EGFR [13].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The impact of the EGFR R776H mutation on response to EGFR inhibition is uncertain due to the rarity of this mutation. In one report, a patient harboring this mutation responded to gefitinib [8], and, in another, a patient with EGFR L858R and R776H mutations achieved a partial response to erlotinib [4]. Another patient with both an L861Q and R776H mutation had stable disease on gefitinib [5].

variants.variant_description: EGFR exon 19 deletion mutations are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]; the specific EGFR exon 19 deletion identified in this patient's tumor (L747_E749del) is uncommon but occurs in a hotspot region for frame-preserving deletions. In addition, a separate EGFR exon 19 missense mutation (K754E) is present in cis arrangement on the same allele as the EGFR exon 19 deletion; while this missense mutation is also relatively uncommon in lung cancer, it has been shown to be oncogenic in preclinical models and has previously been reported co-occuring with an exon 19 deletion [2,3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: EGFR exon 19 deletions are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,4], and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions, including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [5]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [5]. The clinical significance of the EGFR K754E mutation on the same allele as the exon 19 deletion is unclear; however, pre-clinical data suggests that tumors harboring this missense mutation may be less sensitive to some EGFR TKIs, including erlotinib [2].

variants.variant_description: While the EGFR mutation identified in this specimen is rare, this mutation, as well as other exon 19 duplications/insertions, has been reported in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and shown to result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 28089594, 22190593].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Both preclinical [PMID: 28098594] and limited clinical studies [PMID: 28089594, 22190593, 25279299, 29453495, 24736087] have suggested that EGFR exon 19 duplications/insertions are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy (e.g. erlotinib, afatinib and gefitinib). In one report [PMID: 37196448], the response rate among NSCLC harboring exon 19 insertions (n=26) was 69%. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified in this specimen.

variants.variant_description:
EGFR L858R and L861Q:
Two EGFR mutations were detected on separate alleles (in trans). The EGFR L858R and L861Q mutations identified in this specimen is both well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1,2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib, dacomitinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation; however, only afatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR L861Q. Both preclinical [3-5] and clinical [4,6] studies have demonstrated the sensitivity of this mutation to afatinib while preclinical [3,7] and clinical [8,9] studies suggest that erlotinib and gefitinib are less effective for this mutation. In a case report of a patient with both EGFR L858M and L861Q in cis, the combination of these mutations was associated with primary resistance to erlotinib and sensitivity to afatinib [10]. Preclinical studies and a case report have also suggested that osimertinib may be efficacious in tumors with these mutations [3,11]. Treatment of metastatic EGFR-mutated NSCLC with and EGFR inhibitor is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [12]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with acquired TKI resistance (such as T790M) were identified.

variants.variant_description: Two EGFR mutations - L858R and E709K - were identified. EGFR L858R is a common, well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. E709 mutations, including E709K, have also been described in NSCLC [1-10] but has not been biochemically characterized. While L858R mutations may occur in isolation, E709 mutations virtually always co-occur with other EGFR mutations including G719X, L861Q and L858R [3-9].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: EGFR L858R is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,2] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR L858R including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and osimertinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [10]. No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E709 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI reponse is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity. However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitiviting EGFR mutation (G719X, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [3-6].

variants.variant_description: Two nucleotide substitutions (c.2497T>C, L833V and c.2504A>T, H835L) were detected on the same allele of EGFR. This event could either be designated as a single deletion/insertion mutation or as two SNV mutations (albeit on the same allele). Both L833V and H835 are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and nearly always co-occur with another amino acid subsitution, most commonly with each other on the same allele [1-8], as seen in this specimen. L833V has also been known to co-occur with the L858R mutation [9-11].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with specific EGFR mutations (e.g. exon 19 deletions, L858R) including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and osimertinib. These drugs are not approved for the mutation(s) detected in this specimen and little clinical information is available regarding their impact on response to TKI therapy (due to their rarity). However, in one case report, a patient NSCLC harboring the same compound mutation achieved a near-complete response to gefitinib without progression until 34 weeks following the initiation of TKI therapy [1]. Another patient with this mutation (as well as an E709K mutation) achieved a partial response on afatinib [2]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified.

variants.variant_description: The A289T mutation detected in this specimen is well-described in gliomas of varying grade [1-3]. The mutation lies within the extracellular domain of EGFR [4] and has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in ligand-independent MAPK signaling and proliferation [5,6]. Other mutations affecting this residue, including A289V, have also been described in glioma and have been shown to be oncogenic [7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR kinase domain mutations including exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation. However, most EGFR mutations observed in glioma affect the extracellular domain - as seen in this specimen. Preclinical studies have shown that these extracellular mutations are poorly inhibited by the EGFR inhibitors employed in NSCLC [8] and the response to these inhibitors among gliobastoma patients in cliinical studies has been disappointing [9-11]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that inhibitors which bind to the inactive EGFR confirmation (also called "type II" confirmation) - such as neratinib or lapatinib - may be more efficacious [8]. However, clinical studies have shown that lapatinib failes to achieve sufficient intratumor concentrations in glioma patients [8]. Very limited preclinical studies have suggested that another irreversible EGFR inhibitor - afatinib - may have activity in glioblastoma patients with EGFR extracellular domain mutations, including EGFRvIII [12,13]. A phase 1/2 study of afatinib with or without temozolomide in recurrent glioblastoma patients showed a non-statistically significant correlation between EGFRvIII expression and minimally improved outcome with afatinib therapy [13]. However, EGFR targeted therapies are not expected to be efficacious in the context of the KRAS mutation described below since this mutation acts downstream of EGFR within MAPK signaling.

Both L833V and H835 are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and nearly always co-occur with another amino acid subsitution, most commonly with each other on the same allele [1-8], as seen in this specimen. L833V has also been known to co-occur with the L858R mutation [9-11].

However, in one case report, a patient NSCLC harboring the same compound mutation achieved a near-complete response to gefitinib without progression until 34 weeks following the initiation of TKI therapy [1]. Another patient with this mutation (as well as an E709K mutation) achieved a partial response on afatinib [2]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified.

EGFR G719 amino acid substitution mutations, including G719A, are well-described mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive activation of EGFR and downstream MAPK and PIK3CA signalling [1-10]. E709 mutations, including E709V, have also been described in NSCLC [1-10] but has not been biochemically characterized. While G719X mutations may occur in isolation or with other EGFR mutations, E709 mutations always co-occur with other EGFR mutations including G719X, L861Q and L858R [1-7].

No TKI therapies are specifically FDA-approved for EGFR E709 mutations and clinical data concerning the impact of this mutation on TKI reponse is somewhat limited due to its relative rarity. However, the available data suggests that NSCLC patients with E709 mutations in combination with a sensitiviting EGFR mutation (G719X, L861Q or L858R) remain sensitive to these therapies with response rates of approximately 50% [1-4]. variants.variant_description: The EGFR L858R and T790M mutations identified in this specimen is are both well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), resulting in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While EGFR exon 19 deletions (including E746_A750del) are associated with sensitivity to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib) [1,2], EGFR T790M confers resistance to most EGFR inhibitors and is commonly seen as mechanism of acquired resistance to TKI therapy [3]. The third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [4,5] and is currently FDA-approved for this application [6]. No molecular alterations associated with acquired resistance to osimertinib [7,8] were identified in this specimen.

variants.variant_description: An EGFR I706T mutation was also identified. I706T is rare, but has been described in NSCLC [1-7]. This mutation frequently co-occurs with other EGFR mutations, as seen in this case [1-7]. While the impact of I706T on response to TKI therapy is not entirely certain, this mutation - when combined with a TKI-sensitive mutation - appears to remain sensitive to TKI therapy. In one report, a partient harboring both EGFR G719A and I706T who was treated with erlotinib had an overall survival (OS) of 53.1 months [2]. In another report, a patient with G719A and I706T who was treated with gefitinib achieved a partial response that was maintained after 22 months of follow up [3]. A third patient with both G719A and I706T had stable disease of unknown duration while being treated with a TKI [4]. Finally, a patient with EGFR G874S and I706T had stable disease of unknown duration while being treated with erlotinib [6].

The P753S mutation has been described in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma [1] as well as in lung adenocarcinoma [4], melanoma [2], hairy cell leukemia [3], and Wilms tumor [5]. In one case report, a patient with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma harboring a P753S mutation as well as an exon 19 splice site mutation, responded to cetuximab with an mTOR inhibitor [1].

The EGFR L858R mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. This mutation is associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,2] and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR L858R including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and osimertinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehenisve Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [3]. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with TKI resistance were identified. An EGFR V834L mutation was also identified. This mutation was identified on the same allele as the L858R mutation but only on a subset of reads, suggesting that this mutation was acquired after the L858R mutation. EGFR V834L is rare, but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [4-6]. This mutation freqently co-occurs with other activating EGFR mutations including L858R [4-6], as seen in this case. While the impact of this mutation on response to TKI therapy is not entirely certain, this mutation - when combined with a TKI-sensitive mutation - appears to remain sensitive to TKI therapy. In one report, a partient harboring both EGFR L858R and V834L achieved a partial response with a progression free survival (PFS) of 26.1 months and an overall survival (OS) greater than 42.7 months (not reached) [5]. In another report, a patient with an EGFR exon 19 deletion and V834L achieved a partial response with a PFS greater than 45.2 months (not reached) and a OS greater than 52.7 months (not reached) [6].

The EGFR P794S variant detected in this specimen is extremely rare and of uncertain significance. This variant has never been described in gastric carcinoma and has only been described in a single patient with non-small cell lung cancer (germline versus somatic status was not established in this report) [1]. P794 lies within the cytoplasmic domain. While the functional effect of this variant has not been fully characterized, one study suggested that cells with this variant have similar cell proliferation and viability as cells with wild-type EGFR [2]. Other variants affecting this codon, including P794H and P794L have been described in individual samples from prostate cancer [3] and synovial sarcoma [4] and sebeceous adenoma [5], respectively. While this variant is not present in any germline databases, the possibility that this variant is germline cannot be definitively excluded.

The S695I variant detected in this specimen is extremely rare and has only been described in a single non-small cell lung cancer specimen (germline versus somatic status not evaluated) [1]. The functional and clinical significance (including potential response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy) is unknown. While this variant has not been reported in any germline databases, it also remains uncertain if this variant represents heritable germline variant or a somatically acquired mutation.

The EGFR L861Q mutation identified in this specimen is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1,2]. Several EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) - erlotinib, gefinitib, afatinib, osimertinib - are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or the L858R mutation; however, only afatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with EGFR L861Q. Both preclinical [3-5] and clinical [4,6] studies have demonstrated the sensitivity of this mutation to afatinib while preclinical [3,7] and clinical [8,9] studies suggest that erlotinib and gefitinib are less effective for this mutation. Importantly, no EGFR mutations associated with acquired TKI resistance were identified. There are also clinical trials currently recruiting patients with EGFR L861Q that progress on TKI therapy including NCT02496663 (phase 1 of osimertinib and necitumumab; multiple centers outside Michigan) and NCT02503722 (phase 1 of osimertinib and sapanisertib; Moffitt Cancer Center, Tampa, FL).

The EGFR V834L mutation identified in this specimen is rare, but has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-3]. This mutation freqently co-occurs with other activating EGFR mutations [1-3], as seen in this case. The impact of this mutation on response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy is uncertain. In one report, a patient harboring both EGFR V834L and an exon 19 deletion achieved a partial response with a progression free survival of 45 months [3].

The M600_G601delinsIR mutation detected in this specimen affects a cysteine-rich domain of the extracellular portion of the EGFR protein. This muation  has never been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma or any other cancer. Mutations affecting the M600 codon (M600V) and G601 (G601K) codon have been described in one case of Ewing sarcoma and melanoma, respectively. However, the functional effect of these mutations have not explored [1,2]. A mutation affecting a nearby codon (G598V) is well-described in gliobastoma [3] and has been described in two cases of NSCLC. This mutation has been shown to result in oncogenic activation of EGFR [3]. In preclinical studies, cells expressing EGFR G598V were sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibition (erlotinib) with low IC-50 values [3]. It is uncertain if the functional effect of the M600_G601IR mutation detected in this sample is similar to that of G598V.

The L747V mutation detected in this specimen has been described in lung adenocarcinoma, co-occuring with an L858R mutation [1]. No know studies have established the functional effect of this mutation. The patient in whom these mutations were identified had a partial response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy (erlotinib) [1]. Therefore, while it is no known if this mutation confers sensitivity to TKI therapy, this report would suggest that this mutation does not confer resistance to TKI therapy when a co-occuring TKI-sensitizing mutation is present.

The EGFR T790M variant identified in this specimen is well-described as a somatic mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), generally occuring with other activating EGFR mutations, frequently associated with acquired resistance to anti-EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1-3]. However, this variant has also been described as an inherited germline variant associated with an increased risk of lung cancer [4,5]. The variant allele frequency of the T790M variant in this specimen is close to 50% which could be compatible with either a somatic mutation or a heterozygous germline variant. Genetic counseling and possibly germline testing is recommended, if clinically indicated.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While EGFR T790M confers resistance to first and second generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatanib) [1-3], the third generation EGFR TKI osimertinib has proven efficacious in treatment of metastatic NSCLC with the EGFR T790M mutation [6,7] and is currently FDA-approved for this application [8]. Treatment of T790M-mutated metastatic NSCLC with osimertinib is currently a category 1 recommendation in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [9].

name: IDH2
gene_function: IDH2 encodes the mitochondrial enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase that normally converts isocitrate into alpha- ketoglutarate.

variants.variant_description: The mutant protein resulting from this mutation catalyzes the production of 2-hydroxyglutarate which functions as an oncometabolite, inhibiting alpha-ketoglutarate dependent dioxygenases such as TET enzymes, leading to global DNA and histone methylation changes [PMID: 21251613, PMID: 20171147]. In addition, 2-hydroxyglutarate can stimulate the activity of EGLN involved in hypoxia signaling, leading to decreased levels of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and increased tumor proliferation and growth [PMID: 22343896]. IDH2 R172 mutations are reported, but are very rare, in colorectal/appendiceal carcinoma (0.1%) [PMID: 33017591].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The IDH2-targeted inhibitor enasidenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with IDH2-mutant acute myeloid leukemia and the IDH1/2-targeted inhibitor vorasidenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with IDH2-mutant astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma. However, the clinical utility of these inhibitors in patients with colorectal carcinoma harboring IDH2 mutations is not characterized at this time.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: IDH mutation status is incorporated into the WHO classification of diffuse astrocytic and oligodendroglial tumors [WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System 5th ed]. According to NCCN guidelines IDH mutations define WHO grade 2 and 3 astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas, and grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas. Their presence distinguishes lower-grade gliomas from glioblastomas, which are IDH wild-type [NCCN Guidelines Central Nervous System Cancers Version 5.2024].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: The IDH1/2-targeted inhibitor vorasidenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients twelve years and older with WHO grade 2 astrocytoma with a susceptible IDH1 or IDH2 mutation [PMID: 37272516].  NCCN guidelines also recommend vorasidenib for treatment of IDH-mutant astrocytoma in certain circumstances [NCCN Guidelines Central Nervous System Cancers Version 3.2025].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: IDH mutations define WHO grade 2 and 3 astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas, and grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas. Their presence distinguishes lower-grade gliomas from glioblastomas, which are IDH wild-type. Detection of these mutations in a specimen that is otherwise equivocal for tumor may also be regarded as evidence that a diffusely infiltrative glioma is present [7,13].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no targeted therapies currently FDA-approved for the treatment of IDH-mutant glioma. Several IDH- inhibitors with activity against IDH2 have been developed. Enasidenib has been FDA-approved for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with IDH2 mutations; however, the clinical activity of this drug in gliomas has not been evaluated. In preclinical studies, IDH inhibitors have been shown to decrease levels of 2-hydroxyglutarate but have shown mixed ability to inhibit glioma proliferation [8-12].
diseases.prognostic_implications: IDH mutations in glioma impart a significantly better prognosis than grade-matched IDH wild-type gliomas [5,6] and mutations are associated with superior response to chemotherapy.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no targeted therapies currently FDA-approved for the treatment of IDH-mutant non-small cell lung cancer. Several IDH- inhibitors with activity against IDH2 have been developed. Enasidenib has been FDA-approved for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with IDH2 mutations; however, the clinical activity of this drug in non-small cell lung cancer has not been evaluated. Recent studies have shown that once an IDH mutant tumor has been established, IDH-mutant activity and 2-hydroxyglutarate production may no longer be necessary for sustained growth [6]. In addition, blocking 2-hydroxyglutarate production may actually reverse homologous recombination (HR) repair deficiencies associated with elevated 2-hydroxyglutarate, thereby providing a survival advantage in IDH-mutant cells [6]. These HR deficits may result in sensitivity to agents such as poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors. Several PARP inhibitors are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer. Preclinical studies have shown that these drugs may also be effective in cells with IDH mutations [7]. However, results from a recent clinical trial failed to show any efficacy associated with the PARP inhibitor ABT-888 [8].

This missense oncogenic mutation in IDH2 is well-described in myeloid neoplasms and results in a gain of enzymatic function, causing conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG).  2HG then functions as an 'oncometabolite,' inhibiting histone demethylation and resulting in increased DNA methylation.  
 
Gene/Protein Function and Biological Effect of Mutation:
IDH2 encodes mitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase, an enzyme that normally catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate. Oncogenic IDH2 mutations result in a gain of enzymatic function, causing conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG) [1-2]. 2HG then functions as an 'oncometabolite,' inhibiting alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases including histone demethylases and the TET family of DNA hydroxylases [3-4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The IDH2-targeted inhibitor enasidenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with IDH2-mutant acute myeloid leukemia and the IDH1/2-targeted inhibitor vorasidenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with IDH2-mutant astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma. However, the clinical utility of these inhibitors in patients with pancreatic cancer harboring IDH2 mutations is not well characterized at this time.

diseases.diagnostic_implications:
IDH2 mutations are present in approximately 6-7% of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) [5-6] and 3-8% of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) [6-10], but are somewhat more frequent in acute myeloid leukemia (AML; approximately 10-12%) [11-12], particularly cytogenetically normal AML (approximately 12-19%) [13-16]. 
 
IDH2 mutations are uncommon, but have been described at a low incidence in clonal hematopoiesis without an associated overt myeloid neoplasm (CHIP) [17-20].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Enasidenib (Idhifa) was FDA-approved for the treatment of relapse/refractory acute myeloid leukemia with IDH2 mutations. Response to enasidenib has also been reported in MDS with IDH2 mutations [25].
diseases.prognostic_implications: IDH2 mutations have been associated with an inferior prognosis in CMML [5] as well as in MDS (increased risk of leukemic transformation) [6-8]. Mixed results have been published with regard to the prognostic significance of IDH2 mutations in AML with most studies suggesting an inferior prognosis [21-24]. The prognostic significance may vary between R140 and R172 mutations.

While MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and cobimetinib show in vitro inhibition of MAPK signaling and cell growth within KRAS mutated cells and some clinical activity in other RAS-mutated neoplasms, clinical response to these agents (alone or in combination with other therapies) has been disappointing [2-7]. In vitro studies have suggested that these agents may be more effective in combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors [8].
