According to the most recent NCCN guidelines, in patients with KRAS mutation-positive metastatic NSCLC, data suggest the response rate is about 26% for single-agent ICIs. First-line platinum-based chemotherapy (± immunotherapy) is a recommended option for patients with KRAS mutations (eg, carboplatin plus paclitaxel) [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026]. 
 
Preclinical data and limited clinical data suggests that KRAS G12D-mutations may be sensitive to pan KRAS G12X inhibitors including RMC-7977 [PMID: 38589574], RMC-6236 [PMID: 38593348]. Adagrasib (Krazati) and sotorasib (Lumakras) are approved only for KRAS G12C (not G12D).

The absence of an activating EGFR mutation and the presence of a KRAS mutation is associated with primary resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) [1,2]. Some studies have demonstrated a modest response of KRAS-mutant NSCLC to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib [4]. In a phase 2 trial, KRAS-mutant NSCLC treated with trametinib (GSK1120212) showed a similar progression free survival and response rate as docetaxel [4]. While some clinical trials have suggested that the combination of a MEK inhibitor and docetaxel may be more efficacious than docetaxel alone [5,6], a large clinical trial failed to show any improvement in progression free survival for the combination of selumetinib (AZD6244) and docetaxel compared to docetaxel alone [7]. In preclinical studies, treatment of lung cancer cells with a MEK inhibitor induces a compensatory response involving FGFR1 leading to adaptive resistance while the combination of MEK and FGFR1 inhibition resulted in greater sensitivity than MEK inhibition alone [8]. The combination of a MEK inhibitor with other agents such as PI3K inhibitors [9], histone deacetylase inhibitors [10], or CDK4/6 inhibitors [11,12] has also demonstrated improved antitumor activity in preclinical studies.

Erdafinitib (Balversa; JNJ-42756493) is a selective FGFR inhibitor that was recently granted approval by the US Food and Drug Administration for urothelial cancer with FGFR alterations [5]. In a phase 2 trial, a confirmed response rate of 40% was reported in patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma harboring FGFR alterations [6]. Erdafitinib has also demonstrated evidence of preclinical and clinical efficacy in early studies of other cancers with FGFR alterations [6-8]. In a recent case report, a clinically significant response to erdafitinib was reported in a patient with a stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with an FGFR fusion [9].  Multiple other FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have activity against FGFR1 including other selective FGFR inhibitors such as pemigatinib (INCB054828), Debio 1347, AZD4547, BGJ398 and non-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors dovitinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib. Some studies have also demonstrated the clinical efficacy of pemigatinib and pembrolizumab in various solid tumors with FGFR alterations [10]; Debio 1347 in solid tumors with FGFR alterations [11]; AZD4547, BGJ398 and dovitinib, in lung squamous cell carcinoma and with FGFR1 amplification [12-14]; AZD4547 in gastric and breast cancer with high-level FGFR2 amplification [15]; and BGJ398 and lucitanib in various solid tumor malignancies with FGFR1/3 amplification [14]. However, it is unclear how this particular tumor will respond, given the presence of a KRAS mutation (see below), which is downstream of FGFR and may result in intrinsic resistance to FGFR-mediated inhibition.

Erdafitinib (JNJ-42756493) is a selective FGFR inhibitor that was recently FDA-approved for urothelial cancer with FGFR mutations and gene fusions by the US Food and Drug Administration based on clinical studies demonstrating a response rate of approximately 40% in metastatic/locally advanced urothelial carcinomas with these alterations [3]. In a phase 1 trial, erdafitinib demonstrated activity in other tumors with FGFR pathway alterations [4-5]. Some studies have also demonstrated the clinical efficacy of pemigatinib and pembrolizumab in various solid tumors with FGFR alterations [6]; Debio 1347 in solid tumors with FGFR alterations [7]; AZD4547, BGJ398 and dovitinib, in lung squamous cell carcinoma with FGFR1 amplification [8-10]; AZD4547 in gastric and breast cancer with high-level FGFR2 amplification [11]; and BGJ398 and lucitanib in various solid tumor malignancies with FGFR1/3 amplification [10,12].

While there is emerging data suggesting that tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapies such as crizotinib may be efficacious in NSCLC with HIGH-LEVEL MET amplification, tumor with low-level amplification (as seen in this specimen) are less responsive [4-13]. The current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines only recommend the crizotinib treatment for lung cancers with HIGH-LEVEL MET amplification [14]. The KRAS mutation described above is expected to confer resistance to MET targeted therapies.

Patients with colorectal cancer harboring any known KRAS mutation (exon 2, 3, 4) or NRAS mutation (exon 2, 3, 4) should not be treated with either cetuximab or panitumumab unless given as part of a regimen targeting KRAS G12C [NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 2.2026]. Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in KRAS-mutated neoplasms [PMID: 10395327]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have thus far been disappointing [PMIDs: 15483017, 27650277, 26666244]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [PMID: 27338794], CDK4/6 [1PMIDs: 28459468, 28866094, 26728409], ERBB3 [PMID: 29312543], histone deacetylase [PMID: 29079711], STAT3 [PMID: 25961376] and PI3K inhibitors [PMIDs: 23629727, 25342139].

KRAS mutations are associated with primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies such as cetuximab and panitumumab [4-6]. Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in KRAS-mutated neoplasms [7]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [11], CDK4/6 [12-14], ERBB3 [15], histone deacetylase [16], STAT3 [17] and PI3K inhibitors [18-19].

Anti-EGFR antibody therapies such as cetuximab and panitumumab are not expected to have activity against ERBB2 and some studies have suggested that ERBB2 amplification may confer resistance to these treatments [2-5]. While both preclinical [2,3] and limited clinical studies [6-9] have shown a potential clinical benefit to agents targeting ERBB2 including tyrosine kinase inhibitors and anti-ERBB2 antibodies, the KRAS mutation described above is likely to confer resistance to these therapies since RAS is downstream of ERBB2 within the MAPK signaling pathway.

Both preclinical [2,3] and limited clinical studies [2-6] have shown a potential clinical benefit to agents targeting ERBB2 including tyrosine kinase inhibitors and anti-ERBB2 antibodies.  In the HERACLES trial - a phase 2 trial of trastuzumab and lapatinib in treatment-refractory RAS wild-type, ERBB2 positive CRC - 30% (8/27) of patients achieved an objective response with one patient achieving complete remission [5]. In the MyPathway trial - a phase 2 basket trial - the subset that included ERBB2-amplified, metastatic CRC treated with pertuzumab and trastuzumab demonstrated an objective response rate of 32% (18/57) with one patient achieving a complete response [6]. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines now recommends trastuzumab with (lapatinib or pertuzumab) as a subsequent therapy option for ERBB2-amplified, RAS/RAF wild-type CRC [7]; however, the utility of this treatment in the context of low-level copy number gains is uncertain. In addition, the KRAS mutation also detected in this sample is expected to confer resistance to this thereapy.

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for KRAS-mutated melanoma. MEK inhibitors have shown mixed clinical efficacy in the treatment of RAS-mutated melanoma. While response to some MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib has been disappointing [5-6], clinical trials have demonstrated modest clinical efficacy for binimetinib [7-9]. In a phase 3 trial, binimetinib demonstrated a modest improvement in progression free survival (though no statistically significant difference in overall survival) when compared with dacarbazine [7]. The efficacy was most pronounced in patients who had received prior immunotherapy. Preclinical studies have also suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more efficacious when used in combination with immunotherapy [10]. However, as noted above, acquired KRAS mutations have been identified as a potential mechanism of resistance to BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy [11-13].

Of note, the KRAS mutation also detected in this specimen is expected to confer RESISTANCE to these inhibitors since KRAS affects MAPK signaling downstream of FGFR1.

KRAS mutations are associated with primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies such as cetuximab and penitumumab [8-10]. While there are no clinical data available, this mutation is also expected to confer resistance to the FGFR inhibitors described above since KRAS is downstream of FGFR within MAPK signaling. Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in KRAS-mutated neoplasms [10]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have thusfar been disappointing [11-14]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [15], CDK4/6 [15-17], ERBB3 [18], histone deacetylase [19], STAT3 [20] and PI3K inhibitors [21,22].

Fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nkxi is considered a potential subsequent therapy (after disease progression) for advanced/metastatic NSCLC found to have HER2 overexpression by immunohistochemistry (IHC; 3+). While ERBB2 copy number gains are often associated with HER2 overexpression, assessement by immunohistochemistry is recommended prior to any HER2-directed therapy. There is more evidence of efficacy of trastuzumab deruxtecan in NSCLC with ERBB2 mutations (rather than copy number gains or overexpression) [PMID: 34534430, 37694347]. However, phase II studies of trastuzumab emantansine [PMID: 30206164] and trastuzumab deruxtecan PMID: 38547891] have also demonstrated some responses among HER2-overexpressing NSCLC by IHC.

Adagrasib (Krazati) and sotorasib (Lumakras) have been granted accelerated FDA approval for the treatment of patients with KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who received at least one prior systemic therapy [PMID: 35658005, 34096690]. The NCCN NSCLC Panel recommends using PD-L1 level to determine the appropriate first-line systemic therapy regimen (such as immunotherapy and/or chemotherapy) for patients with advanced or metastatic NSCLC with KRAS G12C mutations [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026]. The panel recommends sotorasib or adagrasib as subsequent therapy options for patients who experience disease progression after treatment with first-line systemic therapy. Sotorasib or adagrasib may also be used as third-line therapy or beyond if the patient has not previously received a KRAS G12C-targeted therapy [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Version 5.2026].

Some studies have demonstrated a modest response of KRAS-mutant NSCLC to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib [4]. In a phase 2 trial, KRAS-mutant NSCLC treated with trametinib (GSK1120212) showed a similar progression free survival and response rate as docetaxel [4]. While some clinical trials have suggested that the combination of a MEK inhibitor and docetaxel may be more efficacious than docetaxel alone [5,6], a large clinical trial failed to show any improvement in progression free survival for the combination of selumetinib (AZD6244) and docetaxel compared to docetaxel alone [7]. In preclinical studies, treatment of lung cancer cells with a MEK inhibitor induces a compensatory response involving FGFR1 leading to adaptive resistance while the combination of MEK and FGFR1 inhibition resulted in greater sensitivity than MEK inhibition alone [8]. MAP2K1 P124L:
MAP2K1 encodes the protein MEK1 - a dual specificity kinase involved in growth signaling within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, downstream of BRAF and NRAS/KRAS. The MAP2K1 P124 mutation results in activation of MEK1 and MAPK signaling, but at much lower level than the BRAF V600E or MAP2K1 E203K mutation [PMID: 22197931,22588879] and this mutation frequently co-occurs with other mutations activating MAPK signaling [PMID: 26343386, 26214590] (as seen in this specimen). 
 
While P124L has been seen as a mechanism of acquired resistance to BRAF inhibitor monotherapy (not BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination therapy) [PMID: 19915144], P124 mutations are also frequently observed as a pre-treatment MAP2K1 mutation [PMID: 22588879, 25370473].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
While this mutation is weakly activating, because it activates MAPK signaling, it may confer resistance to KRAS inhibitor therapy. MAP2K1 mutations have been associated with acquired resistance to KRAS G12C inhibition (e.g., sotorasib, adagrasib) [PMID: 34161704, 33824136]. 
 
However, this mutation appears to be highly sensitive to MEK inhibitors (e.g. trametinib) as well as ERK inhibitors (e.g. VX-11e), based on preclinical studies [PMID: 25370473]. Therefore, the combination of a KRAS inhibitor (directed at the mutation described above) and a MEK inhibitor may be more efficacious.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While the impact of ERBB3 mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibodies not entirely certain, the KRAS mutation described above has clear association with resistance to these therapies. name: PIK3CA
gene_function: PIK3CA encodes one of the catalytic subunits of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, a lipid kinase involved in PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling downstream of EGFR.

variants.variant_description:

PIK3CA mutations, including E453K mutation detected in this specimen, results in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation and are well-described in gliomas [1]. However, PIK3CA mutations are not common in pleomorphic xanthoastrocytomas (PXA), including anaplastic PXAs [2].

PIK3CA mutations, including N345K, are are known to result in increased PIK3CA catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation [1,2].

However, the clinical utility in patients with non-small cell lung cancer is not well characterized.

While preclinical studies have suggested that agents such PI3K, mTOR and CDK4/6 inhibitors may be effective [3,4], results from limited clinical studies investigating the utility of PI3K and mTOR inhibitors including PX-866 and everolimus have failed to show a significant response to PI3K [5-7].

Clinical studies in other PIK3CA-mutated cancer types have shown mixed results [9-13]. Mixed results have also been observed in early clinical studies of PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors [14].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Abundant data show that low-dose aspirin therapy after a diagnosis of CRC decreases the risk of recurrence and death. Some evidence suggests that tumor mutations in PIK3CA may be predictive for response to aspirin, although the data are somewhat inconsistent and other predictive markers have also been suggested [PMID: 24062397, 23094721, 25549537]. Based on these data, the NCCN Panel believes that survivors of CRC can consider taking 325 mg daily to reduce their risk of recurrence and death [NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 2.2026].

Currently, there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies available for PIK3CA-mutated gastric cancer. Clinical studies in other PIK3CA-mutated cancer types have shown mixed results [PMID: 25526733, 29126203, 28330462, 27232378, 25902899]. However, the KRAS mutation described above is clearly associated with primary resistance to these therapies. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [7-9].

PIK3CA mutations, including Q546P and G1049R, are very well-described in breast cancer [1], and are known to result in increased PIK3CA catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation [2]. Due to the location on separate amplicons, it is unclear whether these alterations are present on the same or opposite alleles.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: PIK3CA mutations commonly occur in colorectal cancer and co-occur with RAS mutation in about two-thirds of cases, as in this specimen. Alpelisib (Piqray) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer. However, there is a paucity of studies evaluating the efficacy of this drug in colorectal cancer. mTOR inhibitors (e.g. everolimus, temsirolimus) are also FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer; however, clinical response to these agents does not seem to be associated with the presence or absence of PIK3CA mutations [13]. Clinical studies in other PIK3CA-mutated cancer types, including patients with colorectal cancer, have shown mixed results [14-18]. Accoring to the most recent NCCN guidelines abundant data has shown that low-dose aspirin therapy after a diagnosis of CRC decreases the risk of recurrence and death [19-26].  Some evidence suggests that tumor mutations in PIK3CA may be predictive for response to aspirin, although the data are somewhat inconsistent and other predictive markers have also been suggested [26]. In addition, a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs showed that while non-aspirin NSAIDs were better for preventing recurrence, low-dose aspirin was safer and thereby had a more favorable risk-to-benefit profile. Based on these data, the NCCN panel believes that survivors of CRC can consider taking 325 mg aspirin daily to reduce their risk of recurrence and death.

Several PI3K inhibitors are FDA-approved for the treatment of postmenopausal patients with hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer following progression on or after endocrine-based therapy including alpelisib (Piqray; in combination with fulvestrate), capivasertib (Truqap; in combination with fulvestrate) and inavisolisib (Itovebi; in combination with fulvestrate and the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib). Treatment of advanced, HR-positive, HER2-negative, PIK3CA-mutant breast cancer with one of these combinations is currently a category 1 recommendation by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines with inavolisib+palbociclib+fulvestrant useful in certain circumstances first-line and alpelisib+fulvestrant or capivasertib+fulvestrant preferred second- or subsequent-line therapies [Invasive Breast Cancer, version 6.2024] .

PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, including Q546R, are well-described in CRC [1-8].

PIK3CA mutations are well-described in urothelial carcinoma with an incidence of approximately 20% [1,2]. PIK3CA Q546R lies within the helical domain and has been shown to result in constitutive activation of PIK3CA and downstream signaling [3]. This variant has been described in multiple tumor types, most frequently in breast and colonic adenocarcinoma.

The PIK3CA Q546R mutation detected in this specimen has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-4]. Other mutations affecting this residue including Q546K and Q546P, have been shown to be oncogenic resulting in constitutive activation of PI3K signaling [5]. While there is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [6], and the KRAS mutation described above is strongly associated with resistance [7]. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [1,8,9]. While preclinical studies have suggested that PI3K, AKT, mTOR and glutaminase inhibitors may also be effective in treating PIK3CA-mutated neoplasms [10], results from clinical studies investigating the link between activating PIK3CA mutations and response to these agents have been mixed [11-15]. Relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02961283 (phase 1 trial of BRAF/PI3K inhibitor ASN003, multiple centers including START MidWest, Grand Rapids, MI), NCT02861300 (phase 1 and 2 trial of CB-839 + Capecitabine, Cleveland Clinic Taussig Cancer Institute, Cleveland, OH), NCT01226316 (phase 1 of AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan), and NCT02576444 (phase 2 trial of olaparib + AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan).

FGFR2 K659E: 
FGFR2 K659E lies within the protein kinase domain of the FGFR2 protein and results in increased kinase activity and phosphorylation of downstream signaling molecules resulting [1-2]. Activating FGFR2 mutations (as well as other FGFR alterations including gene amplification) are well-described in breast cancer [3-5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Activating FGFR molecular alterations including FGFR2 amplification have been associated with resistance to estrogen receptor targeted therapy [3] and to CDK4/6 inhibitors (e.g. palbociclib, ribociclib) [4].
 
Multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors for the treatment of other cancers have activity against FGFR including selective FGFR inhibitors erdafitinib (Balversa; JNJ-42756493) and pemigatinib (Pemarzyre; INCB054828) and non-selective inhibitors pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib. Erdafitinib (JNJ-42756493) is FDA-approved for urothelial cancer with FGFR mutations and gene fusions [6] while pemigatinib (Pemazyre) and infigratinib (Truseltiq) are FDA-approved for the treatment of cholangiocarcinomas with FGFR2 rearrangements. 
 
Treatment with AZD4547 has shown a response in a subset of gastric and breast cancer with high-level FGFR2 amplification [7]. Various studies have demonstrated clinical efficacy of erdafitinib, dovitinib, AZD4547, BGJ398, and lucitanib in various tumors with FGFR amplifications and alterations [8-13].
 
In a recent phase I study with concurrent alpelisib and infigratinib treatment in patients with both PIK3CA and FGFR alterations in solid tumors, no clear evidence of synergy was observed [14].

variants.variant_description:
BRAF K601E:
BRAF is a serine-threonine kinase involved in growth signaling via the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. The BRAF K601E mutation identified in this specimen is uncommon, but has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1,2] as well as other cancers. In contrast with BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations which result in constitutively active monomers, K601E and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner [3,4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
On April 8, 2020, encorafenib with cetuximab was FDA-approved for metastatic CRC with BRAF V600E with disease progression on one or two prior regimens. Median overall survival was 8.4 months in the encorafenib plus cetuximab arm compared to 5.4 months in the control arm (either irinotecan or FOLFIRI with cetuximab). While "class 2" BRAF mutations are NOT expected to respond to BRAF monomer inhibitors (e.g. vemurafenib, dabrafenib) because their binding to one site within the dimer significantly reduces their affinity for the second [3,4], there is some preclinical evidence in melanoma that class 2 mutations may be sensitive to dual MAPK inhibition, including encorafenib [5]. However, other small studies have found combination treatment to not be very effective in those with K601E mutations [13].
MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have been shown to be effective against BRAF K601E and other "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [3,4,6] as well as limited clinical studies in melanoma patients [7-8]. The significance of the MAP2K1 mutation identified in this tumor in terms of response to MEK inhibition remains to be fully elucidated (see interpretation below). There are also newer BRAF inhibitor compounds such as BGB659, PLX8394 and AZ628 have proven effective against these "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [3,9,10].
 
Anti-EGFR Antibody Therapy: While the current CAP/AMP/ASCO guidelines do not recommend BRAF mutational status be used as a predictive molecular biomarker for this purpose [11], the current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines state that BRAF V600E mutation makes response to panitumumab or cetuximab highly unlikely unless given a BRAF inhibitor [12] CAP/AMP/ASCO guidelines do recommend BRAF testing for prognostic stratification (as well as for CRC with MLH1 loss) [11]. However, the impact of this BRAF mutation on response to anti-EGFR therapy is uncertain.
Other Therapies: While studies have not shown a clinical benefit of BRAF inhibitors as monotherapy in CRC [11] due to activation of EGFR signaling [14], several studies suggest that there is utility when BRAF inhibition is combined with EGFR, MEK and/or PI3K inhibition [15-19]. The latter of which may be particularly advantageous in this patient given the presence of a PIK3CA mutation and PIK3CA amplification.

Amplification of PIK3CA has been described in multiple tumor types including breast carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the lung but is not well-characterized in colorectal carcinoma. diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [4]. However, the KRAS mutation described above is clearly associated with primary resistance to these therapies. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [5-7]. 
 
Alpelisib (Piqray) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer; however, there are no known studies evaluating the efficacy of this drug in colorectal cancer. mTOR inhibitors (e.g. everolimus, temsirolimus) are also FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer; however, clinical response to these agents does not seem to be associated with the presence or absence of PIK3CA mutations [8]. Clinical studies in other PIK3CA-mutated cancer types have shown mixed results [9-13]. Mixed results have also been observed in early clinical studies of PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors [14-20].

variants.variant_description: PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation have been described in pancreatic carcinoma [1,2]. One study found that PIK3CA mutations are capable of initiating pancreatic tumorigenesis [3]. While the Q546L mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon, it has been described as a recurrent, somatic mutation in various cancers including breast [4,5], colorectal [6,7], and bladder [8] and has shown to induce oncogenic transformation [9].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are no FDA-approved therapies for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated pancreatic cancer. Alpelisib (Piqray) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of postmenopausal patients with hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer following progression on or after endocrine-based therapy. In the SOLAR-1 trial, patients with hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, PIK3CA-mutated advanced breast cancer with progression who were treated with alpelisib + fulvestrant achieved a median progression-free survival of 11.0 months compared to 5.7 months among patients treated with fulvestrant alone [10]. mTOR inhibitors (e.g. everolimus, temsirolimus) are also FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer, however, clinical response to these agents does not seem to be associated with the presence or absence of PIK3CA mutations [11]. Mixed results been observed in early clinical studies of other PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors in a variety of cancers [12-23].

The PIK3CA E545_Q546delinsKK mutation detected in this specimen is essentially equivalent to two subsitution mutations (E545K and Q546K) ocurring on the same allele. Both Q545K and Q546K are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-4]. Both mutations have also been shown to be oncogenic resulting in constitutive activation of PI3K signaling [5,6]. While there is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [7], and the KRAS mutation described above is strongly associated with resistance [8]. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [9-11]. While preclinical studies have suggested that PI3K, AKT, mTOR and glutaminase inhibitors may also be effective in treating PIK3CA-mutated neoplasms [12], results from clinical studies investigating the link between activating PIK3CA mutations and response to these agents have been mixed [13-17]. Relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02961283 (phase 1 trial of BRAF/PI3K inhibitor ASN003, multiple centers including START MidWest, Grand Rapids, MI), NCT02861300 (phase 1 and 2 trial of CB-839 + Capecitabine, Cleveland Clinic Taussig Cancer Institute, Cleveland, OH), NCT01226316 (phase 1 of AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan), and NCT02576444 (phase 2 trial of olaparib + AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan).

variants.variant_description: The clinical significance of the PIK3CA E542K mutation is less certain. PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, including E542K, are well described in CRC [1,2]. There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [3], and the CAP/AML/ASCO guidelines do not recommend PIK3CA mutational status be used as a predictive molecular biomarker for this purpose [4]. However, the presence of the KRAS mutation described above is strongly associated with lack of response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [5-7]. Multiple prospective studies are underway to address the potential benefit of aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for CRC. The utility of several other agents including PI3K, AKT, mTOR and glutaminase inhibitors is also being investigated in clinical trials including NCT02861300 (phase 1/2 of capecitabine + the glutaminase inhibitor CB-839, Cleveland, OH).

PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation are well described in several cancers, including NSCLC [1]. While R108H is an uncommon PIK3CA mutation, it has been described in NSCLC [2] and has been shown to be oncogenic [3]. The impact of this mutation on response to TKI therapy is not well established, however activating PIK3CA mutations have been shown to confer resistance to EGFR inhibitors in vitro and have been reported in a small percentage of EGFR-mutated NSCLC with acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy [4]. There are no FDA-approved targeted therapies available for PIK3CA-mutated NSCLC. mTOR inhibitors (e.g. everolimus, temsirolimus) are FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer; however, clinical response to these agents does not seem to be associated with the presence or absence of PIK3CA mutations [5]. Early clinical studies in other PIK3CA-mutated cancer types have shown mixed results [6-10]. Mixed results have also been observed in early clinical studies of PI3K inhibitors [13-16] and AKT inhibitors [17]. The utility of several of these agents is currently being investigated in clinical trials. Relevant trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02861300 (phase 1/2 of capecitabine plus glutaminase inhibitor CB-839, Cleveland, OH), NCT02483858 (phase 1 of PI3K inhibitor PQR309, multicenter including University Hospital of Cleveland), NCT01306045 (phase 2 of AKT inhibitor MK-2206, NIH), NCT02576444 (phase 2 of olaparib plus AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multicenter), NCT01226316 (phase 1 of AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multicenter) and NCT02124148 (phase 1 of prexasertib plus PI3K/mTOR inhibitor LY3023414, multicenter).

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no FDA-approved targeted therapies available for PIK3CA-mutated glioma. Alpelisib (Piqray) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer; however, there are no known studies evaluating the efficacy of this drug in gliomas. One small study did report a response with breast cancer brain metastases [7]. Limited studies also suggest that buparisib, another PI3K inhibitor has been shown to cross the blood-brain barrier [8-10]. The potential benefit derived from treatment of a subclonal mutation is uncertain.

While alpelisib in combination with fulvestrant is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with PIK3CA-mutant ER+/HER2- breast cancer, its clinical utility in patients with PIK3CA-mutant colorectal cancer is unknown. Abundant data show that low-dose aspirin therapy after a diagnosis of CRC decreases the risk of recurrence and death. Some evidence suggests that tumor mutations in PIK3CA may be predictive for response to aspirin, although the data are somewhat inconsistent and other predictive markers have also been suggested [PMID: 24062397, 23094721, 25549537]. Based on these data, the NCCN Panel believes that survivors of CRC can consider taking 325 mg daily to reduce their risk of recurrence and death [NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 4.2025].

variants.variant_description: The PIK3CA P104L mutation detected in this specimen affects the PIK3CA protein between the p85 binding domain and the Ras binding domain. This mutation has been shown to be activating based on increased proliferation in absence of growth factors in Ba/F3 and MCF10A cells [PMID: 29533785]. This mutation has been described as a somatic mutation in colorectal cancer (CRC) [PMID: 28002797] as well as breast cancer [PMID: 27135926], endometrial cancer [PMID: 28481359], ovarian cancer [PMID: 28481359], melanoma [PMID: 26343386], and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma [PMID: 28481359]. This variant has also been described as a germline variant in patients with PIK3CA-related overgrowth syndromes [PMID: 27631024]. Phenotypes that have been described include vascular malformations and syndactyly. The variant allele frequency of the PIK3CA P104L variant in this specimen is not close to 50%; therefore, it is unlikely that this variant is germline. Germline testing and genetic counseling may be indicated if there is concern for a germline PIK3CA mutation.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While alpelisib in combination with fulvestrant is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with PIK3CA-mutant ER+/HER2- breast cancer, its clinical utility in patients with PIK3CA-mutant colorectal cancer is unknown. Abundant data show that low-dose aspirin therapy after a diagnosis of CRC decreases the risk of recurrence and death. Some evidence suggests that tumor mutations in PIK3CA may be predictive for response to aspirin, although the data are somewhat inconsistent and other predictive markers have also been suggested [PMID: 24062397, 23094721, 25549537]. Mixed results have also been observed in early clinical studies of PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors [PMID: 29285035, 25526733, 29126203, 28330462, 27232378, 25902899, 25527417, 28618305, 21216929, 28331003, 25172762, 25605819, 29611022].

variants.variant_description:
CCND1 copy number gain (amplification):
Copy number gain of the CCND1 gene was detected, consistent with amplification. CCND1 encodes cyclin D1, a protein that interacts with cyclin dependent kinases (CDK), regulating Rb activity and cell cycle progression. Amplification of CCND1 has been described in a subset of squamous cell carcinomas of various sites, including head and neck and lung [1,2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck or lung with CCND1 amplification. Preclinical studies have shown that cells with CCND1 amplification may be sensitive to CDK4/6 inhibitors e.g. palbociclib (FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer), ribociclib, and abemaciclib [3]. However, within clinical studies of other cancer types no clear association has been demonstrated between CCND1 amplification status and response to these agents [4,5]. Several ongoing clinical trials are investigating the utility of CDK4/6 inhibitors in neoplasms with CCND1 amplification.

The C378R mutation lies within the C2 domain of exon 6 of PIK3CA and has been characterized as likely oncogenic. Other well characterized activating mutations, such as H1047R also found in this specimen, are more frequently identified in patients with breast cancer [1], and are known to result in increased PIK3CA catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation [2].

The PIK3CA C378R detected in this specimen has been described as a somatic mutation in glioblastoma [1] as well as in breast, colorectal, and endometrial [2-4]. Other PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, are well-described in glioma [5].

Prototypical PIK3CA mutation result in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation and are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-3]. This C378R alteration has been less commonly observed although described in CRC and other cancers [1, 4, 5]; in addition, this alteration within the C2 PI3K-type domain results in constitutive activation and signaling in cell culture [6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Please see interpretation for PIK3CA H1047R.

While preclinical studies have suggested that agents such PI3K, mTOR and CDK4/6 inhibitors may be effective [2,3], results from limited clinical studies investigating the utility of PI3K and mTOR inhibitors including PX-866 and everolimus have failed to show a significant response to PI3K [4-6].  Alpelisib (Piqray) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer; however, there are no known studies evaluating the efficacy of this drug in gliomas. mTOR inhibitors (e.g. everolimus, temsirolimus) are also FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer; however, clinical response to these agents does not seem to be associated with the presence or absence of PIK3CA mutations [7]. Clinical studies in other PIK3CA-mutated cancer types have shown mixed results [8-12]. Mixed results have also been observed in early clinical studies of PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors [13].

There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [7]. However, the KRAS mutation described above is clearly associated with primary resistance to these therapies. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [8-10].

variants.variant_description:
The PIK3CA mutation detected in this specimen has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1], as well as other neoplasms including endometrial, breast, esophageal and bladder cancer [1-5]. While no functional studies have investigated its functional effect, the recurrent nature of this mutation suggests that it is an oncogenic driver.This variant has also been described as a mosaic mutation resulting in overgrowth syndromes [6]. While the allele frequency of this variant in comparison with the reported percentage of neoplastic cells is suggestive of a somatic, cancer-associated mutation, a mosaic mutation cannot be excluded with this assay. Genetic counseling may be indicated if there is clinical concern for an overgrowth syndrome.

The PIK3CA E110del detected in this specimen is rare, but has been described as a somatic mutation in glioblastoma [PMID: 24705251]. This mutation is predicted to confer a gain-of-function as demonstrated by transformation in two different cell lines [PMID: 29533785]. Other PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, are well-described in glioma [PMID: 24120142].

Activating PIK3CA mutations, are well-described in anaplastic thyroid carcinoma [1-5] as well as many other cancers. The PIK3CA E110del mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon, but have been described in colorectal, endometrial, breast, esophageal and bladder cancer [6-10]. While no functional studies have investigated its functional effect, the recurrent nature of this mutation suggests that it is an oncogenic driver. This variant has also been described as a mosaic mutation resulting in overgrowth syndromes [11]. While the allele frequency of this variant in comparison with the reported percentage of neoplastic cells is suggestive of a somatic, cancer-associated mutation, a mosaic mutation cannot be excluded with this assay. Genetic counseling may be indicated if there is clinical concern for an overgrowth syndrome.

While the PIK3CA mutation detected in this specimen has not been described in melanoma, it has been described in other neoplasms including endometrial, breast, colorectal, esophageal and bladder cancer [1-5]. This variant has also been described as a mosaic mutation resulting in overgrowth syndromes [6]. The allele frequency of this variant is similar to that of the other two mutations identified in this specimen suggesting that it is a somatic mutation within melanoma cells. While no functional studies have investigated its functional effect, the recurrent nature of this mutation suggests that it is an oncogenic driver. Activating PIK3CA mutations are well-described in melanoma and frequently co-exist with BRAF (as in this case) or NRAS mutations [7]. There is no clinical or preclinical data concerning efficacy of targeted therapies for this particular PIK3CA variant. While one preclinical study suggested that activating PIK3CA mutations are associated with reduced sensitivity to vemurafenib [7], another study found that these mutations do not seem to play a major role in vemurafenib sensitivity/resistance [8]. Preclinical studies have also suggested that PI3K, AKT, mTOR and glutaminase inhibitors may be effective in treating PIK3CA-mutated neoplasms [9]. Results from clinical studies investigating the link between activating PIK3CA mutations and response to these agents have been mixed [10-14]. Relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02961283 (phase 1 trial of BRAF/PIK3 inhibitor ASN003, multiple centers including START MidWest, Grand Rapids, MI), NCT01226316 (phase 1 of AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan), and NCT02576444 (phase 2 trial of olaparib + AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan).

There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [7]. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [8-10]. Preclinical studies have suggested that PI3K, AKT, mTOR and glutaminase inhibitors may be effective in treating PIK3CA-mutated neoplasms [11]. Results from clinical studies investigating the link between activating PIK3CA mutations and response to these agents have been mixed [12-16].

There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [7] although the above KRAS mutation in this sample is clearly linked to resistance. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [8-10]. 
 
Alpelisib (Piqray) is FDA-approved for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer. mTOR inhibitors (e.g. everolimus, temsirolimus) are also FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer; however, clinical response to these agents does not seem to be associated with the presence or absence of PIK3CA mutations [11]. Clinical studies in other PIK3CA-mutated cancer types have shown mixed results [12-16]. Mixed results have also been observed in early clinical studies of PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors [17-23].

There are no FDA-approved targeted therapies available for PIK3CA-mutated glioma. Alpelisib (Piqray) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer; however, there are no known studies evaluating the efficacy of this drug in gliomas. While preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as PI3K, mTOR and CDK4/6 inhibitors may be effective [PMID: 25371289, 25605819], results from limited clinical studies investigating the utility of PI3K and mTOR inhibitors including PX-866 and everolimus have failed to show a significant response [PMID: 25526733, 29126203].

Mixed results been observed in early clinical studies of other PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors in a variety of cancers [14-25].

A copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected, consistent with amplification. ERBB2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. Amplification of the ERBB2 gene resulting in increased ERBB2 expression and growth signaling is well-described in breast cancer [1]. diseases.therapeutic_implications: Anti-ERBB2 antibodies including trastuzumab, ado-trastuzumab emtansine and pertuzumab, as well as tyrosine kinase inhibitors including lapatinib and neratinib [2-7] have been shown to be effective for ERBB2-amplified breast cancer and have been FDA-approved for the treatment of HER2+ breast cancer [2]. In addition, activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway is frequently seen in carcinomas that progress on HER2-targeted therapy. Early studies evaluating PI3K inhibitors (buparlisib and pictilisib) with trastuzumab in HER-2 positive disease have suggested activity and tolerability [9-10]. Other studies have shown promising preclinical data to suggest efficacy with AKT inhibitors and HER2 therapies in patients with HER2 positive breast carcinoma harboring PIK3CA mutations [11].

variants.variant_description: The PIK3CA mutation identified in this specimen has not been described in the literature; however, a similar mutation -V344M - has been described as a somatic mutation in gliomas [1] as well as many other cancers [2-6]. The PIK3CA V344M mutation has been shown to be oncogenic, conferring transformation ability in two different cell lines [7]. Other PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation are well-described in gliomas [8].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no FDA-approved therapies for the treatment of PIK3CA-mutated gliomas. However, alpelisib (Piqray) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of postmenopausal patients with hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, PIK3CA-mutated metastatic breast cancer following progression on or after endocrine-based therapy. In the SOLAR-1 trial, patients with hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, PIK3CA-mutated advanced breast cancer with progression who were treated with alpelisib + fulvestrant achieved a median progression-free survival of 11.0 months compared to 5.7 months among patients treated with fulvestrant alone [9]. mTOR inhibitors (e.g. everolimus, temsirolimus) are also FDA-approved for the treatment of breast cancer, however, clinical response to these agents does not seem to be associated with the presence or absence of PIK3CA mutations [10]. Mixed results been observed in early clinical studies of other PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors in a variety of cancers [11-22].

variants.variant_description: The S326F mutation identified in this specimen is very rare, but has been described as a somatic mutation in various cancers including papillary thyroid carcinoma [1], melanoma [2,3] and salivary duct carcinoma [4]. There are no known reports of this variant in germline databases and the variant allele frequency in comparison with the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells is consistent with a somatic mutation. However, this mutation has not been biochemically characterized and its clinical significance is unknown.

The PIK3CA R88Q mutation detected in this specimen is well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-5]. This mutation has been shown to result in constitutive activation of PI3K and downstream signaling [6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [7]. However, the KRAS mutation described above is clearly associated with primary resistance to these therapies. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [8-10].

variants.variant_description:
PIK3CA R88Q and R93W:
PIK3CA R88Q and R93W mutations were both identified on the same allele. The PIK3CA R88Q mutation detected in this specimen is well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-5]. The R93W variant is less common but has also been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [6] as well as other neoplasms [7-9]. Both mutations have been shown to result in constitutive activation of PI3K and downstream signaling [10,11].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [12]. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [13-15].

variants.variant_description: The E545K mutation identified in this specimen is a common mutation that has been described in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) [1] as well as other cancers and has been shown to result in weak activation of PIK3CA and downstream signaling [2]. The C378F mutation is much less common, but has been described as a somatic mutation in glioblastoma [3] as well as breast [4], ovarian [4] and pancreatic cancer [5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there are FDA-approved mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, sirolimus and temsiroliums) which have shown activity in PIK3CA-mutated cells in preclinical studies [6,7], phase 2 clinical trials investigating the utility of everolimus have failed to show a clinical benefit both in advanced PIK3CA-mutated solid tumors [8] and recurrent/metastatic head and neck SCC [9]. Similarly disappointing results have been observed for other mTOR inhibitors such as temsirolimus [10,11].

variants.variant_description: While PIK3CA P104T has not been previously described in glioma, this mutation has been described as a somatic mutation in rectal carcinoma and Brenner tumor [1,2]. In addition, other PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, have been described in glioma [3]. While preclinical studies have suggested that agents such PI3K, mTOR and CDK4/6 inhibitors may be effective [4,5], results from limited clinical studies investigating the utility of PI3K and mTOR inhibitors including PX-866 and everolimus have failed to show a significant reponse to PI3K [6-8]. There are no known clinical trials recruiting patients with PIK3CA-mutated glioma.

Two PIK3CA mutations were detected - G359R and Y1021C. Both of these mutations have been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-3]. Y1021C affects the PI3K/PI4K domain and has been shown to be tranforming in cell lines [4]. G469R has not been functionally characterized. There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [5]. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [6-8]. While preclinical studies have suggested that PI3K, AKT, mTOR and glutaminase inhibitors may also be effective in treating PIK3CA-mutated neoplasms [9], results from clinical studies investigating the link between activating PIK3CA mutations and response to these agents have been mixed [10-14]. Relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02961283 (phase 1 trial of BRAF/PI3K inhibitor ASN003, multiple centers including START MidWest, Grand Rapids, MI), NCT02861300 (phase 1 and 2 trial of CB-839 + Capecitabine, Cleveland Clinic Taussig Cancer Institute, Cleveland, OH), NCT01226316 (phase 1 of AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan), and NCT02576444 (phase 2 trial of olaparib + AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan).

The PIK3CA mutation detected in this specimen has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-5]. This mutation has been shown to result in constitutive activation of PI3K and downstream signaling [6]. While there is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [7], and the KRAS mutation described above is strongly associated with resistance [8]. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [9-11]. While preclinical studies have suggested that PI3K, AKT, mTOR and glutaminase inhibitors may also be effective in treating PIK3CA-mutated neoplasms [12], results from clinical studies investigating the link between activating PIK3CA mutations and response to these agents have been mixed [13-17]. Relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02961283 (phase 1 trial of BRAF/PI3K inhibitor ASN003, multiple centers including START MidWest, Grand Rapids, MI), NCT02861300 (phase 1 and 2 trial of CB-839 + Capecitabine, Cleveland Clinic Taussig Cancer Institute, Cleveland, OH), NCT01226316 (phase 1 of AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan), and NCT02576444 (phase 2 trial of olaparib + AKT inhibitor AZD5363, multiple centers outside Michigan).

PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, including H1047R, are well described in CRC [1]. The PIK3CA V344M mutation that was also detected in this specimen is much more rare, but has also been described in CRC and confirmed to be somatically acquired [2-4]. There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [5], and the current CAP/AML/ASCO guidelines do not recommend PIK3CA mutational status be used as a predictive molecular biomarker for this purpose [6]. Some evidence has suggested that PIK3CA mutations in CRC may be predictive of response to aspirin [7-9]. Multiple prospective studies are underway to address the potential benefit of aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for CRC. The utility of several other agents including PI3K, AKT and mTOR inhibitors is also being investigated in clinical trials.

The clinical significance of the PIK3CA mutation identified in this specimen is less certain. PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation are well described in NSCLC [3]. However, the PIK3CA F83L mutation identified in this specimen has only been reported in one publication in a desmoplastic melanoma [4]. While the mutation was not confirmed to be somatic that study, other mutations affecting the same amino acid have been proven somatic in other studies [5,6]. In addition, the mutation frequency observed in this specimen, in comparison with the KRAS mutation as well as the tumor percentage, is in keeping with a somatic mutation. Because KRAS G12V is known to be a strong oncogenic driver mutation that is typically mutually exclusive with other driver mutations, the PIK3CA mutation may represent a secondary or passenger mutation.

ERBB2 V842I:
ERBB2 (HER2) is receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. The V842I mutation detected in this specimen has been described in breast cancer (and other cancers) and has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream growth signaling [1,2]. Other ERBB2 mutations, such as L755S have been described as a mechanism of acquired resistance to ERBB2-targeted therapy [3,4]. In preclinical studies, this mutation was found to be relatively resistant to trastuzumab, cetuximab, panitumumab and lapatinib, but sensitive to neratinib (IC50 1.9 +/- 0.3 nmol/L) and afatinib (IC50 0.42 +/- 0.05 nmol/L) [1,2]. Neratinib is currently FDA-approved for extended adjuvant treatment of HER2+ breast cancer following adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy.

name: ALK
gene_function: ALK is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling.

variants.variant_description: The DCTN1-ALK gene fusion detected in this sample is rare but well-described in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMID: 25813404]. Similar to all previously reported ALK fusion partners in NSCLC DCTN1 contains the coiled coil region, which facilitates constitutive ALK dimerization known to result in constitutive activation of ALK [PMIDs: 26062823]. Approximately 5% of patients with NSCLC have ALK gene rearrangements [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The NCCN NSCLC Panel has preference stratified the first-line therapy options for patients with ALK rearrangement–positive metastatic NSCLC. Alectinib, brigatinib, or lorlatinib are recommended as preferred first-line monotherapy options for patients with ALK rearrangement–positive metastatic NSCLC. Ceritinib is an “other recommended” option, whereas crizotinib is “useful in certain circumstances.” Data suggest that patients with ALK rearrangement–positive metastatic NSCLC do not respond to single-agent immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 5.2026].

variants.variant_description:
Evidence of an ALK gene fusion was detected by initial screening for 5' to 3' imbalance and confirmed by ALK break-apart FISH. ALK gene fusions involving a variety of fusion partners are well-described and result in constitutive activation of ALK kinase domain and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMID: 10216106, 17625570, 8122112].

ALK fusions are well-described in a variety of neoplasms, including inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors and other sarcomas with a variety of fusion partners [1] and result in constitutive activation of ALK and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. An ALK rearrangement was initially detected based on 5'/3' imbalance and then confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).

ALK fusions are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and are known to result in constitutive activation of ALK, as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1-3]. An ALK rearrangement was initially detected based on 5'/3' imbalance and then confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).

diseases.diagnostic_implications: ALK gene fusions have been described at a low incidence (<1%) in papillary thyroid carcinoma [PMID: 25417114].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Studies suggest that ALK inhibitors may be effective in patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma who have ALK gene fusion [PMID: 25501013, 25527510, 24475247, 24613930].

Crizotinib is FDA approved for non-small cell lung cancer with ALK rearrangements. In limited analysis, crizotinib has been shown to be efficacious in ALK-positive sarcoma or sarcomatoid malignancies [2]. Other agents such as brigatinib and alectinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of ALK-positive NSCLC that have progressed on crizotinib. No molecular alterations associated with resistance to TKI therapy were detected.

Several studies have shown a clinical response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) among patients with NSCLC [4-12]. Three of these TKI therapies - crizotinib, alectinib, and ceritinib - are currently FDA-approved for the first-line treatment of metastatic NSCLC with an ALK rearrangement and treatment with one of these agents is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [13]. Other agents such as brigatinib and alectinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of ALK-positive NSCLC that have progressed on crizotinib. The NCCN guidelines currently recommend alectinib as the preferred first-line treatment based on one study which demonstrated a superior efficacy and lower toxicity for alectinib compared to crizotinib [8,13]. No molecular alterations associated with resistance to TKI therapy were detected.

variants.variant_description: ALK gene fusions resulting in constitutive activation of ALK as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling (particularly STRN-ALK, CAD-ALK and EML4-ALK) are rare but have been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-11]. These fusions are much more common in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [11-23]. Studies have suggested that ALK rearrangements in CRC are associated with shorter overall survival [1] and higher stage [2]. An association with proximal location, MSI and mucinous histology was also observed in one study [2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: ALK fusions are extremely rare in CRC; therefore, there are no FDA-approved therapies for CRC with ALK gene fusions. However, several studies have shown a clinical response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) among patients with NSCLC [15-23] and three of these TKI therapies - crizotinib, alectinib, and ceritinib - are FDA-approved for the first-line treatment of metastatic NSCLC with an ALK rearrangement. In one report, a patient with CRC harboring a STRN-ALK rearrangement demonstrated a dramatic response to certinib though progressive disease associated with the acquistion of  KRAS mutation was reported after 9 months of therapy [2]. A response to entrectinib (now approved for NTRK rearranged solid tumors and ROS1 rearranged NSCLC) was also reported in two studies [3,4]. Importantly, no molecular alterations associated with TKI resistanace were detected.

FGFR3-TACC3 Fusion:
This sample demonstrates an in-frame FGFR3 (breakpoint within exon 16) to TACC3 (breakpoint within exon 11) most likely resulting from a deletion extending from  chr4:1,808,294 to chr4:1,741,450. FGFR-TACC fusions including FGFR3-TACC3 fusions are well described in non-small cell carcinoma [1,2] as well as in gliomas [3,4] and bladder cancer [4,5] and head and neck cancer [4]. These rearrangements involve the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR3 and the coiled-coil domain of TACC3 and result in constitutive activation of FGFR and oncogenic transformation independent of canonical signaling downstream of FGFR (pERK and pAKT) [2-4]. Rather, the fusion protein localizes to mitotic spindle poles and induces mitotic and chromosomal segregation defects and aneuploidy. This patient was treated with alectinib for the ALK translocation described above and has now developed progressive disease. While there are no known reports of acquired resistance to ALK inhibitor therapy resulting from FGFR-TACC fusions, the acquisition of FGFR3-TACC3 fusion HAS been described as mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR inhibitor therapy [5,6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have activity against FGFR3 including the non-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors dovitinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib and selective FGFR inhibitors including erdafitinib, AZD4547, BGJ398 and ASP5878. Case reports [8] and phase 1 clinical trials have demonstrated efficacy of several FGFR inhibitors including erdafitinib (JNJ-42756493) [9], Debio 1347 [10], derazantinib [11], BGJ398 [12] and ASP5878 [13] in tumors harboring FGFR fusions. Erdafinitib was recently (April 12, 2019) granted approval by the US Food and Drug Administration for urothelial cancer with FGFR alterations.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several studies have shown a clinical response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) among patients with NSCLC [6-14]. Three of these TKI therapies - crizotinib, alectinib, and ceritinib - are currently FDA-approved for the first-line treatment of metastatic NSCLC with an ALK rearrangement and treatment with one of these agents is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [15]. At least one patient with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer harboring the specific ALK fusion detected in this specimen exhibited good clinical response to crizotinib [4]. Other agents such as brigatinib and alectinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of ALK-positive NSCLC that have progressed on crizotinib. The NCCN guidelines currently recommend alectinib as the preferred first-line treatment based on one study which demonstrated a superior efficacy and lower toxicity for alectinib compared to crizotinib [10,15]. Importantly, no molecular alterations associated with TKI resistance were detected.

Two ALK mutations were detected affecting the same allele. G1269A is a well-described somatic mutation shown to result in acquired resistance to ALK inhibitor therapy in neoplasms with ALK gene fusions (see below) [1-7]. G1263E has not been described in any known study; therefore, it's affect on protein function (if any) is uncertain. As the G1263E variant is on the same allele as the G1269A variant, G1263E could represent a "passenger" mutation.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Putative oncogenic ALK missense mutations have been reported at a low overall incidence of melnoma [8]. In one study, ALK missense mutations were been reported in approximately to 17.4% (13/69) of "pan-negative" melanomas (absence of NRAS, BRAF, KIT, GNAQ, GNA11) melanomas [9]. The specific mutations detetected in this sample were nor reported in that study, but other activating mutations were.
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several preclinical and clinical studies have demonstrated that the ALK G1269A mutation is associated with acquired resistance to crizotinib [1-7,10-16] and lorlatinib [10-12,17]. This mutation appears to confer moderate resistence to alectinib [16]. However, several preclinical and clinical studies have demonstrated that ALK-rearranged tumors with this mutation remain sensitive to ceritinib [16-17] and brigatinib [14-18].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While several tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) have demonstrated clinical efficacy among patients with NSCLC with ALK rearrangements [6-14], ALK L1196Q mutations are associated acquired resistance to TKI therapy. This mutation confers resistance to crizotinib [4,5,15,16], alectinib [15,16] and ceritinib [16]. Some preclinical evidence has suggested that ALK L1196Q-mutant tumors may show sensitivity to second and third generation inhibitors such as brigatinib (AP26113; IC50 0.009293-0.016 uM) [4-5], loratinib [16] and NVP-TAE684 (IC50 0.019 uM) [4-5]. A partial response to brigatinib was reported in one patient who developed an ALK L1196Q after progressing on crizotinib and alectinib [15]. A more common mutation affecting this codon - L1196M - has also demonstrated preclinical evidence of response to brigatinib and lorlatinib [17] though other small case studies/series have found ALK L1196M mutations with or without concomitant alterations has been associated with progression on loratinib therapy [18-19].

ALK copy number gain (amplification; approximately 6 copies)
A copy number gain of the ALK gene was detected (consistent with low-level gene amplification).

diseases.diagnostic_implications: ALK alterations, including translocations, mutations, and amplifications have been characterized in a variety of tumor types. While ALK fusions are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and are known to result in constitutive activation of ALK, the significance of ALK amplification in lung carcinoma is less clear. Studies have found ALK amplification in up to 17% of NSCLC ! [1,2]. ALK amplification has also been described in anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma, among others $. Putative ALK copy number gains have been described rarely in mammary carcinoma ^. ALK amplification has NOT been described in any known studies of cholangiocarcinoma ~.
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Currently, there are no FDA-approved therapies for patients harboring ALK copy number gains in the absence of an identifiable gene fusion. However, in vitro studies of cell lines with ALK copy number gains have shown sensitivity to ALK inhibitors $. Several trials are underway or recently completed which include ALK amplification as an inclusion criteria to assess the efficacy of crizotinib (NCT02034981) and ceritinib (NCT02186821). Results are not yet publicly available. In addition, potential response to these agents in the context of a low-level copy number gain (as observed in this specimen) is uncertain.

The ALK L1196M mutation detected in this specimen is a well-described acquired resistance mutation in ALK-rearranged NSCLC following crizotinib therapy [1,2].

The ALK L1196M mutation detected in this specimen is a well-described acquired mutation in ALK-rearranged NSCLC [1,2]. This patient is noted to have a history of ALK rearrangement which was also detected in this sample by FISH. The patient was initially responsive to crizotinib but later developed acquired resistance. Consistent with this clinical finding, ALK L1196M is associated with acquired resistance to crizotinib [1,2]. The patient was subsequently treated with alectinib, again initially responding but then developing progressive disease. ALK L1196M has been shown to be sensitive to both alectinib [3] (as well as ceritinib [4]), consistent with the patient's initial response to alectinib. However, the recent development of resistance to alectinib likely reflects an alternative resistance mechanism. The clinical efficacy of certinib treatment in the setting of acquired resistance to both crizotinib and alectinib is uncertain. There are case reports of patients responding to certinib after developing progressive disease on alectinib, although many of these patients carried I1171 or V180 mutations which was not dectected in this specimen [5-8].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several studies have shown a clinical response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) among patients with NSCLC [4-12]. Three of these TKI therapies - crizotinib, alectinib, and ceritinib - are currently FDA-approved for the first-line treatment of metastatic NSCLC with an ALK rearrangement and treatment with one of these agents is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [13]. Other agents such as brigatinib and alectinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of ALK-positive NSCLC that have progressed on crizotinib. The NCCN guidelines currently recommend alectinib as the preferred first-line treatment based on one study which demonstrated a superior efficacy and lower toxicity for alectinib compared to crizotinib [8,13]. However, as described above, an ALK L1196M which is a known acquired resistance mutation to TKI therapy, was also detected in this specimen.  Some preclinical evidence has suggested that ALK L1196M-mutant tumors may show sensitivity to second and third generation inhibitors such as ceritinib, brigatinib, and loratinib [14]. However, other small case studies/series have found ALK L1196M mutations with or without concomitant alterations known to confer resistance, associated with progression on alectinib, brigatinib, and loratinib therapy [15-16].

The I1171T [1-7] and G1269A [7-22] mutations have been described in association with acquired resistance to tyrosine kinas inhibitor (TKI) therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with ALK rearrangements (as in this patient).

The EML4-ALK gene fusion detected in this sample is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and is known to result in constitutive activation of ALK as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1-3]. The I1171T [4-10] and G1269A [10-25] mutations have been described in association with acquired resistance to tyrosine kinas inhibitor (TKI) therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with ALK rearrangements (as in this patient).

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Several studies have shown a clinical response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) among patients with NSCLC [26-34]. However, both I1171T [1-6] and G1269A [7-14, 17-22] confer resisent to crizotinib. I117T has also been shown to confer resistance to alectinib [2,3,6], while G1269A is associated with only moderate resistance to alectinib [22]. G1269A is also associated with resistance to lorlatinib [7,15,17,18]. 
 
Importantly, both I1171T [1,2,6,7] and G1269A [7,15,17,18,22] were shown to remain sensitive to ceritinib in both preclinical and clinical studies. More limited studies suggest that both I1171T [1] and G1269A [15,16,20-22] also remain sensitive to brigatinib. Treatment with one of these agents is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [35].

variants.variant_description: The I1171T mutation has been described as a primary activating mutation in neuroblastoma [1], as well as a mutation associated with acquired resistance to tyrosine kinas inhibitor (TKI) therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with ALK rearrangements (as in this patient) [2-12]. This mutation has been shown to confer a gain of function with ligand-independent constitutive activation (phosphorylation) of ALK and downstream MAPK signaling as well as oncogenic transformation [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While this mutation (and other I1171 mutations including I1171N and I1171S) is associated with resistance to crizotinib [3-7] and alectinib [3,4,7] in both prelinical and clinical studies, this mutation has been shown in preclinical [2,3,7,8] and clinical studies [2,3] to be sensitive to ceritinib [2,3]. The same pattern of resistance to crizotinib and alectinib and sensitivity to ceritinib has been reported for other mutations affecting I1171 including I1171N and I1171S [9-11]. Preclinical studies suggest that brigatinib may also be effective [2,12].

variants.variant_description:
EML4 (exon 13) - ALK (exon 20) fusion with G1202R and V1180L mutations:
ALK is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. The EML4-ALK gene fusion detected in this sample is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and is known to result in constitutive activation of ALK as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1-3]. Several studies have shown a clinical response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) among patients with NSCLC [4-12]. Four of these TKI therapies - crizotinib, alectinib, ceritinib and brigatinib - are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with an ALK rearrangement and treatment with one of these agents is currently a category 1 recommendation within the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [13]. 
 
The ALK G1202R mutation also observed in this specimen is a well-decribed, secondary mutation arising in the context of tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1-]. This mutation effects the solvent-exposed region of the ATP-binding pocket and confers high-level resistance to TKI therapies including crizotinib (PF-02341066), alectinib (CH5424802), ceritinib (LDK378), brigatinib (AP26113), NVP-TAE684, ASP3026 [14-22]. However, a third-generation TKI currently with FDA breakthrough designation under priority review - lorlatinib (PF-06463922) - has been shown to active against the G1202R mutation based on preclinical [23,24] and limited clinical studies [22]. In an ongoing phase 1/2 study (NCT01970865), patients who had received prior crizotinib with or without other therapies achieved an overall objective response and intracranial objective response of 69% (n=59) and 68% (n=37), respectively. Among patients who had received one or more TKI other than crizotinib, an overall objective response and intracranial objective response was observed in 33% (n=37) and 42% (n=12), respectively. This trial is no longer recruiting patients. Another study showed that treatment with lorlatinib can result in resensitization to crizotinib [25]. One study showed that sequential treatment of NSCLC cells with various TKI therapies followed by lorlatinib can result in compound ALK mutations (mutations on the same allele) [24]. Other therapies with preclinical evidence of efficacy against the G1202R mutation include a structural analogue of alectinib - JHVII-157-02 [26], 2,4-diarylaminopyrimidines bearing a resorcinol motif [27], and ceritinib with replacement of the terminal piperidine with aliphatic amines [28].
 
A low-level (approximately 3% allele frequency with approximately 95% neoplastic cellularity) ALK V1180L mutation was identified, consistent with a subclonal mutation. Of note, this mutation is present on a different allele (or different cell population) from the G1202R mutation. The V1180L mutation has been reported in the context of tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy and has been shown to confer resistance to TKI therapies including crizotinib and alectinib [29,30]. However, this mutation appears to be sensitive other TKI therapies including ceritinib, brigatinib, and NVP-TAE684 [29,30]. While lorlatinib has been shown to be efficacious against most resistance mutations evaluated thusfar [23,24], the sensitivity of V1180L for lorlatinib has not yet been evaluated.
 
There are no known clinical trials currently recruiting patients that are relevant for NSCLC with the ALK resistance mutations detected in this specimen. However, lorlatinib is reportedly available for compasionate use (http://www.pfizer.com/research/comassionate_use).

name: CTNNB1
gene_function: CTNNB1 encodes the protein beta-catenin, a key component of the Wnt signaling pathway.

variants.variant_description: This variant affects the BCL-interacting region of the CTNNB1 protein. While this variant has been predicted to decrease interation with GSK3B and decreased stability by structural modeling [PMID: 39202333], it has not been functionally characterized in any known study. Therefore, it is unknown if this variant is oncogenic. This variant has been reported in variants neoplasms [PMID: 21901162, 30115035, 3353453, 10213482, 25624430] including one report in a glioblastoma [PMID: 38079020].

The serine residue affected by this mutation is normally phosphorylated prior to ubiquitination. Therefore, mutations affecting this residue, including S45P, lead to increased beta-catenin stability and activation of Wnt signaling [1]. Such oncogenic mutations have been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1,2]. These mutations are NOT mutually exclusive with other driver mutations as seen in this specimen.
