The CTNNB1 S45P mutation detected in this specimen has been well-described in a wide spectrum of cancers including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [1-4]. Studies have shown that CTNNB1 S45P mutations confer a gain of function to the CTNNB1 protein as demonstrated by stabilization of the CTNNB1 protein [5] and increased transcription of the CTNNB1 target genes [6].

diseases.diagnostic_implications:
90-95% of sporadic desmoid tumors harbor CTNNB1 mutations - most commonly T41A, S45P or S45F [PMID: 17721184, 18832571, 23913621, 20197769, 26171757]. 
CTNNB1 mutations are not present in nodular fasciitis (which primarily harbors USP6 rearrangements) and most other mesenchymal tumors that may be in the differential of desmoid fibromatosis.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of CTNNB1-mutated melanoma, mTOR inhibitors [4,5] and gamma secretase inhibitors (inhibition of NOTCH signaling) [6-11] have shown some evidence of efficacy in other CTNNB1-mutated neoplasms such as desmoid tumors.

While there are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of CTNNB1-mutated melanoma, mTOR inhibitors [7] and gamma secretase inhibitors (inhibition of NOTCH signaling) [8-11] have shown some evidence of efficacy in other CTNNB1-mutated neoplasms such as desmoid tumors.

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of CTNNB1-mutated CRC. mTOR inhibitors [3,4] and gamma secretase inhibitors (inhibition of NOTCH signaling) [5-9] have shown some promise in other CTNNB1-mutated neoplasms such as desmoid tumors. The impact of CTNNB1 mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy is uncertain.

While there are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of CTNNB1-mutated NSCLC, mTOR inhibitors [PMID: 21695255, 18768809] and gamma secretase inhibitors (inhibition of NOTCH signaling) [PMID: 28350521, 23868008, 26349011, 25231399] have shown some activity in other CTNNB1-mutated neoplasms such as desmoid tumors.

Amplification of FGFR3 is described at a low incidence in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1,2]. There are no FDA-approved therapies for the treatment of NSCLC with FGFR3 amplification. While there are several early clinical studies demonstrating modest clinical efficacy of various FGFR inhibitors (e.g. dovitinib, JNJ-42756493, AZD4547, BGJ398, lucitanib) in a subset of NSCLC [3-5] and various other solid tumor malignancies [6,7] with FGFR1 amplification, there are no known preclinical or clinical studies evaluating the efficacy of these agent for FGFR3-amplified cancers. As this sample was equivocal for FGFR3 amplification by this assay, evaluation of FGFR3 status using different method (e.g. FISH) is recommended, if clinically indicated.

FGFR-TACC fusions including FGFR3-TACC3 fusions are well described in non-small cell carcinoma [1,2] as well as in gliomas [3,4] and bladder cancer [4,5] and head and neck cancer [4]. These rearrangements involve the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR3 and the coiled-coil domain of TACC3. The fusion results in constitutive activation of FGFR and oncogenic transformation independent of canonical signaling downstream of FGFR (pERK and pAKT) [2-4]. Rather, the fusion protein localizes to mitotic spindle poles and induces mitotic and chromosomal segregation defects and aneuploidy.

diseases.diagnostic_implications:
FGFR-TACC fusions are well-described in gliomas [PMID: 22837387, 25609060], particularly glioblastoma, IDH wild-type (incidence approximately 3%) [PMID: 22837387, 25609060, 28912153, 28976058]. Morphologic features reported in association with glioblastomas with FGFR3-TACC3 rearrangements include monomorphous ovoid nuclei, nuclear palisading, thin parallel cytoplasmic processes, and endocrinoid network of thin capillaries [PMID: 28976058] as wells a neuroepithelial tumors [PMID: 28976058].

FGFR-TACC fusions are well-described in gliomas [1,2], particularly glioblastoma, IDH wild-type (incidence approximately 3%) [1-4]. Morphologic features reported in association with glioblastomas with FGFR3-TACC3 rearrangements include monomorphous ovoid nuclei, nuclear palisading, thin parallel cytoplasmic processes, and enocrinoid network of thin capillaries [4] as wells a neuroepithelial tumors [4]. 
 
FGFR3-TACC3 fusions have also been reported in tumor diagnosed as low grade glioma [3] and low-grade neuroepithelial tumors [5-8] including polymorphous low-grade neuroepithelial tumor of the young [6-7]. In glioblastoma, FGFR3-TACC3 fusions frequently co-occur with TERT promoter mutations and loss of CDKN2A, which can help distinguish these cases from low-grade entities. Some authors have argued that the presence of FGFR3-TACC3 fusions in low-grade neuroepithelial tumors may indicate a need for closer surveillance for evidence of a high grade glioma.
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are no FDA-approved therapies for gliomas with FGFR3 rearrangements. Erdafitinib (Balversa; JNJ-42756493) is a selective FGFR inhibitor that was recently granted approval by the US Food and Drug Administration for urothelial cancer with FGFR alterations and pemigatinib (Pemazyre), infigratinib (Truseltiq) and futibatinib (Lytgobi) are FDA-approved for the treatment of cholangiocarcinomas with FGFR2 rearrangements. Pemigatinib is also FDA-approved for the treatment of relapsed/refractory myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with FGFR1 rearrangements.
 
Erdafitinib has also demonstrated evidence of preclinical and clinical efficacy in early studies of other cancers with FGFR alterations including a small number of glioma patients [PMID: 25609060, 26324363]. There have been case reports demonstrating efficacy of erdafitinib in patients with solid tumors with FGFR3-TACC3 fusions [PMID: 37214414]. In a phase II study, infigratinib demonstrated durable disease control among patient with recurrent gliomas harboring FGFR1/3 point mutations or FGFR3-TACC3 fusions [PMID: 35344029].
 
Multiple other FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have activity against FGFR3 including the non-selective inhibitors dovitinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib and selective FGFR inhibitors including AZD4547, BGJ398.

The FGFR3 P250R mutation detected in this sample has never been described in colorectal carcinoma. This varient has been described as a germline variant associated with craniosynostosis (Muenke syndrome) with a highly variable phenotype, manifesting as unicoronal or bicoronal synostosis, macrocephaly or a normal cranial phenotype  [1-5]. There are no known reports of this variant presenting as an acquired somatic mutation in cancer. In addition, the allele frequency of this variant (approximately 50%) in relation to the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells in the extracted specimen (40%) as well as the allele frequencies of the two somatic mutations described above (each 15%), suggests that the FGFR3 P250R variant may be germline. Genetic counselling is recommended, if clinically indicated.

Because this test was performed using neoplastic tissue, it is not certain whether this variant is germline or somatic. However, the variant allele frequency (near 50%) is consistent with a germline mutation and the patient reportedly has phenotypic features consistent with Muenke Syndrome including craniosynostosis.

variants.variant_description: The FGFR2 N549D variant detected in this specimen affects the kinase domain of the FGFR2 protein and a mutation affecting the same codon (N549K) has been shown to result in oncogenic transformation in vitro with increased MAPK pathway signaling [PMID: 18552176, 19147536]. Variants at the same amino acid position (N549) in FGFR2 and analogous residues in FGFR1 and FGFR3 have been also been associated with various tumors. However, FGFR2 variants have also been associated with Apert and Crouzon syndromes, with variants this particular residue (N549) associated with Crouzon syndrome in at least some reports [PMID: 26003532]. While the variant allele frequency in comparison with the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells is more consistent with a somatic mutation than a germline variant, genetic counseling is recommended If there is any clinical concern for one of these syndromes.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) have activity against FGFR2 including pemigatinib, futinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib. Pemigatinib and and futinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 fusions (not mutations). Endometrial carcinoma cell lines with FGFR2 mutations (including N549K, which at the same site of this mutation) which were treated with ponatinib showed inhibited proliferation and induced apoptosis with a decrease in kinase activity [PMID: 26574622]. In addition, non-selective FGFR inhibitors have been used in the treatment of squamous cell carcinomas of lung origin with FGFR2 kinase mutations [PMID: 24265351]. While N549K has not been previously characterized, it has been identified as a secondary-resistance mutation in patient-derived xenograft models treated with FGFR inhibitors [PMID: 39363320].

variants.variant_description: An in-frame gene fusion was identified involving exons 1-16 of FGFR2 and exons 7-13 of TACC1. While there are no known reports of the exact FGFR2-TACC1 fusion detected in this sample, similar FGFR-TACC fusions fusions are well described in gliomas [1,2]. These rearrangements involve the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR and the coiled-coil domain of TACC. The fusion results in constitutive activation of FGFR and oncogenic transformation independent of canonical signaling downstream of FGFR (pERK and pAKT) [1]. Rather, the fusion protein localizes to mitotic spindle poles and induces mitotic and chromosomal segregation defects and aneuploidy. FGFR-TACC fusions are mutually exclusive with IDH1/2 mutations and frequently co-occur with CDK4 amplification (not seen in this specimen).

name: MTOR
gene_function: MTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) is a serine/threonine kinase involved in growth signaling within the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway.

variants.variant_description: MTOR mutations, in general, are well-described in a wide variety of cancer types, including colorectal carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, and melanoma [PMID: 22810696, 25079552, 24631838]. However, it is within a region of recurrent mutations which have been reported within the TCGA datasets available in cBioPortal.

variants.variant_description:
Multiple PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway alterations (PIK3CA E545K, AKT1 E17K, MTOR E2419K)
PIK3CA, AKT1, and MTOR are all major components of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway involved in growth signaling. PIK3CA encodes one of the catalytic subunits of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, a lipid kinase involved in initiation of the intracellular component signaling that is downstream of EGFR. PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, including E545K, are well-described in a wide variety of neoplasms [1-3] and are not specific to a particular primary. AKT1 is a serine/threonine kinase and the E17K mutation effects the pleckstrin homology domain and results in constitutive activation of PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway and downstream growth signaling [4-5]. These mutations have been well described in a variety of tumors and are also not specific to a particular primary [5]. MTOR is a serine/threonine kinase and the E2419K mutation affects the kinase domain of MTOR and has been shown to result in constitutive activation of MTOR [6]. All 3 of these mutations in this specimen were at allele frequencies lower than expected based on estimated tumor percentage and may reflect tumor heterogeneity or subclonal populations. 
 
Theapeutic Implications:
Alpelisib (Piqray) was shown to be efficacious in PIK3CA-mutant metastatic breast cancer and was recently FDA-approved with trials ongoing for additional applications [7]. In early clinical studies, AKT inhibitors such as capivasertib (AZD5363) and MK-2206 have demonstrated efficacy in advanced solid tumors with AKT1 mutations such as breast cancer [8-9] and others [10]. In addition, recent literature has shown AKT1 E17K mutations are more resistant to radiation treatment due to the increased DNA repair response to double stranded breaks in tumors with this alteration [5]. The mTOR inhibitor everolimus is FDA approved for the treatment of renal cell carcinoma, breast carcinoma, and neuroendocrine carcinomas. It is unclear what the combination of the alterations seen in this case would be on the effects of these therapeutic options, although alterations of alterations downstream from PIK3CA raise concerns about alpelisib efficacy.

The HRAS Q61L mutation identified in this specimen has been described in non-small cell lung cancer [4] as well as many other neoplasms [5-8]. This mutation results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of HRAS as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: HRAS mutations are well-described, somatic mutations in a variety of solid tumors and cutaneous neoplasms. Solid tumors include urothelial carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, colorectal carcinoma, and thyroid cancer [PMID: 28988769, 28481359, 22980975, 26878173]. Cutaneous neoplasms include cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma [PMID: 22256804], as well as melanocytic tumors including benign nevi [PMID: 22499344, 19438459, 223337891, 23599145, 24390138] (particularly Spitz nevi) [PMID: 23599145, 19438459, 10980135] and (less commonly) in melanoma [PMID: 28467829, 28481359, 36219477]. HRAS mutations are also common in other skin tumors including adnexal tumors [PMID: 37074845, 22683711, 223337891, 24890286, 25532942, 25950823], seborrheic keratoses [PMID: 23739246], nevi sebaceous [PMID: 23096712, 24129065, 23096709].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are currently no FDA-approved therapies for HRAS-mutant solid tumors. Although patients with urothelial carcinoma and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma harboring oncogenic HRAS mutations have been treated with the farnesyl transferase inhibitor (FTI) tipifarnib with encouraging results [PMID: 32636318, 33750196].
 
There are also currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for RAS-mutated melanoma. However, MEK inhibitors have shown mixed clinical efficacy in the treatment of RAS-mutated melanoma (more commonly NRAS). While response to some MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib has been disappointing [PMID: 22048237, 22805292], clinical trials have demonstrated modest clinical efficacy for binimetinib [PMID: 28284557, 23414587, 28152546]. In a phase 3 trial, binimetinib demonstrated a modest improvement in progression free survival (though no statistically significant difference in overall survival) when compared with dacarbazine [PMID: 28284557]. The efficacy was most pronounced in patients who had received prior immunotherapy. Preclinical studies have also suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more efficacious when used in combination with immunotherapy [PMID: 28919996].

In a phase 2 trial, KRAS-mutant NSCLC treated with trametinib (GSK1120212) showed a similar progression free survival and response rate as docetaxel [9]. While some clinical trials have suggested that the combination of a MEK inhibitor and docetaxel may be more efficacious than docetaxel alone [10-11], a large clinical trial failed to show any improvement in progression free survival for the combination of selumetinib (AZD6244) and docetaxel compared to docetaxel alone [12]. In preclinical studies, treatment of lung cancer cells with a MEK inhibitor induces a compensatory response involving FGFR1 leading to adaptive resistance while the combination of MEK and FGFR1 inhibition resulted in greater sensitivity than MEK inhibition alone [13]. The combination of a MEK inhibitor with other agents such as PI3K inhibitors [14], histone deacetylase inhibitors [9], or CDK4/6 inhibitors [10,11] has also demonstrated improved antitumor activity in preclinical studies.

Preliminary data from a phase 2 clinical trial (NCT02383927) suggests that HRAS-mutant head and neck squamous cell carcinomas frequently demonstrate a clinical response to the farnesyltransferase inhibitor tipifarnib [4]. Howerver, its clinical significiance in patients with HRAS Q61K mutant colorectal cancer is unknown. Furthermore, pre-clinical data indicates that tipifarnib can inhibit tumor cell growth in mouse models of poorly-differentiated and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, and combination therapy with a MEK inhibitor (i.e., AZD6244) improves response of tumor cells to tipifarnib; however, acquired resistance to tipifarnib was associated with subsequent NF1 or GNAS mutations [4]. Patients with colorectal cancer harboring any known KRAS mutation (exon 2, 3, 4) or NRAS mutation (exon 2, 3, 4) should not be treated with either cetuximab or panitumumab [18]. The MAPK pathway of RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK is downstream of EGFR; mutations in components of this pathway are now established to be strong negative predictive markers, essentially precluding efficacy of these therapies [6]. The potential efficacy of MAPK pathway inhibition downstream of RAS (e.g. ERK inhibitors) is also under investigation.

Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in KRAS-mutated neoplasms [2]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have thusfar been disappointing [3-11]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [12], CDK4/6 [13-15], ERBB3 [16], histone deacetylase [17], STAT3 [18] and PI3K inhibitors [19,20].

HRAS (Harvey Ras) is a membrane-associated GTPase. It plays an important role as an upstream mediator of several pro-proliferative and anti-apoptotic signal transduction pathways, including the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) and PI3 kinase (PI3K) pathways. HRAS, NRAS and KRAS comprise the Ras proto-oncogene family, and all three have a similar structure and function. Transforming, gain-of-function mutations of RAS oncogenes tend to disrupt GTPase activity and promote cell proliferation and angiogenesis. G12S is classified as pathogenic and oncogenic.Patients with Costello syndrome, a hereditary disorder with germline alterations in HRAS, can develop various malignancies at a young age, including neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma and transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder (OncoKb Dec 2022). AKT1 E17K:
AKT1 is a serine/threonine kinase involved in growth signaling within the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway. The AKT1 E17K mutation detected in this specimen affects the pleckstrin homology domain and results in constitutive activation of PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway [PMID: 17611497]. AKT1 is a serine/threonine kinase involved in growth signaling within the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway. AKT1 mutations are often seen in hormone receptor positive (HR+), ERBB2 negative (HER2-) breast cancer (similar to PIK3CA mutations) [3,4] and have been associated with resistance to endocrine therapy [5,6]. ERBB3 D297Y(;)[E332K;K356N]:
Three ERBB3 mutations were detected, two of which affect the same allele. While this protein is kinase-impaired, it is known to form active heterodimers with other members of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, particularly ERBB2 [PMID: 10880430]. The D297Y mutation affects the extracellular domain, resulting in ligand-independent oncogenic signaling by promoting the formation of active heterodimers with ERBB2 [PMID: 23680147, 29963236]. The ERBB3 D297Y mutation has been described in several cancer types [PMID: 29420467, 28481359, 27044931, 22810696]. The E332K mutation is thought to be activating based on in vitro data that shows that it enhances cell survival and proliferation [PMID: 38806620]. There is no functional data for the K356N mutation, and its significance is uncertain.

While there is no available functional data about the ERBB3 R103H mutation, it has been identified as a statistically significant hotspot and is likely to be oncogenic. diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no FDA-approved treatments for ERBB3-mutated cancer. While the impact of this mutation on response to anti-EGFR antibody is not entirely certain, studies have shown that cetuximab does not affect activation of ERBB3 or ERBB2 [PMID: 25474137], and activation of ERBB2/ERBB3 signaling (through heregulin or ERBB2 amplification) has been implicated as a potential mechanism of resistance to anti-EGFR therapy [PMID: 21900593]. However, concurrent treatment with a EGFR/ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g., lapatinib) or an antibody that disrupts ERBB2/ERBB3 dimerization (e.g., pertuzumab or partrimumab) was shown to rescue sensitivity to anti-EGFR therapy in cells with heregulin-mediated resistance [PMID: 21900593, 25961915].

variants.variant_description: While this protein is kinase-impaired, it is known to form active heterodimers with other members of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, particularly ERBB2. The ERBB3 T355I mutation has been described as a recurrent, somatic mutation in colorectal [1] and other cancers [2-6]. ERBB3 T355I affects the extracellular domain and has been shown to be activating with increased cellular proliferation [2,3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While the impact of ERBB3 mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibodies not entirely certain, studies have shown that cetuximab does not affect activation of ERBB3 or ERBB2 [7], and activation of ERBB2/ERBB3 signaling (through heregulin or ERBB2 amplification) has been implicated as a potential mechanism of resistance to anti-EGFR therapy [8]. While concurrent treatment with a EGFR/ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g., lapatinib) or an antibody that disrupts ERBB2/ERBB3 dimerization (e.g., pertuzumab) was shown to rescue sensitivity to anti-EGFR therapy in cells with heregulin-mediated resistance [8,9].

ERRB3 H228Q:
ERBB3 is a member of the ErbB family of receptors and is the only one without receptor tyrosine kinase activity [1-2]. Its role is thought to be related to binding of its biological partners to confer activity. While rare, the H228Q mutation detected in this specimen has been described in gastric carcinomas, including within the TCGA gastric cancer cohort [3]. While functional studies on the oncogenic nature of this mutation are lacking, ERRB3 mutations in gastric carcinoma are common [3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no therapeutic targets for ERBB3 mutations.  In breast cancer, it has been shown that alterations in ERRB3 can be associated with resistance to hormonal and TKI therapies [4]. There have been clinical trails looking at targeting ERRB3 in the presence of HER2 therapy resistance, but the indications of targeting this protein without a concurrent ERRB2 alteration is not known [5].

variants.variant_description: WHO [1]. AML prognosis [2-19]. MDS prognosis [20-26]. MPN prognosis [27-38]. NCCN AML [39]. NCCN MDS [40]. NCCN MPN [41]. Targeted therapies [42-51]. Cryptic [52].

While this protein is kinase-impaired, it is known to form active heterodimers with other members of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, particularly ERBB2 [1]. Mutations of residue 297 affect the extracellular domain resulting in ligand-independent oncogenic signaling by promoting the formation of active heterodimers with ERBB2 [2,3]. While ERBB3 D297H mutation has not been previously described or characteized, mutations affecting codon 297, particularly ERBB3 D297Y mutation has been described in several cancer types [4-7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The potential impact of this mutation or any mutations affecting codon 297 on sensitivity to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) or anti-ERBB antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab, pertuzumab) is uncertain. In a preclinical study, the TKI lapatinib was NOT effective in suppressing cell proliferation of cells with ERBB3 D297Y while trastuzumab and pertuzumab were [3]. In clinical trials, the TKI neratinib showed no clinical activity in an ERBB3-mutant cohort of 16 patients, which included 3 patients with D297Y [4]. The potential impact of these therapies in light of the concomitant ERBB2 amplification described above is uncertain.

variants.variant_description:
ERBB2 (HER2) copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain (approximately 13 copies) of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected (consistent with amplification). ERBB2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. ERBB2 amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression is well-described in urothelial carcinoma (UC) with reported frequencies of approximately 5% [1-4]. Intratumoral heterogeneity with regard to ERBB2 copy number status is common in UC [5,6]. Some studies have suggested that ERBB2 amplification is associated with more aggressive behavior in UC [7].

While this protein is kinase-impaired, it is known to form active heterodimers with other members of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, particularly ERBB2. The ERBB3 D297Y mutation is well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1,2], as well as other cancers [2,3]. Mutations of this residue affect the extracellular domain resulting in ligand-independent oncogenic signaling by promoting the formation of active heterodimers with ERBB2 [2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Anti-ERBB2 antibodies (such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab) and ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI; such as neratinib) are efficacious and currently FDA-approved in the treatment of ERBB2-amplified breast cancer. The potential response to these agents in UC with ERBB2 amplification is uncertain. While studies have shown a response to trastuzumab [8], afatinib [9] combined with chemotherapy in ERBB2 amplified or IHC+, a phase II study of UC with ERBB2 overexpression failed to show a statistically significant difference between gemcitabine, platinum and trastuzumab compared with gemcitabine and platinum alone (possibly due to an inadequate sample size; n=61) [10]. However, the latter study showed that higher ERBB2 copy number correlated with treatment response. Therefore, efficacy of one or more of these therapies may be demonstrable in UC patients if more selective ERBB2 criteria is utilized.

The potential impact of this mutation on sensitivity to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) or anti-ERBB antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab, pertuzumab) is uncertain. In a preclinical study, the TKI lapatinib was NOT effective in suppressing cell proliferation of cells with ERBB3 D297Y while trastuzumab and pertuzumab were [3]. In clinical trials, the TKI neratinib showed no clinical activity in an ERBB3-mutant cohort of 16 patients, which included 3 patients with D297Y [4]. In another study of patients with urothelial carcinoma, 3/3 urothelial carcinoma patients with ERBB3 mutations (one with concomitant ERBB2 and EGFR amplification) treated with afatinib achieved the primary end-point of 3 month progression-free survival [6]. The potential impact of these therapies in light of the concomitant ERBB2 amplifcation described above is uncertain.

While the impact of this mutation on response to anti-EGFR antibody is not entirely certain, studies have shown that cetuximab does not affect activation of ERBB3 or ERBB2 [4], and activation of ERBB2/ERBB3 signaling (through heregulin or ERBB2 amplification) has been implicated as a potential mechanism of resistance to anti-EGFR therapy [5]. However, concurrent treatment with a EGFR/ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g., lapatinib) or an antibody that disrupts ERBB2/ERBB3 dimerization (e.g., pertuzumab or partrimumab) was shown to rescue sensitivity to anti-EGFR therapy in cells with heregulin-mediated resistance [5,6].

variants.variant_description: The ERBB3 M91I mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon but has been described as a somatic mutation in bladder cancer [1], endometrial cancer [1] and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma [2]. The functionaly effect of this variant has not been evaluated.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Currently, there are no FDA-approved treatments for ERBB3-mutated breast cancer; however, dual HER2 blockade (i.e., trastuzumab and lapatinib) in a patient with HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer harboring an activating ERBB3 mutation (G284R) resulted in rapid complete metabolic response [3]. Similarly, tumors harboring ERBB3 mutations have been shown to be sensitive to a number of anti-ERBB family therapies (i.e., lapatinib, trastuzumab, etc.) in pre-clinical models [4,5].

The KIT D816V mutation identified in this specimen affects the protein kinase domain (exon 17) of the Kit protein [1]. This mutation confers a gain of function on Kit, as indicated by constitutive phosphorylation of Kit in cultured cells [PMID: 25148578].

RAS wild-type and BRAF wild-type: 
Cetuximab and panitumumab are monoclonal antibodies directed against EGFR that inhibit its downstream signaling pathways. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines, these therapies have been studied in combination with FOLFIRI and FOLFOX as initial therapy options for treatment of patients with KRAS and NRAS wild type metastatic colorectal cancer. The randomized, phase II PLANET-TTD trial comparing patients treated with panitumumab plus either FOLFOX or FOLFIRI found no significant differences in efficacy between the two regimens. Patients with any known KRAS mutation (exons 2, 3, and 4) or NRAS mutation (exons 2, 3, and 4) should not be treated with either cetuximab or panitumumab, unless given as part of a regimen targeting a KRAS G12C mutation [NCCN Colon v5.2024].

MYC (c-MYC) encodes a transcription factor involved in growth signalling. Oncogenic amplification (as well as rearrangements) have been described in many neoplasms including colorectal cancer (CRC) [1]. Limited studies have reported MYC amplification to be a negative prognostic indicator [2,3]. There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified CRC. Some preclinical studies have suggested that CRC cells with MYC amplification may be more sensitive to 5-fluorouracil and paclitaxel [4,5]. Other preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [6-8]. Clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of some of these agents (particularly BET bromodomain inhibitors) are ongoing. Michigan Medicine is currently participating in one such study - a Phase 1/2 study investigating the safety and preliminary efficacy of the BET bromodomain inhibitor INCB057643 in advanced-stage malignancies (NCT02711137; UMCC 2016.052).

ERBB2 copy number gain (amplification):
ERBB2 (HER2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. A copy number gain of ERBB2 was detected, consistent with gene amplification, that may result in increased ERBB2 expression, resutling in activation of downstream growth signaling.

Low-level MYC copy number gain (equivocal for amplification):
A low-level copy number gain of the MYC gene (considered equivocal for amplification) was detected in this specimen. MYC (c-MYC) is a transcription factor involved in growth signaling. Copy number alterations have been described in many neoplasms including small cell lung cancer (SCLC) [1-2]. MYC amplification has been reported to be a negative prognostic indicator [1].

MET copy number gain (amplification): 
A copy number gain involving the MET gene was detected (approximately 7 copies). MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling and MET amplification, as seen in this specimen, is well-described in multiple tumors types but is rare in pancreatic adenocarcinoma (<1%) [1-2].

Low-level FGFR1 copy number gain (equivocal for amplification):
A low-level copy number gain of the FGFR1 gene was detected (approximately 4-6 copies; considered equivocal for amplification). FGFR1 is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. Amplification of FGFR1 is well-described in a variety of tumor types including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), particularly squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) [1]. There are also rare reports of FGFR1 amplification in pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinomas and thymomas [2-3].

FGFR3 p.[S371R;Y373C]:
FGFR3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. This specimen contained two alterations in FGFR3; Y373C is a well-described mutation in urothelial carcinoma [1-4]. The Y373C mutation results in a gain of function of FGFR3 protein with constitutive activation, signaling, and transformation of cell lines [1,5]. While the variant S371R has been reported in urothelial carcinoma and is likely pathogenic, it is not as well-characterized although increased kinase activity has been reported [2,6,7].

BRAF is a serine-threonine kinase involved in growth signaling, downstream of EGFR within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. The BRAF G466V mutation identified in this specimen is well described in NSCLC. While this mutation is associated with reduced kinase activity, it has been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation in a RAS-dependent manner [1,2]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to CRAF heterodimers. While the combination of dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with a BRAF V600E mutation, the utility of this therapy in NSCLC with non-V600 mutations, like G466V, is uncertain. However, BRAF inhibitors, such as dabrafenib, inhibit activated BRAF monomers but do not affect the formation of heterodimers. As a result, BRAF inhibitors do not suppress MAPK signaling in cells with BRAF G466V mutations [2]. However, unlike cells with activating BRAF mutations such as V600E, cells harboring the BRAF G466V mutation other "class 3" mutations have shown in vitro sensitivity to inhibition of receptor tyrosine kinase activity by desatinib [1] and cetuximab (with or without MEK inhibition) [2].

EGFR p.[L747_E749del;T751I;K754E]:
A complex EGFR mutation within exon 19 that involves a deletion (L747_E749del) and two single nucleotide substitutions (T751I and K754E) all on one allele. Because these variants all affect the same allele, they could also be designated as a single deletion/insertion mutation (L747_K754delinsAISPE). EGFR exon 19 deletion mutations are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of EGFR as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. The specific EGFR exon 19 deletion identified in this patient's tumor (L747_E749del) is uncommon but occurs in a hotspot region for frame-preserving deletions. EGFR T751I is rare variant described in NSCLC [2-4] that has not been biochemically characterized. While K754E is also relatively uncommon in NSCLC, it has been shown to be oncogenic in preclinical models and has previously been reported co-occuring with an exon 19 deletion [5,6].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating mutations in the tyrosine kinase 2 domain (exon 17) of the KIT gene, especially KIT p.D816V, are the molecular hallmark of systemic mastocytosis and are identified in approximately 90% of cases, depending on subtype [WHO Haematolymphoid Tumors (5th ed)].

ERBB2 amplification is described in a variety of different malignancies including breast carcinoma (5-13%) [1-5] and gastric and gastroesophageal carcinoma (13-30%) [6-8]. ERBB2 is less common in colorectal cancer (3%) [9], non-small cell lung cancer (< 2%) [10] and other carcinomas.
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Anti-ERBB2 antibodies including trastuzumab, ado-trastuzumab emtansine and pertuzumab, as well as tyrosine kinase inhibitors including lapatinib and neratinib [11-21] have been shown to be effective for ERBB2-amplified breast cancer and have been FDA-approved for the treatment of HER2+ breast cancer [2]. The anti-ERBB2 antibody trastuzumab (Herceptin) is FDA-approved (in combination with cisplatin and capecitabine or 5-fluorouracil) for the treatment of ERBB2 overexpressing GEA. In the ToGA trial, patients with ERBB2+ advanced GEA who were treated with trastuzumab in addition to chemotherapy achieved significantly improvement in median overall survival compared to chemotherapy alone [22]. Limited clinical studies have suggested a potential benefit from these agents in other cancers [12-21].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified SCLC. However, Aurora kinase inhibitors (e.g., alisertib) may have efficacy towards MYC-amplified SCLC and while studies indicate possible response to CHK1 inhibition or disruption of MYC complexes [2-9]. 
 
Because this sample was found to be equivocal for amplification using this assay, evaluation using an alternative method (e.g. FISH) is recommended before any clinical action is taken based on these results.

While there are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MET-amplified pancreatic carcinoma, emerging data from case reports and small series suggest that tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapies such as crizotinib may be efficacious in cancers with high-level MET amplification such as non-small cell lung cancer [3-13]. There is one phase 2 clinical trial on cMET inhibition in PDAC, now completed, which is yet unpublished.

Multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have activity against FGFR1 including the non-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors dovitinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib and selective FGFR inhibitors including erdafitinib, AZD4547, BGJ398. Some studies have demonstrated the clinical efficacy of dovitinib, AZD4547 and BGJ398 in lung squamous cell carcinoma with FGFR1 amplification [4-6]; AZD4547 in gastric and breast cancer with high-level FGFR2 amplification [7]; and BGJ398 and lucitanib in various solid tumor malignancies with FGFR1/3 amplification [5,8]. In a phase 1 trial, erdafitinib (JNJ-42756493) demonstrated activity in tumors with FGFR pathway alterations [9]. Erdafinitib was recently FDA-approved for for urothelial cancer with FGFR2/3 mutations or gene fusions. The potential utility of these agents in the context of a low-level copy number gain (as detected in this sample) is uncertain.

Erdafinitib was recently granted approval by the US Food and Drug Administration for urothelial cancer with FGFR alterations, with initial response rates of approximately 30% in study BLC2001 NCT02365597 [8]. Trials with other FGFR inhibitors have also shown benefit in other cancers [9-12].

EGFR exon 19 deletions are associated with sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy [1,7], and multiple TKI therapies are currently FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions, including erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib and dacomitinib. Treatment of metastatic NSCLC with one of these agents is recommended by the National Comprehenisve Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [8]. According to these guidelines, osimertinib is currently considered the preferred first-line treatment for NSCLC with a sensitizing EGFR mutation [8]. The clinical significance of the EGFR T751I and K754E on the same allele as the exon 19 deletion is unclear; however, pre-clinical data suggests that tumors harboring this K754E may be less sensitive to some EGFR TKIs, including erlotinib [5].

The following variant of uncertain clinical significance was detected: c.311_313dup, p.G104dup.
This rare variant has been reported as a germline variant detected in patients with acute myeloid leukemia [1,2]. It is not known if this variant is associated with a predisposition to myeloid neoplasms. Unlike the variant detected in this specimen, most germline CEBPA variants associated with familial myeloid neoplasms are frameshift mutations within the N-terminus [3-8]. In addition, CEBPA variants associated predisposed to myeloid neoplasms are generally accompanied by a second mutation affecting the C-terminus of other CEBPA allele when patients present with a myeloid neoplasm [3-8] – not observed in this specimen. However, because the clinical significance of this germline variant is uncertain, a family history and possibly genetic counseling is recommended.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MET-amplified pancreatic carcinoma, emerging data from case reports and small series suggest that tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapies such as crizotinib may be efficacious in cancers with high-level MET amplification such as non-small cell lung cancer [3-13]. There is one phase 2 clinical trial on cMET inhibition in PDAC, now completed, which is yet unpublished [14].

variants.variant_description:
The PDGFRA N659K mutation detected in this specimen is present in a subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumors and has rarely been identified in other human neoplasms [3,4]. The N659K residue lies in the ATP binding domain, and amino acid substitution at this position results in constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation and upregulation of PDGFRA activity [5,6].

PDGFRA mutations have been identified in small subsets adult and pediatric high-grade gliomas [1,2] including the N659K mutation detected in this specimen [3]. The N659K residue lies in the ATP binding domain, and amino acid substitution at this position results in constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation and upregulation of PDGFRA activity [4,5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Patients with GISTs harboriing PDGFRA mutations are unlikely to respond to imatinib and most other approved TKIs for GIST except for avapritinib [8].Therefore, GISTs with imatinib-insensitive mutations are managed differently than most GISTs and the NCCN panel recommends avapritinib as the preferred first-line treatment option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GISTs with imatinib-resistant PDGFRA mutations [8].

Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of various neoplasms with KIT mutations, PDGFRA rearrangements and BCR-ABL1 fusions [6-9]. However, the clinical utility in patients with gliomas harboring PDGFRA mutations is not well characterized.

variants.variant_description: PDGFRA N659 mutations, including the PDGFRA N659Y mutation detected in this specimen, are present in a subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumors and are more common in gastric GISTs [PMID: 15928335, 28481359, 19585585, 16258521, 36119525]. The N659 residue lies in the ATP binding domain, and amino acid substitution at this position results in constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation and upregulation of PDGFRA activity [PMID: 12949711, 29533785].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: According to the most recent NCCN guidelines, most PDGFRA mutations are associated with a response to imatinib, with the exception of D842V [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 2.2024]. Although the N659Y mutation has not been characterized, in vitro evidence suggests that the N659K mutation, affecting the same residue, is sensitive to imatinib [PMID: 15928335].

variants.variant_description: Exon 18 deletion mutations and deletion/insertion mutations, such as D842_D846delinsAC, stabilize the activation loop of the kinase domain of PDGFRA and have been shown to result in constitutive activation of PDGFRA and downstream MAPK, AKT and STAT signaling [PMID: 12522257].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating PDGFRA, particularly exon 18 mutations, are well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and are mutually exclusive with KIT mutations [PMID: 12522257, 15928335, 29312652]. PDGFRA mutations show a strong predilection for gastric GIST often with epithelioid morphology [PMID: 29312652]. These mutations are much less common in intestinal GIST [PMID: 29312652]. Specific mutations in KIT or PDGFRA show some correlation with tumor phenotype, but mutations are not strongly correlated with the biologic potential of individual tumors. The accumulated data show that KIT mutations are not preferentially present in high-grade tumors, and can also be found in small incidental tumors as well as tumors that have an indolent course. Similarly, mutational analysis of PDGFRA cannot be used to predict the behavior of individual tumors [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Most PDGFRA mutations are associated with a response to imatinib, with the exception of D842V, which is unlikely to respond [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. For patients with PDGFRA exon 18 deletion mutations, there is both in vitro and clinical data supporting positive response to both imatinib and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors [PMID: 26130666;  24638008]. Imatinib is included in the NCCN guidelines as a category 1 preferred first-line treatment option for patients with advanced or metastatic GIST with imatinib-sensitive mutations; however, it is not recommended for the treatment of GIST with PDGFRA exon 18 mutations that are insensitive to imatinib, especially D842V [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. 
 
The NCCN panel recommends avapritinib as the preferred first-line treatment option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST with imatinib-resistant PDGFRA D842V mutations or other PDGFRA exon 18 mutations that are known to be imatinib insensitive [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. One study that included both in vitro and clinical trial data showed that none of the patients with the imatinib-resistant D842V mutation responded to imatanib, whereas two of three patients with imatinib-sensitive PDGFRA oncoproteins achieved a PR with imatinib therapy [PMID: 14645423]. Referral to clinical trial is strongly recommended for patients with mutations resistant to imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib, ripretinib, and avapritinib [PMID: 15928335, 15146165, 33465704, 29312652, 32972961].

The N823 residue lies in the protein kinase domain and results in constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation and oncogenic PDGFRA activity [PMID: 29533785, 12949711].

However, the clinical significance in patient with non-small cell lung cancer is unclear at this time.

variants.variant_description:
PDGFRA mutations, including the PDGFRA D842V mutation detected in this specimen, are present in a subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumors and are more common in gastric GISTs [PMID: 15928335, 28481359, 19585585, 16258521, 36119525]. The D842 residue lies in the ATP binding domain, and amino acid substitution at this position results in constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation and upregulation of PDGFRA activity [PMID: 12949711, 29533785].

PDGFRA mutations have been identified in small subsets adult and pediatric high-grade gliomas [1,2]. The PDGFRA D842V mutation detected in this specimen has been reported in pediatric high-grade gliomas [3] and is present in a subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumors and has rarely been identified in other human neoplasms [4,5]. The D842 residue lies in the juxtamembrane domain, and amino acid substitution at this position results in constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation and oncogenic PDGFRA activity [5,6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Avapritinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of unresectable or metastatic GIST with PDGFRA exon 18 mutations, including D842V mutations. Patients with GISTs harboring PDGFRA D842V mutations are unlikely to respond to imatinib and most other approved TKIs for GIST except for avapritinib [PMID: 15928335]. The NCCN panel recommend avapritinib as the preferred first-line treatment option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST with imatinib-resistant PDGFRA D842V mutations or other PDGFRA exon 18 mutations that are known to be imatinib-insensitive [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. No secondary mutations associated with avapritinib resistance [PMID: 32972961] were detected.

Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of various neoplasms with KIT mutations, PDGFRA rearrangements and BCR-ABL1 fusions. While no studies have investigated the utility of TKI therapy in PDGFRA-mutated glioma, studies have also shown that PDGFRA D842V mutations in GIST confer resistance to imatinib [7]. Crenolanib has been shown to be significantly more potent than imatinib in inhibiting the kinase activity of imatinib-resistant PDGFRA kinases (including D842V) [8].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Preclinical studies and structural modeling have demonstrated that PDGFRA exon 18 mutations confer resistance to some tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as imatinib, due to enhanced ATP affinity and decreased inhibitor binding affinity at the kinase active site [PMID: 27349873]. Avapritinib has demonstrated preliminary antitumor activity in gastrointestinal stromal tumors with a PDGFRA exon 18 missense mutation - D842V [PMID: 32615108].

The PDGFRA D846A mutation detected in this specimen is not nearly as common as mutations affecting D842. The D846A variant has not been functionally evaluated in any known study but has been reported in a gastrointestinal stromal tumor [PMID: 21358619]. Therefore, the functional effect of this variant on protein function (if any) is unknown. Other variants affecting this codon - particularly D846Y - have been reported. D846Y has been shown to result in constitutive activation of PDGFRA [PMID: 15928335].

While no know study has evaluated the sensitivity of D846A to TKI therapies, the D846Y mutation has been shown to sensitivity to imatinib in preclinical studies [PMID: 15928335].

variants.variant_description:
Exon 18 deletion mutations and deletion/insertion mutations, such as I843_D846del, reside within the activation loop of the kinase domain of PDGFRA and have been shown to result in constitutive activation of PDGFRA and downstream MAPK, AKT and STAT signaling [PMID: 12522257].

Activating PDGFRA mutations (including I843_D846del) are well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and are mutually exclusive with KIT mutations [1,2]. The exon 18 deletion mutation detected in this specimen affects the activation loop within the kinase domain of PDGFRA and has been shown to result in constitutive activation of PDGFRA and downstream MAPK, AKT and STAT signaling [1].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating PDGFRA, particularly exon 18 mutations, are well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and are mutually exclusive with KIT mutations [PMID: 12522257, 15928335, 29312652]. PDGFRA mutations show a strong predilection for gastric GIST often with epithelioid morphology [PMID: 29312652]. These mutations are much less common in intestinal GIST [PMID: 29312652]. Specific mutations in KIT or PDGFRA show some correlation with tumor phenotype, but mutations are not strongly correlated with the biologic potential of individual tumors. The accumulated data show that KIT mutations are not preferentially present in high-grade tumors, and can also be found in small incidental tumors as well as tumors that have an indolent course. Similarly, mutational analysis of PDGFRA cannot be used to predict the behavior of individual tumors [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2026].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Most PDGFRA mutations are associated with a response to imatinib, with the exception of D842V, which is unlikely to respond [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2025]. For the I843_D846del variant identified in this patients tumor, there is both in vitro and clinical data supporting positive response to both imatinib and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors [PMID: 26130666]. Imatinib is included in the NCCN guidelines as a category 1 preferred first-line treatment option for patients with advanced or metastatic GIST with imatinib-sensitive mutations; however, it is not recommended for the treatment of GIST with PDGFRA exon 18 mutations that are insensitive to imatinib, especially D842V [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2026]. The NCCN panel recommends avapritinib as the preferred first-line treatment option for patients with unresectable, progressive, or metastatic GIST with imatinib-resistant PDGFRA D842V mutations or other PDGFRA exon 18 mutations that are known to be imatinib insensitive [NCCN Guidelines Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors, Version 1.2026]. One study that included both in vitro and clinical trial data showed that none of the patients with the imatinib-resistant D842V mutation responded to imatanib, whereas two of three patients with imatinib-sensitive PDGFRA oncoproteins achieved a PR with imatinib therapy [PMID: 14645423].  In a separate study, a patient with a tumor harboring PDGFRA M844-S847del achieved clinical benefit as well as one year of stable disease following imatinib treatment [PMID: 26130666].  Referral to clinical trial is strongly recommended for patients with mutations resistant to imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib, ripretinib, and avapritinib [PMID: 15928335, 15146165, 33465704, 29312652, 32972961].

While the PDGFRA Y849C mutation has not been reported in colorectal cancer (CRC), this mutation has been reported in several other cancer types including prostate cancer, gliomas, melanomas as well as in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) [1-4]. Other PDGFRA mutations have also been described at a low freqency in CRC [5]. The Y849C mutation has been shown to confer a gain of function on the PDGFRA protein as demonstrated by constitutive phosphorylation of PDGFRA in cell culture [3].

Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of various neoplasms with KIT mutations, PDGFRA rearrangements and BCR-ABL1 fusions. While no studies have investigated the utility of TKI therapy in PDGFRA-mutated CRC, numerous studies have also shown that PDGFRA mutations in GIST (other than D842V) confer sensitivity to imatinib [6-9]. In vitro studies suggest that the Y849C mutation detected in this specimen is also imatinib [3].
The impact of PDGFRA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy is uncertain though these treatments are not expected to impact PDGFRA signaling.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating PDGFRA, particular exon 18 mutations (like  H845_N848delinsP) are well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and are mutually exclusive with KIT mutations [1-3]. PDGFRA mutations show a strong predilection for gastric GIST often with epithelioid morphology [3]. These mutations are much less common in intestinal GIST [3]. Specific mutations in KIT or PDGFRA show some correlation with tumor phenotype, but mutations are not strongly correlated with the biologic potential of individual tumors. The accumulated data show that KIT mutations are not preferentially present in high-grade tumors, and can also be found in small incidental tumors as well as tumors that have an indolent course. Similarly, mutational analysis of PDGFRA cannot be used to predict the behavior of individual tumors [6].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Some PDGFRA mutations are associated with a response to imatinib, with the exception of D842V, which is unlikely to respond to imatinib [6]. One study that included both in vitro and clinical trial data showed that none of the patients with the imatinib-resistant D842V mutation responded to imatanib, whereas two of three patients with imatinib-sensitive PDGFRA oncoproteins achieved a PR with imatinib therapy [8]. One of these patients tumor harbored a similar deletion to the mutation, PDFFRA H842–845, identified in this patients tumor. In a separate study, a patient with a tumor harboring PDGFRA M844-S847del achieved clinical benefit as well as one year of stable disease following imatanib treatment [5]. GISTs with imatinib-insensitive mutations such as PDGFRA D842V are managed differently than most GISTs. Avapritinib is a TKI approved for the treatment of patients with unresectable or metastatic GISTs with a PDGFRA exon 18 mutation, including D842V mutations [6]. Ripretinib is also an option for GIST with PDGFRA exon 18 mutations that are insensitive to imatinib and were previously treated with both avapritinib and dasatinib. An additional clinical benefit may be obtained with the use of ripretinib 150 mg BID upon progression on ripretinib 150 mg daily. Referral to clinical trial is strongly recommended for patients with mutations resistant to imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib, ripretinib, and avapritinib [2-7].

variants.variant_description: While the PDGFRA D842V mutation is well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors [3] and results in constitutive activation of PDGFRA and downstream growth signaling [2-3], there are no known descriptions for PDGFRA P842L. This mutation is presumed to be pathogenic as it affects the same residue as D842V and both mutations result in replacement of the negatively charged aspartic acid with an amino acide with a hydrophic side chain (valine and leucine).

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Avapritinib (Ayvakit; formerly BLU-285) is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) with PDGFRA exon 18 mutations, including D842V [4-5]. The approval of avapritinib was based on a trial containing patients with the D842V mutation - the NAVIGATOR trial (NCT02508532). However, the FDA-approval of avapritinib includes an exon 18 mutation. This TKI demonstrated better efficacy than other TKI therapies such as imatinib to which PDGFRA D842V is resistant [6]. Treatment of GIST harboring PDGFRA exon 18 mutations is recommended by the National Comprehenisve Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [7]. No mutations associated with resistance to PDGFRA [8], were detected in this specimen.

variants.variant_description: Exon 18 deletion mutations and deletion/insertion mutations affect the activation loop within the kinase domain of PDGFRA and have been shown to result in constitutive activation of PDGFRA and downstream MAPK, AKT and STAT signaling [1]. At the protein level, the D842_D842delinsA mutation is analagous to a D842A mutation followed be deletion of I843 through D845.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating PDGFRA, particular exon 18 mutations (like D842_D846delinsA or more commonly D842V) are well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and are mutually exclusive with KIT mutations [1-3]. PDGFRA mutations show a strong predilection for gastric GIST (appproximately 35% of gastric GIST), often with epithelioid morphology [3]. These mutations are much less common in intestinal GIST (approximately 2.7%) [3].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) avapritinib (Ayvakit, formerly BLU-285) was approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in January of 2020 for the treatment of advanced/metastatic GIST with PDGFRA exon 18 mutations. This therapy was found to result in a durable clinical benefit with a median duration of response of 27.6 months [4].
 
PDGFRA exon 18 mutations affecting D842 (particularly D842V but also this mutation) are associated with resistance to imatinib (Gleevec) and sunitib (Sutent) - FDA-approved for GIST with KIT mutations - due to impaired binding of these drugs [2,5]. Treatment of GIST PDGFRA exon 18 mutations that are insensitive to imaginib with avapritinib is a category 1 recommendation in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [6]. Of note, no mutations associated with acquired resistance to avapritinib were detected [7].

No secondary mutations associated with avapritinib resistance [PMID: 32972961] were detected.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib have been FDA-approved for the treatment of various neoplasms with KIT mutations, PDGFRA rearrangements and BCR-ABL1 fusions, the potential utility of these therapies in this context is uncertain since the functional effect of PDGFRA R822H is uncertain. In addition, the KRAS mutation described above is expected to render TKI therapy ineffective since KRAS mutations activated MAPK pathway signaling downstream of PDGFRA.

variants.variant_description:
R841K is a rare PDGFRA mutation which has been identified in at least one melanoma [1] and one gastrointestinal stromal tumor [2]. It has been shown in preclinical studies to be activating/oncogenic [1]. Other activating PDGFRA mutations have been described at a low frequency in breast cancer [3].

R841K is a rare PDGFRA mutation which has been identified in at least one melanoma [1] and one gastrointestinal stromal tumor [2]. It has been shown in preclinical studies to be activating/oncogenic and responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) imatinib and crenolanib [1]. KIT copy number gain (amplification):
KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally involved in regulated activation of RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR and STAT3 signaling in the presence of stem cell factor (SCF). KIT amplification is well described in melanoma, occurring in about 10-15% of cases and having no clear association with location or etiology; it is about equally common in lesions arising on acral, mucosal and chronically sun-damaged skin [3]. While TKIs such as imatinib are recommended in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines for the treatment of KIT-mutated metastatic melanoma [4], their role in KIT-amplified cases is less clear. In a small phase II clinical trial, 5 of 26 patients with melanoma harboring KIT mutations responded to nilotinib, however none of the 8 patients with KIT-amplified melanoma responded [5]. Similarly, a phase II trial of imatinib in 25 patients with melanoma harboring KIT mutations or amplification found that disease control rates were correlated positively with KIT mutations but not KIT amplification [6]. Clinical trials are underway investigating the clinical utility of TKIs and other agents for KIT-amplified and PDGFRA-mutant melanoma. The close homology between KIT and PDGFRA leads to similar sensitivity to TKIs, which in turn results in overlapping clinical trial enrollment criteria and the possibility of a dual mechanism of response to therapy in this case. Michigan Medicine is currently participating in a phase 2 cliinical trial (NCT02272998; UMCC 2015.088) evaluating the efficacy of the TKI ponatinib and a phase 1 clinical trial (NCT02219711; UMCC 2015.040) evaluating the efficacy of the TKI MGCD516. Trials outside of Michigan include a phase I/II trial of pembrolizumab and imatinib at Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center and other locations (NCT02812693), and a Phase I trial of DCC-2618 (NCT02571036, multiple locations in USA).

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of various neoplasms with KIT mutations, PDGFRA rearrangements and BCR-ABL1 fusions. While no studies have investigated the utility of TKI therapy in PDGFRA-mutated breast cancer, numerous studies have also shown that PDGFRA mutations in GIST (other than D842V) confer sensitivity to imatinib [4-7]. Preclinical studies suggest that the R841K mutation detected in this specimen is also sensitive to imatinib [1].

variants.variant_description: The PDGFRA D846G mutation detected in this specimen is extremely rare and has been reported in a single glioma sample [1]. Other somatic mutations affecting this codon have been described in other types of neoplasms including D846Y [2-4], D846V [5], D846E [6] and D846A [2], particularly in gastrointestinal stromal tumor. The allele frequency of this variant is similar to that of the IDH1 mutation described above and also correlated with the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells in the extracted sample, suggesting that the mutation is somatic (not germline). No known study has evaluated the functional effect of this mutation or the potential sensitivity of this mutation to kinase inhibitor therapy.

The V561D mutation detected in this specimen is located within the juxtamembrane domain (exon 12) and is the most common mutation identified in this specific domain in GIST [PMID: 15146165, 17087936, 17566086]. This amino acid substitution results in constitutive, ligand-independent tyrosine phosphorylation and oncogenic PDGFRA activity by disrupting autoinhibitory hydrophobic interactions [PMID: 15221957, 27349873].

PDGFRA mutations have been identified in small subsets adult and pediatric high-grade gliomas [1,2]. The PDGFRA V561D mutation detected in this specimen is present in a subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumors and has rarely been identified in other human neoplasms [3,4]. The V561 residue lies in the juxtamembrane domain, and amino acid substitution at this position results in constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation and oncogenic PDGFRA activity [5,6].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Activating mutations in PDGFRA are identified in approximately 5%–12% of gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and represent an alternative, mutually exclusive oncogenic event to KIT mutations [PMID: 20096441, 15146165, 27349873].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of KIT-positive and PDGFRA-mutated metastatic or unresectable GIST [NCCN Guidelines Version 1.2026 Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors]. While the common PDGFRA D842V mutation is characterized by primary resistance to imatinib, the V561D mutation is highly sensitive to this agent [PMID: 27349873, 17087936, 22745105, 15221957, 17715395, 20473908]. Current NCCN Guidelines list imatinib as the preferred first-line therapy for PDGFRA mutations, specifically excluding those that are imatinib-insensitive, such as D842V [NCCN Guidelines Version 1.2026 Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors].

Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that is FDA-approved for the treatment of various neoplasms with KIT mutations, PDGFRA rearrangements and BCR-ABL1 fusions. While no studies have investigated the utility of TKI therapy in PDGFRA-mutated glioma, numerous studies have also shown that PDGFRA mutations in GIST (other than D842V) confer sensitivity to imatinib [7-10], and pre-clinical studies indicate that the V561D mutation detected in this specimen is also sensitive to imatinib [11,12].

variants.variant_description: I562_E563ins is an in frame insertion within exon 12 involving the juxtamembrane region and has been shown to result in constitutive kinase activation [PMIDs: 12522257].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Myxoid glioneuronal tumors are genetically characterized by a recurrent dinucleotide mutation in the PDGFRA, most commonly  K385L or K385I, and typically occur without concurrent PDGFRA amplification [WHO CNS 5th ed, PMID: 31609499]. K385L and K385I are located within exon 8 which encodes part of the extracellular ligand-binding domain [PMID: 31609499]. The PDGFRA alteration identified in this specimen, I562_E563ins, is located within exon 12 and involves the juxtamembrane region [PMID: 12522257]. PDGFRA exon 12 insertions have not specifically been reported in myxoid glioneuronal tumors and various PDGFRA alterations are identified in other CNS tumors. As such the diagnostic implication of this alteration is not entirely clear and correlation with methylation profiling and microscopic features is needed.
diseases.therapeutic_implications: PDGFRA mutations are well described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and more recently inflammatory fibroid polyps [PMID: 36119525, 15928335, 19448595]. In vitro studies have shown similar exon 12 insertion/deletion mutations to be sensitive to imatanib [PMID: 15928335, 12522257]. Studies have also shown avapritinib to be effective in PDGFRA altered high-grade gliomas [PMID: 40086436].

variants.variant_description: PDGFRA mutations have been identified in a small subset (1%-6%) of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMIDs: 29657128, 32015526, 32791233, 18948947, 22960745, 28445112, 28336552, 29337640, 27158780, 22980975], and the L580M mutation identified in this specimen has been reported in isolated cases [PMIDs: 18948947]. Although the L580M has not been fully functionally characterized, the L580 residue lies in the juxtamembrane domain, and mutations in this domain have been shown to cause constitutive activation. [PMIDs: 15690055, 23773831, 33449152]. The clinical significance of this alteration is not known.

PDGFRA mutations have been identified in small subsets of adult and pediatric high-grade gliomas [PMIDs: 26824661, 27582545]. The S564L mutation identified in this specimen has been reported in isolated cases [PMIDs: 32680567, 27756406], and there is no functional evidence characterizing this mutation; however, the S564L residue lies in the juxtamembrane domain, and mutations in this domain have been shown to cause constitutive activation. [PMIDs: 15690055, 23773831, 33449152]. The clinical significance of this alteration is not known.

CDK4 copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain involving the CDK4 gene was detected, consistent with CDK4 amplification. CDK4 encodes a cyclin dependent kinase that normally phosphorylates the retinoblastoma gene product (Rb) during the G1/S transition. Amplification of CDK4 resulting in increased CDK4 expression has been described at a low incidence in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: A phase 2 study of the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib (PD-0332991) showed clinical efficacy in well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcoma with CDK4 amplification [2].

variants.variant_description: G569R is a rare PDGFRA mutation which has been reported in one melanoma [1]; however, the biological effect and clinical significance of this mutation has not been characterized. Clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of tyrosine kinase inhibitors and other agents for PDGFRA-mutant melanoma are underway, though it is unclear if the mutation detected in this specimen would be sufficient for enrollment given its rarity and lack of literature. Michigan Medicine is currently participating in a phase 2 cliinical trial (NCT02272998; UMCC 2015.088) evaluating the efficacy of the TKI ponatinib and a phase 1 clinical trial (NCT02219711; UMCC 2015.040) evaluating the efficacy of the TKI MGCD516. Trials outside of Michigan include a phase I/II trial of pembrolizumab and imatinib at Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center and other locations (NCT02812693), and a Phase I trial of DCC-2618 (NCT02571036, multiple locations in USA).

PDGFRA alterations have been identified in a variety of tumor types and frequently involve exon 18. Activating PDGFRA mutations are well-described in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST). PDGFRA mutations have also been identified in small subsets adult and pediatric high-grade gliomas [1,2]. In pediatric gliomas, mutations have not been restricted to a single functional domain but have been distributed among different regions of the protein [2]. PDGFR M844_S847del results in the deletion of four amino acids within the protein kinase domain of the Pdgfra protein. This alteration has been identified in sequencing studies but has not been biochemically characterized [3]. Similar alterations, however are activating, and therefore, is predicted to result in a gain of function [4]. PDGFRA G842H also lies within the protein kinase domain but has not previously been reported in the literature. However, D842V is a recurrent hotspot mutation in gastrointestinal stromal tumors which confers resistance to imatinib [4].

variants.variant_description:
PTPRZ1::MET Fusion:
This gene fusion is in-frame and results in fusion of the first 3 exons of PTPRZ1 to exons 2 and above of MET. This gene fusion includes all of the protein-coding sequence of MET and replaces the MET promoter with the PTPRZ1 promoter, thereby driving increased MET expression (promoter "hijacking" rearrangement), enhanced ligand-independent MET phosphorylation, activation of downstream MAPK signaling and oncogenic growth [PMID: 25135958, 25935522, 27748748].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: The PTPRZ1::MET (ZM) gene fusion detected in this sample is well-described in high-grade gliomas [PMID: 25135958, 25935522, 27748748] including grade III astrocytomas and secondary glioblastomas [PMID: 25135958] as well as primary pediatric glioblastomas [PMID: 27748748]. These fusions are typically mutually exclusive with EGFR amplification [PMID: 25135958].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Therapies targeted against MET fusions are centered around MET TRK inhibitor therapy [PMID: 34766555]. Preclinical studies have suggested that this fusion may result in temozolimide chemoresistance [PMID: 28504721] and may be sensitive to MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) including crizotinib [PMID: 27748748], foretinib [PMID: 27748748], SGX523 [PMID: 27748748] and PLB-1001 [PMID: 30343896]. Clinical responses to criztotinib [PMID: 27748748] and tepotinib [PMID: 38815166] have been reported in individual cases of glioblastomas harboring the PTPRZ1::MET fusion.
diseases.prognostic_implications: PTPRZ1::MET fusions have been associated with a poor prognosis [PMID: 25135958].

Autocrine stimulation of MET by HGF has also been implicated in the oncogenesis of some gliomas [4]. MET copy number gains/overexpression have been associated with an inferior prognosis [1,2].

Low-level MET copy number gain (equivocal for amplification):
A low-level copy number gain of the MET gene was detected (approximately 4-6 copies; considered equivocal for amplification). Amplification of MET resulting in increased MET expression is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-2]. While HIGH-LEVEL MET amplification (defined in the literature as a MET:CEP7 ration greater than or equal to 5) is typically mutually exclusive with other oncogenic drivers suggesting a true dependence of neoplastic cells on MET amplification, low-level amplification (as seen in this specimen) is NOT mutually exclusive with other oncogenic drivers [2]. Of note, MET amplification or overexpression has not been identified in thymic carcinomas [3].

A low-level copy number gain (approximately 4-6 copies) involving the MET gene was detected. MET copy number gains are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1,2]

MET copy number gain (not meeting high-level criteria):
A copy number gain involving the MET gene was detected. Amplification of MET resulting in increased MET expression is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMID: 17332337, 19096300, 27262212]. This specimen does NOT appear to meet criteria for high-level MET amplification (defined in the literature and NCCN guidelines as a MET:CEP7 ratio greater than or equal to 5 or NGS copy number greater than 10), which is typically mutually exclusive with other oncogenic drivers suggesting a true dependence of neoplastic cells on MET amplification [PMID: 27262212]. High-level MET gene amplification is associated with an inferior prognosis [PMID: 29805710, 19255323].

Equivocal for MET amplification:
A low-level copy number gain of the MET gene (considered equivocal for amplification) was detected. MET amplification resulting in increased MET expression has been described in squamous cell carcinoma from various primaries including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-3] and head and neck [4]. In NSCLC, high-level MET amplification (defined in the literature as a MET:CEP7 ration greater than or equal to 5) is typically mutually exclusive with other oncogenic drivers suggesting a true dependence of neoplastic cells on MET amplification [3]. The current specimen was found to be equivocal for MET amplification. In addition, because previous clinical studies were based on MET copy number status as determined by FISH, confirmation testing using MET FISH (with a CEP7 probe) is recommended prior to any clinical action being taken based on this result. While there are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MET-amplified squamous cell carcinoma, emerging data suggest that tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapies such as crizotinib may be efficacious in NSCLC with HIGH-LEVEL MET amplification [5,6]. In addition, high-level MET gene amplification in NSCLC is associated with an inferior prognosis and has been implicated as a mechanism of acquired resistance to epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKI) [7,8]. Treatment of NSCLC with high-level MET amplification is currently a category 2A recommendation with National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [9]. Multiple clinical trials are currently enrolling patients with MET mutated advanced solid tumors. Relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT02219711 (phse 1 of MET inhibitor MGCD516; University of Michigan), NCT02544633 (phase 2 trial of MGCD265 for NSCLC, multicenter including Henry Ford), NCT02920996 (phase 2 study of mesertinib in NSCLC, Dana Farber Cancer Institute), NCT02132598 (phase 2 trial of cabozantinib in NSCLC with brain metastases, University of Pittsburgh), NCT02648724 (phase 1/2 of Sym015, multiple centers including University of Chicago) and NCT00585195 (a phase 1 study of PF-02341066, multiple centers including Karmanos Cancer Center).

An NRAS G12D mutation was detected at a low variant allele frequency (2%). While NRAS mutations are exceedingly rare in hairy cell leukemia [1], they have been described at a very low incidence in age-related clonal hematopoiesis (ARCH) / clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) / clonal cytopenias of uncertain significance (CCUS) [2-9] and at a higher incidence (approximately 5-13%) in monoclonal gammopathies [10-12]. However, MEK inhibitors (often in combination with other agents such as AKT inhibitors) have demonstrated preclinical [PMID: 20923857, 22169769, 22392911, 25961376] and early clinical [PMID: 25517890] evidence of efficacy. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [7], CDK4/6 [8-10], ERBB3 [11], histone deacetylase [12], STAT3 [13] and PI3K inhibitors [14,15].
