diseases.therapeutic_implications:
NRAS mutations are associated with primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies such as cetuximab and panitumumab [PMID: 16618717, 20921462, 20921465, NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 2.2025]. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines all patients with metastatic colorectal cancer should have tumor genotyped for RAS (KRAS and NRAS) and BRAF mutations individually or as part of an NGS panel. Patients with any known KRAS mutation (exons 2, 3, and 4) or NRAS mutation (exons 2, 3, and 4) should not be treated with either cetuximab or panitumumab [NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 2.2025].  
 
Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in RAS-mutated neoplasms [PMID: 10395327]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have thusfar been disappointing [PMID: 15483017, 27650277, 26666244]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [PMID: 27338794], CDK4/6 [PMID: 28459648, 28866094, 26728409], ERBB3 [PMID: 29312543], histone deacetylase [PMID: 29079711], STAT3 [PMID: 25961376] and PI3K inhibitors [PMID: 23629727, 25342139].

While there is promising clinical data in patients with oncogenic NRAS-mutant melanoma treated with the MEK1/2-targeted inhibitor binimetinib either as monotherapy or in combination with the CDK4/6-targeted inhibitor ribociclib, its clinical utility in patients with NRAS G12V mutant non-small cell lung cancer is unknown [PMID: 28284557]

diseases.diagnostic_implications: RAS mutations (most commonly NRAS) occur in approximately 30% of poorly differentiated thyroid carcinomas [PMID: 26878173], 30% of follicular thyroid carcinomas [PMID: 33224857] and 10% of papillary thyroid carcinomas [PMID: 25417114].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no therapies FDA-approved specifically for NRAS-mutated thyroid cancer and no therapies specifically recommended for NRAS-mutated thyroid cancer in NCCN guidelines [v.5.2024]. MEK inhibitors and other agents have been investigated in preclinical studies.

NCCN Guidelines for Melanoma recommend (category 2B) the use of binimetinib for metastatic/unresectable melanomas harboring NRAS mutations that progress following immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy [NCCN Guidelines Melanoma: Cutaneous, Version 1.2026]. 
 
While response to some MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib has been disappointing [PMIDs: 22048237, 22805292], clinical trials have demonstrated modest clinical efficacy for binimetinib [PMIDs: 28284557, 23414587, 28152546]. In a phase 3 trial, binimetinib demonstrated a modest improvement in progression free survival (though no statistically significant difference in overall survival) when compared with dacarbazine [PMID: 28284557]. The efficacy was most pronounced in patients who had received prior immunotherapy. Preclinical studies have also suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more efficacious when used in combination with immunotherapy [PMID: 28919996]. ERK inhibitors which act even further downstream with the MAPK signaling pathway are also being investigated in clinical trials.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The FDA has granted the MEK1/2-targeted inhibitor selumetinib orphan drug designation for adjuvant treatment of differentiated thyroid cancer. Selumetinib, both in combination with or as upfront therapy prior to radioiodine uptake therapy, has been shown to produce meaningful increases in radioiodine uptake in thyroid cancers refractory to iodine which may be more effective in RAS-mutated thyroid cancers [PMID: 23406027].

There are no FDA-approved targeted therapies specifically for the treatment of NRAS-mutated follicular thyroid carcinoma. There is promising clinical data in patients with oncogenic NRAS-mutant thyroid cancer treated with the FDA-approved MEK1/2-targeted inhibitor selumetinib, both in combination with or as upfront therapy prior to radioiodine uptake therapy (4).

The absence of an activating EGFR mutation and the presence of a NRAS mutation is associated with primary resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib and gefitinib) [2]. Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in RAS-mutated neoplasms [3]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have thusfar been disappointing [4-6]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [7], CDK4/6 [8-10], ERBB3 [11], histone deacetylase [12], STAT3 [13] and PI3K inhibitors [14,15].

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of KRAS-mutated gastric cancer. While MEK inhibitors, such as trametinib and cobimetinib, show in vitro inhibition of MAPK signaling and cell growth within KRAS-mutated cells (including gastric carcinoma cell lines) and demonstrate some clinical activity in other RAS-mutated neoplasms, clinical response to these agents (alone or in combination with other therapies) has been disappointing [4-10]. Recently, the MEK inhibitor selumetinib (in combination with docetaxel) has been used in the treatment of KRAS-mutated gastric cancer in a phase 2 clinical trial, and a subset of the tumors showed partial clinical response [11]. Finally, in vitro studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective in combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors [12].

variants.variant_description: NRAS T50I does not lie within any known functional domains of the NRAS protein, but is predicted to lead to gain of function as it has been shown to increase phosphorylation of ERK in cell culture [1], potentially through altering NRAS membrane orientation and strengthening effector binding based on structural modeling of the HRAS protein [2]. This mutation has been described as a somatic mutation in melanoma [3] and other NRAS mutations are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [4]. However, the T50I mutation has also been described as a germline mutation associated with Noonan syndrome [1]. It is not known if the mutation in this sample is germline or somatic - the variant allele frequency is approximately 47%. Germline testing and genetic counseling is recommended if there is clinical concern for Noonan syndrome.

NRAS G13D mutation is well-described in many cancer types, including melanoma, and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of NRAS as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [1]. BRAF is a serine-threonine kinase involved in growth signaling, downstream of EGFR (and upstream of RAS) within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. The BRAF K601E mutation detected in this specimen is uncommon but has been described in many cancer types [2-4]. In contrast to BRAF V600E and other "class 1" BRAF mutations, which result in constitutively active monomers, K601E and other "class 2" mutations have been shown to increase MAPK signaling and cell proliferation by forming constitutively active dimers in a RAS-independent manner [5,6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for NRAS-mutated melanoma or “class 2” BRAF mutations. There is some preclinical evidence in melanoma that class 2 mutations may be sensitive to dual MAPK inhibition, including encorafenib [4], however, multiple small studies have found combination treatment to not be very effective in those with K601E mutations [7,8].
MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of BRAF within MAPK signaling) have been shown to be effective against BRAF K601E and other "class 2" mutations in preclinical studies [2,3,5] as well as limited clinical studies in melanoma patients [6,9]. However, little is known about therapeutic effects of these drugs in patients with a second activating mutation in the MAPK pathways such as this patient.

According to most recent NCCN guidelines patients with any known KRAS mutation (exons 2, 3, and 4) or NRAS mutation (exons 2, 3, and 4) should not be treated with either cetuximab or panitumumab, unless given as part of a regimen targeting a KRAS G12C mutation [NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer v3.2024, PMID: 16618717, 20921462, 20921465]. Patients with oncogenic NRAS-mutant melanoma treated with the MEK1/2-targeted inhibitor binimetinib either as monotherapy or in combination with the CDK4/6-targeted inhibitor ribociclib have shown encouraging clinical responses. However, the clinical significance in patients with colorectal cancer harboring NRAS mutations is not well characterized [PMID: 28284557].

IDH1 R132C:
IDH1 encodes cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase, an enzyme that normally catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate. The IDH R132C mutation detected in this sample has been described at a low incidence in melanomas [1], non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [2] and other cancers and is known to result in a gain of enzymatic function, causing conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG) [4]. 2HG then functions as an 'oncometabolite,' inhibiting histone demethylation and resulting in increased DNA methylation [5,6]. One study did describe a relatively frequent co-occurrence of NRAS mutations in IDH1-mutant melanoma, as seen in this case [10].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved therapies for the treatment of IDH-mutant melanomas. Ivosidenib (Tibsovo) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with IDH1 mutations. Various other IDH inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical studies [7-9]. There have been no studies investigating the utility of these agents in melanomas.

NRAS E132K lies within the G domain of the NRAS protein and is very rare but has been identified in three tumor samples from Filipino young-onset, sporadic colorectal cancer patients as well as reported three colorectal cancer cases in the Catalogue of Somatic COSMIC database [1]. While confirmed somatic, there has been little functional characterization of this variant. One in vitro study utilizing NRAS E132K mutant cell lines found that E132K does not affect cell proliferation or migration, but results in cytoskeletal disruption, decreased expression and aberrant localization of E-cadherin, and decreased cell adhesion compared to wild-type NRAS in culture.

Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in RAS-mutated neoplasms [5]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have thusfar been disappointing [6-8]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [9], CDK4/6 [10-12], ERBB3 [13], histone deacetylase [14], STAT3 [15] and PI3K inhibitors [16,17].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The absence of an activating EGFR mutation and the presence of KRAS and NRAS mutations is associated with primary resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) [1,2]. Some studies have demonstrated a modest response of RAS-mutant NSCLC to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib [3]. In a phase 2 trial, KRAS-mutant NSCLC treated with trametinib (GSK1120212) showed a similar progression free survival and response rate as docetaxel [3]. In preclinical studies, treatment of lung cancer cells with a MEK inhibitor induces a compensatory response involving FGFR1 leading to adaptive resistance while the combination of MEK and FGFR1 inhibition resulted in greater sensitivity than MEK inhibition alone [7]. The combination of a MEK inhibitor with other agents such as PI3K inhibitors [8], histone deacetylase inhibitors [9], or CDK4/6 inhibitors [10,11] has also demonstrated improved antitumor activity in preclinical studies.

BRAF G466R:
BRAF is a serine-threonine kinase involved in growth signaling, downstream of EGFR within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. The BRAF G466R mutation detected in this specimen is a rarely described variant in melanoma [15046639, 14681681] [1-3]. G466R (like other "class 3" BRAF mutations) is thought to result in absent kinase activity (kinase-dead), but is associated with RAS-dependent augmentation of MAPK signaling [4-6]. More specifically, these mutations cause increased binding to activated RAS resulting in the formation of mutant BRAF to wild-type CRAF heterodimers. Therefore, this mutation is expected to augment the MAPK activation initiated by the weakly activating NRAS Q61R mutation also present in this tumor (described below).

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The BRAF inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib are NOT effective in treating "class 3" BRAF mutations since they preferentially inhibit activated BRAF monomers (class 1 mutations) [6]. Newer RAF inhibitors such as PLX8394, BGB659 and AZ628 have demonstrated an ability to inhibit RAF dimers [5,7,8]. In epithelial tumors including NSCLC, the requisite RAS activation associated "class 3" BRAF mutations appears to come from activated receptor tyrosine kinases including EGFR. NSCLC cell lines and patient derived xenografts harboring "class 3" BRAF mutations were shown to be sensitive to the anti-EGFR antibody cetuximab [6]. In another preclinical study, "class 3" BRAF mutations conferred sensitivity to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib [9]. In addition, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib (which act downstream of RAS and BRAF) also inhibit the growth of cell lines and patient-derived xenografts with these mutations [6]. Finally, ERK inhibitors also act downstream of BRAF and in a recent phase 1 clinical trial, a subset of NSCLC with class 2 or 3 BRAF mutations responded to the ERK inhibitor ulixertinib (BVD-523) [10].

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for NRAS-mutated melanoma. However, MEK inhibitors have shown mixed clinical efficacy in the treatment of NRAS-mutated melanoma. While response to some MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib has been disappointing [5,6], clinical trials have demonstrated modest clinical efficacy for binimetinib [7-9]. In a recent phase 3 trial, binimetinib demonstrated a modest improvement in progression free survival (though no statistically significant difference in overall survival) when compared with dacarbazine [7]. The efficacy was most pronounced in patients who had received prior immunotherapy. Preclinical studies have also suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more efficacious when used in combination with immunotherapy [10].

PIK3CA E542K:
PIK3CA encodes one of the catalytic subunits of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, a lipid kinase involved in PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling, also downstream of RAS and EGFR. PIK3CA mutations resulting in increased catalytic activity and oncogenic transformation, including E542K, are well-described in CRC [1-3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There is conflicting data regarding the impact of CRC PIK3CA mutations on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies [4]. However, the NRAS mutation described above is clearly associated with primary resistance to these therapies. There is also conflicting data from observational studies regarding the impact of PIK3CA mutations on the clinical utility of aspirin [5-7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
NRAS mutations (as is true for KRAS mutations) are associated with primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies such as cetuximab and penitumumab [2-4]. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommends KRAS and NRAS genotyping of all metastatic colorectal cancers and states that patients with any known KRAS or NRAS mutation in exons 2-4 should NOT be treated with either cetuximab or panitumumab [5].
Preclinical studies have suggested that agents such as MEK inhibitors may be efficacious in KRAS-mutated neoplasms [6]. However, clinical studies investigating the utility of these agents have thusfar been disappointing [7-9]. Preclinical studies have suggested that MEK inhibitors may be more effective when combined with other agents such as inhibitors of FGFR [10], CDK4/6 [11-13], ERBB3 [14], histone deacetylase [15], STAT3 [16] and PI3K inhibitors [17,18].

variants.variant_description:
ERBB2 S310F:
The absence of an activating EGFR mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) generally results in a primary resistance to anti-EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies [1,2]. However, ERBB2 (HER2) is another receptor tyrosine kinase. The ERBB2 S310F mutation identified in this specimen has been described in NSCLC [3,4]. This mutation affects the extracellular domain of the ERBB2 protein causing C-terminal tail phosphorylation, hyperphosphorylation and consistitutive activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [5]. 
 
While there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC, the S310F mutation appears to be sensitive to anti-ERBB2 antibodies (trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib), based on in vitro studies [6]. In one case report, a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring an S310F mutation responded to afatinib [7]. Similar reports in breast cancer patients have shown a clinical response to trastuzumab and lapatinib [8,9]. Several case reports and small series examining NSCLC with other ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [10-14]. Treatment of NSCLC harboring ERBB2 mutations with TKI and/or antibody therapies is currently a National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) category 2B recommendation [15]. However, it should be noted that the NRAS mutation that was also identified in this specimen results in constitutive activation growth signaling downstream of ERBB2 within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. Therefore, this mutation would be expected to result in resistance to both anti-ERBB2 antibodies and tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
 
Clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of these types of anti-ERBB2 agents in advanced solid tumors with ERBB2 mutations are ongoing. The NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060) includes an afatinib treatment arm for advanced stage solid tumors with ERBB2 mutations. Other relevant clinical trials include NCT01953926 (phase 2 trial of neratinib, multicenter), NCT03066206 (phase 2 trial of poziotinib, MD Anderson), NCT01306045 (phase 2 trial of lapatinib, NCI), and NCT02716116 (phase1/2 of AP32788, multicenter).

PAX8 (exon 8) - PPARG (exon 2):
The PAX8-PPARG fusion is found in approximately 30-35% of follicular thyroid carcinomas [PMID: 10958784, 12161538, 12727991, 12651598], follicular adenomas [PMID: 12161538, 12727991], and a subset of follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma [PMID: 12651598]. This fusion protein includes the N-terminal DNA-binding of PAX8 and the entire coding coding sequence of PPARG [PMID: 10958784]. Transcription of the fusion transcript is under control from the PAX8 promoter which is highly active in thyroid follicular cells [PMID: 11789384]. While the oncogenic mechanism of this fusion protein has not been completely elucidated, it is thought to act as a dominant negative inhibitor of tumor suppressive effect of wild-type PPARG [PMID: 10958784] and/or a transcriptional activator of various genes [PMID: 15608688].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for thyroid neoplasms with PAX8-PPARG fusions. In preclinical studies, PPARG agonists such as pioglitazone have been shown to be effective [PMID: 21952241]. One case report also demonstrated some clinical benefit from pioglitazone treatment [PMID: 29373711].

This fusion protein includes the N-terminal DNA-binding of PAX8 and the entire coding coding sequence of PPARG [1]. name: ERBB2
gene_function: ERBB2 (HER2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling.

variants.variant_description:
ERBB2 (HER2) Y772_A775dup (also designated A775_G776insYVMA):
ERBB2 (HER2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling similar to EGFR. The in-frame exon 20 insertion (duplication) identified in this specimen is well-described in NSCLC and affects the kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein. This mutation results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [PMID:15753357, 15457249].

While ERBB2 amplification is seen in 15-20% of breast carcinoma, ERBB2 mutations are much more infrequent (2-4%), with L755S being the most common mutation [1-3]. ERBB2 exon 20 insertions, including Y775_G776insYVMA are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [4-8] and have been rarely reported in breast carcinoma [9-10]. These mutations affect the kinase domain of ERBB2, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [6-7,11].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The HER2-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors zongertinib and sevabertinib and the antibody-drug conjugate fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) are FDA-approved as single agents for the treatment of patients with non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring an ERBB2 tyrosine kinase domain activating mutation [NCCN NSCLC v2.2026, PMID:41104928, 40293180, 34534430].

Several studies have evaluated alterations within the tyrosine kinase domain of ERBB2 in breast carcinoma and have found these tumors to be sensitive to the irreversible Tk inhibitor neratinib [12]. Both preclinical [13] and clinical [14-16] studies have also shown that neratinib can overcome acquired trastuzumab resistance and improve outcomes when administered following trastuzumab therapy. The SUMMIT trial, found that neratinib was most effective in breast cancer patients, with patients containing L755S and V777L [17] Based on these findings, Neratinib is currently FDA-approved for extended adjuvant treatment of HER2+ breast cancer following adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy. While Y775_G776insYVMA is very rare and has not been studied extensively in breast carcinoma, one study evaluated patients with HER2-amplified/mutant breast carcinoma and found one patient harboring Y775_G776insYVMA who had stable disease following treatment with Neratinib [9]. There is also some variable response to afatinib in lung carcinoma patients harboring Y775_G776insYVMA, although the majority of patients did still have progressive disease.

A copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected (consistent with amplification). Copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected, consistent with gene amplification. Amplification of ERBB2 results in increased ERBB2 expression, driving activation of ERBB2 and downstream growth signaling.

A copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected (consistent with amplification). ERBB2 amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression is well-described in urothelial carcinoma (UC) with reported frequencies of approximately 5% [PMID: 24476821, 28988769, 12370744, 15029496]. Intratumoral heterogeneity with regard to ERBB2 copy number status is common in UC [PMID: 19889613, 29601842]. Some studies have suggested that ERBB2 amplification is associated with more aggressive behavior in UC [PMID: 23087329].

Amplification resulting in increase ERBB2 expression has been described in biliary tract cancer [PMID: 32353192, 17322545, 33279901] and has been associated with inferior survival [PMID: 32353192.].

A copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected, consistent with ERBB2 gene amplification. HER2 is rarely amplified/overexpressed in CRC (approximately 3% overall), but the prevalence is higher in RAS/BRAF–wild type tumors (reported at 5%–14%) [PMID: 22810696; NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 5.2025].

A copy number gain of ERBB2 was detected, consistent with gene amplification, that may result in increased ERBB2 expression, resutling in activation of downstream growth signaling.

A copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected (consistent with amplification). There are no known reports of ERBB2 amplification in salivary basal cell adenocarcinoma, though this rare neoplasm has not been extensively investigated for molecular alterations.

A copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected (approximately 8 copies), consistent with amplification. ERBB2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase and amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression. ERBB2 amplification is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)  [1,2].

ERBB2 (HER2) copy number gain (amplification):
High-level amplification (>20 copies) of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected. ERBB2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase and amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression is well-described in NSCLC [1,2]. While the impact of ERBB2 amplification on response to EGFR inhibition is uncertain, some studies have suggested that ERBB2 amplification could be a mechanism of resistance [3,4]. Anti-ERBB2 antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. afatinib) have been shown to be effective in other ERBB2-amplified neoplasms such as breast cancer [5]. A phase 2 study of dacomitinib (PF-00299804), none of the four NSCLC patients with ERBB2 amplification demonstrated a response [6]. In a recent phase 2 study of trastuzumab in patients with HER2+ NSCLC by IHC (NCT02289833), an objective response was observed in 20% (5/20) of patients with HER2 3+ and no patients (0/29) with HER2+ [unpublished results available at clinicaltrials.gov]. Another phase 2 trial evaluating the efficacy of trastuzumab in HER2+ NSCLC was terminated early due to limited efficacy [7]. Recent precelinical studies have suggested that osimertinib may have activity in NSCLC with ERBB2 amplification and other aberrations [8]. Clinical trials currently recruiting NSCLC with ERBB2 amplification include NCT01306045 (phase 2 of lapatinib, NCI).

ERBB2 (HER2) copy number gain (amplification):
A high-level copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected (considered positve for amplification). ERBB2 amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression has been described in several cancer types including colorectal cancer [1] and pancreatic adenocarcinoma [2].

Amplification resulting increased expression of ERBB2 has been described at a low frequency in melanoma [1,2].

Copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene was detected, consistent with amplification. Amplification of ERBB2 has been described at a low frequency in squamous cell carcinomas of various sites, including head and neck and lung [1,2].

A high-level copy number gain of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene, consistent with ERBB2 amplification, was detected. Amplification of ERBB2 resulting in overexpression of the ERBB2 protein is well-described in peri-ampullary adenocarcinoma [1-7]. In studies thusfar, no prognostic significance has been associated with ERBB2 amplification [5-7]. While anti-ERBB2 antibodies (such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab) and ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (such as neratinib) are efficacious and currently FDA-approved in the treatment of ERBB2-amplified breast cancer, there are no available clinical data concerning the efficacy of targeted therapies for the treatment of periampullary  with ERBB2 amplification. There are, however, multiple clinical trials currently recruiting patients with ERBB2-amplified advanced stage solid tumor cancers including the NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060; PI Ajjai Alva), TAPUR trial (NCT02693535; PI Ajjai Alva; group 8; trastuzumab and pertuzumab), NCT03065387 (phase 1 study of neratinib with everolimus, palbociclib or trametinib; MD Anderson Cancer Institute; Houston, TX), and NCT03410927 (phase 1/2 of ERBB2 inhibitor TAS0728; multiple centers outside Michigan).

ERBB2 amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression has been described in pancreatic adenocarcinoma [1,2]. Anti-ERBB2 antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab) and ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) are effective in the treatment of other ERBB2-amplified neoplasms such as breast cancer. Studies targeting ERBB2 in pancreatic cell lines and xenografts have shown suggested a potential response to anti-ERBB2 antibodies [3,4] and TKI therapies [5]. However, clinical studies of ERBB2 pancreatic adenocarcinoma have shown a LACK of response to trastuzumab [6]. Several studies have also failed to show any significant prognostic significance of ERBB2 amplification [7,8]. There are ongoing clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of various agents in solid tumors with ERBB2 amplification including the NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060; trastuzumab treatment arm for ERBB2-amplified solid tumors) and NCT02451553 (phase 1 trial of afatinib with capecitibine in pancreatic cancer; Indiana University and University of Washington),

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The HER2-targeted antibody trastuzumab (in combination with chemotherapy with or without the anti-PD-1 antibody pembrolizumab) and the antibody-drug conjugate trastuzumab deruxtecan are FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with HER2-positive gastric cancer. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines clinical trial results suggest that the combinations of trastuzumab with capecitabine and oxaliplatin or with mFOLFOX are effective regimens with acceptable safety profiles in patients with HER2 overexpression-positive gastroesophageal cancers. Trastuzumab should be added to first-line chemotherapy for patients with advanced HER2 overexpression-positive adenocarcinoma (combination with a fluoropyrimidine and a platinum agent is preferred [category 1 for cisplatin; category 2A for oxaliplatin]). Pembrolizumab can also be added to this regimen for treatment of advanced HER2 overexpressionpositive adenocarcinoma. Trastuzumab may be combined with other chemotherapy agents for first-line therapy, but should not be continued in second-line therapy [NCCN Gastric Cancer v2.2025].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Amplification of ERBB2 has been described at a low frequency in squamous cell carcinomas of various sites, including head and neck and lung [PMID: 25631445].
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu) is approved for HER2-positive (immunohistochemistry 3+) advanced solid tumors. 
 Anti-ERBB2 antibodies (such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab) and ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI; such as neratinib) are efficacious and currently FDA-approved in the treatment of ERBB2-amplified breast cancer. The clinical utility of these therapies for ERBB2-amplified squamous cell carcinoma is currently unknown.

Trastuzumab deruxtecan is an FDA-approved therapy in patients with unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive solid tumors (IHC 3+). It showed a 51% response rate in a range of solid tumors, including biliary, bladder, endometrial, lung, colorectal, and other tumor types [PMID: 37870536, 38547891, 37286557].

There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of biliary tract cancers; however, anti-ERBB2 antibody therapies, such as trastuzumab, are FDA-approved for the treatment of ERBB2-amplified breast cancer. Limited clinical studies have shown a response to trastuzumab in ERBB2-amplifed biliary tract cancers [3-5]. In a phase 2 trial of trastuzumab in extrahepatic bile duct cancer and gallbladder cancer showed a complete response, partial response and progressive disease, each in one of three treated patients (NCT00478140; clinicaltrials.gov).

According to the most recent NCCN guidelines, four different regimens are recommended as options for subsequent treatment of patients with metastatic CRC with HER2 amplifications: famtrastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki (T-DXd) monotherapy or trastuzumab in combination with pertuzumab, lapatinib, or tucatinib. These regimens (with the exception of T-DXd) may also be appropriate for patients with previously untreated HER2-amplified mCRC when intensive therapy is not recommended. The NCCN Panel notes that FDA-approved biosimilars may be substituted for trastuzumab wherever the therapy is recommended within these Guidelines [NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 5.2025].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
First-line systemic treatment of HER2-positive uterine serous adcarcinoma or carcinosarcoma with a regimen containing anti-ERBB2 antibodies - carboplatin/paclitaxel/trastuzumab - is currently a category 2A recommendation from the National Comprehensive Cancer Network [NCCN, version 1.2024]. 
 
In a phase II study, the addition of tastuzumab to carboplatin and paclitaxel resulted in an increased progression-free survival - 8.0 months versus 12.6 months (HR 0.44) for all patient; 9.3 months versus 17.9 months (HR 0.40) for stage III and stage IV [PMID: 29584549].

Anti-ERBB2 antibodies (such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab) and ERBB2 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI; such as neratinib) are efficacious and currently FDA-approved in the treatment of ERBB2-amplified breast cancer. The potential response to these agents in endometrial carcinoma with ERBB2 amplification is uncertain. While studies have shown a response to trastuzumab [8] and afatinib [9] combined with chemotherapy in ERBB2 amplified or IHC+ UC, a phase II study with ERBB2 overexpression failed to show a statistically significant difference between gemcitabine, platinum and trastuzumab compared with gemcitabine and platinum alone (possibly due to an inadequate sample size; n=61) [10]. However, the latter study showed that higher ERBB2 copy number correlated with treatment response. Lapatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor of both HER2 and EGFR, currently FDA approved for metastatic breast cancer, showed a 59% response rate when combined with gemcitabine and cisplatin in urothelial carcinoma in a phase I trial [11].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: ERBB2 amplification is described in a variety of different malignancies including breast carcinoma (5-13%) [1-5] and gastric and gastroesophageal carcinoma (13-30%) [6-8]. ERBB2 is less common in colorectal cancer (3%) [9], non-small cell lung cancer (< 2%) [10] and other carcinomas.
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Anti-ERBB2 antibodies including trastuzumab, ado-trastuzumab emtansine and pertuzumab, as well as tyrosine kinase inhibitors including lapatinib and neratinib [11-21] have been shown to be effective for ERBB2-amplified breast cancer and have been FDA-approved for the treatment of HER2+ breast cancer [2]. The anti-ERBB2 antibody trastuzumab (Herceptin) is FDA-approved (in combination with cisplatin and capecitabine or 5-fluorouracil) for the treatment of ERBB2 overexpressing GEA. In the ToGA trial, patients with ERBB2+ advanced GEA who were treated with trastuzumab in addition to chemotherapy achieved significantly improvement in median overall survival compared to chemotherapy alone [22]. Limited clinical studies have suggested a potential benefit from these agents in other cancers [12-21].

There are no known reports of ERBB2 targeted therapy in salivary basal cell adenocarcinoma. However, in phase 2 clinical trials, treatment of HER2-positive locally-advanced and/or recurrent or metastic salivary duct carcinoma with trastuzumab and docetaxel was associated with overall response rates of 70% and median progression-free and overall survivals of 8.9 months and 39.7 months, respectively [1]. In the MyPathway basket trial an objective response rate of 60% (9/15) was reported among salivary gland carcinomas with HER2 amplification/overexpression treated with trastuzumab and pertuzumab [2]. Clinical responses among HER2-amplified salivary gland cancers have also been reported for ado-transtumab emtansine (TDM-1) [3], single agent trastuzumab [4]. 
 
Treatment of HER2-positive salivary gland tumors with trastuzumab, ado-trastuzumab emtansine (TDM-1), trastuzumab/pertuxumab or docetaxel/trastuzumab is currently a category 2A recommendation with the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Clinical Practice Guidelines for Head and Neck Cancers [5].

Anti-ERBB2 antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. afatinib) have been shown to be effective in other ERBB2-amplified neoplasms such as breast cancer [3]. In a phase II study of dacomitinib (PF-00299804), none of the four NSCLC patients with ERBB2 amplification demonstrated a response [4], and another phase II trial evaluating the efficacy of trastuzumab in HER2-positive (HER2+) NSCLC was terminated early due to limited efficacy [5]. On the other hand, in a recent phase II study of trastuzumab in patients with HER2+ NSCLC by immunohistochemistry (IHC; NCT02289833), an objective response was observed in 20% (4/20) of patients with 3+ HER2 staining and no patients (0/29) with 2+ HER2 IHC staining [6]. Finally, recent preclinical studies have suggested that osimertinib may have activity in NSCLC with ERBB2 amplification and other aberrations [7].

While both preclinical [3,4] and limited clinical studies [5-9] have shown a potential clinical benefit to agents targeting ERBB2 including tyrosine kinase inhibitors and anti-ERBB2 antibodies, the KRAS mutation described above is likely to confer resistance to these therapies since RAS is downstream of ERBB2 within the MAPK signaling pathway.

The current National Comprehenisve Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines recommend treating small bowel adenocarcinoma with systemic therapy according the NCCN Guidelines for colon cancer [2]. Both preclinical [3,4] and limited clinical studies [3-7] have shown a potential clinical benefit to agents targeting ERBB2 including tyrosine kinase inhibitors and anti-ERBB2 antibodies.  In the HERACLES trial - a phase 2 trial of trastuzumab and lapatinib in treatment-refractory RAS wild-type, ERBB2 positive colon cancer - 30% (8/27) of patients achieved an objective response with one patient achieving complete remission [6]. In the MyPathway trial - a phase 2 basket trial - the subset that included ERBB2-amplified, metastatic CRC treated with pertuzumab and trastuzumab demonstrated an objective response rate of 32% (18/57) with one patient achieving a complete response [7]. Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations, including L755S, are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC), as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [PMID: 22810696, 26243863, 23220880,  28481359,29420467].

The L755S and V842I mutations detected in this specimen lie within the protein kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein [1]. These variants have been shown to result in increased phosphorylation of ERBB2, activation of downstream growth signaling and transformation in cell culture. Both variants have been reported in patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma [2]. It is  noted that this patient has metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma of possible colorectal primary location.

While ERBB2 amplification is seen in 15-20% of breast carcinoma, ERBB2 mutations are much more infrequent (2-4%), with L755S being the most common mutation [1-3]. ERBB2 exon 20 duplications (insertions), including Y772_A775dup are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [4-8] and have been rarely reported in breast carcinoma [9-10]. These mutations affect the kinase domain of ERBB2, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [6-7,11].

The L755S mutation detected in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein [1]. This variant has been shown to result in increased phosphorylation of ERBB2, activation of downstream growth signaling and transformation in cell culture ~. This mutation has been described in gastric adenocarcinoma | as well as other cancers such as breast, colorectal, endometrial and ovarian |&. ERBB2 mutations have been described in approximately 3-9% of gastric adenocarcinomas ^.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: HER2-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors zongertinib and sevabertinib are FDA-approved for patients with non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring an ERBB2 tyrosine kinase domain activating mutation. The antibody-drug conjugate fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with ERBB2-mutant NSCLC. However, the clinical utility of these inhibitors in patients with colorectal cancer is unknown at this time.

According to most recent NCCN guidelines, anti-HER2 therapy with signal transduction inhibition (eg, trastuzumab/pertuzumab, trastuzumab/tucatinib, trastuzumab/lapatinib) is only indicated in HER2-amplified tumors that are also RAS and BRAF wild-type. Activating mutations in ERBB2 in patients with colorectal cancer are not associated with RAS/BRAF wild-type status and it is unclear if anti-HER2 therapy is indicated in patients with ERBB2 mutated disease without associated HER2 overexpression/amplification [4]. In this specimen there is no evidence of ERBB2 DNA amplification. As such, additional testing for HER2 amplification by immunohistochemistry or FISH is recommended, if clinically indicated.

Several studies have evaluated alterations within the tyrosine kinase domain of ERBB2 in breast carcinoma and have found these tumors to be sensitive to the irreversible tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) neratinib [4]. Both preclinical [5] and clinical [6-8] studies have also shown that neratinib can overcome acquired trastuzumab resistance and improve outcomes when administered following trastuzumab therapy. The SUMMIT trial, found that neratinib was most effective in breast cancer patients, with patients containing L755S and V777L [9]. Neratinib is currently FDA-approved for extended adjuvant treatment of HER2+ breast cancer following adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy.

In preclinical studies, L755S was associated with relative resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as lapatinib !$, but appears to remain sensitive to irreversible inhibitors such as afatinib and neratinib $.

Summary: ERBB2 (also HER2) is a transmembrane receptor that is a member of the ERBB family of receptor tyrosine kinases, including EGFR, ERBB3, and ERBB4. ERBB2 does not directly bind its own ligand; instead, it potentiates the activity of other ligand-bound ERBB receptors by binding to them (PMID: 12620236).  Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations, including D769Y, are reported in patients with urothelial carcinoma.  Activation of ERBB2-mediated signaling ultimately results in cellular proliferation, migration, and differentiation (PMID: 18045542). ERBB2 is activated by gene amplification and overexpression in a range of human cancers including breast, gastric, and endometrial tumors, among others (PMID: 24656976). Preclinical and clinical studies have demonstrated that many of these mutations are transforming and sensitive to FDA-approved ERBB targeted therapies, including trastuzumab, ado-trastuzumab emtansine, lapatinib, and pertuzumab (PMID: 24799465).

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, anti-EGFR antibodies, such as cetuximab and panitumumab, are not expected to be effective in CRC with activating ERBB2 mutations since these therapies do not affect ERBB2 signaling (as shown in cell line experiments) [2]. Studies have shown that colorectal cancer cell lines with ERBB2 activating mutations (such as D769Y) are sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), such as neratinib and afatinib, as well as anti-ERBB2 antibodies such as trastuzumab [2,6]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated CRC, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [5, 7-13]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [14-15], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective.

While the anti-HER2 antibody ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) is NCCN-compendium listed for the treatment of patients with ERBB2 mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and there is promising clinical data in patients with breast and NSCLC with known oncogenic ERBB2 alterations treated with the ERBB-targeted inhibitor neratinib, their clinical utility in patients with ERBB2 D769Y mutant bladder urothelial carcinoma is unclear [16,17].

The ERBB2 S310Y mutation identified in this specimen has been described in multiple neoplasms including melanoma and biliary, breast, colorectal, urothelial, and gastroesophageal cancers [1-4]. This mutation affects the extracellular domain of the ERBB2 protein causing C-terminal tail phosphorylation, hyperphosphorylation and constitutive activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [5].

The absence of an activating EGFR mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) generally results in a primary resistance to anti-EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies [1,2]. The ERBB2 S310Y mutation identified in this specimen is rare, but has been described in NSCLC [3,4] as well as other neoplasms including breast cancer, urothelial cancer, colorectal cancer, and cervical cancer [5,6]. In addition, other ERBB2 mutations affecting the S310 residue including S310F have been described in NSCLC [7,8]. These mutations affect the extracellular domain of the ERBB2 protein causing C-terminal tail phosphorylation, hyperphosphorylation and consistitutive activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [9].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While the anti-HER2 antibody ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) is NCCN-compendium listed for the treatment of patients with ERBB2 mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and there is promising clinical data in patients with breast and NSCLC with known oncogenic ERBB2 alterations treated with the ERBB-targeted inhibitor neratinib, the clinical utility in patients with bladder urothelial carcinoma is not well characterized. In vitro studies have shown that the S310Y mutation is sensitive to anti-ERBB2 antibodies (trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib) [8] and several case reports and small series examining lung cancer with ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [9-13]. However, a phase II trial of neratinib resulted in mixed results in bladder cancer patients with this S310Y variant, with stable disease in 2 patients and progressive disease in 2 patients [2]; other tumors types in the same trial with ERBB2 S310Y alterations generally did not show benefit to treatment with neratinib. Several case reports and small series examining solid tumors with other ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [14-19]. Of note, ERBB2 (HER2) amplification was not identified in this specimen.

In one case report, a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring an S310F mutation responded to afatinib [11]. Similar reports in breast cancer patients have shown a clinical response to trastuzumab and lapatinib [12,13]. Several case reports and small series examining NSCLC with other ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [14-18]. Treatment of NSCLC harboring ERBB2 mutations with ado-trastuzumab emtansine is currently a National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) category 2A recommendation [19].

variants.variant_description: The D769H mutation detected in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein [1]. This variant has been shown to result in increased phosphorylation of ERBB2, activation of downstream growth signaling and transformation in cell culture. Activating ERBB2 mutations, such as D769H, are reported in approximately 17% of patients with urothelial carcinoma [2,3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The FDA has approved the use of fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki for adult patients with unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive (IHC3+) solid tumors who have received prior systemic treatment and have no satisfactory alternative treatment options [4]. However, the use of anti-HER2 therapy in patients with urothelial carcinomas harboring oncogenic mutations in ERBB2 is unclear. There is promising clinical data in patients with breast and non-small cell carcinoma with known oncogenic ERBB2 alterations treated with the ERBB-targeted inhibitor neratinib, but the clinical utility in patients with urothelial carcinoma is unknown. Of note, no copy number gains in ERBB2 (HER2) were identified in this specimen. Therefore, additional testing to assess for ERBB2 (HER2) amplification, such as immunohistochemistry or FISH, may be helpful, if clinically indicated.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: According to most recent NCCN guidelines the NSCLC Panel recommends fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki as a subsequent therapy option for patients with metastatic NSCLC and ERBB2 (HER2) mutations based on clinical trial data and FDA approval. The NCCN NSCLC Panel also recommends ado-trastuzumab emtansine as a subsequent therapy option for patients with ERBB2 (HER2) mutation–positive metastatic NSCLC. The panel preference stratified the recommended regimens for patients with ERBB2 (HER2) mutation–positive metastatic NSCLC and voted that fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki is a preferred subsequent therapy option; ado-trastuzumab emtansine is an other recommended subsequent therapy option. The NCCN NSCLC Panel does not recommend single-agent therapy with trastuzumab or afatinib for patients with ERBB2 (HER2) mutations, because response rates are lower and treatment is less effective with these agents [6].

Fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki was granted accelerated approval by the FDA for the treatment of adults with unresectable or metastatic NSCLC with activating ERBB2 (HER2) mutations, who have received a prior systemic therapy. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines, after disease progression, fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki is recommended as a preferred subsequent therapy options for patients with metastatic NSCLC and ERBB2 (HER2) mutations, while ado-trastuzumab emtansine is categorized as an "other recommended" option. Data suggest that ICI monotherapy may be less effective in NSCLC with ERBB2 (HER2) mutations [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 3.2026].

The ERBB2 V777L mutation identified in this specimen has been described in NSCLC and affects the kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein [1-3]. This mutation results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [2,4-6].

While ERBB2 amplification is seen in 15-20% of breast carcinoma, ERBB2 mutations are much more infrequent (2-4%) [PMIDs: 26451490, 30205045]. While exon 20 mutations such as V777L are uncommon, ERBB2 exon 20 insertions, including Y775_G776insYVMA are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMIDs: 22761469, 16825508, 15753357, 26598547, 15457249] and have been rarely reported in breast carcinoma [PMIDs: 30301790, 28164408]. These mutations affect the kinase domain of ERBB2, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [PMIDs: 15753357, 26598547, 15457249].

Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC), as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [PMID: 22811876, 16775247, 26598547, 24516025]. The V777L mutation identified in this case has been described in CRC [PMID: 16397024, 29420467] as well as other cancers [PMID: 27034166]. This mutation results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [PMID: 26508629, 23220880, 22046346, 26243863].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC, preclinical studies, case reports and small series have shown a potential benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [3-13]. The tyrosine kinase inhibitor poziotinib resulted in a confirmed objective response rate of 42% among 12 patient with ERBB2-mutated NSCLC. In a basket trial with ado-trastuzumab emtansine, the overall response rate among ERBB2-mutant lung adenocarcinoma was 44% (8/18) [11]. In another study, ado-trastuzumab emtansine, a response rate of 51% was reported among 49 patients with ERBB2-amplified or mutant lung cancer [12]. In a phase 2 trial of trastuzumab deruxtecan  (T-DXd; DESTINY-Lung01), which was presented at the 2020 ASCO Annual Meeting, the confirmed objective response rate was 61.9%, the disease control rate was 90.5% and the estimated median progression-free survival was 14.0 months among 42 patients treated with T-DXd [13]. Treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC with ado-trastuzumab emtansine or fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki are currently category 2A recommendations in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [14].

Several studies have evaluated alterations within the tyrosine kinase domain of ERBB2 in breast carcinoma and have found these tumors to be sensitive to the irreversible tyrosine kinase inhibitor neratinib [PMID: 32256585]. Both preclinical [PMID: 24009064] and clinical [PMIDs: 27406346, 26874901] studies have also shown that neratinib can overcome acquired trastuzumab resistance and improve outcomes when administered following trastuzumab therapy. The SUMMIT trial, found that neratinib was most effective in breast cancer patients, with patients containing L755S and V777L [PMID: 29420467].

While there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of ERBB2-mutated urothelial carcinoma, the V777L mutation appears to be sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors including lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib, based on in vitro studies [2,4-6]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated urothelial carcinoma, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [12-20]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [21-22], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective.

While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, anti-EGFR antibodies, such as cetuximab and panitumumab, may not expected to be effective in CRC with activating ERBB2 mutations, since these therapies do not affect ERBB2 signaling (as shown in cell line experiments) [PMID: 22811876]. There is limited clinical data on the efficacy of tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies in ERBB2-mutated CRC, however, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [PMID: 28481359, 23610105, 26358791, 26001389, 29420467, 23220880, 22810696, 28164408].
 
The V777L mutation appears to be sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors including lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib, based on in vitro studies [PMID: 26508629, 23220880, 22046346, 26243863]. In vitro studies have also shown that colorectal cancer cell lines with ERBB2 activating mutations are sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), such as neratinib and afatinib, as well as anti-ERBB2 antibodies such as trastuzumab [PMID: 22811876, 21737652]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated CRC, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [PMID: 28481359, 23610105, 26358791, 26001389, 29420467, 23220880, 22810696, 28164408]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [PMID: 26487584, 26243863], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective.

RAS Wild-Type and BRAF wild-type:
No KRAS, NRAS or BRAF mutations were detected. In colorectal cancer (CRC), therapeutic response to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies (including cetuximab and panitumumab) is associated with the absence of RAS mutations [1-3] or BRAF mutations [4,5]. Treatment of RAS wild-type CRC with one of these agents is currently a category 2A recommendation in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [6].

Amplification of the ERBB2 gene resulting in increased ERBB2 expression and growth signaling is well-described in breast cancer [1]. While ERBB2-amplification is associated with an inferior prognosis including a higher risk of relapse [1], this alteration confers sensitivity to anti-ERBB2 antibodies including trastuzumab, ado-trastuzumab emtansine and pertuzumab, as well as tyrosine kinase inhibitors including lapatinib and neratinib [2-6]. All of these agents are FDA-approved for the treatment of HER2+ breast cancer. An ERBB2 V842I mutation was also detected. This mutation has been described in breast cancer (and other cancers) and has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream growth signaling [7,8]. Other ERBB2 mutations, such as L755S have been described as a mechanism of acquired resistance to ERBB2-targeted therapy [9,10]. In preclinical studies, this mutation was found to be relatively resistant to trastuzumab, cetuximab, panitumumab and lapatinib, but sensitive to neratinib (IC50 1.9 +/- 0.3 nmol/L) and afatinib (IC50 0.42 +/- 0.05 nmol/L) [7,8]. Neratinib is currently FDA-approved for extended adjuvant treatment of HER2+ breast cancer following adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy. Both preclinical [11] and clinical [3-6] studies have shown that neratinib can overcome acquired trastuzumab resistance and improve outcomes when administered following trastuzumab therapy.

Trastuzumab emtansine is NCCN-compendium listed for the treatment of patients with ERBB2 mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and there is promising clinical data in patients with breast and NSCLC with known oncogenic ERBB2 alterations treated with the ERBB-targeted inhibitor neratinib. However, the ERBB2 V842I mutation may be resistant to anti-ERBB2 antibodies (trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (lapatinib), based on in vitro studies [7].

Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations described in urinary tract cancers as well as other neoplasms such as small bowel adenocarcinomas, breast cancer and colorectal carcinoma [1-6]. The R678Q mutation (annotated R648Q using transcript NM_001005862) lies within the juxtamembrane domain of the Erbb2 (Her2) protein and has been reported most frequently in stomach, colon and breast carcinomas [7-8]. While R678Q, by itself, did not impact receptor kinase activity or tumor growth in vitro in some studies [6], this mutation was recurrently identified (at a low frequency) in many cancer types suggesting that it plays some role in oncogenesis [12-21]. Moreover, other studies, in contrast to that above, have shown that this mutation results increased phosphorylation and activation of downstream signaling [22-23]. This mutation also frequently co-occurs with other ERBB2 mutations suggesting that other mutations may facilitate oncogenesis.

Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations are well-described in ampullary cancer as well as other neoplasms such as colorectal and breast cancer [1-3]. The R678Q mutation (annotated R648Q using transcript NM_001005862), however, has been reported only rarely [4]. While R678Q, by itself, did not impact receptor kinase activity or tumor growth in vitro [3], this mutation is recurrently identified (at a low frequency) many cancer types suggesting that it plays some role in oncogenesis [4-7]. This mutation also frequently co-occurs with other ERBB2 mutations suggesting that other mutations may facilitate oncogenesis [5].

ERBB2 (HER2) Y772_A775dup (also designated A775_G776insYVMA) and low-level ERBB2 (HER2) copy number gain (equivocal for amplification):
ERBB2 (like EGFR) is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. ERBB2 exon 20 duplications (insertions), including Y772_A775dup are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-4], particularly adenocarcinomas in patients without a history of smoking [1-3]. These mutations affect the kinase domain of ERBB2, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [3-5]. A low-level copy number gain involving the ERBB2 gene was also detected (approximately 4-6 copies; considered equivocal for amplification) that appears to affect the mutated ERBB2 allele. ERBB2  amplification resulting in increased ERBB2 expression is well-described in NSCLC [6,7].

While ERBB2 amplification is seen in 15-20% of breast carcinoma, ERBB2 mutations are much more infrequent (2-4%), with L755S being the most common mutation [1-3]. ERBB2 exon 20 duplications (insertions), including Y772_A775dup are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [4-8] and have been rarely reported in breast carcinoma [9-10]. These mutations affect the kinase domain of ERBB2, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [6-7,11].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki (Enhertu; 5.4mg/kg) was approved on 8/11/2022 for the treatment of adult patients with unresectable or metastatic NSCLC harboring activating HER2 (ERBB2) mutations who have received a prior systemic therapy based on the results from the DESTINY-Lung01 [PMID: 34534430] and DESTINY-Lung02 trials [PMID: 37694347]. 
 
Zongertinib (Hernexeos) was granted accelerated approval for unresectable or metastatic, non-squamous NSCLC with ERBB2 tyrosine kinase domain activating mutations based on the Beamion LUNG-1 trial [PMID: 40030100].
 
According to NCCN Guidelines for NSCLC [NSCL-36; v.8.2025], fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki or zongertinib is the preferred subsequent therapy for ERBB2-mutated NSCLC progressing on prior systemic therapy. Ado-trastuzumab emtansine is another recommended therapy.

Several case reports and small series examining NSCLC with other ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibody therapies and tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including trastuzumab [5,8-13], afatinib [7-9,14-16], neratinib [5,17] and lapatinib [5]. Treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC with ado-trastuzumab emtansine is currently a category 2A recommendation according the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [18].

Several studies have evaluated alterations within the tyrosine kinase domain of ERBB2 in breast carcinoma and have found these tumors to be sensitive to the irreversible Tk inhibitor neratinib [12]. Both preclinical [13] and clinical [14-16] studies have also shown that neratinib can overcome acquired trastuzumab resistance and improve outcomes when administered following trastuzumab therapy. The SUMMIT trial, found that neratinib was most effective in breast cancer patients, with patients containing L755S and V777L [17] Based on these findings, Neratinib is currently FDA-approved for extended adjuvant treatment of HER2+ breast cancer following adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy. While Y772_A775dup is very rare and has not been studied extensively in breast carcinoma, one study evaluated patients with HER2-amplified/mutant breast carcinoma and found one patient harboring Y772_A775dup who had stable disease following treatment with Neratinib [9]. There is also some variable response to afatinib in lung carcinoma patients harboring Y772_A775dup, although the majority of patients did still have progressive disease.

variants.variant_description:
In patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma, mutations in ERBB2 are most commonly insertion/duplication events in exon 20, and less commonly, other activating mutations are observed, such as T733I within exon 18. While some mutations are known to be activating, including mutations in the extracellular domain (eg, p.S310X) and exon 20 insertion/ duplication mutations, not all single-nucleotide or double-nucleotide changes in ERBB2 are activating and not all potentially activating mutations were studied in pivotal trials [3]. The ERBB2 T733I mutation identified in this specimen lies within the protein kinase domain, is within a hot spot domain, and has been characterized as likely oncogenic [2]. Cell line data demonstrates increased kinase activity [1,2].

The ERBB2 (HER2) T733I variant has been described as somatic mutation in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1,2], as well as in gastric, bladder and bile duct cancers [3-6]. However, this variant has been shown to have weak [6] or no tranformation activity [7].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The ERBB2 T733I mutation appears to be sensitive to anti-ERBB2 antibodies (trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib), based on in vitro studies [1]. The antibody-drug conjugate fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki (T-DXd) is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with ERBB2-mutant non-small cell lung cancer [3].

While the impact of this variant on response to ERBB2 targeted therapies is not entirely certain, some studies have shown that this mutation confers resistance to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor lapatinib [6].

variants.variant_description: Two ERBB2 (HER2) mutations detected - it is uncertain if these mutations affect the same allele or different alleles. The ERBB2 S310Y mutation identified in this specimen has been described in multiple neoplasms including melanoma and biliary, breast, colorectal, urothelial, and gastroesophageal cancers [1-4]. This mutation affects the extracellular domain of the ERBB2 protein causing C-terminal tail phosphorylation, hyperphosphorylation and consistitutive activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [5]. E717K has been described in breast carcinoma [6-7], but has not been functionally characterized.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The ERBB2 S310Y mutation identified in this specimen is sensitive to anti-ERBB2 antibodies (trastuzumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib), based on in vitro studies [8] and several case reports and small series examining lung cancer with ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [9-13]. However, a phase II trial of neratinib resulted in mixed results in bladder cancer patients with this S310Y variant, with stable disease in 2 patients and progressive disease in 2 patients [2]; other tumors types in the same trial with ERBB2 S310Y alterations generally did not show benefit to treatment with neratinib. The potential sensitivity or resistance associated with the E717K mutation also detected in this specimen is unknown. 
 
Afatinib demonstrated significant activity in patients with platinum-refractory urothelial carcinoma with ERBB2 or ERBB3 alterations [14]. Several case reports and small series examining solid tumors with other ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [15-19].

variants.variant_description: ERBB2 L841V mutation identified in this specimen has been reported in small bowel adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer (CRC) as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [1-2]. L841V lies within the protein kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein and results in increased cell proliferation and cell viability in two different cell lines [3] and demonstrates transformation in cell culture [4] and therefore, is predicted to result in gain of ERBB2 protein function.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, anti-EGFR antibodies, such as cetuximab and panitumumab, are not expected to be effective in CRC with activating ERBB2 mutations since these therapies do not affect ERBB2 signaling (as shown in cell line experiments) [5]. Studies have shown that colorectal cancer cell lines with ERBB2 activating mutations are sensivitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), such as neratinib and afatinib, as well as anti-ERBB2 antibodies such as trastuzumab [5,6]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated small bowel adenocarcinoma and CRC, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [7-13]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [14-15], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective.

variants.variant_description: Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC), as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [1-5]. The E874K mutation identified in this case is very rare but has been described in at least one case of colon cancer [6]. The E874K codon resides in the ERBB2 kinase domain; however, this particular mutation has not been functionally characterized. Thus, the biologic significance is unknown at this time.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, anti-EGFR antibodies, such as cetuximab and panitumumab, may not expected to be effective in CRC with activating ERBB2 mutations, since these therapies do not affect ERBB2 signaling (as shown in cell line experiments) [2]. Studies have shown that colorectal cancer cell lines with ERBB2 activating mutations are sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), such as neratinib and afatinib, as well as anti-ERBB2 antibodies such as trastuzumab [2,7]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated CRC, particularly those that harbor alterations in BRAF, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [5, 8-14]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [15,16], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective. There is also preliminary evidence that combination strategies with BRAF/TKI inhibitors may be more effective in BRAF-mutated carcinomas which express higher levels of ERBB2 [17]

variants.variant_description: Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations are well described in several tumor types including breast, colorectal carcinoma, and bladder carcinoma [1]. Alterations in ERBB2 are seen in around 17% of gastric adenocarcinoma, however gene amplification comprise the majority of alterations with only about 5% containing oncogenic mutations [2]. ERBB2 L755S lines within the protein kinase domain and is a well-described hotspot mutation frequently seen in breast carcinoma. In vitro studies have shown that it results in increased phosphorylation of Her2 and activation of downstream signaling including PI3K/Akt and MAPK signaling pathways [3][4]. There have been rare documented reports of gastric carcinoma harboring ERBB2 L755S mutation [5]. ERBB2 T686A lies within the juxtamembrane domain and has been shown to increase cell survival compared to wild-type HER2 in culture, predicting a gain of protein function [6]. However, alterations at T686 are incredibly rare in carcinoma and its clinical significance is not well-established.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: In preclinical trials, ERBB2 L755S mutation has been associated with primary resistance to lapatinib [3] and has also been associated with acquired resistance to trastuzumab therapy in breast cancer [7]. However, in vitro studies have shown sensitivity to afatinib plus neratinib [3][7]. The SUMMIT trial found that neratinib was most effective in breast cancer patients containing L755S and V777L [8]. However, it has been shown that Her2-targeted therapies may have variable effects in different tumor types, and there is currently no clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated gastric adenocarcinomas. In addition, there is no clinical data on the efficacy of Her2-targeted therapies in tumors with ERBB2 T686A alterations or those with L755S and T686A combined mutations.

variants.variant_description: The T686A mutation detected in this specimen lies within the juxtamembrane domain of the ERBB2 protein [1]. This variant has been shown to increase cell survival in culture compared with wild-type ERBB2 and is therefore predicted result in a gain of protein function [1]. ERBB2 mutations have been described in approximately 3-9% of gastric adenocarcinomas [2-6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The potential sensitivity of ERBB2 T686A to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) is uncertain due the rarity of this variant. There is also no known clinical data concerning the use of ERBB2 TKI therapy in ERBB2-mutated gastric adenocarcinoma.

variants.variant_description: Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC), as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [1-5]. The R897G mutation identified in this case is very rare but has been described in at least one case of breast cancer; the R897 codon resides in the ERBB2 kinase domain, and in vitro characterization of the R897G mutation suggests that it results in increased ERBB2 phosphorylation and downstream MAPK signaling pathway activation [6].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, anti-EGFR antibodies, such as cetuximab and panitumumab, may not expected to be effective in CRC with activating ERBB2 mutations, since these therapies do not affect ERBB2 signaling (as shown in cell line experiments) [2]. Studies have shown that colorectal cancer cell lines with ERBB2 activating mutations are sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), such as neratinib and afatinib, as well as anti-ERBB2 antibodies such as trastuzumab [2,7]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated CRC, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [5, 8-14]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [15,16], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective.

variants.variant_description: The S305C mutation detected in this specimen is rare, but has been described in breast cancer [1,2]. This mutation has not been biochemically characterized and its clinical significance is uncertain.

ERBB2 (HER2) G776S:
The absence of an activating EGFR mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) generally results in a primary resistance to anti-EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies [1-2]. The G776S identified in this specimen is uncommon, but has been reported in cancer types including gastric, colorectal, and urinary tract [3-5]. Other point mutations have been described in lung and breast cancer including the same G776 residue, such as G776L and G776V [6-7]. The G776S mutation occurs in the kinase domain and results in increased kinase activity of ERBB2 and activation of MAPK pathway including transformation and increased proliferation in cell culture [8]

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC, preclinical studies, case reports and small series have shown a potential benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [9-14]. A patient with a similar G776V metastatic breast cancer treated with trastuzumab and pertuzumab experienced clinical benefit [7]. Treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC with ado-trastuzumab emtansine is currently a category 2A recommendations in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [15].

variants.variant_description: Activating oncogenic ERBB2 mutations are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC), as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [1-3]. The L726I mutation is rare and has not been previously described in CRC, however, L726 lies within the protein kinase domain, suggesting that this mutation is also oncogenic.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, anti-EGFR antibodies, such as cetuximab and panitumumab, are not expected to be effective in CRC with activating ERBB2 mutations, since these therapies do not affect ERBB2 signaling (as shown in cell line experiments) [2]. Studies have shown that colorectal cancer cell lines with ERBB2 activating mutations are sensivitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), such as neratinib and afatinib, as well as anti-ERBB2 antibodies such as trastuzumab [2,4]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated CRC, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [5-11]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [12-13], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective. Importantly, in preclinical models, L726 mutations are associated with acquired resistance to gefinitib and lapatinib [14,15], although L726-mutant tumors may remain sensitive to EXEL-7647 (tesevanitib) [15].

The impact of ERBB2 copy number gain on response to anti-EGFR antibody therapies such as cetuximab and panitumumab is uncertain, however, these agents are not expected to have activity against ERBB2, and some studies have suggested that ERBB2 amplification may confer resistance to these treatments [2-5]. Indeed, both preclinical [2,3] and limited clinical studies [6-9] have shown a potential clinical benefit to agents targeting ERBB2, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

variants.variant_description:
ERBB2 Y772_A775dup and H878Y:
The absence of an activating EGFR mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) generally results in a primary resistance to anti-EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies [1-2]. The in-frame exon 20 insertion (Y772_A775dup) identified in this specimen is well-described in NSCLC and results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [3,4]. The H878Y mutation is much less uncommon, but has been in NSCLC [3]. This mutation has also been shown to result in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [3,4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC, preclinical studies, case reports and small series have shown a potential benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [5-10]. In a recent basket trial with ado-trastuzumab emtansine, the overall response rate among ERBB2-mutant lung adenocarcinoma was 44% (8/18). The vast majority of the mutations in these studies are exon 20 insertions (similar to the mutation detected in this specimen). However, in preclinical studies the H878Y mutation was shown to also be sensitive to TKI therapies such as neratinib and laptinib [3,4]. Treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC with ado-trastuzumab emtansine is currently a category 2A recommendations in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [11].
