The H878Y identified in this specimen is uncommon, bu has been in NSCLC [3]. This mutation results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [3,4].

In a recent basket trial with ado-trastuzumab emtansine, the overall response rate among ERBB2-mutant lung adenocarcinoma was 44% (8/18). The vast majority of these mutations are exon 20 insertions. However, in preclinical studies this mutations was shown to also be sensitive to TKI therapies such as neratinib and laptinib [3,4]. Treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC with ado-trastuzumab emtansine is currently a category 2A recommendations in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [11].

variants.variant_description: ERBB2 exon 20 duplications (insertions), including G778_P780dup, are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1-4], particularly adenocarcinomas in patients without a history of smoking [1-3]. These mutations affect the kinase domain of ERBB2, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling [3-5]. Several case reports and small series examining NSCLC with other ERBB2 mutations have shown a potential clinical benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibody therapies and tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including trastuzumab [5-11], afatinib [5-7,12-14], neratinib [5,15] and lapatinib [5]. Treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC with ado-trastuzumab emtansine is currently a category 2A recommendation according the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [16]. The University of Michigan is currently participating in a phase 1/2 study (NCT02716116; UMCC 2017.110; PI Shirish Gadgeel) investigating the utility of the oral EGFR/ERBB2 inhibitor AP32788. Other relevant clinical trials currently recruiting patients include NCT03318939 (phase 2 trial of posiotinib; multiple centers including Karmanos Cancer Institute, Detroit, MI), NCT02675829 (phase 2 of ado-trastuzumab; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY), NCT03066206 (phase 2 trial of poziotinib, MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, TX), NCT01306045 (phase 2 trial of lapatinib, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD), and NCT02716116 (phase1/2 of AP32788, multiple centers outside Michigan). The University of Michigan is no longer participating in a phase 2 trial (NCT01953926) investigating neratinib alone or in combination with trastuzumab in ERBB2-mutated lung cancer.

Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations, including V842I, are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [1-3]. While there is insufficient clinical data to draw definitive conclusions, anti-EGFR antibodies, such as cetuximab and panitumumab, are not expected to be effective in CRC with activating ERBB2 mutations since these therapies do not affect ERBB2 signaling (as shown in cell line experiments) [2]. Studies have shown that colorectal cancer cell lines with ERBB2 activating mutations (such as V842I) are sensivitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI), such as neratinib and afatinib, as well as anti-ERBB2 antibodies such as trastuzumab [2,4]. While there is limited clinical data on the efficacy of these therapies in ERBB2-mutated CRC, such therapies have shown efficacy in other ERBB2-mutated neoplasms including breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer [5-11]. However, some studies have shown limited efficacy for TKI monotherapy [12-13], suggesting that anti-ERBB2 antibodies or combined TKI/antibody therapy may be more effective. Various clinical trials are underway investigating the utility of these and other agents, both for colorectal cancer and, more broadly, for advanced stage cancer. Relevant trials currently recruiting patients include NCT01953926 (phase 2 of neratinib and trastuzumab; multiple centers outside Michigan). Relevant trials that are not yet recruiting include NCT03457896 (phase 2 of neratinib with trastuzumab; NSABP Foundation) and NCT03410927 (phase 1/2 of the TKI TAS0728; multiple centers; closest Nashville, TN).

Activating, oncogenic ERBB2 mutations are well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC) as well as other neoplasms such as breast cancer [1-3]. The T862A mutation identified in this specimen is a rare variant that has been reported in CRC [4,5]. The T862 residue forms the base of the ATP binding site with the ERBB2 kinase domain. The T862A mutation has been shown to oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of ERBB2 and downstream signaling [6]. In preclinical studies, this mutation was sensitive to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor lapatinib, albeit with somewhat higher IC50 likely necessitating higher doses in patients [6]. However, the KRAS mutation described above is expected to confer resistance to targeted therapies directed at ERBB2.

While activating ERBB2 mutations have been described in NSCLC, there are no reports of the ERBB2 V665A variant observed in this specimen. While this assay cannot definitively distinguish between somatic (acquired) and germline (inherited) variants, the variant allele frequency in comparison with the reported percentage of neoplastic cells within the specimen is suggestive of a somatic mutation. Given the lack of any previous description, this variant may represent a passenger mutation.

The absence of an activating EGFR mutation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) generally results in a primary resistance to anti-EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies [1-2]. The in-frame exon 20 insertion identified in this specimen is well-described in NSCLC and affects the kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein. This mutation results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [3,4]. While there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC, preclinical studies, case reports and small series have shown a potential benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [5-9]. Treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC with trastuzumab or afatinib is currently a category 2B recommendations in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [10]. Clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of these types of agents in this setting are ongoing. The NCI-MATCH trial (NCT02465060) includes an afatinib treatment arm for advanced stage solid tumors with ERBB2 mutations. Other relevant clinical trials include NCT01953926 (phase 2 trial of neratinib, multicenter), NCT03066206 (phase 2 trial of poziotinib, MD Anderson), NCT01306045 (phase 2 trial of lapatinib, NCI), and NCT02716116 (phase1/2 of AP32788, multicenter).

The in-frame exon 20 insertion (duplication) identified in this specimen is well-described in NSCLC and affects the kinase domain of the ERBB2 protein. This mutation results in constitutive, oncogenic activation of ERBB2 as well as the downstream MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [3,4]. While there are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of ERBB2-mutated NSCLC, preclinical studies, case reports and small series have shown a potential benefit to ERBB2 TKI and anti-ERBB2 antibodies therapies, including trastuzumab and afatinib [5-9]. Clinical trials investigating the clinical utility of these agents in this setting are ongoing.

name: GNA11
gene_function: GNA11 encodes a subunit of a guanine nucleotide binding protein (G protein) receptor involved in growth signaling [PMID: 19458711].

variants.variant_description: The Q209P mutation occurs at a statistically significant hotspot and is predicted to result in constitutive activation of GNA11 and downstream mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling [PMID: 21083380, 29490280].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Mutations of GNA11 (as well as GNAQ) are well-described in uveal melanoma [PMID: 21083380], less commonly in mucosal melanoma [PMID: 27498141] including rarely genitourinary [PMID: 27498141, 27089234]. GNA11 mutations are typically mutually exclusive with other oncogenic mutations such as those involving BRAF, NRAS, and KIT.
diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted treatments for GNAQ-mutated melanoma. In preclinical studies, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib induce cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis in uveal melanoma cell lines [PMID: 22733540, 25952648]. However, in clinical trials, GNAQ and GNA11 mutation status did not appear to affect response to MEK inhibitors [PMID: 24938562,: 26059332, 24938562, 26059332]. In vitro studies suggest that resistance may be mediated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF; the ligand for MET) and/or neuregulin 1 (NRG1) [PMID: 25952648] and that co-targeting of MEK and MET or PI3K may have greater efficacy [PMID: 22733540, 28138035].

variants.variant_description:
This mutation results in constitutive activation of GNA11 and downstream mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling [PMID: 21083380].

Mutations of GNA11, including Q209L, are well-described in uveal melanoma [2], less commonly in mucosal melanoma [3] including rarely genitourinary [3,4]. These mutations result in constitutive activation of GNA11 and downstream mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling [2]. GNA11 mutations are typically mutually exclusive with other oncogenic mutations such as those involving BRAF, NRAS and KIT.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Mutations of GNA11 (as well as GNAQ) are well-described in uveal melanoma [PMID: 21083380], less commonly in mucosal melanoma [PMID: 27498141] including rarely genitourinary [PMID: 27498141, 27089234]. GNA11 mutations are typically mutually exclusive with other oncogenic mutations such as those involving BRAF, NRAS, and KIT.
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
In preclinical studies, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib induce cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis in uveal melanoma cell lines [PMID: 22733540, 25952648]. However, in clinical trials, GNAQ and GNA11 mutation status did not appear to affect response to MEK inhibitors [PMID: 24938562,: 26059332, 24938562, 26059332]. In vitro studies suggest that resistance may be mediated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF; the ligand for MET) and/or neuregulin 1 (NRG1) [PMID: 25952648] and that co-targeting of MEK and MET or PI3K may have greater efficacy [PMID: 22733540, 28138035].

In preclinical studies, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib induce cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis in uveal melanoma cell lines [5,6]. However, in clinical trials, MEK inhibitors have shown limited efficacy [7,8]. In a phase 2 trial of 120 patients with metastatic uveal melanoma, selumetinib monotherapy showed a modest improvement in progression-free survival and response rate, but no improvement in overall survival compared with standard chemotherapy [7]. The presence of GNAQ or GNA11 mutations did not seem to affect the likelihood of response in this study. A recent phase 3 trial of selumetinib and dacarbazine failed to show any improvement in progression-free survival over chemotherapy alone [8] (results available at clinicaltrials.gov). In vitro studies suggest that resistance may be mediated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF; the ligand for MET) and/or neuregulin 1 (NRG1) [6] and that co-targeting of MEK and MET or PI3K may have greater efficacy [5,9].

However, in clinical trials, MEK inhibitors have shown limited efficacy [7,8]. variants.variant_description: The R181Q mutation detected in this specimen has never been described as a somatic mutation but has been described as a germline mutation associated with autosomal dominant hypocalcemia [1]. While this test cannot definitively distinguish somatic from germline variants, the variant allele frequency in comparison with the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells suggests that the variant is somatic rather than germline. If there is any clinical concern for inherited hypocalcemia, germline testing and genetic counseling is recommended. If this variant is indeed a somatic mutation, the clinical significance is uncertain.

name: ETV1
gene_function: ETV1 is an ETS-family transcription factor which have been shown to be oncogenic in other tumors including Ewing sarcoma and prostatic adenocarcinoma.

variants.variant_description:
PTPRZ1 (exon 1) - ETV1 (exon 4) Gene Fusion: 
A gene fusion involving exon 1 of PTPRZ1 and exon 4 of ETV1 was detected. Recurrent gene fusions involving these two have recently been described [PMID: 31381204]. The fusion detected in this specimen results in the promoter of PTPRZ1 in frame with the DNA-binding domain of ETV1. This is expected to result in ETV1 expression being controlled by the PTPRZ1 promoter, and other fusions involving the PTPRZ1 promoter such as PTPRZ1::MET have been shown to result in increased expression of partner gene (in this case ETV1) [PMID: 27748748, 25935522, 25135958].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: This gene fusions has been described in glioblastomas and individual cases of anaplastic oligodendroglioma and pilocytic astrocytoma, and has been shown to co-exist with other oncogenic mutations in glioma  [PMID: 31381204].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no therapies directed at ETV1 alterations that have established clinical efficacy. An ETV1 small molecular inhibitor has shown preclinical evidence of efficacy in cell lines [PMID: 21559405, 28553168] and in a prostate cancer mouse xenograft model [PMID: 25479232]. Preclinical experiences have also demonstrated that ETS transcription factor activity was dependent on PARP1 expression and that inhibition of PARP could potentiate ETS-induced DNA damage [PMID: 22287547, 21575865]. Multiple clinical trials have been initiated to evaluate PARP inhibitors in patients with prostate cancer and Ewings sarcoma harboring ETS fusions [PMID: 37375228, 24958807]. However, the multi-institutional randomized phase II trial NCT01576172 in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer found that neither the addition of veliparib nor ETS status influenced response in this trial [Hussain M et al. J Clin Oncol. 2017; 35(suppl 15); Abstract 5001]. A gene fusion involving exon 1 of PTPRZ1 and exon 5 of ETV1 was detected. Recurrent gene fusions involving these partners have been described in gliomas at low frequency [PMID: 31381204]. The fusion detected in this specimen results in the promoter of PTPRZ1 in frame with the DNA-binding domain of ETV1. This is expected to result in ETV1 expression being controlled by the PTPRZ1 promoter, and other fusions involving the PTPRZ1 promoter such as PTPRZ1-MET have been shown to result in increased expression of the partner gene (in this case ETV1) [PMID: 27748748, 25935522,: 25135958].

A gene fusion involving exon 1 of SCAF11 and exon 4 of ETV1 was detected. The fusion detected in this specimen putatively links the promoter of SCAF11 with the DNA-binding domain of ETV1. An ETV1 small molecular inhibitor has shown preclinical evidence of efficacy in cell lines [3-4] and in a prostate cancer mouse xenograft model [5]. Preclinical experiences have also demonstrated that ETS transcription factor activity was dependent on PARP1 expression and that inhibition of PARP could potentiate ETS-induced DNA damage [6-7]. Multiple clinical trials have been initiated to evaluate PARP inhibitors in patients with prostate cancer and Ewings sarcoma harboring ETS fusions. However, the multi-institutional randomized phase II trial NCT01576172 in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer found that neither the addition of veliparib nor ETS status influenced response in this trial [8]. In a phase I, dose-escalation NCT00749502 trial testing niraparib (MK4827), no evidence of an association between ETS rearrangements and treatment benefit was identified [9].

variants.variant_description:
CDK4 R24L
CDK4 (cyclin-dependent kinase 4) is a serine/threonine kinase that regulates the cell cycle G1 to S phase transition. Upon stimulation, CDK4 forms a complex with cyclin D and cyclin-dependent kinase 6 (CDK6), therby leading to activation of the kinases [1]. The active CDK4/CDK6 complex phosphorylates and inactivates retinoblastoma (RB), inducing  gene expression program important in cell cycle progression. CDK4 R24L lies within the protein kinase domain and although not functionally characterized is considered likely oncogenic. Additionally, the CDK4 R24C mutation is known to be oncogenic and in the ClinVar database this variant is classified as likely pathogenic.
 
Interpretation: Palbociclib is NCCN-compendium listed for the treatment of patients with well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas. However, the clinical signficance of CDK4 R24L mutant non-small cell lung cancer is not currently well characterized [4,5].

The CDK4 K22R detected in this specimen has been described as a rare somatic mutation in melanoma [1-3]. While no functional studies have investigated its functional effect, the recurrent nature of this mutation and the location of this mutation within the p16/CDKN2A binding region [4] suggests that it is an oncogenic driver. Other recurrent mutations of CDK4 are also described in melanoma [4,5]. While the impact of this mutation on response to BRAF inhibitor therapy is not entirely certain, on melanoma cell line carrying this mutation remained sensitive to vemurafenib [3]. Open clinical trials investigating the ultility of CDK4/6 inhibitors in melanoma and other advanced solid tumors with CDK4 alterations include NCT01037790 (phase 2 of CDK4/6 inhibitor PD-0332991, Abramson Cancer Center, Univ. Pennsylvania), and NCT03310879 (phase 2 of CDK4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib, Dana Farber Cancer Insititute).

name: MAP2K1
gene_function: MAP2K1 encodes the protein MEK1 - a dual specificity kinase involved in growth signaling within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, downstream of EGFR, NRAS/KRAS and BRAF.

variants.variant_description: Although the G128A has not been functionally characterized, other mutations at the G128 residue have been shown to be activating [PMID: 25899310, 28115009, 32641410]. Activating MAP2K1 mutations are well-described in various neoplasms [PMID: 22197931, 35123694, 22817889, 24982505, 25202140].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved therapies for MAP2K1-mutated solid tumors. Limited clinical data suggest that MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and cobimetinib may be effective against various cancers harboring oncogenic MAP2K1 mutations [PMID: 36455195].

variants.variant_description:
The MAP2K1 Q56P mutation has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of MEK1 and downstream signaling [PMID: 25351745, 22327936, 19915144, 32641410].

The Q56P mutation detected in this specimen has been described in many neoplasms including colorectal cancer (CRC) [1], gastric carcinoma [2-3], lung adenocarcinoma [1][4] and hairy cell leukemia [5]. This mutation has been shown to confer a gain of function, resulting in constitutive activation and MEK1 and downstream signaling [6-7].

The Q56P mutation detected in this specimen has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [1-3] and has been shown to be ongenic resulting in constitutive activation and MEK1 and downstream signaling [4]. While neither the CAP/AMP/ASCO guidelines nor the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend MAP2K1 mutational status be used as a predictive molecular biomarker for response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy (cetuximab, panitumumab) [5,6], colorectal cancers with activating MAP2K1 mutations are not expected to respond to these therapies since MEK1 is downstream of EGFR within MAPK signaling. Multiple studies have identified MAP2K1 mutations as a potential mechanism of primary resistance to anti-EGFR therapies [7,8]. This mutation has also been shown to be resistant to at least some MEK inhibitors such as selumetinib (AZD6244) [9]. Clinical trials investigating the utility of ERK inhibitors in patients with advanced stage cancer including CRC include NCT02711345 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LTT462; New York, NY and Houston, TX) and NCT02857270 (phase 1 trial of ERK inhibitor LY3214996 alone or in combination with other agents; multiple centers outside the midwest).

diseases.diagnostic_implications: According to the 5th edition WHO, splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukaemia with prominent nucleoli has been shown to harbor MAP2K1 mutations in approximately 38-42% of cases [PMID: 19641528, 22210875, 22594855, 24241536, 27241017].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Cell line experiments suggest that the MAP2K1 Q56P mutation may be sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib [PMID: 32641410].
In case reports, clinical responses to MEK1/2-targeted inhibitors such as trametinib and cobimetinib have been reported in patients with MAP2K1-mutant NSCLC [PMID:36455195].

This mutation has also been shown to be resistant to BRAF inhibitors such as dabrafenib and regorafenib [8][9] and at least some MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib (AZD6244) [8][10], but appears to be sensitive to other MEK inhibitors such as U0126 [11]. In addition, preclinical studies have suggested that cells with this mutation may be sensitive to inhibition of ERK (downstream of MEK in MAPK signaling) using agents such as ulixertinib [8].

variants.variant_description: The K57N mutation detected in this specimen has been described in colorectal cancer (CRC) [PMID: 26644315, 26030179] and has been shown to be oncogenic resulting in constitutive activation and MEK1 and downstream signaling [PMID: 18632602, 25351745].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: MAP2K1 mutations have been described in approximately 17-28% of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) cases [PMID: 24982505, 25202140]. These mutations are generally mutually exclusive with BRAF mutations [PMID: 24982505, 25202140].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several MEK inhibitors including trametinib (GSK1120212), selumetinib (AZD6244) and cobimentinib (XL518) are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600 mutated melanoma.  Limited clinical studies have shown a response to trametinib in LCH patients with MAP2K1 (as well as BRAF) mutations [PMID: 32991018]. Based on preclinical studies, the MAP2K1 K57N mutation appears to be sensitive to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib [PMID: 25351745, 32641410, 36442478] and selumetinib [PMID: 18632602, 25351745, 29753091]. Clinical response to trametinib have been reported in other neoplasms harboring MAP2K1 K57N including non-small cell lung cancer [PMID: 36455195] and Erdheim-Chester [PMID: 26566875]. Inhibition of ERK (downstream of MEK in MAPK signaling) is another potential treatment option.

The absence of an activating EGFR mutation and the presence of a downstream MAP2K1 mutation is associated with primary resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib) [1-4]. There is promising clinical data from case studies in patients with MAP2K1-mutant NSCLC treated with FDA-approved MEK1/2 inhibitors trametinib and cobimetinib.  Several MEK inhibitors including trametinib (GSK1120212), selumetinib (AZD6244) and cobimentinib (XL518) are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600 mutated melanoma. Based on preclinical studies, the MAP2K1 K57N mutation appears to be sensitive to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib [1] and selumetinib [3]. Another preclinical study suggested that the combination of sorafenib and selumetinib was more efficacious in a colorectal carcinoma patient-derived cell line harboring a MAP2K1 K57T mutation [5]. Inhibition of ERK (downstream of MEK in MAPK signaling) is another potential treatment option.

While neither the CAP/AMP/ASCO guidelines nor the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend MAP2K1 mutational status be used as a predictive molecular biomarker for response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy (cetuximab, panitumumab) [PMID: 28165299; NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer, Version 3.2025], colorectal cancers with activating MAP2K1 mutations are not expected to respond to these therapies since MEK1 is downstream of EGFR within MAPK signaling. However, the KRAS mutation seen in this specimen is clearly associated with lack of response to these therapies (see above). Multiple studies have identified MAP2K1 mutations as a potential mechanism of primary and acquired resistance to anti-EGFR therapies [PMID: 26644315, 26030179, 31226844, 26416732]. 
 
Several MEK inhibitors including trametinib (GSK1120212), selumetinib (AZD6244) and cobimentinib (XL518) are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600 mutated melanoma. Based on preclinical studies, the MAP2K1 K57N mutation appears to be sensitive to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib [PMID: 26644315] and selumetinib [PMID: 26030179]. Another preclinical study suggested that the combination of sorafenib and selumetinib was more efficacious in a CRC patient-derived cell line harboring a MAP2K1 K57T mutation [PMID: 28819429]. Inhibition of ERK (downstream of MEK in MAPK signaling) is another potential treatment option.

Activating MAP2K1 mutations, including E203K, are well-described in melanoma [1-3], and are frequently seen as a mechanism of acquired resistance to BRAF and/or MEK inhibitor therapy [2,3]. However, BRAF V600E mutation was not identified in this specimen. Laboratory and some clinical data support the use of MEK1/2-targeted inhibitors such as FDA-approved trametinib or cobimetinib in pateints with melanoma harboring MAP2K1 mutations.

The E203K mutation detected in this specimen has been described in several cancer types including colorectal cancer (CRC) and non-small cell lung cancer [1,2] and has been shown to be oncogenic resulting in constitutive activation and MEK1 and downstream signaling [3,4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There has been encouraging clinical data from case studies in patients with MAP2K1-mutant NSCLC treated with FDA-approved MEK1/2-targeted inhibitors such as trametinib and cobimetinib [4].

There is some promising clinical data supporting the use of FDA-approved MEK1/2-targeted inhibitors such as trametinib and cobimetinib in patients with various cancers harboring known oncogenic MAP2K1 mutations. However, their clinical utility in patients with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors is unknown [3].

Several MEK inhibitors including trametinib (GSK1120212) and cobimentinib (XL518) are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRAF V600 mutated melanoma. The sensitivity of the MAP2K1 E203K mutation to MEK inhibitors has not been evaluated in any known studies. ERK inhibitors, which act downstream of MEK, are another potential therapeutic option for targeting cancers with MAP2K1 mutations [5-9].

KRAS V14I and N116H:
KRAS is a membrane-bound GTPase normally involved in signal transduction upon activation by a growth factor receptor (e.g. EGFR). The KRAS V14I and N116H mutations detected in this sample are both extremely rare. V14I has been previously described in one case of colon cancer [1], as well as in two cases of pancreatic cancer and one case of endometrial cancer [1-3]. N116H has been described in two cases of colon cancer [4,5]. Both variants have been shown to cause weak activation of KRAS and downstream signaling (weaker than mutations affecting codons 12, 13 and 61) [6-8]. However, both V14I and a variant similar to N116H - N116S - have also been described as an inherited germline variant associated with Noonan syndrome [6,7,9]. While this assay cannot definitively determine if the variant is germline or somatic, evaluation of the variant allele frequency in comparison with the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells is more suggestive of a somatic mutation. If there is clinical concern for Noonan syndrome, genetic counseling with possible germline testing is recommended. While more strongly activating KRAS mutations affecting codons 12, 13 and 61 have been associated with primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody-based therapies such as cetuximab and penitumumab [10-12], it is not known if, and to what degree, KRAS V14I and N116H will affect response to these agents. name: IDH1
gene_function: IDH1 encodes cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase, an enzyme that normally catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate.

variants.variant_description:
The IDH1 R132 mutations are known to result in a gain of enzymatic function, causing conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG) [PMID: 19935646]. 2HG then functions as an 'oncometabolite,' inhibiting histone demethylation and resulting in increased DNA methylation [PMID: 22343901, 21130701].

Molecular alteration with diagnostic and prognostic implications
IDH1 R132G:
IDH1 encodes the cytoplasmic enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase that normally converts isocitrate into alpha- ketoglutarate. The mutant protein resulting from this mutation catalyzes the production of 2-hydroxyglutarate which functions as an oncometabolite, inhibiting alpha-ketoglutarate dependent dioxygenases such as TET enzymes, leading to global DNA and histone methylation changes [1,2]. In addition, 2-hydroxyglutarate can stimulate the activity of EGLN involved in hypoxia signaling, leading to decreased levels of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and increased tumor proliferation and growth [3].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: IDH1 mutations have been described at a low incidence (approximately <1-2%) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMID: 22980975, 25079552, 27158780, 27346245, 29337640].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: While not approved for NSCLC, ivosidenib (Tibsovo) was FDA-approved for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with IDH1 mutations. Various other IDH inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical studies [PMID: 28124097, 26368816, 28193778] and clinical trials are evaluating inhibitors in solid tumors such as gliomas. There have been no studies investigating the clinical utility of these agents in NSCLC.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: According to the most recent NCCN guidelines IDH mutations define WHO grade 2 and 3 astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas, and grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas. Their presence distinguishes lower-grade gliomas from glioblastomas, which are IDH wild-type. Detection of these mutations in a specimen that is otherwise equivocal for tumor may also be regarded as evidence that a diffusely infiltrative glioma is present. IDH mutations are commonly associated with MGMT (O6-methylguanineDNA methyltransferase) promoter methylation. IDH1 or 2 mutations are associated with a relatively favorable prognosis and are important in stratification for clinical trials. In grade 2 or 3 infiltrative gliomas, wild-type IDH1 or 2 is associated with increased risk of aggressive disease. IDH1 or 2 mutations are associated with a survival benefit for patients treated with radiation or alkylating systemic therapy [4-7,16].
diseases.therapeutic_implications: According to the most recent NCCN guidelines vorasidenib is a dual inhibitor of IDH1 and IDH2 mutations. In a phase 3 study of vorasidenib versus placebo in patients with residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma (after surgery and no prior treatment), vorasidenib improved median PFS (27.7 mo vs. 11.1 mo), compared to placebo. Although the FDA approval process for vorasidenib is ongoing, eligible patients with newly diagnosed WHO grade 2 disease can obtain vorasidenib through an expanded access program (NCT05592743)[16].  Several IDH-inhibitors with activity against IDH1 have been developed. Ivosidenib (Tibsovo) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with IDH1 mutations. Studies with IDH inhibitors have been shown to decrease levels of 2-hydroxyglutarate but have shown mixed ability to inhibit glioma proliferation [8-12]. Recent studies have shown that once an IDH mutant tumor has been established, IDH-mutant activity and 2-hydroxyglutarate production may no longer be necessary for sustained growth [12]. In addition, blocking 2-hydroxyglutarate production may actually reverse homologous recombination (HR) repair deficiencies associated with elevated 2-hydroxyglutarate, thereby providing a survival advantage in IDH-mutant cells [12]. These HR deficits may result in sensitivity to agents such as poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors. Several PARP inhibitors are FDA-approved for the treatment of BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer. Preclinical studies have shown that these drugs may also be effective in cells with IDH mutations [13]. However, results from a recent clinical trial failed to show any efficacy associated with the PARP inhibitor ABT-888 [14]. Finally, there is some evidence that IDH1/2 mutations may contribute to immune suppression in gliomas and raise the possibility that these tumors may be sensitive to immunotherapeutic agents [15].

Molecular alteration with diagnostic and prognostic implications
IDH1 R132S:
IDH1 encodes the cytoplasmic enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase that normally converts isocitrate into alpha-ketoglutarate. The mutant protein resulting from this mutation catalyzes the production of 2-hydroxyglutarate which functions as an oncometabolite, inhibiting alpha-ketoglutarate dependent dioxygenases such as TET enzymes, leading to global DNA and histone methylation changes [1,2]. In addition, 2-hydroxyglutarate can stimulate the activity of EGLN involved in hypoxia signaling, leading to decreased levels of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and increased tumor proliferation and growth [3]. IDH1 R132S, this mutation is well described in gliomas [4].

IDH1 utilizes NADP(+) as an electron acceptor and it is predominantly expressed in the cytosol and peroxisomes, playing a role in the cytoplasmic production of NADPH. Cancer-associated mutations in the catalytic site of IDH1 confer a gain-of-function of neomorphic enzymatic activity, allowing the mutant enzyme to convert α-KG to the “oncometabolite” D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (PMID: 20171147). 2-HG promotes tumor development by inhibiting a variety of enzymes that require α-KG as a substrate, including enzymes involved in DNA demethylation, histone demethylation, adaptation to hypoxia and collagen maturation. R132S is classified as onogenic and pathogenic (1,2).

While the IDH1 inhibitor ivosidenib is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with IDH1-mutant acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and cholangiocarcinoma, its clinical utility in patients with IDH1 R132S mutant chondrosarcoma is not as well defined. A multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation and expansion phase 1 trial in patients with IDH1-mutant advanced solid tumors, including 21 patients with advanced chondrosarcoma, evaluated the response to ivosidenib, a selective IDH1 inhibitor. Median PFS was 5.6 months (95% CI, 1.9–7.4 months), PFS at 6 months was 39.5%, and 52% of patients had stable disease. All patients demonstrated decreased plasma 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) levels following treatment. Ivosidenib has thus been added as a treatment option for patients with IDH1-mutant conventional or dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma (3).

There are currently no FDA-approved therapies for the treatment of IDH-mutant NSCLC. Ivosidenib (Tibsovo) was recently FDA-approved for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with IDH1 mutations. Various other IDH inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical studies [5-7]. There have been no studies investigating the utility of these agents in NSCLC.

variants.variant_description:
G2032R is a likely oncogenic mutation that has been classified as activating in in vitro studies. This variant has been described as a resistance mutation in patients with non-small cell lung cancer with ROS1 mutations treated with crizotinib. Detailed patient history is unknown at this time. However, the final diagnosis is a malignant neoplasm with melanocytic differentiation with an immunoprofile most suggestive of melanoma. ROS1 mutations have been reported in approximately 15-30% of patients with various types of melanoma [Cerami E et al Cancer Discov (2012) 2 (5): 401–404 and Gao J et al. Sci Signal 2013 Apr 2;6(269):pl1 (cBioPortal.org Aug 2025).

The G2032R mutation detected in this sample is a known resistance mechanism acquired in some non-small cell lung cancers harboring oncogenic ROS1 fusions following treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as crizotinib [1-3]. This case is unusual in that no ROS1 fusion is present. While ROS1 fusion-positive tumors with G2032R-induced resistance have been shown in in vitro studies to respond to cabozantinib [4], tumors with G2032R but lacking a ROS1 fusion have not been similarly studied. In addition, the impact of the BRAF mutation described above on response to these agents is unknown.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Currently there is clinical data in ROS1 G2032R mutant non-small cell lung cancer treated with the ROS1/NTRK tyrosine kinase inhibitor taletrectinib. Although, the clinical significance in patients with ROS1 G2032R mutant melanoma is unknown.

In the current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines, entrectinib or crizotinib are preferred first-line therapy for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC with a ROS1 rearrangement (category 2A) [7]. diseases.therapeutic_implications:
There are no FDA-approved targeted therapies for gliomas with ROS1 rearrangements. Entrectinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with ROS1 rearrangements. This medication has been shown to cross the blood-brain barrier [PMID: 26939704, 27003761] and has demonstrated tumor responses in brain metastases of NSCLC patients with ROS1 and other susceptible rearrangements [PMID: 28183697, 30050303]. Another brain-permeable TKI, lorlatinib was shown in preclinical studies of glioblastoma xenografts to be efficacious [PMID: 30171048]. While lorlatinib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) harboring ALK rearrangements, several studies have demonstrated clinical activity of this drug in NSCLC with ROS1 rearrangements, including patients with brain metastases [PMID: 29074098, 30683630]. Certinib is another TKI FDA-approved for ALK-rearranged NSCLC that also has shown clinical activity in ROS1-rearranged NSCLC including patients with brain metastases [PMID: 28520527]. 
 
Importantly, no molecular alterations associated with TKI resistance [PMID: 31124056] were detected.

name: ESR1
gene_function: ESR1 encodes the alpha subunit of the estrogen receptor (ER), a transcription factor activated by estrogen.

variants.variant_description:
The ESR1 Y537 mutations including Y537N (as well as Y537S and Y537C) have been described in breast adenocarcinoma, particularly as a mechanism of acquired resistance in patients receiving anti-estrogen and aromatase inhibitor therapy [PMID: 24185510, 24185512, 26836308]. This mutation occurs in the ligand binding domain (LBD) and results in constitutive (estrogen-independent) ER activity [PMID: 24185510, 24185512, 26836308].

ESR1 mutations are reported in approximately 20% of patients with breast cancer [7]. ESR1 Y537N results in constitutive (estrogen-independent) ER activity and is characterized as likely oncogenic [1-2].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Elacestrant is FDA-approved for postmenopausal women or adult men for ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer with disease progression following at least one line of endocrine therapy. ESR1 LBD mutations are associated with complete or partial resistance to a number of first-line hormone-based therapies, including tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors [PMID: 31647985, 27986707]; however, newer agents, such as selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs; e.g., fulvestrant, AZD9496, etc.), may remain effective against tumors with ESR1 LBD mutations [PMID: 27986707]. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines some patients with tumors harboring ESR-1 mutations retain sensitivity to fulvestrant and may benefit by adding one of the following to fulvestrant: a CDK 4/6-inhibitor or an mTOR-inhibitor [NCCN Breast v4.2025].

ESR1 activating mutations are associated with resistance to a number of first-line hormone-based therapies, including tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors, although new agents such as selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs; e.g., fulvestrant) may remain effective against tumors with ESR1 ligand binding domain mutations [3,4]. Additionally, ESR1 activating mutations have been associated with resistance to alpelisib [5]. According to the most recent NCCN guidelines ESR1 activating mutations, such as Y537N, are frequently detected in patients with prior exposure to aromatase inhibitors (AI). Tumors with these mutations are generally resistant to both AIs and tamoxifen. Certain tumors with these mutations retain sensitivity to fulvestrant. All may benefit by adding one of the following to fulvestrant - a CDK 4/6-inhibitor, or an mTOR-inhibitor [6].

ETV6 (exon 5) - NTRK3 (exon 15) Gene Fusion:
NTRK3 (also known as TRKC) is a receptor tyrosine kinase that activates mitogen activated protein kinase signaling. This in-frame fusion involves the first 5 exons of ETV6 and exons 15 and greater of NTRK3 and results in fusion of the helix-loop-helix dimerization domain of ETV6 and the protein tyrosine kinase domain of NTRK3 [PMID: 10702799]. This gene fusion results in ligand-independent dimerization of the fusion protein and constitutive activation of NTRK3 (a receptor tyrosine kinase) as well as downstream growth signaling [PMIDs: 10702799, 9462753].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: The ETV6-NTRK3 fusion is characteristic of mammary analogue secretory carcinoma [PMIDs: 20410810, 25651470]. name: GNAQ
gene_function: GNAQ encodes a subunit of a guanine nucleotide binding protein (G protein) receptor involved in growth signaling [PMID: 19458711].

variants.variant_description:
Mutations of GNAQ, including Q209L, result in constitutive activation of GNAQ and downstream mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling [PMIDs: 18719078, 21083380, 19078957]. Activating GNAQ mutations are well described in melanoma (particularly uveal melanoma and, less commonly, mucosal melanoma) [PMIDs: 18719078, 21083380, 19078957, 32064597] as well as in up to 80% of blue nevi [PMIDs: 21056896, 21366456]. In melanocytic lesions, GNAQ mutations are typically mutually exclusive with other oncogenic mutations such as those involving BRAF, NRAS and KIT.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
According to the most recent NCCN guidelines "… data show that some patients with uveal melanoma may respond to the MEK inhibitor selumetinib, and there are limited data suggesting that trametinib may also be marginally effective. Although the data are strongest for selumetinib, it was not FDA approved for use in humans at the time of the most recent Guidelines update, so it could not be included as a recommended option. Trametinib is included as a recommended option based on the positive data for selumetinib and the general lack of systemic therapy options for patients with uveal melanoma. Further study of trametinib for uveal melanoma is needed." [NCCN Guidelines Melanoma: Uveal, v1.2025].
 
In preclinical studies, MEK inhibitors such as trametinib and selumetinib induce cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis in uveal melanoma cell lines [PMID: 22733540, 25952648]. However, in clinical trials, MEK inhibitors have shown limited efficacy as single agents [PMID: 24938562, 26059332]. In a phase 2 trial of 120 patients with metastatic uveal melanoma, selumetinib monotherapy showed a modest improvement in progression-free survival and response rate, but no improvement in overall survival compared with standard chemotherapy [PMID: 24938562]. The presence of GNAQ or GNA11 mutations did not seem to affect the likelihood of response in this study. A phase 3 trial of selumetinib and dacarbazine failed to show any improvement in progression-free survival over chemotherapy alone [PMID: 26059332] (results available at clinicaltrials.gov). In vitro studies suggest that resistance may be mediated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF; the ligand for MET) and/or neuregulin 1 (NRG1) [PMID: 25952648] and that co-targeting of MEK and MET or PI3K may have greater efficacy [PMIDs: 22733540, 28138035].
 
There are currently no FDA-approved targeted treatments for GNAQ-mutated melanoma. Clinical studies show that some patients with uveal melanoma may respond to the MEK inhibitor selumetinib, and there is limited data suggesting that trametinib may be marginally effective; however, GNAQ and GNA11 status did not appear to impact response rate or outcome in patients treated with MEK inhibitors [PMID: 24938562, 29528792, 22805292].

name: FGFR1
gene_function: FGFR1 is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling.

variants.variant_description:
FGFR1 copy number gain (amplification):
An FGFR1 copy number gain was detected, consistent with FGFR1 amplification. FGFR1 amplification has been described in patients with colorectal carcinoma, approximately 2-3% [PMID: 22810696, cBioPortal.org February 2025].

FGFR1 copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain of the FGFR1 gene was detected, consistent with FGFR1 amplification. Amplification of FGFR1 resulting in overexpression of the FGFR1 protein has been described in approximately 10% of breast cancers, particularly those which are hormone receptor positive [PMID: 9331099, 23000897, 20179196]. This finding has been correlated with poorer outcomes in breast cancer patients [PMID: 20179196, 10706127].

FGFR1 copy number gain (amplification):
A copy number gain (approximately 9 copies) of the FGFR1 gene was detected, consistent with FGFR1 amplification. Putative amplification of FGFR1 has been described at a low incidence in melanoma [1].

FGFR1 amplification has been described in a small subset of pancreatic adenocarcinoma [1,2]. In one study, proliferation of a cell line derived from an FGFR1-amplified pancreatic carcinoma was inhibited by an FGFR1 inhibitor. Multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have putative activity against FGFR1 including pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib. While there is no clinical data concerning the efficacy of FGFR inhibitors in pancreatic adenocarcinoma patients, several studies have demonstrated the clinical efficacy of various FGFR inhibitors in other types of cancer including dovitinib and AZD4547 in NSCLC [2,3] and BGJ398 and lucitanib in various solid tumor malignancies [4-6].

ERBB3 D297Y:
ERBB3 is a membrane-bound growth factor receptor. While this protein is kinase-impaired, it is known to form active heterodimers with other members of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, particularly ERBB2. The ERBB3 D297Y mutation is well-described in colorectal cancer (CRC), bladder carcinoma, and occasionally lung carcinoma, among others [1-3]. The frequency of ERBB3 in squamous cell carcinomas of the head and neck is relatively low [4]. Mutations of this residue affect the extracellular domain resulting in ligand-independent oncogenic signaling by promoting the formation of active heterodimers with ERBB2 [2].

Amplification of FGFR1 is described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), particularly squamous cell carcinoma [1]. Multiple FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have activity against FGFR1 including pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib. Several studies have demonstrated modest clinical efficacy of various FGFR inhibitors in cancer with FGFR1 amplification including dovitinib and AZD4547 in NSCLC [2,3] and BGJ398 and lucitanib in various solid tumor malignancies [4,5]. Relevant clinical trials currently enrolling patients include NCT02272998 (phase 2 of ponatinib, University of Michigan), NCT02393248 (phase 1 of INCB054828, University of Michigan),NCT02160041 (phase II study for BGJ398, multiple centers including Cancer and Hematology Centers of West Michigan Dept. of Oncology, Grand Rapids), NCT01976741 (phase I for BAY1163877, multiple centers including Chicago, IL), NCT02052778 (phase I study for TAS-120, multiple centers outside Michigan), and NCT01948297 (phase I for Debio1347, multiple centers outside Michigan), NCT02608125 (phase I for PRN1371, multiple centers outside Michigan). diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no FDA-approved treatments for ERBB3-mutated cancer. One small study suggested that patients with somatic ERBB3 mutations may respond to anti-ERBB antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab) and/or tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. lapatinib, afatinib) [5]. A separate case report documented a clinical response to lapatinib in a patient with metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the skin [6]. In another study, no clinical response to neratinib was observed among 13 patients with ERBB3-mutated cancer [7].

variants.variant_description:
FGFR1 fusion: BAG4 (exon 1) - FGFR1 (exon 2) 
Transcripts: BAG4 NM_004874.3 ; FGFR1 NM_023110.2

The BAG4-FGFR1 gene fusion detected in this sample has been described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [1].

FGFR alterations, including fusions, are well-described in non-small cell lung cacinoma (NSCLC) and more frequently occur in squamous cell carcinomas. FGFR fusions involve the tyrosin kinase domain of FGFR and result in constitutve activation of FGFR and oncogenic transformation independent of canonical signaling downstream of FGFR 9pERK and pAKT) [2-3]. The BAG4-FGFR1 gene fusion is very rare but has been detected in NSCLC [1]. While FGFR fusions are often present in the absence of other known alterations, a subset of cases have been seen co-occuring with other driver alterations, including KRAS, as is seen in this case [4].

Erdafinitib (Balversa; JNJ-42756493) is a selective FGFR inhibitor that was recently granted approval by the US Food and Drug Administration for urothelial cancer with FGFR alterations [5]. In a phase 2 trial, a confirmed response rate of 40% was reported in patients WITH locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma harboring FGFR alterations [6]. Erdafitinib has also demonstrated evidence of preclinical and clinical efficacy in early studies of other cancers with FGFR alterations [6-8]. In a recent case report, a clinically significant response to erdafitinib was reported in a patient with a stage IV lung adencarcinoma with an FGFR fusion [9].
 
Multiple other FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have activity against FGFR1 including other selective FGFR inhibitors such as pemigatinib (INCB054828), Debio 1347, AZD4547, BGJ398 and non-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors dovitinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib. Some studies have also demonstrated the clinical efficacy of pemigatinib and pembrolizumab in various solid tumors with FGFR alterations [10]; Debio 1347 in solid tumors with FGFR alterations [11]; AZD4547, BGJ398 and dovitinib, in lung squamous cell carcinoma and with FGFR1 amplification [12-14]; AZD4547 in gastric and breast cancer with high-level FGFR2 amplification [15]; and BGJ398 and lucitanib in various solid tumor malignancies with FGFR1/3 amplification [14]. However, it is unclear how this particular tumor will respond, given the presence of a KRAS mutation, which is downstream of FGFR and may result in intrinsic resistance to FGFR-mediated inhibition.

variants.variant_description:
An in-frame gene fusion was identified involving FGFR1 and TACC1. FGFR-TACC1 rearrangements involve the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR and the coiled-coil domain of TACC. The fusion results in constitutive activation of FGFR1 and oncogenic transformation independent of canonical signaling downstream of FGFR1 (pERK and pAKT) [1]. 
 
Diagnostic and Therapeutic Implications:
FGFR-TACC fusions have been described in several CNS tumors, including low grade neuroepithelial tumors, as well as a variety of other neoplasms [1-12].  One study reported specific FGFR1-TACC1 fusions in dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors, diffuse oligodendroglial tumors  and diffuse astrocytoma [13]. Other papers report the identification of FGFR1-TACC1 fusions in patients with pilocytic astrocytomas [4,5,14]. Laboratory data suggest that tumors with certain oncogenic FGFR1 alterations may be sensitive to selective FGFR-targeted inhibitors.

A gene fusion was identified involving exon 17 of FGFR1 and exons 7 of TACC1. This fusion, as well as other FGFR-TACC fusions, is well described in gliomas [1-2]. These rearrangements involve the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR and the coiled-coil domain of TACC. The fusion results in constitutive activation of FGFR and oncogenic transformation independent of canonical signaling downstream of FGFR (pERK and pAKT) [1]. Rather, the fusion protein localizes to mitotic spindle poles and induces mitotic and chromosomal segregation defects and aneuploidy. FGFR-TACC fusions are mutually exclusive with IDH1/2 mutations [2].

FGFR-TACC fusions including FGFR1-TACC1 fusions are well described in breast adenocarcinoma [1], non-small cell carcinoma [2,3] as well as in gliomas [4,5] bladder cancer [5,6] and head and neck cancer [5]. These rearrangements involve the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR1 and the coiled-coil domain of TACC1. The fusion results in constitutive activation of FGFR and oncogenic transformation independent of canonical signaling downstream of FGFR (pERK and pAKT) [2-4]. Rather, the fusion protein localizes to mitotic spindle poles and induces mitotic and chromosomal segregation defects and aneuploidy.

diseases.diagnostic_implications:
FGFR-TACC fusions are well-described in gliomas [1-2], particularly glioblastoma, IDH wild-type (incidence approximately 3%) [1-4]. Morphologic features reported in association with glioblastomas with FGFR3-TACC3 rearrangements include monomorphous ovoid nuclei, nuclear palisading, thin parallel cytoplasmic processes, and enocrinoid network of thin capillaries [3] as wells a neuroepithelial tumors [3]. 
 
FGFR-TACC fusions have also been reported in tumor diagnosed as low grade glioma [4] and low-grade neuroepithelial tumors [5-8] including polymorphous low-grade neuroepithelial tumor of the young [6-7]. In glioblastoma, FGFR-TACC fusions frequently co-occur with TERT promoter mutations and loss of CDKN2A, which may help distinguish these cases from low-grade entities.
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Erdafitinib (Balversa; JNJ-42756493) is a selective FGFR inhibitor that was recently granted approval by the US Food and Drug Administration for urothelial cancer with FGFR alterations [9] and pemigatinib (Pemazyre) and infigratinib (Truseltiq) are FDA-approved for the treatment of cholangiocarcinomas with FGFR2 rearrangements. In a phase 2 trial of erdafitinib, a confirmed response rate of 40% was reported in patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma harboring FGFR alterations [10]. Erdafitinib has also demonstrated evidence of preclinical and clinical efficacy in early studies of other cancers with FGFR alterations including a small number of glioma patients [2,11-12].
 
Multiple other FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors have activity against FGFR3 including the non-selective inhibitors dovitinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, sunitinib and lenvatinib and selective FGFR inhibitors including AZD4547, BGJ398. Small trials with these other FGFR inhibitors have also shown a benefit in various cancers with FGFR alterations [13-16].
diseases.prognostic_implications: A case control study of patients with diffuse gliomas showed that the presence of FGFR3-TACC3 fusions was associated with improved prognosis. However, the prognostic implications of FGFR3-TACC3 fusions in low-grade neuroepithelial tumors is not well understood.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Erdafitinib (JNJ-42756493) is a selective FGFR inhibitor that was recently FDA-approved for urothelial cancer with FGFR mutations and gene fusions by the US Food and Drug Administration based on clinical studies demonstrating a response rate of approximately 40% in metastatic/locally advanced urothelial carcinomas with these alterations [7]. In a phase 1 trial, erdafitinib demonstrated activity in other tumors with FGFR pathway alterations [8-9]. There are no known clinical studies of erdafitinib in breast adenocarcinoma. Erdafitinib may be available for compassionate use in other neoplasms from US Bioservices (877-757-0667, https://www.usbioservices.com). name: RAF1
gene_function: RAF1 encodes the CRAF protein - a serine/threonine kinase similar to BRAF involved in growth signaling within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.

variants.variant_description: S259 is a residue normally phosphorylated in the RAF1 inactive state. The S259A mutation prevents phosphorylation of this site and therby results in constitutive (mitogen-independent) membrane localization and activation of RAF1 [PMID: 11756411].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: While there are no clinical or in vitro studies that have evaluated the utility of targeted therapy for the RAF1 S257L mutation detected in this specimen, there are several small molecule inhibitors with activity against CRAF, including regorafenib and sorafenib [PMID: 24896071]. Paradoxically, some RAF1 mutations appear to confer resistance to subsets of RAF inhibitors [PMID: 23737487]. However, there is some evidence to suggest that at least a subset of RAF1 mutations may be sensitive to combined MEK and type II RAF inhibitors (such as Sorafenib) [PMID: 31285551, 24569458].

While, the S259P mutation has not been biochemically characterized, other mutations affecting codon 259 including S259F has been shown to be oncogenic, resulting in constitutive activation of MAPK signaling [PMID: 24569458].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are no known clinical studies demonstrating efficacy of targeted therapies for cancers with RAF1 mutations. In preclinical studies, RAF1 S259F was shown to be inhibited by MEK inhibitors as well as class II RAF inhibitors e.g. sorafenib [PMID: 24569458].

diseases.diagnostic_implications: Oncogenic RET mutations, in general, occur frequently in medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) [PMID: 7906866, 7824936, 8570194]. These mutations can be acquired somatic mutations or germline mutations associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) [PMID: 7906866, 23059849]. This test cannot definitively differentiate between germline and somatic mutations. Genetic counseling and germline testing may be indicated.
diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Selpercatinib (Retevmo; LOXO-292), a selective RET tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), is FDA-approved for the treatment of adult and pediatric patient over 2 years-old with advanced or metastatic RET-mutant MTC who require systemic therapy. Treatment of RET-mutant MTC with selpercatinib is currentlly a category 1 recommendation in the NCCN guidelines [version 4.024]. Within the LIBRETTO-001 study, the overall response rate (ORR) among 55 previously treated patients (cabozantinib, vandetanib, or both) was 69% with 76% of responding patients having responses lasting longer than 6 months [PMID: 32846061]. The ORR among 88 patients without previous treatment was 73% with 61% of responding patients having responses lasting longer than 6 months.
 
Pralsetinib (BLU-667) was granted FDA accelerated approval for the treatment of RET fusion (not mutation) positive thyroid cancer. Treatment of MTC with pralsetinib is currently a category 2B recommendation in the NCCN guidelines [version 4.024].

Oncogenic RET mutations, including V648I, occur frequently in medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) [1-3] and have been described in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)[4]. These mutations can be acquired somatic mutations or germline mutations associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) [1-3]. This test cannot definitively differentiate between germline and somatic mutations.

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The RET-targeted inhibitor selpercatinib is FDA-approved for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients with metastatic RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer. However, its clinical utility in patients with RET V648I mutant non-small cell lung cancer is not well characterized [5].

Selpercatinib (Retevmo; LOXO-292), a selective RET tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), was FDA-approved (May 8, 2020) for the treatment of advanced or metastatic RET-mutant MTC who require systemic therapy. Within the LIBRETTO-001 study [5], the overall response rate (ORR) among 55 previously treated patients (cabozantinib, vandetanib, or both) was 69% with 76% of responding patients having responses lasting longer than 6 months. The ORR among 88 patients without previous treatment was 73% with 61% of responding patients having responses lasting longer than 6 months.
 
Several other selective RET inhibitors have also been developed including BLU-667 and RXDX-105. In a phase 1 trial of BLU-667 presented at the AACR meeting [6], an ORR of 40% in MTC (n = 29) was reported. RXDX-105 is another selective RET inhibitor with preclinical evidence of greater potency than MKI therapies [7].
 
Multi-kinase inhibitors (MKI) including vandetanib and cabozantinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic or unresectable MTC (regardless of RET mutation status). Reported response rates to these agents range from 20%-45% [8-10]. Other MKI including sunitinib, lenvatinib and sorafenib have also demonstrated activity in MTC with reported response rates ranging from 6% to 36% [11-14]. MKI therapy is often associated with toxicities, some (e.g. impaired wound healing, fistula formation, hemorrhage) related to inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR-2).

variants.variant_description:
MYC copy number gain (amplification): 
A copy number gain involving the MYC gene was detected, consistent with MYC amplification. MYC (c-MYC) is a transcription factor involved in growth signaling. Amplification of MYC, as seen in this specimen, is well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and may be associated with a poor prognosis, particularly in early stage disease [1-4].

Available data concerning the functional effect of S649L is conflicting. In one in vitro study, this variant reportedly resulted in increased kinase activity and cell proliferation and moderate transforming activity [2]. In another study, S649L was not found to result in transforming activity in culture and led to RET pathway signaling similar to wild-type RET in reporter assays [3].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: There are currently no FDA-approved targeted therapies for the treatment of MYC-amplified NSCLC; however, some preclinical studies have implicated agents such as BET bromodomain inhibitors and Aurora kinase inhibitors [5-7]. In addition, MYC amplification is associated with DNA damage [8] raising the possible utility of therapies targeting DNA damage repair deficiencies such as PARP inhibitors and ATR kinase inhibitors.

diseases.diagnostic_implications: While this mutation has not been described in gliomas, RET S649L (like other RET mutations) has been described in kindreds with evidence of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) [2]. RET S649L has also been reported as a somatic mutation in medullary thyroid carcinoma [4]. This test cannot definitively differentiate between germline and somatic mutations.

variants.variant_description:
CCDC6 (exon 1) / RET (exon 12) gene fusion:
The CCDC6-RET fusion results from a translocation fusing the 3'-end of the CCDC6 gene with the 5' end of the RET gene. This fusion has been reported in 4-6% of patients with thyroid carcinoma [1] and is characterized as activating and oncogenic [2].

CCDC6 (exon 1) - RET (exon 12) Gene Fusion:
RET (Rearranged during Transfection) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neural crest development. This rearrangement results in the fusion of the kinase domain of RET with a dimerization domain of another protein, creating a constitutively active protein that causes oncogenic growth [PMID: 29284153]. Rearrangements of RET (including the gene fusion detected in this specimen) are well-described in papillary thyroid cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMID: 32326537, 29468981, 28911727, 37882481, 32495721].

CCDC6 (exon 1) / RET (exon 12) Gene Fusion:
RET (Rearranged during Transfection) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neural crest development [PMID: 8306871]. Rearrangements of RET (including CCDC6 (exon 1) - RET (exon 12) are well-described in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMID: 22327623]. This rearrangement results in the fusion of the kinase domain of RET with a dimerization domain of another protein, creating a constitutively active protein that causes oncogenic growth [PMID: 9083029].

CCDC6 (exon 1) / RET (exon 12) gene fusion:
RET (Rearranged during Transfection) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neural crest development [1]. Rearrangements of RET (including the gene fusion detected in this specimen) are well-described in papillary thyroid cancer, anaplastic thyroid cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [2-4]. This rearrangement results in the fusion of the kinase domain of RET with a dimerization domain of another protein, creating a constitutively active protein that causes oncogenic growth [5].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: The phase I–II LIBRETTO-001 study evaluated the efficacy of the RET inhibitor selpercatinib in 19 patients with previously treated RET fusion positive thyroid cancer (2 patients with anaplastic disease). The ORR was 79% (95% CI, 54%–94%), and 1-year PFS was 64% (95% CI, 37%– 82%). In the ongoing phase I–II ARROW study, pralsetinib, another RET inhibitor, is being evaluated in patients with RET fusion-positive disease (NCT03037385). In an analysis including 9 patients with RET fusionpositive thyroid cancer, the ORR was 89% (95% CI, 52%–100%) with  durable responses (100% DCR). In 2020, the FDA approved both of these RET inhibitors for RAI-refractory RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer requiring systemic therapy [3].

The selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors pralsetinib and selpercatinib are FDA-approved for treatment of RET gene fusion-positive thyroid cancers that require systemic therapy [NCCN Guidelines Thyroid Carcinoma, Version 1.2025].

Selpercatinib (Retevmo) and pralsetinib (Gavreto) are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with RET gene fusions. According to NCCN Guidelines, selpercatinib or pralsetinib are preferred monotherapy options for patients with RET rearrangement-positive metastatic NSCLC [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 8.2025]. Cabozantinib is considered useful in certain circumstances.

The selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor (selpercatinib) has been FDA approved for treatment of RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer. Results from phase 1/2 trial of selpercatinib showed a response rate of 79% in patients with RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer whose disease was no longer responding to radioactive iodine treatment and had received previous systemic therapy and 100% in patients who had received only prior radioactive iodine.  Recently, pralsetinib, a selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor with much greater RET inhibitory potency (BLU-667), has also received FDA approval for RET-fusion positive, radioactive iodine-refractory thyroid cancer requiring systemic therapy based on the data from the ARROW study, which showed an overall response rate of 89% in patients with RET fusion-positive thyroid carcinoma [7]. RXDX-105 has also been shown to have activity in tumors with some RET gene fusions [8]. Importantly, no mutations associated with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [9,10] were detected.

KIF5B (exon 15) / RET (exon 12) Gene Fusion:
RET (Rearranged during Transfection) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neural crest development [PMID: 8306871]. Rearrangements of RET (including the gene fusion detected in this specimen) are well-described and occur in approximately 1-2% of NSCLC [PMID: 22327623; NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 8.2025]. The KIF5B-RET fusion is activating as it causes aberrant activation of RET kinase resulting in a constitutively active protein [PMID: 9083029].

variants.variant_description:
RET Rearrangement (fusion partner unknown):
A RET rearrangement was initially detected based on 5'/3' imbalance and then confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Rearrangements of RET (including the gene fusion detected in this specimen) are well-described in papillary thyroid cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [2-4]. These rearrangements typically result in the fusion of the kinase domain of RET with a dimerization domain of another protein, creating a constitutively active protein that causes oncogenic growth [5].

Suspicious for RET rearrangement:
Next-generation sequencing results were suspicious for a rearrangement involving the RET gene and an unknown fusion partner. RET break-apart FISH was performed in order to confirm this finding. This FISH study was also strongly suspicious for a RET rearrangement, although the results were somewhat subtle, possibly due to an intrachromosomal fusion. Confirmation using another method (e.g. MiOncoseq) is recommended. Rearrangements of RET have described at a very low frequency in colorectal cancer (CRC) [2,3]. This rearrangements result in the fusion of the kinase domain of RET with a dimerization domain of another protein, creating a consitutively active that causes oncogenic growth [4]. Fusion partners described in CRC include CCDC6, NCOA4, RRBP1. RET rearrangements in CRC are generally mutually exclusive with KRAS, NRAS, or BRAF mutations [2,3]. RET rearrangements have also been described at a higher frequency in papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) [5] and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [6]. Several multi-kinase inhibitors (MKI) including vandetanib, cabozantinib, sunitinib, levatinib and sorafenib have demonstrated in vitro and in vivo growth inhibition of RET-driven NSCLC and PTC cells [7-9]. Vandetinib and cabozantinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) and lenvatinib and sorafenib are FDA-approved for the treatment of differentiated thyroid cancers. These drugs have shown limited clinical efficacy in thyroid cancer [10] and NSCLC [11-13] patients, but are often associated with toxicities, some (e.g. impaired wound healing, fistula formation, hemorrhage) related to inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR-2). Recently, a TKI with specificity for RET - BLU-667 - has been described that has > 10-fold increased potency over approved MKI in various RET-driven cell lines [14]. This drug also potently inhibited growth in NSCLC and PTC xenografts without inhibiting VEGFR-2. Clinical reponses have been observed in two MTC and two NSCLC patients treated with BLU-667 as part of a clinical trial [a]. Other TKI with RET specificity including LOXO-292 [15] and RXDX-105 [16] have shown early clinical evidence of efficacy in published abstracts. Of note, RXDX-105 has been shown to activity in tumors with some RET rearrangements but not others (e.g. KIF5B-RET) [16]. Importantly, no mutations associated acquired resistance to TKI therapy [17-18] were detected. Michigan Medicine is currently participating in a phase 1 clinical trial (NCT03037385; UMCC 2017.152; PI Shirish Gadgeel) investigating the utility of BLU-667 in advanced solid tumors with RET activation. Another phase 1 Michigan Medicine clinical trial (NCT02219711; UMCC 2015.040) is investigating the utility of an MKI (MGCD516) in advanced solid tumors with tyrosine kinase alterations including RET rearrangements. Other relevant clinical trials currently enrolling patients include NCT03157128 (phase 1 of LOXO-292; multiple centers including START Midwest, Grand Rapids, MI).

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
The selective RET inhibitors selpercatinib and pralsetinib are FDA approved for NSCLC with RET gene fusions. 
 
In a phase 1-2 trial, selpercatinib (LOXO-292) achieved an objective response rate of 64% (n = 30; confirmed ORR 74%) in NSCLC patients with RET fusions [6]. The median duration of response was 12.1 months. Among previously untreated patients, the objective response rate was 85% with 90% of responses ongoing at 6 months. Activity was independent of the RET fusion partner and prior therapy. Responses were also seen in patients with intracranial metastases. Consistent with a more selective therapy, only minor side effects were observed with no maximum tolerated dose achieved.  
 
In a phase 1-2 trial, pralsetinib (BLU-667) efficacy for RET-fusion positive NSCLC was evaluated in 87 patients previously treated with platinum chemotherapy [7]. The overall response rate ws 57%; 80% of responding patients had responses lasting 6 months or longer. Overall response rate was 70% for patients who never received systemic treatment.

Selpercatinib (Retevmo) and pralsetinib (Gavreto) are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with RET gene fusions. According to NCCN Guidelines, selpercatinib or pralsetinib are preferred monotherapy options for patients with RET rearrangement-positive metastatic NSCLC [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 8.2025]. Cabozantinib is considered useful in certain circumstances .

While this specific mutation has not been biochemically characterized due to its rarity, activating, oncogenic RET mutations, in general, occur frequently in medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) [5-7]. These mutations can be acquired somatic mutations or germline mutations associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) [5,8]. diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Multi-kinase inhibitors (MKI) including vandetanib and cabozantinib are FDA-approved for the treatment of metastic or unresectable MTC (regardless of RET mutation status) [9-11]. Reported response rates to these agents range from 20%-45%. Other MKI including sunitinib, levatinib and sorafenib have also demonstrated activity in MTC with reported response rates ranging from 6% to 36% [12-15]. MKI therapy is often associated with toxicities, some (e.g. impaired wound healing, fistula formation, hemorrhage) related to inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR-2).
Recently, several selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) with much greater RET inhibitory potency including LOXO-292, BLU-667 and RXDX-105 have been developed. LOXO-292 was granted breakthrough therapy designation for the treatment of lung and thyroid cancers with RET abnormalities in September of 2018. Results from a phase 1 trial of LOXO-292 were presented at the last ASCO meeting [16]. In RET-mutant MTC, LOXO-292 achieved an overall response rates (ORR) of 45% (n = 22; confirmed ORR 33%). Most of the patients in this study had previously received MKI therapy. Consistent with a more selective therapy, only minor side effects were observed with no maximum tolerated dose achieved.  Results from a phase 1 trial of BLU-667 were presented at the last AACR meeting [17]. An ORR of 40% in MTC (n = 29) was reported. RXDX-105 is another selective RET inhibitor with preclinical evidence of greater potency the MKI therapies [18].

variants.variant_description: While activating mutations and rearrangements involving RET are well described in various neoplasms (including NSCLC), the RET E884X mutation identified in this specimen has NOT been previously described and is expected to result in loss of function of the RET protein. The allele frequency of this variant is similar to that of the other somatic mutations detected in this specimen suggesting that RET E884X was somatically acquired (rather than germline). However, because this mutation has not been previously described and there is no known oncogenic role of loss of function RET mutations, RET E884X may represent a "passenger" mutation that does not play a role in the oncogenesis of this tumor.

FGFR1 copy number gain (amplification):
A low-level copy number gain involving the FGFR2 gene was detected (considered  amplification. FGFR1 is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling. Amplification of FGFR1 has been described multiple tumors and is present in approximately 10% of urothelial carcinomas [1-2].

This variant affects the intron 7 splice acceptor site and is expected to result in altered splice, possibly skipping of exon 7.

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
Erdafitinib (JNJ-42756493) is a selective FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that has been FDA-approved for urothelial cancer with FGFR mutations and gene fusions by the US Food and Drug Administration based on clinical studies demonstrating a response rate of approximately 40% in metastatic/locally advanced urothelial carcinomas with these alterations [3]. In a phase II study of erdafitinib in cancers with FGFR amplification (NCI-MATCH), erdafitinib showed limited efficacy [4]. In a review of several clinical trials, one study found that FGFR mutations and fusions correlated better with response to FGFR TKI than those with FGFR amplification [5].

AR encodes a transcription factor activated by androgen hormones. Amplification of AR resulting in increased AR expression is well-described in prostate cancer, particularly castration-resistant prostate cancer [PMID: 9000575, 22722839].

variants.variant_description:
The JAK2 V617F (Val617Phe) mutation is very well-described and affects the pseudokinase (JH2) domain, resulting in constitutive activation of JAK2 signaling (see below). The mutation in this specimen is present at a high variant allele frequency - approximately 20%.

Low-level JAK2 V617F mutation detected. See Interpretation.
 
JAK2 V617F:
A low-level JAK2 V617F mutation was detected. The source of this mutation is uncertain; however, the presence of this mutation at a low allele frequency despite a high percentage of carcinoma cells within the extracted sample suggests that this mutation could come from contaminating leukocytes rather than carcinoma cells. While JAK2 V617F mutation resulting in constitutive activation of JAK2 kinase activity and JAK-STAT signaling is commonly seen in myeloproliferative neoplasms including polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis [1-3], low-level JAK2 V617F mutations have also been described in healthy individuals with asymptomatic clonal hematopoiesis [4-10]. This mutation was not identified among several large studies of thyroid cancer. Clinical correlation and possible evaluation of peripheral blood for JAK2 V617F mutation is recommended if a myeloproliferative neoplasm is suspected.
