Low-level JAK2 V617F mutations have also been described in healthy individuals [4-6]. This mutation was not identified among several large studies of colorectal cancer [7-9]. Clinical correlation and possible evaluation of peripheral blood for JAK2 V617F mutation is recommended if a myeloproliferative neoplasm is suspected.

A low-level JAK2 V617F mutation was also detected. This mutation has not been described in esophageal adenocarcinoma but is well-described in myeloproliferative neoplasms. The source of the mutation detected in this (a subclone of carcinoma cells vs. contaminating leukocytes) is uncertain. Clinical correlation and possible evaluation of peripheral blood for JAK2 V617F mutation is recommended if a myeloproliferative neoplasm is suspected.

diseases.diagnostic_implications:
JAK2 mutations are well-described in myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), including polycythemia vera [1], essential thrombocythemia (ET) and primary myelofibrosis [2-4]. The presence of a JAK2 mutation is a major diagnostic criterion for each of these MPN according to the WHO Classification of Tumours of Hematopoietic and Lymphoid Tissues [5]. 
 
JAK2 mutations can also be detected in individuals without a demonstrable MPN and can be associated with age-related clonal hematopoiesis [6-10]. However, JAK2 V617F unrelated to an MPN are present at low variant allele frequencies - the large majority less than 1%, rarely as high as 4% [6-10].

variants.variant_description: ERBB4 is receptor tyrosine kinase involved in growth signaling similar to EGFR and HER2. The R711C mutation detected in this specimen has been described in melanoma [1-5]. This mutation has not been biochemically characterized and its effect on protein function is unknown. ERBB4 mutations in melanoma often co-occur with NRAS or BRAF mutations [6]. Targeted therapies directed at ERBB4 are not expected to be efficacious in light of the BRAF mutation described above.

TMPRSS2 - ERG Fusion:
Recurrent gene fusions involving the ETS transcription factors including ERG are well-described in prostatic adenocarcinoma [1-4]. TMPRSS2 is the most common fusion partners for ERG [1-4]. These fusions result in androgen-induced ERG expression [1,4].

diseases.therapeutic_implications: Several targeted therapies employing inhibitory RNA or peptides have shown preclinical evidence of potential efficacy [5-8].

name: SMO
gene_function: SMO (smoothened) encodes a G protein-coupled receptor that is involved in transducing Hedgehog growth signaling by interacting with the PTCH1 (Patched) receptor.

variants.variant_description:
Activating mutations in SMO lead to constitutive activation of GLI-mediated transcription and have been identified in several tumor types, most notably basal cell carcinoma as in this case [1,2]. SMO L412F has been reported in basal cell carcinoma [1,3]. SMO L412F is within transmembrane domain 5 in a pivot region of the Smo protein and confers activation of Hedgehog signaling [3]. Therapeutic Significance:
Smoothened (SMO) inhibitors are under investigation for the treatment of several cancers. Vismodegib and sonidegib are FDA-approved for the treatment of locally advanced and metastatic basal cell carcinoma. However, SMO variants may account for much of targeted therapy resistance in basal cell carcinoma. Preclinical studies have shown that SMO activating alterations, including SMO L412F, confers decreased response to Hedgehog pathway inhibitors taladegib, vismodegib, and sonidegib [3,4]. Specifically, preclinical studies with SMO L412F has shown Hedgehog pathway inhibitor (vismodegib) resistance, although there was still suppression by GLI antagonists [3].

Activating mutations in SMO lead to constitutive activation of GLI-mediated transcription and have been identified in several tumor types, most notably basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastomas (Sonic Hedgehog subtype) [1,2]. The SMO I408V is rare but has been reported in several tumors. SMO I408V lies within the drug-binding pocket of the transmembrane domain 5 of the Smo protein, and although it has not been fully biochemically characterized, it is predicted by some to confer oncogenic properties [3]. Therapeutic Significance:
Smoothened (SMO) inhibitors are under investigation for the treatment of several cancers. Vismodegib and sonidegib are FDA-approved for the treatment of locally advanced and metastatic basal cell carcinoma. Sonidegib and vismodegib have also been shown to have anti-tumor activity in clinical trials of SHH-driven pediatric and adult medulloblastomas [4]. Per the NCCN guidelines for adult medulloblastomas, vismodegib may be considered in certain circumstances for tumor recurrence in patients treated with prior chemotherapy and a mutation in sonic hedgehog pathway [5]. However, preclinical studies have shown that SMO I408V, due to its location within the drug-binding pocket, confers decreased response to Hedgehog pathway inhibitors including taladegib, vismodegib, and sonidegib [3].
The R512H mutation has not been described in the current literature and its functional effect and clinical significance is uncertain. References: 1. None

NCOA4 (exon 7) / RET (exon 12) Gene Fusion:
RET (Rearranged during Transfection) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neural crest development [1]. While RET gene fusions have not been described in gliomas (including diffuse midline glioma, H3 H27M-mutant), the fusion between NCOA4 (formerly PTC3) and RET that was detected in this specimen is well described in papillary thyroid carcinoma [2], non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [3,4], salivary gland intraductal carcinoma [5,6], salivary duct carcinoma [7], breast cancer [8], and colorectal cancer [9,10]. These rearrangements result in the fusion of the kinase domain of RET with a dimerization domain of another protein, creating a constitutively active protein that causes oncogenic growth [11]. While RET fusions have not been described in diffuse midline glioma, H3 H27M-mutant, other molecular alterations involving tyrosine kinases including NTRK1/2/3 gene fusion [12] and FGFR1 mutations and fusions [13] have been described.

NCOA4 (exon 7) / RET (exon 12) Gene Fusion:
RET (Rearranged during Transfection) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neural crest development [PMID: 8306871]. Rearrangements of RET (including the gene fusion detected in this specimen) are well-described in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [PMID: 22327623]. These rearrangements result in the fusion of the kinase domain of RET with a dimerization domain of another protein, creating a constitutively active protein that causes oncogenic growth [PMID: 9083029].

diseases.therapeutic_implications:
While several multi-kinase inhibitors (MKI) including vandetanib, cabozantinib, sunitinib, lenvatinib and sorafenib have demonstrated in vitro and in vivo growth inhibition of RET-driven NSCLC and PTC cells [14-16]; these drugs have shown limited clinical efficacy in thyroid cancer [17] and NSCLC [18-20] patients and are often associated with toxicities, some (e.g. impaired wound healing, fistula formation, hemorrhage) related to inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR-2). In addition, the CNS penetration of many of these agents is poor [21].
 
Recently, several selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) with much greater RET inhibitory potency including selpercatinib (LOXO-292), pralsetinib (BLU-667) and RXDX-105 have been developed. LOXO-292 was granted breakthrough therapy designation for the treatment of lung and thyroid cancers with RET abnormalities in September of 2018. Results from a phase 1 trial of LOXO-292 were presented at the last ASCO meeting [22]. LOXO-292 achieved an overall response rate (ORR) of 77% (n = 30; confirmed ORR 74%) in NSCLC patients with RET fusions. Activity was independent of the RET fusion partner and prior therapy. Importantly, this drug penetrates the blood-brain barrier and esponses were also seen in patients with intracranial metastases (3/3). Consistent with a more selective therapy, only minor side effects were observed with no maximum tolerated dose achieved.  
 
Results from a phase 1 trial of BLU-667 were presented at the last AACR meeting [23]. An ORR of 50% in NSCLC with RET gene fusions (n = 14; confirmed ORR 36%) was reported. Again, activity was independent of fusion partner and prior therapy and responses were observed in patients with intracranial disease. Hypertension and elevated ALT was seen in some patients. RXDX-105 has been shown to have activity in tumors with some RET rearrangements but not for KIF5B-RET [24]. 
 
Importantly, no mutations associated with acquired resistance to TKI therapy [25,26] were detected.

Selpercatinib (Retevmo) and pralsetinib (Gavreto) are FDA-approved for the treatment of NSCLC with RET gene fusions. According to NCCN Guidelines, selpercatinib or pralsetinib are preferred monotherapy options for patients with RET rearrangement-positive metastatic NSCLC [NCCN Guidelines Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 8.2025]. Cabozantinib is considered useful in certain circumstances .
